concepts.name: 12-Lead ECG
concepts.shortExplanation: A recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 angles — the key bedside test for diagnosing a heart attack and identifying arrhythmias.

sections.purpose: Capture a detailed electrical snapshot of the heart to detect ischemia/infarction, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and electrolyte effects.
sections.careConsiderations: Place limb and precordial leads in correct anatomic positions (misplacement mimics pathology); prep skin for a clean signal; minimize motion artifact; get it within 10 minutes for chest pain and compare with prior tracings.

concepts.name: Absence Seizure
concepts.shortExplanation: A generalized seizure, most common in children, causing brief (seconds-long) staring spells with abrupt loss of awareness and no postictal confusion. Distinguished by its brevity, the lack of aura or postictal state, preserved posture, and provocation by hyperventilation.

sections.presentation: Sudden, brief (usually under 10-20 seconds) staring spells or 'daydreaming' with abrupt onset and offset, no loss of postural tone (the patient does not fall), and sometimes subtle eye fluttering or lip movements. There is no postictal confusion, and episodes may occur many times a day and be mistaken for inattention. Classic EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, and hyperventilation can provoke an episode.
sections.typicalTreatments: Ethosuximide is first-line; valproate or lamotrigine are alternatives (valproate is preferred when generalized tonic-clonic seizures also occur). Avoid carbamazepine, phenytoin, and gabapentin, which can worsen absence seizures. Hyperventilation during EEG helps provoke and confirm the diagnosis.
sections.riskFactors: Childhood absence epilepsy (typical onset ages 4-10), family history or genetic predisposition, and more common in girls.

concepts.name: Acetaminophen
concepts.shortExplanation: A common pain reliever and fever reducer that, unlike NSAIDs, has little anti-inflammatory effect and does not thin the blood or irritate the stomach.

sections.mechanism: Analgesic and antipyretic believed to act centrally; it does not meaningfully reduce inflammation or affect platelets.
sections.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated at recommended doses.
sections.adverseEffects: Liver injury (hepatotoxicity) in overdose or with chronic high doses, especially with alcohol use or existing liver disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Add up the total daily dose from all sources, including combination products, and stay within accepted daily limits (lower in liver disease). Acetylcysteine is the antidote for overdose.

concepts.name: ACLS Cardiac Arrest Algorithm
concepts.shortExplanation: The standardized team response to cardiac arrest — high-quality CPR, rhythm checks, shocks for shockable rhythms, and timed medications.

sections.triggerCriteria: Pulseless patient — confirmed cardiac arrest. Rhythm sorted into shockable (VF/pulseless VT) or non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
sections.steps: Start high-quality CPR and attach the monitor/defibrillator. Shockable: defibrillate, resume CPR, give epinephrine every 3–5 min, add amiodarone, shock with each rhythm check. Non-shockable: CPR with epinephrine every 3–5 min. Throughout, search for and treat reversible causes (the Hs and Ts) and minimize interruptions in compressions.

concepts.name: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
concepts.shortExplanation: A clotting test of the intrinsic and common pathways, most often used to monitor unfractionated heparin.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 25-35 seconds (lab dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Prolonged aPTT is seen with heparin therapy, hemophilia, clotting-factor deficiencies, and lupus anticoagulant. When titrating a heparin drip, the goal aPTT is set by protocol. It is often ordered alongside PT/INR to evaluate bleeding.

concepts.name: Acute Agitation
concepts.shortExplanation: A state of severe restlessness, distress, or aggression that can pose a safety risk to the patient and others and needs prompt, calm management.

sections.presentation: Escalating motor restlessness, loud or threatening speech, pacing, clenched fists, and hostility, which may stem from psychiatric illness, intoxication or withdrawal, delirium, or a medical cause.
sections.typicalTreatments: Begin with verbal de-escalation and a safe, low-stimulation environment. Look for and treat underlying medical causes such as hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or infection. Medications (benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics) are used when behavioral measures are insufficient, with physical restraint reserved as a last resort with close monitoring.
sections.riskFactors: Psychosis, mania, substance intoxication or withdrawal, delirium and dementia, and untreated pain or metabolic derangements.

concepts.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery starving heart muscle of oxygen — the umbrella term for unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI (heart attack).

sections.presentation: Chest pressure or pain (often radiating to the arm/jaw), shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea; women, older adults, and diabetics may present atypically.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aspirin plus a second antiplatelet, anticoagulation, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, statin; emergent cardiac catheterization (PCI) for STEMI; serial troponins and ECGs.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, family history, older age, obesity.

concepts.name: Acute Ischemic Stroke
concepts.shortExplanation: A blocked artery cuts off blood flow to part of the brain, causing sudden neurologic deficits. Rapid treatment can save brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden face droop, arm or leg weakness (often one-sided), slurred or garbled speech, vision changes, severe imbalance, or confusion. Time of last known well is critical.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent non-contrast CT to rule out bleeding, IV thrombolytics (such as alteplase or tenecteplase) within the treatment window, and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Careful blood pressure management, glucose control, and swallow screening before oral intake.
sections.riskFactors: Atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, prior stroke or TIA, and older age.

concepts.name: Acute Kidney Injury
concepts.shortExplanation: A sudden drop in kidney function over hours to days, shown by rising creatinine and/or falling urine output, common in critically ill patients.

sections.presentation: Decreased urine output, rising creatinine and BUN, fluid overload, and electrolyte disturbances such as hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Often detected on labs before symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause, restore perfusion and volume, stop or dose-adjust nephrotoxic drugs, and manage electrolytes and fluid balance. Dialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy for severe or refractory cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypotension or shock, sepsis, nephrotoxic medications, contrast exposure, major surgery, heart failure, and pre-existing kidney disease.

concepts.name: Acute Liver Failure
concepts.shortExplanation: Rapid loss of liver function in a person without prior liver disease, causing coagulopathy and confusion. A medical emergency, often from acetaminophen overdose.

sections.presentation: Jaundice, confusion (hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy with easy bleeding, nausea, and right upper quadrant discomfort developing over days to weeks. Can progress to cerebral edema, multi-organ failure, and hypoglycemia.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU care with treatment of the cause (N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity), management of cerebral edema and coagulopathy, glucose monitoring, and early transfer to a transplant center. Emergency liver transplant may be lifesaving.
sections.riskFactors: Acetaminophen overdose, viral hepatitis, drug reactions, autoimmune hepatitis, and ischemia (shock liver).

concepts.name: Acute Pancreatitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often from gallstones or alcohol. Ranges from mild and self-limited to severe with organ failure.

sections.presentation: Severe, steady epigastric pain that radiates to the back, nausea and vomiting, and abdominal tenderness. Fever, tachycardia, and hypotension in severe disease. Elevated lipase (and amylase). Rare bruising around the flanks (Grey Turner) or umbilicus (Cullen) signals hemorrhagic disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, pain control, antiemetics, and bowel rest with early feeding as tolerated. Treat the cause (gallstone removal via ERCP, alcohol cessation). Monitor for complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, and organ failure.
sections.riskFactors: Gallstones, heavy alcohol use, high triglycerides, certain medications, ERCP, and hypercalcemia.

concepts.name: Acute Pulmonary Edema
concepts.shortExplanation: Sudden fluid accumulation in the alveoli, most often from acute heart failure, causing severe shortness of breath and hypoxemia.

sections.presentation: Acute severe dyspnea, orthopnea, restlessness, pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles, tachypnea, tachycardia, and low oxygen saturation. Patients often sit upright and appear anxious/diaphoretic.
sections.typicalTreatments: Sit upright, high-flow oxygen or noninvasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP), IV loop diuretics (furosemide), nitroglycerin for preload reduction, and treatment of the underlying cardiac cause. Intubation if refractory.
sections.riskFactors: Heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, severe hypertension, valvular disease, arrhythmia, and volume overload (including renal failure).

concepts.name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: Sudden, severe lung inflammation that floods the air sacs with fluid, causing dangerously low oxygen levels that often require a ventilator.

sections.presentation: Rapidly worsening shortness of breath and low oxygen levels not explained by heart failure, with diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, usually within a week of a known insult such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, or trauma.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause; lung-protective mechanical ventilation using low tidal volumes; prone positioning for severe cases; careful fluid management; and sedation with or without paralysis as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, severe trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, and inhalation injury.

concepts.name: Acute Respiratory Failure
concepts.shortExplanation: The lungs suddenly cannot get enough oxygen into the blood (hypoxemic) or clear enough carbon dioxide (hypercapnic), a common reason for ICU admission and intubation.

sections.presentation: Shortness of breath, rapid or labored breathing, use of accessory muscles, restlessness or confusion, and low oxygen saturation. Rising carbon dioxide can cause drowsiness. An arterial blood gas confirms the type and severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen, treating the underlying cause, noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) for selected patients, and intubation with mechanical ventilation when these fail or the airway is at risk.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, pneumonia, heart failure, asthma, ARDS, neuromuscular weakness, opioid overdose, and chest wall or airway problems.

concepts.name: Acyclovir
concepts.shortExplanation: An antiviral medication used to treat herpes simplex and varicella-zoster infections, including herpes encephalitis and severe shingles. IV therapy is used for serious disease.

sections.mechanism: A nucleoside analog that, after activation by viral thymidine kinase, inhibits viral DNA polymerase and stops viral DNA replication; selective for herpesviruses.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, and malaise.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, especially with IV use and dehydration (crystal formation in the kidneys); neurotoxicity (confusion, tremor) particularly in renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Ensure adequate hydration and infuse IV doses slowly to protect the kidneys; monitor renal function and adjust dose for renal impairment. Start early for best effect; for herpes encephalitis, treatment should not be delayed.

concepts.name: Adenosine
concepts.shortExplanation: A very fast-acting drug that briefly "pauses" the heart to break certain rapid rhythms (SVT) and reset a normal beat.

sections.mechanism: Transiently blocks AV node conduction, interrupting reentrant SVT. Extremely short half-life (seconds) — must be given as a rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush, ideally at a site close to the heart.
sections.sideEffects: Brief flushing, chest tightness, a sense of impending doom, a short sinus pause — all typically last seconds.
sections.adverseEffects: Transient asystole, bronchospasm in asthmatics, brief high-grade AV block.
sections.nursingImplications: Give as fast IV push with an immediate flush (two-syringe or stopcock technique); warn the patient about the brief uncomfortable feeling; have continuous ECG running and a defibrillator nearby.

concepts.name: Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis)
concepts.shortExplanation: A condition in which the adrenal glands produce too little cortisol (and sometimes aldosterone). An acute crisis causes life-threatening low blood pressure.

sections.presentation: Chronic: fatigue, weakness, weight loss, low appetite, salt craving, and skin darkening (in primary disease). Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis: severe hypotension and shock, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia, often triggered by illness or stress.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate IV hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroids) and aggressive IV fluids with dextrose for crisis; treat the precipitant. Chronic disease is managed with daily glucocorticoid (and mineralocorticoid in primary disease) replacement. Patients need stress dosing during illness and a medical alert identification.
sections.riskFactors: Autoimmune adrenal destruction, abrupt withdrawal of long-term steroids, pituitary disease, and physiologic stress (infection, surgery) in a person with limited adrenal reserve.

concepts.name: Advance Directives
concepts.shortExplanation: Legal documents that let people state their wishes for medical care if they become unable to speak for themselves. They include living wills and the naming of a healthcare decision-maker.

sections.triggerCriteria: Relevant to all adults, and especially important for patients with serious or terminal illness. They guide care when a patient loses the capacity to make or communicate decisions.
sections.steps: Key forms include a living will (preferences for treatments such as CPR, intubation, and artificial nutrition), a durable power of attorney for healthcare or healthcare proxy (naming a surrogate decision-maker), and portable medical orders such as POLST/MOLST that translate wishes into actionable clinician orders. Nurses confirm documents are on the chart and honored, clarify code status, help patients and families discuss goals, and ensure directives are communicated across care transitions.

concepts.name: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
concepts.shortExplanation: A liver enzyme that is more specific to the liver than AST and rises with liver-cell injury.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 7-56 U/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high ALT is a fairly specific sign of liver injury from viral hepatitis, medications (including acetaminophen toxicity), alcohol, or fatty liver disease. It is trended with AST, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase to distinguish liver-cell injury from bile-duct obstruction.

concepts.name: Albumin
concepts.shortExplanation: The main protein in blood; low levels can flag malnutrition or illness and are linked to poor wound healing.

sections.normalRange: About 3.5-5.0 g/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low albumin can reflect malnutrition, inflammation, liver disease, or protein loss through the kidneys or gut, and is associated with poor wound healing and edema. It is a marker of nutrition and overall illness rather than a specific diagnosis.

concepts.name: Albuterol
concepts.shortExplanation: A fast-acting inhaled medication that opens the airways to make breathing easier — commonly used during a COPD or asthma flare.

sections.mechanism: Short-acting beta-2 agonist — relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Onset within minutes, often given via nebulizer or inhaler during acute exacerbations.
sections.sideEffects: Tremor, tachycardia, nervousness.
sections.adverseEffects: Significant tachyarrhythmia in sensitive patients, hypokalemia with frequent dosing.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate, especially with frequent/repeated dosing; assess respiratory status before and after administration.

concepts.name: Alcohol Withdrawal
concepts.shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person dependent on alcohol suddenly stops or reduces drinking, which can become life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension begin within hours. More severe stages include hallucinations, withdrawal seizures, and delirium tremens, which features confusion, severe autonomic instability, and can be fatal.
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines are the mainstay, often dosed using a symptom-triggered approach guided by the CIWA-Ar scale. Add thiamine (before glucose) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, along with IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and a calm monitored environment.
sections.riskFactors: Long-term heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal episodes or seizures, prior delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation.

concepts.name: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person who drinks heavily suddenly stops, ranging from tremors and anxiety to seizures and life-threatening delirium tremens.

sections.presentation: Tremors, anxiety, sweating, fast heart rate, hypertension, nausea, and insomnia within hours to days of the last drink. Severe cases progress to hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens (confusion, agitation, fever, and autonomic instability).
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines titrated to symptoms (often using a scoring tool such as CIWA-Ar), a calm and monitored environment, IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and correction of electrolytes (magnesium, potassium, phosphorus). ICU care for severe delirium tremens.
sections.riskFactors: Long-standing heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation, often during hospitalization for another reason.

concepts.name: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
concepts.shortExplanation: An enzyme found mainly in the liver's bile ducts and in bone; useful for detecting bile-duct and bone disease.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 44-147 U/L in adults (higher in growing children and pregnancy).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high ALP suggests bile-duct obstruction (cholestasis) or bone disorders such as Paget disease and bony metastases. Checking GGT helps tell whether the source is liver or bone. Physiologic elevation is normal in growing children and in pregnancy.

concepts.name: Alkylating Agents (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: A class of chemotherapy drugs, including cyclophosphamide, that damage cancer cell DNA so the cells cannot divide. They are used across many cancer types.

sections.mechanism: Attach alkyl groups to DNA, causing cross-links and strand breaks that prevent DNA replication and trigger cell death; they work regardless of cell cycle phase.
sections.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, hair loss, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Hemorrhagic cystitis with cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide (mesna and hydration are protective), infertility, pulmonary fibrosis with some agents, and a long-term risk of secondary cancers.
sections.nursingImplications: Ensure adequate hydration and, with cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide, encourage frequent voiding and give mesna as ordered. Monitor blood counts, watch for infection and bleeding, and manage nausea with antiemetics.

concepts.name: Alprazolam
concepts.shortExplanation: A short-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety and panic disorder.

sections.mechanism: Enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at the GABA-A receptor, producing sedation, anxiety relief, and muscle relaxation.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, impaired coordination, and memory problems.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and profound sedation, especially with opioids or alcohol; tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal seizures with abrupt discontinuation.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess sedation and fall risk and avoid combining with opioids or alcohol. Do not stop abruptly; taper to prevent withdrawal. Flumazenil is a reversal agent but is used cautiously because it can precipitate seizures. Teach caution with driving.

concepts.name: Alteplase (tPA)
concepts.shortExplanation: A clot-dissolving thrombolytic given IV for acute ischemic stroke within a specific time window, and also used for pulmonary embolism and STEMI. Its main danger is bleeding.

sections.mechanism: A tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin, breaking down fibrin and dissolving the clot obstructing blood flow.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising or bleeding at puncture sites.
sections.adverseEffects: Serious hemorrhage, including intracranial hemorrhage; angioedema; must screen carefully for contraindications (recent surgery, bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension).
sections.nursingImplications: Verify eligibility and time from symptom onset; control blood pressure below target before and after; weight-based dosing. Monitor for signs of bleeding and neurologic change with frequent neuro checks; avoid invasive procedures and hold antithrombotics for the initial period after administration.

concepts.name: Alveoli
concepts.shortExplanation: The tiny air sacs at the end of the airways where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

sections.purpose: Provide the vast, thin surface where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. A film of surfactant keeps the alveoli open by lowering surface tension.
sections.careConsiderations: Alveolar disease impairs gas exchange: fluid (pulmonary edema, ARDS), infection (pneumonia), or collapse (atelectasis) cause hypoxemia. Nurses use incentive spirometry, positioning, and early mobility to keep alveoli open, and surfactant deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

concepts.name: Alzheimer Disease and Dementia
concepts.shortExplanation: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia, marked by gradual decline in memory, thinking, and function.

sections.presentation: Insidious, progressive memory loss (especially recent events), word-finding difficulty, impaired judgment and problem-solving, disorientation, and later loss of ability to perform daily activities. Behavioral and psychological symptoms and agitation are common in later stages.
sections.typicalTreatments: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine may modestly help symptoms; structured routines, safety measures, and caregiver support; nonpharmacologic strategies for behavioral symptoms; treat superimposed delirium and reversible contributors.
sections.riskFactors: Advancing age, family history and genetics (including APOE), cardiovascular risk factors, head injury, low physical and cognitive activity.

concepts.name: Amiodarone
concepts.shortExplanation: An antiarrhythmic medication used to control or convert abnormal heart rhythms, most often atrial fibrillation.

sections.mechanism: Class III antiarrhythmic — prolongs the cardiac action potential, affecting multiple ion channels. Long half-life (weeks); IV loading followed by oral maintenance is common.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, photosensitivity, injection site phlebitis (IV).
sections.adverseEffects: Pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction (hyper- or hypothyroidism), liver toxicity, bradycardia/hypotension with IV administration.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate/rhythm and blood pressure during IV administration; monitor liver and thyroid function with long-term use.

concepts.name: Amlodipine
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for hypertension and chronic stable angina.

sections.mechanism: Blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing arterial vasodilation that lowers blood pressure and reduces cardiac afterload.
sections.sideEffects: Peripheral edema (especially ankles), flushing, headache, dizziness, and palpitations.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive hypotension and reflex tachycardia; peripheral edema can be dose-limiting. Unlike diltiazem/verapamil, it has little effect on heart rate.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure and check for ankle/leg swelling. Counsel about rising slowly to avoid dizziness. Effect is gradual and long-lasting; not for acute BP lowering.

concepts.name: Ammonia
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test of a nitrogen waste product that can build up when the liver fails to clear it, contributing to confusion in hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 15-45 mcg/dL in adults, though reference ranges vary by laboratory and method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels are associated with hepatic encephalopathy and other causes of impaired ammonia clearance. The level does not always correlate tightly with the degree of confusion, so treatment is guided mainly by the clinical picture. Proper sample handling (kept on ice and processed promptly) is important because delays falsely raise results.

concepts.name: Amoxicillin
concepts.shortExplanation: A penicillin-class antibiotic commonly used in children for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, killing susceptible bacteria.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, and rash.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions ranging from hives to anaphylaxis in penicillin-allergic patients, and rarely severe skin reactions or C. difficile-associated diarrhea.
sections.nursingImplications: Dosing in children is weight-based; confirm the child has no penicillin allergy before giving. Encourage completing the full course, shake liquid suspensions well, and report any rash, which may signal allergy.

concepts.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate
concepts.shortExplanation: A combination oral antibiotic pairing amoxicillin with clavulanate to treat sinus, ear, respiratory, skin, and urinary infections including some resistant bacteria.

sections.mechanism: Amoxicillin is a penicillin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects amoxicillin from enzymes that would otherwise inactivate it, broadening coverage.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and vaginal yeast infection; diarrhea is more common than with amoxicillin alone.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, Clostridioides difficile colitis, and rare cholestatic liver injury.
sections.nursingImplications: Screen for penicillin allergy. Give with food to reduce GI upset. Teach patients to complete the full course and report persistent diarrhea, which may signal C. difficile. Monitor for rash or signs of allergic reaction.

concepts.name: Anaphylactic Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: Life-threatening distributive shock from a severe allergic reaction, with massive histamine-driven vasodilation, capillary leak, and bronchospasm. The distinguishing treatment priority is immediate intramuscular epinephrine - antihistamines and steroids are only adjuncts.

sections.presentation: Rapid onset (minutes to a couple of hours) after an allergen, with hypotension plus airway and skin findings: urticaria, angioedema, throat tightness, stridor, wheezing, dyspnea, nausea/vomiting, and a sense of impending doom. Distinguished from other distributive shock by the allergic features (hives, angioedema, bronchospasm) and clear temporal link to an exposure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral (mid-outer) thigh is first-line and given immediately, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed; use IV/IO epinephrine for refractory shock. Remove the trigger, give high-flow oxygen, and rapid IV fluid boluses for hypotension. Adjuncts (second-line, not substitutes): inhaled beta-agonists for bronchospasm, H1/H2 antihistamines, and corticosteroids. Observe for a delayed biphasic reaction.
sections.riskFactors: Known food, drug, latex, or insect-sting allergy; prior anaphylaxis; and asthma (a risk factor for severe or fatal reactions).

concepts.name: Anemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A reduced red blood cell mass or hemoglobin, lowering the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. A broad category with many causes; it is classified by red cell size (micro-, normo-, macrocytic) to narrow the diagnosis.

sections.presentation: Fatigue, weakness, pallor, dyspnea on exertion, tachycardia, palpitations, and lightheadedness. Severe or rapid drops can cause chest pain and hemodynamic instability.
sections.typicalTreatments: Directed at the cause: iron, B12, or folate replacement; transfusion of packed red cells for symptomatic or severe anemia; erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in CKD; and controlling any source of bleeding.
sections.riskFactors: Blood loss (GI, menstrual, surgical), nutritional deficiency, chronic disease and inflammation, chronic kidney disease, hemolysis, and bone marrow disorders.

concepts.name: Anemia of Chronic Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: Anemia driven by chronic inflammation, where hepcidin traps iron in storage so it cannot reach the marrow. The key contrast with iron-deficiency anemia is that ferritin is normal or high and TIBC is low despite a low serum iron.

sections.presentation: Usually mild, normocytic anemia (can become microcytic over time) in a patient with a chronic inflammatory, infectious, malignant, or kidney condition. Labs show low serum iron, LOW TIBC, and normal-to-high ferritin.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying disorder. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (with iron) are used in CKD and selected chemotherapy or perioperative patients. Iron alone is generally avoided unless true iron deficiency is also present.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease, chronic infection, malignancy, and heart failure.

concepts.name: Anion Gap
concepts.shortExplanation: A calculated value from the metabolic panel used to work out the cause of a metabolic acidosis.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 8-12 mEq/L (varies by lab and whether potassium is included).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high anion gap points to acidosis from accumulated acids - classic causes include DKA, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, and toxic ingestions. A normal-gap acidosis is more typical of bicarbonate loss such as diarrhea. It is calculated as sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate.

concepts.name: Aortic Stenosis
concepts.shortExplanation: The aortic valve narrows and stiffens, forcing the heart to work harder to push blood out — leading to chest pain, fainting, and heart failure as it worsens.

sections.presentation: Exertional chest pain, syncope, and dyspnea; a harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids; narrowed pulse pressure in severe disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Valve replacement when symptomatic or severe — surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVR); careful management of blood pressure and volume; avoid abrupt vasodilation.
sections.riskFactors: Older age (calcific degeneration), bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic heart disease, chronic kidney disease.

concepts.name: APGAR Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A quick assessment of a newborn's condition just after birth, done at 1 and 5 minutes of life.

sections.purpose: Rapidly assesses a newborn's transition to life outside the womb at 1 and 5 minutes (and beyond if needed) to determine whether resuscitation support is required.
sections.steps: Five signs - Appearance (color), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration - each scored 0-2; total 0-10.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 7-10 is generally reassuring, 4-6 moderately depressed, and 0-3 severely depressed and needing resuscitation. A low or non-improving 5-minute score prompts continued support; the score guides care but does not by itself predict long-term outcome.

concepts.name: Apixaban
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral anticoagulant (DOAC) used to prevent strokes in atrial fibrillation and to treat clots — no routine INR monitoring needed, unlike warfarin.

sections.mechanism: Directly inhibits factor Xa. Predictable dosing without routine coagulation monitoring; shorter half-life than warfarin.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding (GI, intracranial); reversal with andexanet alfa when available.
sections.nursingImplications: Reinforce not to skip doses (short half-life means clot risk returns quickly); assess for bleeding; note dose reductions for age, weight, and renal function; usually held before procedures per orders.

concepts.name: Apnea of Prematurity
concepts.shortExplanation: Pauses in breathing in premature infants caused by an immature respiratory control center in the brain.

sections.presentation: Breathing pauses, often lasting 20 seconds or longer or shorter pauses accompanied by a slow heart rate or drop in oxygen saturation, in a preterm infant.
sections.typicalTreatments: Gentle stimulation, caffeine to stimulate the respiratory center, and respiratory support such as CPAP when needed. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is essential, and new or worsening apnea should prompt evaluation for infection or other causes.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (more frequent the earlier the gestational age); apnea may also be worsened by infection, anemia, or reflux.

concepts.name: Appendicitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the appendix, usually from obstruction, that can progress to rupture. A common surgical emergency.

sections.presentation: Pain that begins near the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point), anorexia, nausea, low-grade fever, and rebound tenderness. Sudden relief followed by worsening diffuse pain suggests rupture and peritonitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Appendectomy is standard; antibiotics are given and, in selected uncomplicated cases, may be used alone. IV fluids, pain control, and NPO status while awaiting surgery. Avoid applying heat or laxatives, which may promote rupture.
sections.riskFactors: Most common between the ages of 10 and 30, but can occur at any age.

concepts.name: Aripiprazole
concepts.shortExplanation: An atypical antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and as add-on for depression, available orally and as a long-acting injection.

sections.mechanism: A partial agonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT1A receptors and an antagonist at 5-HT2A, stabilizing dopamine activity with generally less sedation and metabolic effect than some other agents.
sections.sideEffects: Akathisia (restlessness), insomnia, anxiety, nausea, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic changes, impulse-control problems (such as compulsive gambling), and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess for akathisia, which patients may find distressing, and for other movement effects. Monitor weight, glucose, and lipids. Ask about new impulsive behaviors. The long-acting injection supports adherence; do not stop abruptly.

concepts.name: Arterial Blood Gas
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test drawn from an artery that measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acid-base balance to assess how well the lungs and metabolism are working.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low pH is acidosis, high pH is alkalosis. A high PaCO2 points to respiratory acidosis (inadequate ventilation); a low PaCO2 to respiratory alkalosis. Abnormal HCO3 reflects metabolic disturbances. Low PaO2 or SaO2 indicates hypoxemia. Results guide ventilator settings and treatment of acid-base disorders.

concepts.name: Arterial Line Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of a catheter into an artery (commonly radial) for continuous blood pressure monitoring and frequent blood draws without repeated needle sticks.

sections.targetConcern: Need for beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring, e.g. while titrating a vasopressor, or frequent arterial blood gas sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Waveform quality, distal perfusion/pulses of the cannulated limb, insertion site for bleeding, accidental disconnection (risk of significant blood loss).

concepts.name: Ascites
concepts.shortExplanation: Buildup of fluid in the abdominal cavity, most often from cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Large volumes cause distension and breathing difficulty.

sections.presentation: Abdominal distension and discomfort, weight gain, a fluid wave or shifting dullness on exam, and early satiety. Large ascites can cause shortness of breath. Fever and abdominal pain raise concern for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Sodium restriction and diuretics (typically spironolactone with furosemide), therapeutic paracentesis for large or tense ascites, and albumin replacement after large-volume taps. Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with antibiotics. Monitor daily weights and abdominal girth.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension, heart failure, malignancy, and kidney disease.

concepts.name: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
concepts.shortExplanation: A liver enzyme (also found in heart and muscle) that rises when those tissues are injured.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 10-40 U/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated AST indicates liver-cell injury from hepatitis, alcohol, medications, or fatty liver, but because AST is also in muscle and heart, it can rise with muscle injury. It is interpreted alongside ALT; an AST:ALT ratio above 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease.

concepts.name: Aspiration Pneumonia
concepts.shortExplanation: Lung infection or inflammation that develops after inhaling food, stomach contents, or secretions into the airways, common in patients with impaired swallowing or reduced consciousness.

sections.presentation: Cough, fever, shortness of breath, low oxygen, and purulent sputum, often after a witnessed aspiration event or in a patient at risk. Infiltrates typically appear in dependent lung regions.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen and airway support, suctioning, and antibiotics guided by severity and risk. Supportive care and treatment of respiratory failure as needed. Swallow evaluation and aspiration precautions to prevent recurrence.
sections.riskFactors: Impaired swallowing, stroke, decreased consciousness, sedation, tube feeding, gastroesophageal reflux, and intubation or extubation.

concepts.name: Aspirin
concepts.shortExplanation: An antiplatelet that makes platelets less sticky — given early in a suspected heart attack and taken long-term to prevent clots in the coronary arteries.

sections.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1), blocking thromboxane A2 and reducing platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. In suspected ACS, a non-enteric 162–325 mg tablet is chewed for rapid absorption.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset, easy bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding/ulceration, allergic reaction/bronchospasm, Reye syndrome in children with viral illness.
sections.nursingImplications: Have the patient chew (don't swallow whole) in suspected MI for faster onset; assess for bleeding and GI symptoms; ask about aspirin allergy before giving.
sections.commonBrandName: Bayer, Ecotrin. Often written as ASA.

concepts.name: Asthma
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible bronchospasm, causing episodic wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath triggered by allergens, exercise, or irritants.

sections.presentation: Wheezing, chest tightness, dry cough (often nocturnal), prolonged expiration, and dyspnea. Severe attacks show accessory muscle use, inability to speak full sentences, and a silent chest with low peak flow.
sections.typicalTreatments: Short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol) for rescue; inhaled corticosteroids for control, often combined with long-acting beta-agonists; leukotriene modifiers (montelukast) and systemic steroids for exacerbations. Trigger avoidance and an asthma action plan.
sections.riskFactors: Atopy/allergies, family history, eczema, tobacco or air-pollution exposure, obesity, and viral respiratory infections.

concepts.name: Atelectasis
concepts.shortExplanation: Collapse of alveoli or a region of lung, reducing gas exchange. Very common after surgery and in immobile patients; it is a leading cause of early postoperative fever and hypoxemia.

sections.presentation: Often asymptomatic when small; larger collapse causes dyspnea, low-grade fever (classically in the first 24-48 hours after surgery), hypoxemia, decreased breath sounds and dullness over the affected area, and sometimes tachypnea. Chest imaging shows volume loss with opacification.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prevention and re-expansion: incentive spirometry, deep breathing and coughing, early mobilization, and adequate pain control so the patient can breathe deeply. Add chest physiotherapy and, for refractory or mucus-plugging cases, positive-pressure therapy or bronchoscopy to clear plugs. Supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia.
sections.riskFactors: Recent surgery (especially thoracic or upper-abdominal) and general anesthesia, immobility, shallow breathing from pain, thick secretions or mucus plugging, obesity, and smoking.

concepts.name: Atenolol
concepts.shortExplanation: A cardioselective beta-blocker used for hypertension, angina, and some arrhythmias.

sections.mechanism: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart, lowering heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure and reducing myocardial oxygen demand.
sections.sideEffects: Fatigue, dizziness, bradycardia, cold extremities, and depression.
sections.adverseEffects: Marked bradycardia and hypotension, worsening heart block, and rebound hypertension or angina if stopped abruptly; it is largely renally cleared, so it accumulates in kidney impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Check heart rate and blood pressure before dosing and hold and notify the provider for significant bradycardia or hypotension. Do not stop abruptly; taper. Teach diabetic patients that it can mask signs of hypoglycemia except sweating.

concepts.name: Atorvastatin
concepts.shortExplanation: A statin that lowers cholesterol — used to slow plaque buildup in arteries and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, lowering LDL and stabilizing atherosclerotic plaque. High-intensity dosing is standard after ACS.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle aches, GI upset, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain with dark urine), elevated liver enzymes.
sections.nursingImplications: Ask about new muscle pain or weakness; monitor liver function per orders; typically dosed in the evening; counsel to avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice.

concepts.name: Atrial Fibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: An irregular, often rapid heart rhythm originating in the atria that increases the risk of stroke and can reduce the heart's pumping efficiency.

sections.presentation: Irregularly irregular pulse, palpitations, fatigue, sometimes asymptomatic and found incidentally on telemetry.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control (beta-blockers, amiodarone), rhythm control (antiarrhythmics, cardioversion), anticoagulation (warfarin or other agents) to reduce stroke risk.
sections.riskFactors: Advanced age, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, excessive alcohol use.

concepts.name: Atrial Fibrillation with RVR
concepts.shortExplanation: Atrial fibrillation in which the ventricular rate runs fast (typically over 100-120 bpm), often causing palpitations, hypotension, or chest pain. The priority is rate control, with urgent cardioversion if the patient is hemodynamically unstable.

sections.presentation: Irregularly irregular pulse with a rapid ventricular rate (often 110-160+ bpm). Palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pressure, lightheadedness, and fatigue. May progress to hypotension, altered mental status, angina, or acute pulmonary edema when the rate is too fast to allow adequate filling and cardiac output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control is the first goal in stable patients: IV diltiazem or IV metoprolol (beta blocker); digoxin or amiodarone in select cases (heart failure, hypotension). Treat reversible drivers (fever, sepsis, hypovolemia, hyperthyroidism, PE, pain). If the patient is unstable (hypotension, ischemia, shock, or pulmonary edema), perform immediate synchronized cardioversion. Anticoagulation is assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc score to reduce stroke risk.
sections.riskFactors: Underlying atrial fibrillation, sepsis or infection, heart failure exacerbation, hyperthyroidism, pulmonary embolism, dehydration, alcohol, electrolyte disturbances, and missed rate-control medications.

concepts.name: Atrial Flutter
concepts.shortExplanation: A fast, organized atrial rhythm from a re-entry circuit (usually in the right atrium) producing classic sawtooth flutter waves on ECG. It often conducts 2:1, giving a strikingly regular ventricular rate near 150 bpm, and carries a stroke risk similar to atrial fibrillation.

sections.presentation: Palpitations, breathlessness, fatigue, or chest discomfort. ECG shows sawtooth flutter (F) waves, typically at an atrial rate of about 250-350 bpm; with 2:1 AV conduction the ventricular rate is often near 150 bpm and regular, which distinguishes it from the irregularly irregular rhythm of AFib. Can become unstable if conduction accelerates.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control with beta blockers or diltiazem, and anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc (same stroke-risk approach as AFib). Atrial flutter is often less responsive to drugs but very responsive to synchronized cardioversion, frequently at low energy. Cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation is highly effective and often curative for typical (right atrial) flutter. Perform immediate synchronized cardioversion if unstable.
sections.riskFactors: Coexisting atrial fibrillation, COPD, heart failure, valvular and structural heart disease, prior cardiac surgery, hyperthyroidism, and older age.

concepts.name: Atropine
concepts.shortExplanation: Speeds up a dangerously slow heart rate by blocking the vagal "brake" on the heart — first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia.

sections.mechanism: Anticholinergic — blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing vagal tone and increasing sinus node firing and AV conduction. ACLS dose is 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes (max 3 mg) for symptomatic bradycardia.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, flushing.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive tachycardia worsening myocardial ischemia; confusion/delirium especially in older adults; may be ineffective in high-grade (infranodal) heart block.
sections.nursingImplications: Push rapidly (slow push can paradoxically slow the heart); monitor rhythm and heart rate response; prepare transcutaneous pacing as a backup if atropine fails.

concepts.name: AV Fistula and Graft Care
concepts.shortExplanation: Care and protection of the surgically created blood vessel access used to perform hemodialysis.

sections.targetConcern: Provides durable access for hemodialysis needles - a fistula directly joins an artery and vein, while a graft uses a synthetic tube between them.
sections.whatToMonitor: Check for a thrill (a palpable buzz) and listen for a bruit (a whooshing sound) each shift, and assess circulation to the hand. Protect the access limb: no blood pressure cuffs, blood draws, or IVs in that arm. Watch for bleeding, infection, and steal syndrome (a cold, painful hand).

concepts.name: Azithromycin
concepts.shortExplanation: A macrolide antibiotic used for respiratory infections, some sexually transmitted infections, and skin infections, often given as a short course such as a Z-Pak.

sections.mechanism: Binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, giving a broad but generally bacteriostatic effect with a long tissue half-life.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: QT-interval prolongation with risk of arrhythmia, hepatotoxicity, and rare severe allergic or skin reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Review the ECG and other QT-prolonging drugs and correct low potassium or magnesium. Can be taken with or without food. Teach patients to finish the course and report palpitations or jaundice.

concepts.name: Bacteremia
concepts.shortExplanation: The presence of viable bacteria in the bloodstream, confirmed by blood cultures. Distinguished from sepsis, which is the body's dysregulated systemic response to infection - bacteremia may be transient and asymptomatic or may progress to sepsis.

sections.presentation: May be asymptomatic and transient (for example, after dental work) or cause fever, chills, rigors, and tachycardia. It can progress to sepsis or septic shock with hypotension and organ dysfunction. Positive blood cultures are the defining finding.
sections.typicalTreatments: Obtain blood cultures (ideally before antibiotics), start empiric IV antibiotics and narrow them by culture and sensitivity, and identify and control the source (for example, remove an infected central line). Monitor for progression to sepsis, and obtain follow-up cultures to confirm clearance for certain organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus.
sections.riskFactors: Indwelling catheters and central lines, recent invasive procedures or surgery, immunosuppression, IV drug use, prosthetic devices or valves, and urinary tract infection.

concepts.name: Bacterial Meningitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord caused by bacterial infection. It is a medical emergency that can rapidly become fatal.

sections.presentation: Classic triad of fever, headache, and neck stiffness; also photophobia, altered mental status, nausea, seizures, and petechial or purpuric rash (meningococcal). Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Infants may show poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, and irritability.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent empiric IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone plus vancomycin) started immediately, ideally after blood cultures without delaying treatment; lumbar puncture for CSF analysis; adjunctive dexamethasone in certain cases; droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy for suspected meningococcal disease.
sections.riskFactors: Recent respiratory or ear infection, close-quarters living, immunocompromise, absent or nonfunctioning spleen, missing vaccinations, age extremes, CSF leak or neurosurgery.

concepts.name: Bell Palsy
concepts.shortExplanation: Sudden weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face from dysfunction of the facial nerve. Most cases recover over weeks to months.

sections.presentation: Rapid-onset unilateral facial droop involving the forehead (unable to raise the eyebrow or close the eye on the affected side), loss of the nasolabial fold, drooling, altered taste, and sensitivity to sound. Forehead involvement helps distinguish it from stroke.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral corticosteroids started early; antivirals may be added in some cases; eye protection is essential (lubricating drops, taping the eye at night) because the eye may not close fully; most patients recover.
sections.riskFactors: Recent viral illness, pregnancy, diabetes, and possible reactivation of herpes simplex virus.

concepts.name: Benzonatate
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral non-opioid antitussive that suppresses cough by numbing stretch receptors in the airways.

sections.mechanism: A topical anesthetic (related to tetracaine) that anesthetizes the stretch receptors in the respiratory passages and lungs, dampening the cough reflex.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and GI upset.
sections.adverseEffects: Chewing or sucking the capsule can cause oropharyngeal numbness, laryngospasm, and severe reactions. Overdose (especially in children) can be fatal, causing seizures and cardiac arrest.
sections.nursingImplications: Instruct patients to swallow capsules whole and never chew or dissolve them. Keep away from children; even a small ingestion can be lethal.

concepts.name: Betamethasone
concepts.shortExplanation: A corticosteroid given to the mother before an anticipated preterm birth to speed up the baby's lung development and reduce complications of prematurity.

sections.mechanism: Crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal surfactant production and lung maturation, lowering the risk of respiratory distress syndrome.
sections.sideEffects: Maternal elevated blood glucose, transient reduction in fetal movement, insomnia.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsened hyperglycemia in mothers with diabetes; potential immunosuppression with concurrent infection.
sections.nursingImplications: Given as a course of intramuscular injections spaced apart; the benefit builds over about 24-48 hours, so timing matters. Monitor maternal blood glucose, especially in diabetics, and continue to assess fetal well-being.

concepts.name: BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure)
concepts.shortExplanation: A noninvasive ventilation device that delivers two pressure levels - higher on inhalation and lower on exhalation - to support breathing without intubation.

sections.purpose: Provides a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) to assist breaths and a lower expiratory pressure (EPAP) to keep alveoli open. Used for COPD exacerbations with CO2 retention, acute heart failure, and to avoid intubation in respiratory failure.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm the patient is awake enough to protect the airway; avoid in patients unable to clear secretions or at high aspiration risk. Monitor ABGs, mental status, respiratory rate, and mask fit. Watch for gastric distension, aspiration, and facial pressure injury; be ready to escalate to intubation if the patient worsens.

concepts.name: Bisacodyl
concepts.shortExplanation: A stimulant laxative available as oral tablets or a rectal suppository for constipation or bowel preparation.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates the colonic mucosa to increase peristalsis and promotes fluid accumulation in the bowel.
sections.sideEffects: Abdominal cramping, nausea, and rectal burning with the suppository.
sections.adverseEffects: Fluid and electrolyte disturbances with overuse and laxative dependence with chronic use.
sections.nursingImplications: Oral tablets act in about 6 to 12 hours; suppositories work within about an hour. Do not crush enteric-coated tablets or give with antacids or milk, which can cause premature dissolution and cramping. Encourage fluids.

concepts.name: Bishop Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A cervical exam score that predicts how ready the cervix is for labor induction.

sections.purpose: Assesses cervical readiness (ripeness) to predict the likelihood of a successful labor induction and guide whether cervical ripening is needed first.
sections.steps: Five cervical parameters: dilation, effacement, and fetal station (each 0-3), plus cervical consistency and position (each 0-2); total 0-13.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A higher score means a more favorable cervix: generally 8 or more is favorable with good chances of vaginal delivery, while 6 or less is unfavorable and often prompts cervical ripening before induction.

concepts.name: Bladder Scanner
concepts.shortExplanation: A portable ultrasound device that noninvasively measures the volume of urine in the bladder.

sections.purpose: Estimates bladder volume and post-void residual to evaluate urinary retention, decide whether catheterization is needed, and avoid unnecessary catheter insertions that risk infection.
sections.careConsiderations: Position the patient supine, apply gel, and aim toward the pubic bone for an accurate reading. Select the correct sex/gender setting; a prior hysterectomy affects the setting. A large post-void residual may prompt intermittent catheterization per protocol rather than an indwelling catheter.

concepts.name: Blood Culture Collection
concepts.shortExplanation: Drawing blood into special bottles to detect bacteria or fungi in the bloodstream, ideally before antibiotics.

sections.targetConcern: Identifies bloodstream infection (bacteremia or fungemia) and guides targeted antibiotic therapy in suspected sepsis or endocarditis.
sections.whatToMonitor: Draw before starting antibiotics whenever possible. Meticulous skin and bottle-top antisepsis prevents contamination and false positives. Collect the recommended blood volume in aerobic and anaerobic bottles and obtain two sets from separate sites. Note any fever or line source, and watch for the preliminary Gram stain and final sensitivities.

concepts.name: Blood Cultures
concepts.shortExplanation: A test that grows and identifies bacteria or fungi in the blood to diagnose bloodstream infection and guide antibiotic choice. Proper collection is key to accurate results.

sections.normalRange: No growth (negative) after incubation. Results are qualitative rather than a numeric range.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive culture indicates organisms in the blood (bacteremia or fungemia), supporting diagnoses such as sepsis, endocarditis, or line infection, and guides targeted therapy. A single positive with a common skin organism may reflect contamination. Draw before starting antibiotics when possible, using proper skin antisepsis, and collect at least two sets from separate sites; report results promptly so therapy can be tailored.

concepts.name: Blood Glucose Meter (Glucometer)
concepts.shortExplanation: A handheld device that measures blood sugar from a drop of capillary blood at the bedside.

sections.purpose: Gives a rapid point-of-care glucose reading to guide insulin dosing, catch hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, and monitor diabetic and critically ill patients.
sections.careConsiderations: Use control solutions and quality checks per policy, and confirm the test strips are not expired. Cleanse the site, wipe away the first drop if needy, and use the side of the fingertip. Very high or very low readings, or values that do not fit the patient, should be confirmed with a venous lab sample before major treatment.

concepts.name: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test reflecting kidney function and hydration; it measures a nitrogen waste product from protein breakdown.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 7-20 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High with kidney impairment, dehydration, GI bleeding, high protein intake, or tissue breakdown; low with overhydration or liver disease. It is interpreted alongside creatinine, and the BUN-to-creatinine ratio helps identify dehydration-related (prerenal) causes.

concepts.name: BNP
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone released when the heart's chambers are stretched by fluid overload — helps confirm and gauge the severity of heart failure.

sections.normalRange: Typically <100 pg/mL for BNP; NT-proBNP cutoffs are higher and rise with age. Interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels suggest cardiac wall stretch from heart failure/volume overload; higher values generally mean more severe decompensation. Levels can also rise with renal dysfunction and are lower in obesity.

concepts.name: Braden Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A tool that scores a patient's risk of developing pressure injuries so prevention can be started early.

sections.purpose: Predicts risk of pressure injury (bedsores) so preventive measures like repositioning and support surfaces can be started before skin breaks down.
sections.steps: Six subscales - sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition (each 1-4), and friction/shear (1-3); total 6-23. Lower scores mean higher risk.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Lower scores indicate greater risk: roughly 15-18 mild, 13-14 moderate, 10-12 high, and 9 or below very high risk. A score of 18 or less generally triggers pressure-injury prevention protocols.

aliases.text: Braden Scale for Predicting Pressure Sore Risk

concepts.name: Bronchiolitis
concepts.shortExplanation: A common lower respiratory infection in infants, most often from RSV, that inflames the small airways and causes wheezing and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Begins with runny nose and cough, then progresses to wheezing, tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, and feeding difficulty in a child under 2 years. Apnea can occur in young infants.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mainly supportive: nasal suctioning to clear secretions, adequate hydration, and supplemental oxygen for low saturations. Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely effective. Monitor respiratory status and hydration closely.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 2 years (especially under 6 months), prematurity, RSV season, secondhand smoke exposure, and daycare attendance.

concepts.name: Bronchoscopy
concepts.shortExplanation: Passing a thin camera-tipped scope into the airways to look inside the lungs, clear secretions or blockages, and collect samples.

sections.targetConcern: Diagnosing and managing airway and lung problems - clearing mucus plugs or blood, sampling for infection or masses (biopsy, bronchoalveolar lavage), and evaluating persistent respiratory issues.
sections.whatToMonitor: Oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory status during and after the procedure. Watch for bleeding, low oxygen, bronchospasm, and pneumothorax. Keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns after topical airway anesthesia.

concepts.name: Budesonide
concepts.shortExplanation: An inhaled corticosteroid used for long-term control of asthma and COPD by reducing airway inflammation.

sections.mechanism: Corticosteroid that suppresses airway inflammation and reduces bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
sections.sideEffects: Oral thrush (candidiasis), hoarseness, sore throat, and cough.
sections.adverseEffects: Long-term high-dose use may cause adrenal suppression, reduced bone density, and (in children) slowed growth. Not a rescue inhaler.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach patients to rinse and spit after each dose to prevent thrush. Emphasize daily controller use even when feeling well; effect builds over days to weeks.

concepts.name: Bupropion
concepts.shortExplanation: An atypical antidepressant also used for smoking cessation, notable for not causing sexual side effects or weight gain.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine; it does not act primarily on serotonin, which explains its different side-effect profile.
sections.sideEffects: Insomnia, dry mouth, headache, agitation, and decreased appetite.
sections.adverseEffects: Lowers the seizure threshold (contraindicated in seizure disorders, eating disorders, and abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal), hypertension, and possible increased suicidal thoughts early in treatment.
sections.nursingImplications: Screen for seizure risk and eating disorders before use. Give doses earlier in the day to limit insomnia and do not crush extended-release tablets. Monitor blood pressure and mood. Teach that it may take weeks to work.

concepts.name: Butalbital-Acetaminophen-Caffeine
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral combination product for tension (muscle-contraction) headache that blends a barbiturate, acetaminophen, and caffeine.

sections.mechanism: Butalbital is a barbiturate that depresses the central nervous system and relaxes muscle contraction; acetaminophen relieves pain; caffeine is a stimulant that enhances analgesia and constricts cerebral vessels.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, nausea, and abdominal pain.
sections.adverseEffects: Habit formation and dependence with the barbiturate, medication-overuse (rebound) headache, sedation, and acetaminophen hepatotoxicity if the daily limit is exceeded; withdrawal can occur with abrupt discontinuation.
sections.nursingImplications: Reserve for intermittent use because of dependence and rebound-headache risk. Track total daily acetaminophen. Caution against driving until effects are known and against combining with alcohol or other sedatives. Taper rather than stop abruptly after prolonged use.

concepts.name: C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood marker of inflammation that rises with infection, tissue injury, and inflammatory disease. It is used to detect and monitor inflammation over time.

sections.normalRange: Generally less than about 10 mg/L (roughly under 1 mg/dL) in healthy adults; high-sensitivity CRP is reported in lower ranges for cardiovascular risk. Reference values vary by lab and assay.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated CRP indicates inflammation from infection, autoimmune disease, tissue injury, or other causes; it is sensitive but not specific. Rising or persistently high levels can suggest worsening or uncontrolled infection, while falling levels often indicate response to treatment. Interpret alongside the clinical picture and other markers such as ESR and procalcitonin.

concepts.name: Caffeine Citrate
concepts.shortExplanation: A stimulant given to premature infants to reduce episodes of apnea by supporting their immature breathing control.

sections.mechanism: A methylxanthine that stimulates the central respiratory drive and increases sensitivity to carbon dioxide, reducing apnea episodes.
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, jitteriness, and feeding intolerance.
sections.adverseEffects: Signs of toxicity include marked tachycardia, agitation, and, rarely, seizures.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given once daily with a loading dose followed by maintenance dosing. Monitor heart rate, for apnea frequency and response, and for feeding tolerance. It has a wide safety margin and long half-life in neonates, so routine level monitoring is often not required.

concepts.name: Calcium Gluconate
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV calcium salt used to protect the heart in hyperkalemia, to treat low calcium, and as the antidote for magnesium toxicity.

sections.mechanism: Raises extracellular calcium, which stabilizes cardiac cell membranes; in hyperkalemia it protects the heart but does not lower potassium.
sections.sideEffects: Warmth or flushing during infusion.
sections.adverseEffects: Bradycardia if pushed too fast and tissue injury with extravasation (less severe than calcium chloride).
sections.nursingImplications: Used for hyperkalemia with ECG changes, symptomatic low calcium, and magnesium toxicity. Monitor the ECG, give slowly, and ensure a patent IV.

concepts.name: CAM-ICU
concepts.shortExplanation: A bedside tool to detect delirium in ICU patients, including those on a ventilator who cannot speak.

sections.purpose: Screens for delirium in critically ill patients, including nonverbal and ventilated patients, so it can be recognized and addressed early.
sections.steps: Assesses four features: (1) acute change or fluctuating course of mental status, (2) inattention, (3) altered level of consciousness (using RASS), and (4) disorganized thinking. It is applied only when the patient is arousable (not RASS -4 or -5).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Delirium is present (CAM-ICU positive) when features 1 and 2 are both present plus either feature 3 or feature 4. A positive screen prompts a search for causes and delirium-reducing measures.

aliases.text: Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU

concepts.name: Cancer Pain Management
concepts.shortExplanation: A structured approach to relieving pain in cancer patients, often guided by the WHO analgesic ladder. It combines scheduled and as-needed medications with attention to side effects and quality of life.

sections.triggerCriteria: Applies to patients with cancer-related pain from the tumor, treatment, or procedures. Pain is assessed regularly with a consistent scale and characterized by type (for example nociceptive versus neuropathic) to guide therapy.
sections.steps: Match analgesia to pain severity along the WHO ladder: non-opioids such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs for mild pain, adding opioids as pain increases, plus adjuvants (for example agents for neuropathic pain) at any step. Use around-the-clock dosing for constant pain with breakthrough doses available, prevent opioid-induced constipation with a proactive bowel regimen, and monitor for sedation and respiratory depression. Reassess response frequently and involve palliative care for complex pain.

concepts.name: Capillary Blood Glucose Check
concepts.shortExplanation: A fingerstick test that measures blood sugar at the bedside using a glucometer.

sections.targetConcern: Provides a rapid blood glucose value to guide insulin dosing and to detect and treat hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Time checks with meals and insulin per orders. Treat lows promptly (fast-acting carbohydrate or, if unable to swallow, IV dextrose or glucagon) and recheck. Cleanse the site and use the side of the fingertip. Confirm implausible readings with a venous sample before acting, and correlate results with the patient's symptoms.

concepts.name: Capnography Monitor
concepts.shortExplanation: A monitor that measures exhaled carbon dioxide (end-tidal CO2) breath by breath, used to confirm airway placement and watch breathing in real time.

sections.purpose: Continuously measure end-tidal CO2 to confirm and monitor endotracheal tube placement, detect early respiratory depression during sedation, and assess ventilation and the effectiveness of CPR.
sections.careConsiderations: Recognize the normal waveform and values (end-tidal CO2 roughly 35-45 mmHg). A sudden loss of waveform can mean a dislodged tube, disconnection, or cardiac arrest. During procedural sedation it detects hypoventilation earlier than pulse oximetry. Keep the sensor free of secretions and moisture.

concepts.name: Cardiac Ablation
concepts.shortExplanation: A catheter is guided to the heart to burn (radiofrequency) or freeze (cryo) the small area of tissue causing an abnormal rhythm — destroying the faulty electrical pathway so a normal rhythm can hold.

sections.targetConcern: Recurrent or drug-refractory arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, SVT, or ventricular tachycardia originating from an identifiable focus.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site (usually femoral) for bleeding or hematoma, cardiac rhythm for recurrence or new arrhythmia, signs of cardiac tamponade (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD), distal pulses.

concepts.name: Cardiac Arrest
concepts.shortExplanation: The heart abruptly stops pumping effectively, so blood flow to the brain and body ceases — reversible only with immediate CPR and ACLS.

sections.presentation: Sudden unresponsiveness, no pulse, and no normal breathing (or only gasping). Underlying rhythm may be shockable (VF/pulseless VT) or non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR, defibrillation for shockable rhythms, epinephrine per ACLS, advanced airway, and identifying/treating reversible causes (the Hs and Ts).
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease/MI, heart failure, severe electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, drug overdose, prior arrest.

concepts.name: Cardiac Conduction System
concepts.shortExplanation: The heart's built-in electrical wiring that sets the beat — starting at the SA node and traveling through the AV node to the ventricles.

sections.purpose: Generate and coordinate each heartbeat. The SA node (natural pacemaker) fires, the impulse pauses at the AV node to let the ventricles fill, then travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles.
sections.careConsiderations: Where the signal fails maps to the arrhythmia: SA node problems cause bradycardia; AV node/His block causes heart block; abnormal ventricular foci cause VT/VF. This system is the target of pacemakers, ablation, and rate/rhythm drugs.

concepts.name: Cardiac Stress Test
concepts.shortExplanation: Monitors the heart while it's made to work harder — by exercise or medication — to reveal blocked coronary arteries that don't cause symptoms at rest.

sections.targetConcern: Suspected coronary artery disease — evaluating exertional chest pain or risk before certain procedures.
sections.whatToMonitor: ECG for ischemic changes, blood pressure and heart rate response, chest pain or shortness of breath — stop the test for significant symptoms or ECG changes.

concepts.name: Cardiac Tamponade
concepts.shortExplanation: Fluid building up in the sac around the heart squeezes it so it can't fill properly — a life-threatening emergency that drops blood pressure fast.

sections.presentation: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), pulsus paradoxus, tachycardia, dyspnea, low-voltage ECG or electrical alternans.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage, IV fluids as a temporizing measure to support filling, treat the underlying cause.
sections.riskFactors: Pericarditis, chest trauma, recent cardiac procedure, malignancy, aortic dissection, post-MI wall rupture.

concepts.name: Cardiac Telemetry Monitor
concepts.shortExplanation: Continuous wireless heart-rhythm monitoring that lets staff watch for arrhythmias in real time from a central station.

sections.purpose: Continuously track heart rhythm and rate to catch arrhythmias, ischemic changes, or dangerous rate changes early.
sections.careConsiderations: Place and change electrodes on clean, dry skin; know each patient's alarm parameters and respond to alarms (avoid alarm fatigue); ensure leads stay connected and the battery is charged; correlate any rhythm change with the patient's symptoms and a 12-lead ECG.

concepts.name: Cardiogenic Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: The heart is too weak to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs — organs start to fail from poor perfusion. Most often follows a large heart attack.

sections.presentation: Hypotension, cool/mottled extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, low urine output, pulmonary congestion, rising lactate.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause (e.g. urgent revascularization for MI), inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors, and mechanical support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Large myocardial infarction, advanced heart failure, severe arrhythmia, acute valve failure.

concepts.name: Carvedilol
concepts.shortExplanation: A combined alpha- and beta-blocker used to treat heart failure, hypertension, and post-heart-attack patients.

sections.mechanism: Blocks beta-1, beta-2, and alpha-1 receptors, lowering heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure; improves survival in systolic heart failure.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, fatigue, hypotension, bradycardia, and weight gain from fluid retention.
sections.adverseEffects: Can worsen acute decompensated heart failure if started or up-titrated too fast; masks hypoglycemia symptoms; may cause bronchospasm in reactive airway disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Check apical pulse and blood pressure before giving; hold and notify provider for significant bradycardia or hypotension. Give with food to slow absorption and reduce orthostasis. Do not stop abruptly.

concepts.name: Catheter-Associated UTI
concepts.shortExplanation: A urinary tract infection linked to an indwelling urinary catheter. It is a common, largely preventable healthcare-associated infection.

sections.presentation: New fever, suprapubic or flank pain or tenderness, and change in urine appearance or character in a catheterized patient, often with few localized symptoms; altered mental status may be the only sign in older adults. Diagnosis requires symptoms plus a positive urine culture, not merely cloudy urine or asymptomatic bacteriuria.
sections.typicalTreatments: Remove or replace the catheter when possible; antibiotics guided by urine culture; avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. Prevention centers on inserting catheters only when indicated, sterile insertion, maintaining a closed system, and removing them as early as possible.
sections.riskFactors: Prolonged catheterization, breaks in the closed drainage system, poor insertion technique, female sex, older age, diabetes, and immobility.

concepts.name: Cefazolin
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic commonly used for surgical infection prevention and skin and soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible bacteria.

sections.mechanism: A beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; active against many gram-positive organisms including methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions, diarrhea, nausea, and rash.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypersensitivity and allergic reactions (use caution with penicillin allergy); Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; rarely seizures at high doses in renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Screen for beta-lactam allergy. For surgical prophylaxis, give within the recommended window before incision and redose for long procedures or major blood loss. Adjust dose in renal impairment; monitor for signs of allergic reaction and for C. difficile.

concepts.name: Ceftriaxone
concepts.shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum injectable antibiotic used for many common infections, including pneumonia and urinary tract/kidney infections.

sections.mechanism: Third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, injection-site reactions, rash.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions (caution with penicillin allergy) and C. difficile infection. Avoid co-administration with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess allergy history before giving. Monitor for rash or anaphylaxis and for diarrhea suggesting C. difficile.

concepts.name: Cellulitis
concepts.shortExplanation: A bacterial infection of the skin and underlying tissue that causes a spreading area of redness, warmth, and swelling.

sections.presentation: Warm, red, swollen, tender skin with poorly defined borders, most often on a lower leg; may have fever, chills, and red streaking toward lymph nodes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics targeting skin bacteria, limb elevation, marking the border of redness to track spread, and pain control.
sections.riskFactors: Breaks in the skin, edema and venous insufficiency, diabetes, obesity, and lymphedema.

concepts.name: Central Line Insertion
