concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of a catheter into a large central vein for reliable IV access — used for vasopressors, certain medications, or when peripheral access is inadequate.

sections.targetConcern: Need for reliable central venous access, e.g. to safely administer vasopressors in septic shock.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion site for bleeding/infection, chest x-ray to confirm placement and rule out pneumothorax, signs of catheter-related bloodstream infection.

concepts.name: Central Venous Catheter (Device)
concepts.shortExplanation: A catheter whose tip sits in a large central vein, used for medications, fluids, and monitoring that a peripheral IV cannot handle.

sections.purpose: Provides reliable access for vesicant or irritating drugs (vasopressors, chemotherapy, TPN), rapid large-volume resuscitation, central venous pressure monitoring, and long-term therapy. Types include internal jugular/subclavian lines, PICCs, and tunneled catheters and ports.
sections.careConsiderations: Follow strict sterile technique and central-line bundle practices to prevent CLABSI: scrub the hub, keep the dressing clean/dry/occlusive, and remove the line as soon as it is no longer needed. Assess the site for redness or drainage, confirm blood return before use, and watch for air embolism when caps or tubing are open.

concepts.name: Central Venous Oxygen Saturation
concepts.shortExplanation: The oxygen saturation of blood returning through a central line, used as a marker of the balance between oxygen delivery and how much tissue is using.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 65-70% or higher for ScvO2 measured from a central venous catheter.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low value suggests oxygen delivery is not keeping up with demand - from low cardiac output, anemia, hypoxemia, or increased consumption - as seen in shock. An unusually high value can reflect impaired oxygen extraction by tissues, as in some cases of septic shock. Trends help guide resuscitation.

concepts.name: Central-Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection
concepts.shortExplanation: A serious bloodstream infection that develops in a patient with a central venous catheter and is not from another source. It is largely preventable with proper line care.

sections.presentation: Fever and chills, and possibly hypotension or signs of sepsis; the catheter exit site may show redness, tenderness, or purulence. Confirmed with blood cultures, ideally drawn from the catheter and a peripheral site.
sections.typicalTreatments: Blood cultures then prompt empiric IV antibiotics (often covering MRSA) adjusted to culture results; consider removing the catheter, especially with instability or certain organisms; source control. Prevention uses insertion bundles, chlorhexidine skin prep, maximal sterile barriers, daily necessity review, and scrupulous hub disinfection.
sections.riskFactors: Prolonged catheter dwell time, femoral or multiple-lumen access, frequent line access, parenteral nutrition, immunocompromise, and breaks in sterile technique.

concepts.name: Cephalexin
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-generation oral cephalosporin antibiotic used for skin, soft-tissue, respiratory, and urinary infections.

sections.mechanism: A beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect against many gram-positive and some gram-negative organisms.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and vaginal yeast infection.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions (cross-reactivity is possible with penicillin allergy, especially severe reactions) and C. difficile colitis.
sections.nursingImplications: Ask about penicillin and cephalosporin allergy. May be given with food to reduce GI upset. Teach patients to finish the full course and report persistent diarrhea or rash.

concepts.name: Cerebral Lobes
concepts.shortExplanation: The four lobes of the cerebrum - frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital - each with distinct functions.

sections.purpose: Divide the cerebrum by function: the frontal lobe governs movement, judgment, and personality; the parietal lobe processes sensation and spatial awareness; the temporal lobe handles hearing, language, and memory; and the occipital lobe processes vision.
sections.careConsiderations: Localizing deficits helps interpret strokes and injuries - for example, frontal changes in behavior, temporal language deficits (aphasia), or occipital visual field loss. Nurses perform focused neuro checks and note new deficits, which guide stroke recognition and management.

concepts.name: Cetirizine
concepts.shortExplanation: A once-daily second-generation antihistamine for allergic rhinitis and hives, effective with relatively low sedation.

sections.mechanism: Selectively blocks peripheral histamine H1 receptors, relieving allergy symptoms with limited central nervous system penetration.
sections.sideEffects: Mild drowsiness (more than some other second-generation agents), dry mouth, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Generally well tolerated; more sedation than loratadine in some patients but far less anticholinergic effect than first-generation antihistamines.
sections.nursingImplications: Give once daily, typically in the evening if it causes drowsiness. Teach caution with driving until effects are known. Preferred over diphenhydramine in older adults.

concepts.name: CHA2DS2-VASc Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A score that estimates stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation to help decide on anticoagulation.

sections.purpose: Estimates annual stroke risk in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation to guide the decision about anticoagulation.
sections.steps: Points for Congestive heart failure (1), Hypertension (1), Age 75 or older (2), Diabetes (1), prior Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), and Sex category female (1); total 0-9.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher scores mean higher stroke risk. Anticoagulation is generally recommended at a score of 2 or more in men and 3 or more in women, considered at 1 (men) or 2 (women), and often not needed at 0, per guidelines.

concepts.name: Chemotherapy
concepts.shortExplanation: The use of cytotoxic drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, usually given in cycles. Because it also affects fast-dividing healthy cells, it causes predictable side effects like low blood counts, hair loss, and nausea.

sections.targetConcern: Destroys or controls cancer by targeting rapidly dividing cells; it may be curative, used to shrink tumors before surgery, given after surgery to reduce recurrence, or used for palliation.
sections.whatToMonitor: Complete blood counts for myelosuppression (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia), signs of infection, nausea and vomiting, mucositis, kidney and liver function, and infusion or hypersensitivity reactions. Watch the IV site closely for vesicant extravasation and monitor for tumor lysis syndrome with bulky, rapidly dividing tumors.

concepts.name: Chemotherapy Extravasation
concepts.shortExplanation: The accidental leakage of chemotherapy from the vein into surrounding tissue during infusion. With vesicant drugs this can cause severe pain, blistering, and tissue death.

sections.presentation: Burning or pain, swelling, redness, and lack of blood return at the IV site during or after infusion. Vesicant extravasation can progress over days to blistering, ulceration, and necrosis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the infusion immediately while leaving the catheter in place to aspirate residual drug, then remove it and elevate the limb. Apply cold or warm compresses and give a specific antidote depending on the drug, mark and photograph the area, and involve the provider and pharmacy; surgery may be needed for severe injury.
sections.riskFactors: Vesicant drugs such as anthracyclines and vinca alkaloids, small or fragile peripheral veins, poor catheter placement, patient movement, and infusing vesicants peripherally rather than through a central line or port.

concepts.name: Chest Drainage System (Pleur-evac)
concepts.shortExplanation: A closed collection system connected to a chest tube that drains air, blood, or fluid from the pleural space and prevents it from re-entering.

sections.purpose: Uses a three-chamber design - collection, water seal, and suction control - to evacuate air or fluid, re-expand the lung, and restore negative pleural pressure after pneumothorax, hemothorax, effusion, or thoracic surgery.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep the unit upright and below chest level. Assess for tidaling in the water-seal chamber (normal) and continuous bubbling (indicates an air leak or loose connection). Monitor drainage amount, color, and rate; report sudden increases in bright red drainage. Never clamp the tube routinely; if it disconnects, place the end in sterile water. Keep an occlusive dressing and clamp at the bedside.

concepts.name: Chest Pain Protocol
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized first response to new chest pain to quickly identify or rule out a heart attack.

sections.triggerCriteria: New or ongoing chest pain or an anginal equivalent (e.g. unexplained dyspnea, especially in higher-risk patients).
sections.steps: Get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, draw troponin (trended serially), apply continuous cardiac monitoring, establish IV access, and consider the initial "MONA" measures — aspirin, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, and pain control — while escalating to the STEMI pathway if ECG shows ST elevation.

concepts.name: Chest Tube Placement
concepts.shortExplanation: Insertion of a tube into the pleural space to drain air, blood, or fluid and re-expand the lung — commonly used for pneumothorax or significant pleural effusion.

sections.targetConcern: Pneumothorax or large pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise.
sections.whatToMonitor: Drainage amount/color, air leak (bubbling in the water seal chamber), respiratory status, insertion site for bleeding/infection, subcutaneous emphysema.

concepts.name: CHF Exacerbation
concepts.shortExplanation: Acute worsening of heart failure symptoms, often from fluid overload.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles on lung auscultation, jugular venous distension, peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Loop diuretics (furosemide), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, fluid and sodium restriction.
sections.riskFactors: Prior heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension, medication/dietary non-adherence.

concepts.name: Cholecystitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a gallstone blocking the cystic duct. Causes right upper quadrant pain and can become infected.

sections.presentation: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often after fatty meals, that may radiate to the right shoulder. Nausea, vomiting, fever, and a positive Murphy sign (pain and arrest of inspiration on palpation under the right costal margin).
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest, IV fluids, pain control, antiemetics, and antibiotics for infection. Cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment; a cholecystostomy tube may be used in poor surgical candidates.
sections.riskFactors: Gallstones, female sex, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss, and age over 40.

concepts.name: Chronic Bronchitis
concepts.shortExplanation: A clinical subtype of COPD defined by a productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, from chronic airway inflammation and mucus hypersecretion. Classically the 'blue bloater' phenotype.

sections.presentation: Chronic productive (mucus-heavy) cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. The classic 'blue bloater' picture: cyanosis and CO2 retention (hypoxemia), often overweight, with signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale) such as peripheral edema and jugular venous distention. Coarse rhonchi and wheezes on auscultation. In practice most COPD patients overlap with emphysema features.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, inhaled bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-agonists and anticholinergics), inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, and supplemental oxygen for chronic hypoxemia. Exacerbations: bronchodilators, systemic steroids, and antibiotics when sputum is purulent.
sections.riskFactors: Cigarette smoking (leading cause), long-term air-pollution or occupational-dust/fume exposure, and recurrent respiratory infections.

concepts.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: A gradual, long-term loss of kidney function; at its end stage (ESRD) it requires dialysis or a transplant.

sections.presentation: Often silent early on; later fatigue, edema, anemia, itching, poor appetite, and mineral and bone disease. It is staged by the GFR.
sections.typicalTreatments: Control blood pressure and diabetes, avoid nephrotoxins, manage anemia with ESAs and iron, use phosphate binders, and adjust diet. End-stage disease requires dialysis or transplant.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes, hypertension, older age, cardiovascular disease, family history, and repeated episodes of acute kidney injury.

concepts.name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
concepts.shortExplanation: A progressive, largely irreversible airflow limitation from emphysema and chronic bronchitis, most often caused by smoking, producing chronic dyspnea and cough.

sections.presentation: Chronic productive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea, wheezing, prolonged expiration, and barrel chest. Advanced disease shows pursed-lip breathing, hypoxemia, and cor pulmonale with peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, long-acting bronchodilators (tiotropium, LABA), inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehab, and long-term oxygen for chronic hypoxemia. Target controlled oxygen (SpO2 roughly 88-92 percent) to avoid CO2 retention.
sections.riskFactors: Cigarette smoking (primary), occupational dust/chemical exposure, biomass smoke, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

concepts.name: Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A quick three-part check for stroke, the basis of the public FAST message, used to rapidly identify likely stroke.

sections.purpose: Rapidly screens for stroke in the field or at the bedside so patients can be triaged quickly to definitive stroke care.
sections.steps: Checks three signs: facial droop (ask the patient to smile), arm drift (ask them to hold both arms out), and abnormal speech (ask them to repeat a phrase). The public FAST version adds Time - note symptom onset and act fast.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Any one abnormal finding strongly suggests stroke and should trigger urgent stroke workup and transport. Establishing time of onset is critical for treatment eligibility.

concepts.name: Ciprofloxacin
concepts.shortExplanation: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for urinary, GI, respiratory, and other infections, with strong activity against many gram-negative bacteria.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication; broad gram-negative coverage including Pseudomonas.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, and dizziness; photosensitivity.
sections.adverseEffects: Tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm risk, and blood glucose disturbances; C. difficile infection. Boxed warnings note serious, potentially permanent effects.
sections.nursingImplications: Separate from dairy, antacids, and products containing calcium, magnesium, iron, or zinc, which impair absorption. Monitor for tendon pain (stop the drug if it occurs), neuropathy, and QT-affecting drug combinations; encourage hydration; adjust for renal function.

concepts.name: Cirrhosis
concepts.shortExplanation: Advanced scarring of the liver from chronic injury that replaces healthy tissue and impairs liver function. Leads to portal hypertension and its complications.

sections.presentation: Often silent early. Later: fatigue, jaundice, easy bruising and bleeding, ascites, leg edema, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy). Signs of portal hypertension include varices and an enlarged spleen.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause (alcohol cessation, antivirals for hepatitis) and manage complications: diuretics and sodium restriction for ascites, lactulose and rifaximin for encephalopathy, and variceal screening and prophylaxis. Transplant evaluation for end-stage disease.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic alcohol use, chronic hepatitis B or C, and fatty liver disease (metabolic/nonalcoholic).

concepts.name: Cisplatin
concepts.shortExplanation: A platinum-based chemotherapy drug used for many solid tumors, including testicular, ovarian, bladder, and lung cancers. It is notable for kidney toxicity, severe nausea, and hearing loss.

sections.mechanism: A platinum compound that forms DNA cross-links, blocking DNA replication and transcription and triggering cancer cell death.
sections.sideEffects: Severe nausea and vomiting, myelosuppression, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (hearing loss and tinnitus), peripheral neuropathy, and electrolyte wasting such as low magnesium.
sections.nursingImplications: Give aggressive IV hydration before and after the dose to protect the kidneys and monitor urine output, creatinine, and electrolytes (especially magnesium and potassium). Provide strong antiemetic prophylaxis, ask about hearing changes and numbness, and replace electrolytes as ordered.

concepts.name: CIWA-Ar
concepts.shortExplanation: A symptom scale that rates the severity of alcohol withdrawal to guide how much and how often to give benzodiazepines.

sections.purpose: Grades the severity of alcohol withdrawal so treatment (usually symptom-triggered benzodiazepines) can be titrated to the patient's actual symptoms.
sections.steps: 10 items: nausea/vomiting, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile, auditory, and visual disturbances, headache (each 0-7), and orientation/clouding of sensorium (0-4); total 0-67.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Lower scores (often under 8-10) suggest minimal withdrawal; higher scores indicate more severe withdrawal with rising risk of seizures and delirium tremens. Medication is commonly triggered at a threshold (frequently 8-10 or higher) per protocol.

aliases.text: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol

concepts.name: CK-MB
concepts.shortExplanation: The heart-associated fraction of creatine kinase; historically used to detect heart-muscle injury, now largely replaced by troponin.

sections.normalRange: Generally 0-3 ng/mL, or under about 5% of total CK (assay dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rise in CK-MB indicates heart-muscle injury, as in myocardial infarction. Because it clears faster than troponin, it was once used to detect reinfarction, but troponin is now the preferred cardiac marker. Skeletal muscle injury can also raise CK-MB modestly.

concepts.name: CKD Stage 3
concepts.shortExplanation: Moderately reduced kidney function with an eGFR of 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73m2 (3a 45-59, 3b 30-44). This is often where CKD first becomes symptomatic and where slowing progression becomes the priority.

sections.presentation: Frequently still asymptomatic; may show early fatigue, mild edema, hypertension, and rising creatinine. Complications such as anemia and mineral-bone disease can begin, especially in stage 3b.
sections.typicalTreatments: Focus on slowing progression: blood pressure and glycemic control, ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, avoiding nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast), and renal dosing of medications. Monitor eGFR, potassium, and albuminuria.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes, hypertension, older age, cardiovascular disease, and recurrent acute kidney injury.

concepts.name: CKD Stage 4
concepts.shortExplanation: Severely reduced kidney function with an eGFR of 15 to 29 mL/min/1.73m2. The distinguishing focus of this stage is preparing for renal replacement therapy - dialysis access and transplant evaluation - before failure arrives.

sections.presentation: Symptomatic uremia may appear: fatigue, nausea, pruritus, edema, and worsening hypertension. Anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and mineral-bone disease are common and need active management.
sections.typicalTreatments: Nephrology co-management, dietary protein/potassium/phosphate restriction, phosphate binders, ESAs for anemia, and treatment of acidosis. Key stage-specific step: create dialysis access (AV fistula) and begin transplant workup ahead of need.
sections.riskFactors: Progression of diabetic or hypertensive nephropathy, glomerular disease, and repeated nephrotoxic or ischemic insults.

concepts.name: Clindamycin
concepts.shortExplanation: A lincosamide antibiotic used for skin and soft-tissue infections (including some MRSA), dental and anaerobic infections, and as a penicillin alternative in allergy.

sections.mechanism: Binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; it has good activity against gram-positive and anaerobic organisms.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and a metallic taste.
sections.adverseEffects: One of the antibiotics most strongly associated with Clostridioides difficile colitis; esophageal irritation and rare severe skin reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Have patients take oral doses with a full glass of water and remain upright to prevent esophageal irritation. Monitor for and teach patients to report new or persistent diarrhea, which may signal C. difficile. Complete the full course.

concepts.name: Clonazepam
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting benzodiazepine used for panic disorder and certain seizure disorders.

sections.mechanism: Enhances GABA activity at the GABA-A receptor, raising the seizure threshold and producing anxiolytic and sedative effects.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, impaired coordination, and depression.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and oversedation, especially with opioids or alcohol; tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal seizures with abrupt discontinuation.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess sedation, mood, and fall risk. Avoid combining with opioids or alcohol and do not stop abruptly. Teach caution with driving and report worsening depression or suicidal thoughts.

concepts.name: Clopidogrel
concepts.shortExplanation: An antiplatelet often paired with aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy) after a stent or heart attack to keep the coronary arteries from re-clotting.

sections.mechanism: Irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, inhibiting aggregation. A prodrug activated in the liver — effect is reduced in poor CYP2C19 metabolizers.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding, GI upset.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding; rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
sections.nursingImplications: Emphasize adherence after coronary stenting (stopping early risks stent thrombosis); assess for bleeding; note it's usually held several days before surgery per orders.

concepts.name: Clostridioides difficile Infection
concepts.shortExplanation: An antibiotic-associated intestinal infection that causes profuse watery diarrhea and is spread by spores.

sections.presentation: Frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever, and an elevated white blood cell count, typically after recent antibiotic use.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the offending antibiotic when possible and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (metronidazole in select cases), plus fluids. Use contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene, since alcohol gel does not kill the spores. Fecal transplant is used for recurrences.
sections.riskFactors: Recent antibiotics, hospitalization, older age, and proton pump inhibitor use.

concepts.name: Codeine-Acetaminophen
concepts.shortExplanation: A combination oral analgesic pairing the opioid codeine with acetaminophen for mild to moderate pain.

sections.mechanism: Codeine is metabolized to morphine and acts on mu-opioid receptors to reduce pain; acetaminophen adds non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, drowsiness, nausea, dizziness, and lightheadedness.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, sedation, and dependence; ultra-rapid metabolizers can develop dangerously high morphine levels, and acetaminophen overdose causes hepatotoxicity. Contraindicated in children after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor pain, respiratory rate, and sedation. Track total daily acetaminophen. Anticipate constipation and manage bowels. Avoid in young children and breastfeeding mothers because of variable metabolism. Keep naloxone available.

concepts.name: Colonoscopy
concepts.shortExplanation: A procedure using a flexible scope to examine the lining of the colon. Used to screen for colorectal cancer, remove polyps, and investigate bleeding or bowel changes.

sections.targetConcern: Screens for and prevents colorectal cancer through polyp removal, and evaluates rectal bleeding, chronic diarrhea, iron-deficiency anemia, and inflammatory bowel disease; biopsies can be taken.
sections.whatToMonitor: After the procedure, monitor vital signs and level of consciousness as sedation wears off. Passing gas is expected. Watch for warning signs of perforation or bleeding: severe or persistent abdominal pain, distension, fever, or significant rectal bleeding. Confirm the patient has a ride home after sedation.

concepts.name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)
concepts.shortExplanation: Pneumonia acquired outside a hospital, most often from Streptococcus pneumoniae or atypical organisms. It is distinguished from hospital-acquired pneumonia mainly by its lower risk of drug-resistant pathogens and its narrower empiric antibiotic coverage.

sections.presentation: Fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and tachypnea; older adults may present atypically with confusion or malaise. Focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds on exam and a lobar or patchy infiltrate on chest imaging. Severity and disposition are guided by tools such as CURB-65.
sections.typicalTreatments: Empiric antibiotics chosen by setting and comorbidities. Healthy outpatients: amoxicillin, doxycycline, or a macrolide. Outpatients with comorbidities or hospitalized (non-ICU) patients: a beta-lactam (e.g., ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (e.g., levofloxacin). Add supportive oxygen, fluids, and antipyretics; de-escalate based on cultures. Standard (not resistant-pathogen) coverage is usually sufficient.
sections.riskFactors: Age over 65, smoking, COPD or asthma, chronic heart/liver/kidney disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, and aspiration risk.

concepts.name: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
concepts.shortExplanation: A common panel measuring the red cells, white cells, and platelets to screen for infection, anemia, and bleeding risk.

sections.normalRange: Includes white blood cells (about 4.5-11 x10^9/L), hemoglobin (about 12-16 g/dL in women and 13.5-17.5 in men), hematocrit, and platelets (about 150-400 x10^9/L).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high white count suggests infection or inflammation and a low count suggests marrow suppression; low hemoglobin and hematocrit indicate anemia or blood loss; low platelets raise bleeding risk.

concepts.name: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy
concepts.shortExplanation: A slow, continuous form of dialysis used in critically ill patients who cannot tolerate the rapid fluid shifts of standard hemodialysis.

sections.targetConcern: Removing fluid, waste, and correcting electrolyte and acid-base imbalances gradually in hemodynamically unstable patients with acute kidney injury, severe fluid overload, or dangerous electrolyte disturbances.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hourly fluid balance and hemodynamics, the dialysis circuit for clotting and pressure alarms, anticoagulation status, and electrolytes (especially potassium, calcium, and phosphorus). Monitor for hypothermia, hypotension, and access-site integrity.

concepts.name: COPD Exacerbation
concepts.shortExplanation: Acute worsening of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease symptoms — increased shortness of breath, cough, and sputum production, often triggered by infection.

sections.presentation: Increased dyspnea, wheezing, increased sputum production or change in sputum color, use of accessory muscles, low oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bronchodilators (albuterol), corticosteroids, supplemental oxygen, antibiotics if infection is suspected, possibly BiPAP or intubation in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking history, respiratory infection, air pollution exposure, poor medication adherence.

concepts.name: Coronary Arteries
concepts.shortExplanation: The vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen-rich blood — the ones that get blocked in a heart attack.

sections.purpose: Deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium. The left main branches into the LAD (anterior wall) and circumflex (lateral wall); the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes.
sections.careConsiderations: ECG lead groupings map to territories (inferior II/III/aVF ≈ RCA; anterior V1–V4 ≈ LAD; lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 ≈ circumflex), which helps localize an infarct; RCA involvement often causes bradycardia and heart block.

concepts.name: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft
concepts.shortExplanation: Open-heart surgery that reroutes blood around blocked coronary arteries using a healthy vessel taken from elsewhere in the body — restoring blood supply to heart muscle beyond the blockage.

sections.targetConcern: Severe multi-vessel or left main coronary disease that isn't well suited to stenting, often with angina or reduced heart function.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hemodynamics and cardiac rhythm (arrhythmias are common postoperatively), chest tube output, sternal incision and graft harvest sites for bleeding/infection, respiratory status and pain control, neuro status after bypass.

concepts.name: Cortisol
concepts.shortExplanation: The body's main stress hormone, made by the adrenal glands. Blood levels are measured to evaluate adrenal and pituitary disorders.

sections.normalRange: Levels follow a daily rhythm, highest in the early morning and lowest at night, so timing matters. Reference ranges vary by lab and by the time of the draw; dynamic tests (such as ACTH stimulation) are often needed for diagnosis.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low cortisol suggests adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) or pituitary failure and can indicate risk of adrenal crisis. High cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome (from tumors or steroid medication) or acute stress. Because of the daily rhythm and stress effects, single random values are interpreted cautiously and often confirmed with stimulation or suppression testing.

concepts.name: COVID-19
concepts.shortExplanation: A respiratory and multisystem illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Severity ranges from mild cold-like symptoms to severe pneumonia and respiratory failure.

sections.presentation: Fever, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, sore throat, congestion, loss of taste or smell, body aches, and GI symptoms. Severe disease brings hypoxemia, ARDS, thromboembolism, and multiorgan involvement.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care and oxygen; antivirals and immunomodulators (such as corticosteroids for those needing oxygen) per current guidance; anticoagulation as indicated; prone positioning and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemia; standard, contact, and airborne precautions per facility policy; vaccination for prevention.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular and chronic lung disease, immunocompromise, pregnancy, and being unvaccinated.

concepts.name: COWS
concepts.shortExplanation: A clinician-rated scale for the severity of opioid withdrawal, used especially to time buprenorphine induction.

sections.purpose: Grades the severity of opioid withdrawal to guide treatment and, importantly, to time the start of buprenorphine so it is given once enough withdrawal is present.
sections.steps: 11 items including resting pulse, sweating, restlessness, pupil size, bone/joint aches, GI upset, tremor, yawning, anxiety/irritability, gooseflesh skin, and runny nose/tearing; total roughly 0-48.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Common bands: 5-12 mild, 13-24 moderate, 25-36 moderately severe, and over 36 severe withdrawal. Higher scores support the need for treatment; buprenorphine induction is typically started once moderate withdrawal is present.

concepts.name: CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure)
concepts.shortExplanation: A noninvasive device that delivers one constant level of positive airway pressure to keep the airways and alveoli open.

sections.purpose: Maintains a single continuous pressure throughout the breathing cycle, splinting open the upper airway and alveoli. Used chiefly for obstructive sleep apnea and to improve oxygenation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure a good mask seal without excessive tightness; watch for pressure injury on the nose bridge and facial skin. Monitor for gastric distension, aspiration risk, and claustrophobia. The patient must be able to protect their own airway and breathe spontaneously.

concepts.name: Creatine Kinase (CK)
concepts.shortExplanation: An enzyme released when muscle is damaged; a marker of muscle injury including rhabdomyolysis.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 30-200 U/L (varies by sex, race, and muscle mass).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Very high CK indicates muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) from crush injury, prolonged immobility, seizures, intense exertion, or statins, and threatens the kidneys. Milder elevations occur after IM injections or strenuous activity. Trend CK and protect kidneys with fluids when it is markedly high.

concepts.name: Creatinine
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood waste product filtered by the kidneys; it is the main marker used to track kidney function.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.6-1.2 mg/dL, varying with muscle mass, sex, and age.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rising creatinine indicates worsening kidney function and is used to estimate the GFR for staging kidney disease. Low values usually reflect low muscle mass.

concepts.name: Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool
concepts.shortExplanation: A behavioral pain scale for critically ill adults who cannot self-report, including patients on a ventilator.

sections.purpose: Assesses pain through observable behavior in ICU adults who cannot communicate, including intubated patients, so analgesia can be guided appropriately.
sections.steps: Four items - facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and compliance with the ventilator (or vocalization if extubated) - each scored 0-2, for a total of 0-8. Observe at rest and during a procedure such as turning.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher scores indicate more pain-related behavior; a score above 2 (some guidelines use 3 or more) suggests significant pain and the need for intervention.

concepts.name: Crohn Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract, from mouth to anus, in patchy full-thickness segments. Marked by flares and remissions.

sections.presentation: Crampy abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant), chronic diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Perianal disease (fistulas, abscesses) is common. Complications include strictures, obstruction, and fistulas. Skip lesions and transmural inflammation distinguish it from ulcerative colitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating therapy: corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators, and biologics (anti-TNF and others). Nutritional support, smoking cessation, and surgery for complications. Monitor for malnutrition and vitamin deficiencies.
sections.riskFactors: Family history, smoking, and age (often diagnosed in adolescence or young adulthood).

concepts.name: Croup
concepts.shortExplanation: A viral infection that swells the upper airway in young children, producing a distinctive barking cough and noisy breathing.

sections.presentation: A seal-like barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night and preceded by cold symptoms. Retractions and stridor at rest signal more severe airway narrowing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone reduce airway swelling in most cases, and nebulized racemic epinephrine is added for moderate to severe stridor. Keep the child calm, since agitation worsens obstruction, and provide humidified air and oxygen as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 3 years, fall and winter viral season, and prior episodes of croup.

concepts.name: Cushing Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A disorder caused by prolonged exposure to high cortisol, most often from long-term steroid medication. Causes weight gain and characteristic body changes.

sections.presentation: Central (truncal) obesity with thin arms and legs, a rounded face, a fatty hump between the shoulders, purple stretch marks, easy bruising, thin skin, muscle weakness, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and mood changes.
sections.typicalTreatments: For exogenous cases, gradually taper the steroid when possible. For endogenous causes, treat the source: surgery to remove a pituitary or adrenal tumor, and medications that lower cortisol. Monitor and manage hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and infection risk.
sections.riskFactors: Long-term glucocorticoid therapy (most common), pituitary tumors (Cushing disease), adrenal tumors, and ectopic ACTH-producing tumors.

concepts.name: Cyclobenzaprine
concepts.shortExplanation: A skeletal muscle relaxant used short term for muscle spasm from acute musculoskeletal conditions.

sections.mechanism: Acts centrally in the brainstem to reduce tonic motor activity, relieving muscle spasm; it is structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Anticholinergic effects, serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, and additive sedation with CNS depressants; caution in the elderly and in heart disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Recommend short-term use, typically two to three weeks. Assess sedation and fall risk and advise caution with driving and alcohol. Avoid with MAO inhibitors and use cautiously with other serotonergic agents.

concepts.name: D-dimer
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood marker of clot breakdown used mainly to help rule out venous clots when suspicion is low.

sections.normalRange: Typically negative below about 500 ng/mL FEU (assay dependent; some labs use age-adjusted cutoffs).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A negative D-dimer in a low-risk patient helps rule out DVT or PE. An elevated D-dimer is nonspecific - it rises with clots but also with infection, surgery, trauma, pregnancy, and advanced age - so a positive result usually prompts imaging rather than confirming a clot.

concepts.name: Dabigatran
concepts.shortExplanation: A direct oral anticoagulant (direct thrombin inhibitor) used to prevent stroke in atrial fibrillation and to treat venous thromboembolism.

sections.mechanism: Directly and reversibly inhibits thrombin (factor IIa), preventing conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin and blocking clot formation.
sections.sideEffects: Dyspepsia and gastritis-like stomach upset, and bruising.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding including gastrointestinal hemorrhage; bleeding risk rises with renal impairment because the drug is largely cleared by the kidneys.
sections.nursingImplications: Instruct patients to swallow capsules whole and keep them in the original bottle because they degrade with moisture. Do not stop abruptly. Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for life-threatening bleeding. Assess renal function.

concepts.name: Dantrolene
concepts.shortExplanation: A skeletal muscle relaxant that is the specific antidote for malignant hyperthermia. It stops the runaway muscle metabolism that drives the crisis.

sections.mechanism: Blocks the ryanodine receptor in skeletal muscle, reducing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum so muscle contraction and the hypermetabolic state subside.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle weakness, drowsiness, dizziness, and phlebitis at the IV site.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory muscle weakness, hepatotoxicity with prolonged oral use, and tissue injury if it extravasates.
sections.nursingImplications: In an MH crisis, reconstitute and give rapidly; older formulations require vigorous shaking with many vials, while the concentrated formulation reconstitutes faster. Monitor muscle strength, respiratory status, temperature, and IV site, and continue dosing until the crisis resolves.

concepts.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, that can break loose and travel to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

sections.presentation: Unilateral leg swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness, most often in the calf; some clots are asymptomatic.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin or LMWH transitioning to oral agents) and leg elevation. Do not massage the affected limb, which could dislodge the clot.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, cancer, hormone therapy, prior clots, and obesity - reflecting the Virchow triad of stasis, hypercoagulability, and vessel injury.

concepts.name: Defibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: An unsynchronized electrical shock delivered to a pulseless, chaotic rhythm (VF or pulseless VT) to stop it and give the heart a chance to restart a normal rhythm.

sections.targetConcern: Ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia — a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation.
sections.whatToMonitor: Rhythm and pulse immediately after each shock, quality of CPR between shocks, airway and oxygenation, skin at pad sites.

concepts.name: Defibrillator
concepts.shortExplanation: The device that delivers a shock to the heart — used unsynchronized to defibrillate arrest rhythms, or synchronized to cardiovert unstable ones; many also pace.

sections.purpose: Deliver a controlled electrical shock to terminate life-threatening arrhythmias (defibrillation for VF/pulseless VT; synchronized cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias) and provide transcutaneous pacing.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure pads have good skin contact and clear everyone before discharge ("I'm clear, you're clear"); select sync mode for cardioversion but not for defibrillation; keep it charged and checked each shift; remove medication patches and avoid pad placement over an implanted device.

concepts.name: Delirium
concepts.shortExplanation: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying medical problem. It is usually reversible when the cause is treated.

sections.presentation: Acute onset with fluctuating course, inattention, disorganized thinking, altered level of consciousness. Hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (drowsy, withdrawn), or mixed forms. Often worse at night (sundowning). Screen with tools such as CAM-ICU.
sections.typicalTreatments: Identify and treat the underlying cause (infection, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, medications, pain, urinary retention); nonpharmacologic measures first (reorientation, sleep-wake regulation, early mobility, glasses and hearing aids, minimizing lines and restraints); reserve low-dose antipsychotics for severe agitation.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, dementia, severe illness, surgery, infection, polypharmacy and sedatives, dehydration, sensory impairment, ICU stay, sleep disruption.

concepts.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
concepts.shortExplanation: A synthetic form of antidiuretic hormone used to treat central diabetes insipidus and certain bleeding disorders, and bedwetting.

sections.mechanism: A synthetic analog of vasopressin (ADH) that acts on kidney receptors to increase water reabsorption, concentrating urine; it also raises certain clotting factors (von Willebrand factor and factor VIII).
sections.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, facial flushing, and nasal irritation with the nasal spray.
sections.adverseEffects: Water retention leading to hyponatremia, which can cause confusion and seizures; overdose risk with excess fluid intake.
sections.nursingImplications: Available by oral, intranasal, subcutaneous, and IV routes. Monitor sodium, fluid balance, daily weights, and urine output. Counsel patients to avoid excessive fluid intake to prevent hyponatremia.

concepts.name: Dexmedetomidine
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV sedative that calms patients while keeping them relatively easy to arouse and without suppressing breathing, often used for light ICU sedation and to ease weaning from the ventilator.

sections.mechanism: Selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow, producing sedation and analgesia with minimal respiratory depression.
sections.sideEffects: Bradycardia, hypotension, and dry mouth are common. A transient rise in blood pressure can occur with rapid loading.
sections.adverseEffects: Marked bradycardia and hypotension; rebound hypertension and agitation can follow abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure closely. Because it does not blunt respiratory drive, it can be continued during ventilator weaning and extubation. Titrate to a sedation goal and taper rather than stopping abruptly after long infusions.

concepts.name: Diabetes Insipidus
concepts.shortExplanation: A disorder of water balance where the kidneys cannot concentrate urine, causing large volumes of dilute urine and intense thirst. Unrelated to blood sugar diabetes.

sections.presentation: Excessive urination (polyuria) with dilute urine, intense thirst, and frequent drinking, and risk of dehydration and hypernatremia if intake cannot keep up. Central DI results from lack of ADH; nephrogenic DI results from kidneys not responding to ADH.
sections.typicalTreatments: Central DI is treated with desmopressin (a synthetic ADH). Nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the cause, low-salt diet, and sometimes thiazide diuretics. Ensure access to water, monitor intake and output, daily weights, and sodium levels.
sections.riskFactors: Head injury, pituitary or hypothalamic surgery or tumors, certain medications (lithium for nephrogenic DI), and kidney disorders.

concepts.name: Diabetes Mellitus
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic disorder of high blood glucose caused by inadequate insulin production, insulin resistance, or both. The parent diagnosis that includes type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes.

sections.presentation: Classic hyperglycemia symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, fatigue, blurred vision, and weight change. Long-standing disease drives microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular (coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral arterial) complications.
sections.typicalTreatments: Glucose self-monitoring, diet and activity, and pharmacologic therapy tailored to type (oral agents such as metformin, injectable GLP-1 agonists, and/or insulin). A1c is trended as the marker of long-term control; treatment goals are individualized.
sections.riskFactors: Family history, obesity, physical inactivity, and older age favor type 2; autoimmune predisposition and genetics favor type 1. History of gestational diabetes raises future risk.

concepts.name: Diabetic Foot Ulcer
concepts.shortExplanation: A wound on the foot of a person with diabetes, driven by nerve damage and poor circulation, that heals slowly and can become infected.

sections.presentation: Often painless (because of neuropathy) ulcers over pressure points such as the sole or toes, frequently with surrounding callus; may show infection or poor healing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Offloading pressure from the wound, debridement, moist dressings, glucose control, treating infection, and assessing blood flow. Watch for underlying bone infection (osteomyelitis).
sections.riskFactors: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, poor glucose control, foot deformity, and prior ulcers.

concepts.name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A serious complication of diabetes where the body produces high levels of blood acids (ketones) due to insufficient insulin — a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment.

sections.presentation: Hyperglycemia, fruity-smelling breath, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations), altered mental status in severe cases.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV fluids, IV insulin infusion, potassium replacement (insulin drives potassium into cells), correction of the underlying trigger (e.g. infection, missed insulin doses).
sections.riskFactors: Missed insulin doses, infection, new-onset type 1 diabetes, physiologic stress (illness, surgery).

concepts.name: Diazepam
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety, muscle spasm, seizures, and alcohol withdrawal.

sections.mechanism: Potentiates GABA at the GABA-A receptor, producing sedation, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation, and anticonvulsant effects.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, fatigue, muscle weakness, ataxia, and dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and oversedation, particularly with opioids or alcohol; dependence and withdrawal, including seizures, with abrupt discontinuation. Its long half-life can cause accumulation in older adults.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor respiratory rate, sedation, and fall risk. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use. Use cautiously in the elderly and in liver disease. Flumazenil can reverse it but may precipitate seizures.

concepts.name: Digoxin
concepts.shortExplanation: Strengthens the heart's contraction and slows the heart rate — used in some heart failure and atrial fibrillation patients. Has a narrow safety margin.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits the Na-K-ATPase pump, increasing intracellular calcium (positive inotropy) and enhancing vagal tone to slow AV conduction. Narrow therapeutic index — levels and potassium matter.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, anorexia, visual changes (yellow-green halos), bradycardia.
sections.adverseEffects: Digoxin toxicity — worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal impairment — causing dangerous arrhythmias; reversed with digoxin immune Fab.
sections.nursingImplications: Check apical pulse for a full minute and hold for bradycardia (commonly <60) per parameters; monitor potassium, magnesium, and renal function; know signs of toxicity.

concepts.name: Digoxin Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood level checked to keep digoxin in its narrow safe range — too high risks toxicity and dangerous arrhythmias.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.5–2.0 ng/mL, with lower targets (about 0.5–0.9) often preferred in heart failure. Drawn at least 6 hours after the dose.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels (worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal impairment) point to toxicity — nausea, visual changes, and arrhythmias. Interpret alongside symptoms and potassium.

concepts.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
concepts.shortExplanation: A disease of the heart muscle in which the left ventricle enlarges and weakens, contracting poorly. It is the most common cause of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and predisposes to arrhythmias and clot formation.

sections.presentation: Signs and symptoms of systolic heart failure: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema, and reduced exercise tolerance. Echocardiogram shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with a low ejection fraction. Patients are prone to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and to mural thrombus/embolism.
sections.typicalTreatments: Guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) and diuretics for congestion. Treat the underlying cause where identifiable (ischemia, alcohol, tachyarrhythmia, myocarditis, peripartum, chemotherapy). ICD for sudden-death prevention in eligible patients; anticoagulation if thrombus or AFib is present.
sections.riskFactors: Ischemic heart disease, chronic alcohol use, viral myocarditis, chemotherapy (anthracyclines), genetic/familial forms, uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia, and peripartum state.

concepts.name: Diltiazem
concepts.shortExplanation: A calcium channel blocker used to slow a fast heart rate (e.g. in atrial fibrillation) and lower blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker — slows AV node conduction (rate control) and relaxes vascular smooth muscle. IV for acute rate control, PO for maintenance.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, peripheral edema, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Symptomatic bradycardia or heart block; worsening heart failure in reduced ejection fraction; hypotension with IV use.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure closely during IV administration; avoid combining with IV beta-blockers (additive AV block); hold per bradycardia/hypotension parameters.

concepts.name: Diphenhydramine
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-generation antihistamine used for allergies, allergic reactions, sleep, and motion sickness.

sections.mechanism: Blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve allergy symptoms and crosses into the brain, producing sedation and antiemetic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and constipation.
sections.adverseEffects: Strong anticholinergic effects causing confusion, delirium, and falls, especially in older adults; paradoxical excitation in children and additive CNS depression with sedatives.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess sedation and fall risk and avoid in older adults when possible because of anticholinergic burden. May be given for allergic reactions or as premedication. Teach caution with driving and combining with alcohol or other sedatives.

concepts.name: Discharge Planning
concepts.shortExplanation: The process of preparing a patient to leave the hospital safely and arranging the care and resources they will need afterward. Good discharge planning reduces complications and avoidable readmissions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Begins early in the hospital stay, ideally at admission, for all patients and is intensified for those with complex needs, limited support, or high readmission risk.
sections.steps: Assess the patient's functional status, home situation, support system, and post-discharge needs; determine the appropriate next level of care (home, home health, or a facility); reconcile medications and arrange prescriptions and equipment; schedule follow-up appointments and any home services; and provide clear, teach-back-verified education on medications, warning signs, and self-care. Confirm transportation and communicate the plan to the patient, family, and receiving providers.

concepts.name: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
concepts.shortExplanation: A life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy in which widespread clotting activation uses up platelets and clotting factors, causing simultaneous microthrombi and bleeding. Distinguished by the paradox of clotting and bleeding together, with low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/aPTT, and high D-dimer.

sections.presentation: Simultaneous bleeding (oozing from IV and line sites, petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, mucosal or GI bleeding) and microvascular thrombosis (organ ischemia, oliguria, altered mentation, limb ischemia). Labs show thrombocytopenia (often the earliest, down-trending finding), prolonged PT and aPTT, low or falling fibrinogen, a markedly elevated D-dimer, and schistocytes on the peripheral smear.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause - this is the cornerstone (for example, sepsis, an obstetric emergency, trauma, or malignancy). In bleeding patients, give supportive blood-product replacement - platelets, fresh frozen plasma (clotting factors), and cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen). Heparin is used in selected thrombosis-predominant or chronic cases. Monitor the coagulation panel and D-dimer closely.
sections.riskFactors: Sepsis (especially gram-negative), major trauma, obstetric complications (placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP), malignancy (especially acute promyelocytic leukemia), severe burns, and transfusion reactions.

concepts.name: Distributive Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: A category of shock caused by widespread blood-vessel dilation (low systemic vascular resistance), so blood pools and fails to perfuse organs despite a normal or high cardiac output. Includes septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock.

sections.presentation: Hypotension with a WARM, flushed periphery early on (vasodilation) and a wide pulse pressure, unlike the cold, clamped-down periphery of hypovolemic or cardiogenic shock. Tachycardia is usual (the exception is neurogenic shock, which causes bradycardia). Low systemic vascular resistance with a normal-to-high cardiac output is the hemodynamic hallmark; ScvO2 is often high because tissues cannot extract oxygen. Progresses to altered mental status, rising lactate, and reduced urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis, IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis, spine stabilization for neurogenic). Restore perfusion with IV isotonic crystalloid fluids, then add vasopressors when fluids alone do not restore mean arterial pressure - norepinephrine is the usual first-line pressor to counter vasodilation. Trend lactate and MAP; target adequate urine output.
sections.riskFactors: Severe infection (sepsis), severe allergic reaction, acute spinal cord injury above T6, and adrenal insufficiency.

concepts.name: Diverticulitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation or infection of small pouches (diverticula) in the colon wall, most often in the sigmoid colon. Causes left lower quadrant pain.

sections.presentation: Left lower quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and change in bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea). Complications include abscess, perforation, obstruction, and fistula.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest and a clear liquid diet advancing as tolerated, antibiotics for complicated or higher-risk cases, and pain control. Abscesses may need drainage; perforation or recurrent disease may need surgery. A high-fiber diet is recommended to prevent recurrence.
sections.riskFactors: Age, low-fiber diet, obesity, smoking, and physical inactivity.

concepts.name: Dobutamine
concepts.shortExplanation: An inotrope that strengthens the heart's pumping — used when a weak heart can't maintain adequate output, as in cardiogenic shock or decompensated heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Primarily a beta-1 agonist — increases contractility and cardiac output with modest effect on systemic vascular resistance (can lower blood pressure via beta-2 vasodilation).
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, palpitations, mild blood pressure changes.
sections.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, increased myocardial oxygen demand and ischemia, hypotension.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring (ideally arterial line); titrate to hemodynamic goals; watch for arrhythmias and ischemic chest pain.

concepts.name: Docusate
concepts.shortExplanation: A stool softener used to prevent constipation and straining, often alongside opioids.

sections.mechanism: An emollient (surfactant) laxative that lets water and fat penetrate stool, softening it so it passes more easily.
sections.sideEffects: Mild abdominal cramping, throat irritation with the liquid form, and diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: Generally well tolerated; limited effectiveness for established constipation, so it works better as prevention than treatment.
sections.nursingImplications: Encourage fluids, fiber, and activity to support bowel function. Commonly paired with opioids or bedrest to prevent constipation. Advise that it may take one to three days to work and is not for rapid relief.

concepts.name: Doxorubicin
concepts.shortExplanation: An anthracycline chemotherapy drug used for many cancers, including breast cancer, lymphoma, and leukemia. It is known for cumulative heart toxicity and for turning the urine red.

sections.mechanism: Intercalates into DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, and generates free radicals, blocking DNA and RNA synthesis in dividing cells.
sections.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, hair loss, mucositis, and harmless red-orange discoloration of urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Dose-related cardiotoxicity that can lead to cardiomyopathy and heart failure, and severe tissue necrosis if it extravasates (it is a potent vesicant).
sections.nursingImplications: Track the lifetime cumulative dose and monitor cardiac function (for example ejection fraction). Give through a reliable, well-placed IV or central line, monitor the site constantly for extravasation, and reassure the patient about red urine. Report any signs of heart failure such as dyspnea or edema.

concepts.name: Doxycycline
concepts.shortExplanation: A tetracycline antibiotic used for respiratory and skin infections, tick-borne illnesses, atypical pathogens, and acne. It is broad-spectrum and generally well tolerated.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; covers many atypical, gram-positive, and gram-negative organisms including tick-borne pathogens and some community MRSA.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset, nausea, photosensitivity (increased sunburn risk), and esophageal irritation.
sections.adverseEffects: Esophagitis or ulceration if not taken properly; tooth discoloration and effects on bone growth in young children and during pregnancy; rare intracranial hypertension; C. difficile infection.
sections.nursingImplications: Take with a full glass of water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes to prevent esophageal irritation; separate from antacids, dairy, iron, and calcium. Advise sun protection. Generally avoided in pregnancy and in children under 8 except for specific indications.

concepts.name: Duloxetine
concepts.shortExplanation: A serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) used for depression, anxiety, and several chronic pain conditions including diabetic neuropathy and fibromyalgia.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, improving mood and modulating pain pathways.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, dry mouth, constipation, drowsiness, and decreased appetite.
sections.adverseEffects: Serotonin syndrome, elevated blood pressure, hepatotoxicity (avoid in significant liver disease or heavy alcohol use), increased bleeding risk, and discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly.
sections.nursingImplications: Instruct patients to swallow capsules whole and not to stop suddenly. Monitor blood pressure, mood, and suicidality early in therapy. Useful for combined depression and neuropathic pain. Review serotonergic drug interactions.

concepts.name: Echocardiogram
concepts.shortExplanation: An ultrasound of the heart that shows how well it pumps, how the valves move, and whether there's fluid around it — a painless bedside or lab test.

sections.targetConcern: Need to assess heart function (ejection fraction), valve disease, wall motion after MI, or a pericardial effusion.
sections.whatToMonitor: For a transthoracic study, no special monitoring; for a transesophageal (TEE) study, airway, sedation level, and gag reflex/NPO status before eating.

concepts.name: Eclampsia
concepts.shortExplanation: The onset of seizures in a woman with preeclampsia, representing a life-threatening obstetric emergency for mother and baby.

sections.presentation: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a pregnant or recently delivered woman with preeclampsia, often preceded by severe headache, visual disturbances, and hyperreflexia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury during the seizure, give magnesium sulfate to control and prevent further seizures, control severe hypertension, and expedite delivery once the mother is stabilized.
sections.riskFactors: Untreated or severe preeclampsia, and the same risk factors as preeclampsia.

concepts.name: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
concepts.shortExplanation: A test that records the brain's electrical activity through scalp electrodes. It is used to diagnose seizures and evaluate altered consciousness.

sections.targetConcern: Detecting abnormal electrical activity to diagnose and classify seizures and epilepsy, evaluate unexplained altered mental status, identify nonconvulsive status epilepticus, and assess brain function; continuous EEG is used in the ICU.
sections.whatToMonitor: Painless and noninvasive. Hair should be clean and free of products; sleep deprivation or photic stimulation may be used to provoke findings. Note any clinical events and their timing during recording. After the study, help remove electrode paste; resume medications per orders.

concepts.name: Embolic (Cardioembolic) Ischemic Stroke
concepts.shortExplanation: An ischemic stroke caused by a clot or debris that travels from elsewhere - most often the heart in atrial fibrillation - and lodges in a cerebral artery. Distinguished by abrupt, maximal-at-onset deficits and by anticoagulation (rather than antiplatelet therapy) for prevention when the source is cardioembolic.

sections.presentation: Sudden, maximal-at-onset focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, arm or leg weakness, aphasia, neglect), often affecting a larger territory with more severe deficits than a lacunar stroke, and sometimes multiple vascular territories. There is frequently a history of atrial fibrillation, recent MI, or valvular disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Acute management follows ischemic stroke care - IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) if within the treatment window, and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Identify the source with echocardiography and telemetry for atrial fibrillation. Secondary prevention uses anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC) when cardioembolic, in contrast to the antiplatelet therapy used for atherothrombotic stroke.
sections.riskFactors: Atrial fibrillation (the leading cause), recent myocardial infarction with left ventricular thrombus, reduced ejection fraction, valvular heart disease, prosthetic heart valves, infective endocarditis, and patent foramen ovale.

concepts.name: Empagliflozin
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral SGLT2 inhibitor that lowers blood glucose and also benefits heart failure and chronic kidney disease.

sections.mechanism: Blocks the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the kidney's proximal tubule, causing glucose and sodium to be excreted in the urine, which lowers glucose and produces a mild diuretic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination, and thirst.
sections.adverseEffects: Volume depletion and hypotension, euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (ketoacidosis with only modestly elevated glucose), and rare serious genital infection (Fournier gangrene).
sections.nursingImplications: Give in the morning. Encourage hydration and teach genital hygiene and UTI symptom awareness. Hold before major surgery per protocol because of DKA risk. Note that urine glucose testing is unreliable on this drug; monitor blood glucose and renal function.

concepts.name: Emphysema
concepts.shortExplanation: A subtype of COPD in which the alveolar walls are destroyed, reducing surface area for gas exchange and causing air trapping and loss of elastic recoil. Classically the 'pink puffer' phenotype.

sections.presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnea with minimal cough or sputum. The classic 'pink puffer': thin, barrel-chested, using pursed-lip breathing and accessory muscles, often adopting a tripod posture, with oxygenation relatively preserved until late. Hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds on exam; hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms on chest imaging. Most real patients show a mix of emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, inhaled long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA/LABA) with inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, and supplemental oxygen for chronic hypoxemia. Advanced disease may warrant lung-volume-reduction procedures or transplant evaluation; consider alpha-1 antitrypsin testing in early-onset or nonsmoking cases.
sections.riskFactors: Cigarette smoking (leading cause), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and long-term air-pollution or occupational exposures.

concepts.name: Encephalitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, most often from a viral infection such as herpes simplex virus. It differs from meningitis by prominent brain dysfunction.

sections.presentation: Fever with altered mental status, confusion, personality or behavior changes, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and decreased level of consciousness. Headache and neck stiffness may overlap with meningitis. HSV encephalitis often affects the temporal lobes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Empiric IV acyclovir started promptly when herpes encephalitis is suspected (do not wait for confirmation); supportive ICU care, seizure control, and management of intracranial pressure; lumbar puncture with CSF PCR to identify the pathogen.
sections.riskFactors: Viral infections (HSV, arboviruses such as West Nile), immunocompromise, mosquito or tick exposure, age extremes, unvaccinated status.

concepts.name: End-Stage Renal Disease (CKD Stage 5)
concepts.shortExplanation: Kidney failure with an eGFR under 15 mL/min/1.73m2, or the patient is on dialysis. Unlike earlier stages, survival now depends on renal replacement therapy (dialysis or transplant) because the kidneys can no longer clear wastes or manage fluid and electrolytes.

sections.presentation: Uremic symptoms (nausea, anorexia, pruritus, encephalopathy, pericarditis), fluid overload and pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and anemia. Life-threatening hyperkalemia and volume overload are the emergent concerns.
sections.typicalTreatments: Hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplant. Ongoing management of anemia (ESAs, iron), bone-mineral disease (phosphate binders), fluid limits, and dialysis access care. Protect the non-dominant arm from BP cuffs and venipuncture in fistula patients.
sections.riskFactors: Progression of diabetes and hypertension (the leading causes), glomerulonephritis, and polycystic kidney disease.

concepts.name: Endotracheal Intubation
concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of a breathing tube into the trachea to secure the airway and allow mechanical ventilation — used in respiratory failure or when a patient can't protect their own airway.

sections.targetConcern: Respiratory failure or inability to protect the airway.
sections.whatToMonitor: Tube placement (breath sounds, capnography, chest x-ray), oxygen saturation, blood pressure during and after the procedure, signs of accidental extubation.

concepts.name: Enoxaparin
concepts.shortExplanation: A low-molecular-weight heparin injected under the skin to prevent and treat blood clots.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits clotting factor Xa, reducing clot formation.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising and irritation at the injection site.
sections.adverseEffects: Bleeding and, less often than with unfractionated heparin, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; it accumulates in kidney impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously (often the abdomen); do not expel the air bubble in the prefilled syringe and do not rub the site. Monitor platelets and for bleeding. Dose is reduced or avoided in severe renal impairment; anti-Xa levels are used when monitoring is needed.

concepts.name: Enteral Feeding Administration
concepts.shortExplanation: Delivering nutrition through a feeding tube, either continuously by pump or as scheduled bolus feeds.

sections.targetConcern: Provides nutrition and hydration to patients who cannot safely eat by mouth but have a working gut, using nasogastric or gastrostomy tubes.
sections.whatToMonitor: Keep the head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees during and after feeds to prevent aspiration. Confirm tube placement, check gastric residuals or tolerance per policy, and watch for distension, nausea, and diarrhea. Flush the tube before and after feeds and medications, and monitor blood glucose, electrolytes, and weight; refeeding syndrome is a risk in malnourished patients.

concepts.name: Enteral Feeding Pump
concepts.shortExplanation: A pump that delivers tube feeding formula at a controlled rate through a feeding tube.

sections.purpose: Delivers enteral nutrition at a set rate (continuous, cyclic, or bolus) through a nasogastric, PEG, or other feeding tube for patients who cannot eat safely by mouth.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep the head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees to reduce aspiration risk. Verify tube placement and check residuals per policy, flush the tube to prevent clogging, and use only enteral (ENFit) connectors so tube feeding can never be connected to an IV line.

concepts.name: Enteral Feeding Tube (Device)
concepts.shortExplanation: A tube placed into the stomach or small intestine to deliver nutrition, fluids, and medication when a patient cannot eat safely.

sections.purpose: Provides a route for enteral nutrition and medications. Short-term options include nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes; long-term options include surgically or endoscopically placed gastrostomy (PEG) and jejunostomy tubes.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm placement before use per policy (initial x-ray for new NG tubes; check external length and markings before each feed). Flush before and after feeds and medications to prevent clogs, give medications in liquid form when possible, and keep the head of bed elevated to reduce aspiration. Assess the insertion or stoma site for skin breakdown.

concepts.name: Epidural Analgesia
concepts.shortExplanation: A regional anesthesia technique in which medication is delivered through a small catheter near the spinal nerves to relieve labor pain.

sections.targetConcern: Provides effective pain relief during labor and delivery while keeping the mother awake, and can be dosed further if a cesarean becomes necessary.
sections.whatToMonitor: Watch for maternal hypotension, which is the most common complication and can reduce placental blood flow, so monitor blood pressure frequently and continue fetal heart rate monitoring. Also assess for urinary retention, degree of motor block and fall risk, itching, fever, and postdural puncture headache. A fluid bolus is often given beforehand to reduce hypotension.

concepts.name: Epilepsy (Seizure Disorder)
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic brain disorder marked by recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain.

sections.presentation: Varies by seizure type: generalized tonic-clonic (loss of consciousness, stiffening then rhythmic jerking, postictal confusion), focal seizures (localized motor, sensory, or behavioral changes), absence spells (brief staring). May include aura, incontinence, tongue biting.
sections.typicalTreatments: Long-term antiseizure medications (e.g. levetiracetam, phenytoin, valproate, lamotrigine); identify and avoid triggers; ketogenic diet or epilepsy surgery for refractory cases. Treat prolonged or repeated seizures as status epilepticus.
sections.riskFactors: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, brain tumor, congenital malformation, family history, alcohol or drug withdrawal, medication nonadherence, sleep deprivation.

concepts.name: Epinephrine
concepts.shortExplanation: A powerful medication that stimulates the heart and blood vessels — a cornerstone drug in cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis.

sections.mechanism: Alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonist — increases heart rate, contractility, and systemic vascular resistance. In cardiac arrest, 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes per ACLS.
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, hypertension.
sections.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, severe hypertension, myocardial ischemia; tissue necrosis with extravasation of concentrated infusions.
sections.nursingImplications: Know the concentration and route — arrest dosing (1 mg of 1:10,000 IV) differs sharply from anaphylaxis dosing (IM); double-check the code-cart dose; monitor rhythm and blood pressure continuously.

concepts.name: Epoetin Alfa
concepts.shortExplanation: A synthetic form of erythropoietin that stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells, used for anemia of chronic kidney disease.

sections.mechanism: An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) that signals the marrow to produce red blood cells.
sections.sideEffects: Elevated blood pressure, injection-site reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsening hypertension, clotting events (stroke, MI, clots), and higher cardiovascular risk if hemoglobin is raised too high or too quickly.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor hemoglobin and blood pressure. Ensure adequate iron stores for the drug to work. Target a conservative hemoglobin rather than a normal level.

concepts.name: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that measures how quickly red blood cells settle, serving as a nonspecific marker of inflammation. It changes more slowly than CRP.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 0 to 15 mm/hr in adult men and 0 to 20 mm/hr in adult women; values rise with age and vary by lab. Often summarized with the Westergren method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: An elevated ESR reflects inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, or certain malignancies but is nonspecific and rises and falls gradually. It is useful for conditions such as osteomyelitis, temporal arteritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica and for monitoring disease activity over time. Interpret together with CRP and the clinical context; very high values warrant further evaluation.

concepts.name: Escitalopram
concepts.shortExplanation: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used for depression and generalized anxiety disorder.

sections.mechanism: Blocks serotonin reuptake at the synapse, increasing serotonin available to nerve cells to improve mood and anxiety over several weeks.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, insomnia or drowsiness, sexual dysfunction, and dry mouth.
sections.adverseEffects: Serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, QT prolongation at higher doses, hyponatremia, increased bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, and possible increased suicidal thoughts early in treatment, especially in younger patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach that full benefit takes several weeks and not to stop abruptly to avoid discontinuation symptoms. Monitor mood and suicidal ideation early on. Review serotonergic and QT-prolonging drugs and monitor sodium in at-risk patients.

concepts.name: Esomeprazole
concepts.shortExplanation: A proton pump inhibitor used for GERD, erosive esophagitis, and ulcer prevention or treatment.
