sections.mechanism: The S-isomer of omeprazole; irreversibly inhibits the gastric proton pump to suppress acid secretion.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and flatulence.
sections.adverseEffects: With prolonged use: low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, increased fracture risk, and C. difficile infection.
sections.nursingImplications: Give at least 30 to 60 minutes before a meal. Delayed-release capsules can be opened and sprinkled on applesauce if needed. Reassess long-term need and monitor magnesium with extended therapy.

concepts.name: Esophageal Varices
concepts.shortExplanation: Swollen, fragile veins in the lower esophagus caused by portal hypertension from cirrhosis. They can rupture and bleed massively.

sections.presentation: Often silent until they bleed. Variceal hemorrhage causes large-volume hematemesis, melena, hypotension, and shock. A history of cirrhosis or portal hypertension is typical.
sections.typicalTreatments: For acute bleeding: resuscitation, octreotide to reduce portal pressure, prophylactic antibiotics, and urgent endoscopic band ligation. Non-selective beta-blockers and banding are used to prevent bleeding. A balloon tamponade tube or TIPS procedure may be needed for uncontrolled hemorrhage.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension; larger varices and advanced liver disease raise bleeding risk.

concepts.name: Essential Hypertension
concepts.shortExplanation: Chronically elevated blood pressure without an identifiable secondary cause; a major modifiable risk factor for stroke, heart disease, and kidney disease.

sections.presentation: Usually asymptomatic ("silent killer") and found on routine measurement. Long-standing disease may cause headache, and end-organ damage shows as retinopathy, LVH, proteinuria, or elevated creatinine.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifestyle changes (low-sodium diet, weight loss, exercise, limiting alcohol) plus antihypertensives: thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (lisinopril, losartan), and calcium channel blockers (amlodipine). Home BP monitoring and adherence are key.
sections.riskFactors: Age, family history, obesity, high sodium intake, physical inactivity, excess alcohol, and Black race.

concepts.name: Famotidine
concepts.shortExplanation: An H2 blocker that reduces stomach acid, used for heartburn, GERD, and ulcers. Available over the counter and by prescription.

sections.mechanism: Blocks histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, dizziness, constipation, or diarrhea; generally well tolerated.
sections.adverseEffects: Confusion (especially in older adults or with kidney impairment). Dose reduction is needed in renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Can be given orally or IV. Less potent than proton pump inhibitors for healing ulcers. Assess renal function and adjust dose accordingly; watch for CNS effects in the elderly.

concepts.name: Febrile Neutropenia
concepts.shortExplanation: A fever in a patient with a very low neutrophil count, treated as an oncologic emergency. Because the immune system is impaired, infection can become life-threatening within hours.

sections.presentation: A single oral temperature at or above roughly 38.3 degrees Celsius, or a sustained temperature around 38 degrees, in a neutropenic patient. Localizing signs of infection may be minimal, and the patient can deteriorate quickly to sepsis and shock.
sections.typicalTreatments: Draw blood cultures and a full workup, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics that cover Pseudomonas without delay, ideally within about an hour. Support hemodynamics, consider growth factors, and adjust antibiotics based on cultures and the clinical course.
sections.riskFactors: Recent chemotherapy (highest risk at the neutrophil nadir), deeper and longer neutropenia, indwelling catheters, mucositis, and older age or comorbidities.

concepts.name: Febrile Seizure
concepts.shortExplanation: A convulsion triggered by fever in a young child, usually brief and harmless, occurring most often between 6 months and 5 years of age.

sections.presentation: A generalized seizure during a febrile illness, typically lasting a few minutes, followed by drowsiness. Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalized, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex ones are prolonged, focal, or recurrent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury, control the fever, and identify and treat the underlying infection. Simple febrile seizures are self-limited and generally do not require antiseizure medication. Reassure and educate caregivers.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 5 years, high or rapidly rising fever, viral infections, and a family history of febrile seizures.

concepts.name: Fentanyl
concepts.shortExplanation: A potent, fast-acting IV opioid used for pain control and sedation in critically ill and post-operative patients and during intubation.

sections.mechanism: Binds mu-opioid receptors to block pain signaling and blunt the stress response. Rapid onset and short duration when given as a single dose, but it accumulates with prolonged infusion.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypotension, constipation, nausea, and pruritus.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and apnea; chest-wall rigidity with rapid high-dose IV push; tolerance and dependence with prolonged infusion.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor respiratory rate, sedation level, and oxygenation. Keep naloxone available for reversal. Pair analgesia with sedation goals (analgesia-first sedation). Anticipate withdrawal and titrate down after long infusions.

concepts.name: Ferritin
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood protein that stores iron; ferritin is the best single marker of the body's iron stores.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 12-300 ng/mL (varies by sex and lab; lower in menstruating women).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low ferritin confirms iron-deficiency anemia. High ferritin can mean iron overload but is also an acute-phase reactant, rising with infection, inflammation, and liver disease, so a normal or high ferritin does not fully exclude iron deficiency in an ill patient.

concepts.name: Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
concepts.shortExplanation: Tracking the baby's heart rate and the mother's contractions during labor to assess how well the fetus is tolerating labor.

sections.targetConcern: Detects signs of fetal hypoxia or distress so the team can intervene before harm occurs, most often using external Doppler and a contraction sensor.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assess baseline rate (normal roughly 110-160 beats per minute), variability, accelerations, and decelerations in relation to contractions. Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency, and variable decelerations suggest cord compression. For nonreassuring patterns, reposition the mother, give IV fluids and oxygen, stop oxytocin, and notify the provider.

concepts.name: Fibrinogen
concepts.shortExplanation: A clotting protein (factor I) that forms the fibrin mesh of a clot; a key value in bleeding and DIC.

sections.normalRange: About 200-400 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low fibrinogen occurs with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), massive hemorrhage, and severe liver disease and increases bleeding risk; it may be replaced with cryoprecipitate. As an acute-phase reactant, fibrinogen also rises with inflammation and pregnancy.

concepts.name: Filgrastim
concepts.shortExplanation: A granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that stimulates the bone marrow to make more neutrophils. It is used to shorten neutropenia and lower infection risk after chemotherapy.

sections.mechanism: A recombinant form of G-CSF that stimulates the production, maturation, and release of neutrophils from the bone marrow.
sections.sideEffects: Bone and muscle pain (often in the back and long bones), low-grade fever, and injection-site reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Splenic enlargement or rare rupture, allergic reactions, and (uncommonly) acute respiratory distress or capillary leak.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by subcutaneous injection or IV, usually starting after chemotherapy and stopped before the next cycle. Monitor blood counts, manage bone pain with analgesics as needed, and report severe left-upper-abdominal or shoulder-tip pain (possible splenic issue) or breathing difficulty. It should not be given close to the time chemotherapy is administered.

concepts.name: First-Degree AV Block
concepts.shortExplanation: A conduction delay through the AV node shown as a consistently prolonged PR interval; usually benign and asymptomatic.

sections.presentation: PR interval greater than 0.20 seconds on ECG with every P wave conducting to a QRS. Patients are typically asymptomatic; found incidentally on telemetry.
sections.typicalTreatments: Usually no treatment needed. Review medications that slow AV conduction (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) and monitor for progression to higher-degree block.
sections.riskFactors: Increased vagal tone, AV-nodal blocking drugs, aging conduction system, ischemia, and electrolyte disturbances.

concepts.name: FLACC Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: An observational pain scale for young children or others who cannot self-report, scoring behaviors like facial expression and crying.

sections.purpose: Estimates pain in preverbal children (about 2 months to 7 years) and other nonverbal patients by observing behavior rather than self-report.
sections.steps: Five behaviors - Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, and Consolability - each scored 0-2 and summed for a total of 0-10.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher scores mean more pain: roughly 1-3 mild discomfort, 4-6 moderate pain, and 7-10 severe pain, prompting comfort measures and analgesia with reassessment.

concepts.name: Fluconazole
concepts.shortExplanation: An antifungal medication used to treat and prevent yeast infections such as candidiasis and cryptococcal meningitis. It is available orally and IV with good absorption.

sections.mechanism: An azole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis (via CYP450-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase), damaging the fungal cell membrane.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and serious skin reactions; many drug interactions as a CYP enzyme inhibitor (e.g. warfarin, certain statins).
sections.nursingImplications: Review for interacting medications and QT-prolonging drugs; monitor liver function with prolonged therapy and INR in patients on warfarin. Adjust dose for renal impairment. Oral and IV doses are largely interchangeable.

concepts.name: Flumazenil
concepts.shortExplanation: The reversal drug for benzodiazepines, used in select cases of oversedation. It is given cautiously because it can trigger seizures.

sections.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor, reversing benzodiazepine sedation and respiratory depression.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, dizziness, agitation, and flushing.
sections.adverseEffects: Seizures, especially in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses with pro-convulsant drugs; resedation when the benzodiazepine outlasts flumazenil.
sections.nursingImplications: Avoid in patients on chronic benzodiazepines or with suspected tricyclic co-ingestion because of seizure risk. Support airway and breathing first. Monitor for resedation because it is short-acting and redosing may be required.

concepts.name: Fluoxetine
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting SSRI used for depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, and bulimia.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits serotonin reuptake, increasing synaptic serotonin; it has an unusually long half-life and active metabolite.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, insomnia, headache, nervousness, and sexual dysfunction.
sections.adverseEffects: Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, QT prolongation, hyponatremia, increased bleeding risk, and possible increased suicidal thoughts early in treatment, especially in younger patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach that effect builds over several weeks; its long half-life self-tapers but also prolongs drug interactions after stopping. Monitor mood and suicidality early. Review serotonergic drugs, including tramadol and MAO inhibitors.

concepts.name: Fluticasone
concepts.shortExplanation: An inhaled corticosteroid for maintenance control of asthma and COPD; also available as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis.

sections.mechanism: Corticosteroid that reduces airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness. Often combined with a long-acting beta-agonist (salmeterol) as a controller.
sections.sideEffects: Oral thrush, hoarseness, throat irritation, and cough; nasal form can cause epistaxis.
sections.adverseEffects: Adrenal suppression and reduced bone density with prolonged high doses; increased pneumonia risk in COPD patients on inhaled steroids.
sections.nursingImplications: Rinse and spit after inhaled doses to prevent thrush. It is a controller, not a rescue inhaler. Reinforce consistent daily use and proper inhaler/spacer technique.

concepts.name: Focal (Partial) Seizure
concepts.shortExplanation: A seizure that begins in one area of a single cerebral hemisphere. Distinguished from generalized seizures by localized symptoms and by whether awareness is retained (focal aware) or impaired (focal impaired awareness), often with automatisms such as lip-smacking.

sections.presentation: Localized motor or sensory symptoms (focal twitching, tingling, unusual smells or tastes), automatisms such as lip-smacking or picking at clothing, and staring. Awareness may be preserved (focal aware, formerly simple partial) or impaired (focal impaired awareness, formerly complex partial). Focal seizures can spread and secondarily generalize into a tonic-clonic seizure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Ensure safety and carefully observe and document the semiology - where symptoms began, how they progressed, and whether awareness was preserved. Antiseizure medications include carbamazepine, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or oxcarbazepine. Give a benzodiazepine if the seizure evolves to prolonged or generalized activity.
sections.riskFactors: Structural brain lesions (prior stroke, tumor, traumatic injury, cortical scarring), mesial temporal sclerosis, CNS infection, congenital malformations, and epilepsy.

concepts.name: Foley Catheter Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of an indwelling urinary catheter to drain the bladder and allow accurate output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Urinary retention, need for precise hourly output monitoring (e.g. in shock or with diuretic therapy), or immobility complicating toileting.
sections.whatToMonitor: Urine color/clarity/amount, signs of catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), skin integrity around the insertion site, bladder distension if the catheter appears blocked.

concepts.name: Free Thyroxine (Free T4)
concepts.shortExplanation: The active, unbound form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine in the blood. Used with TSH to assess thyroid function.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 0.8-1.8 ng/dL in adults (reference ranges vary by laboratory).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low free T4 with a high TSH confirms primary hypothyroidism. A high free T4 with a low TSH confirms hyperthyroidism. Free T4 helps distinguish primary from central thyroid disorders and gauges severity when interpreting an abnormal TSH.

concepts.name: Furosemide
concepts.shortExplanation: Helps the body get rid of extra fluid by making the kidneys release more sodium and water — commonly used when fluid buildup makes it hard to breathe or puts strain on the heart.

sections.mechanism: Loop diuretic — inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle. Watch for hypokalemia, hypotension, and ototoxicity with rapid IV push.
sections.sideEffects: Increased urination, dehydration, low potassium (hypokalemia), dizziness or low blood pressure.
sections.adverseEffects: Hearing changes or ringing in the ears (ototoxicity) with rapid IV push; severe electrolyte imbalance; allergic reaction in patients with sulfa sensitivity.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor potassium and renal function, watch for orthostatic hypotension, track daily weights and I&Os.
sections.commonBrandName: Lasix. Usually given IV push or PO depending on acuity.

concepts.name: Gabapentin
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication for nerve (neuropathic) pain and seizures, often used as part of multimodal pain control.

sections.mechanism: Modulates voltage-gated calcium channels, dampening abnormal nerve signaling.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, drowsiness, unsteadiness, peripheral edema.
sections.adverseEffects: Excess sedation and respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants; accumulates in kidney impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Renally cleared, so the dose is reduced in kidney disease. Monitor sedation, especially with opioids. Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid withdrawal.

concepts.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
concepts.shortExplanation: Chronic backflow of stomach acid into the esophagus, causing heartburn and regurgitation. Long-standing reflux can injure the esophageal lining.

sections.presentation: Heartburn (burning behind the breastbone), acid regurgitation, worse when lying flat or after meals. May cause chronic cough, hoarseness, sore throat, or a sensation of a lump in the throat. Chest pain that can mimic cardiac pain.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifestyle changes (weight loss, elevating the head of the bed, avoiding late meals and trigger foods), acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers, and antacids for breakthrough symptoms. Surgery (fundoplication) for refractory cases.
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, large or fatty meals, and delayed gastric emptying.

concepts.name: Gastrointestinal Bleed
concepts.shortExplanation: Bleeding anywhere along the digestive tract, which can range from slow and hidden to rapid and life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Upper GI bleeds cause vomiting of blood or coffee-ground material and black tarry stools (melena); lower GI bleeds cause bright red blood per rectum. Large bleeds cause fatigue, low blood pressure, and a fast heart rate.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV access and fluids, blood transfusion as needed, proton pump inhibitors, endoscopy to locate and treat the source, and holding anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs.
sections.riskFactors: NSAID or aspirin use, anticoagulation, peptic ulcer disease, liver disease with varices, and H. pylori infection.

concepts.name: Gastrointestinal Tract
concepts.shortExplanation: The digestive tube running from mouth to anus that breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, and eliminates waste.

sections.purpose: Digests food and absorbs nutrients and water. It includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), and large intestine, supported by the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
sections.careConsiderations: GI problems are common on every unit: bleeding, obstruction, ileus, and impaired absorption. Nurses assess bowel sounds, distension, nausea, and stool, verify feeding-tube placement, and monitor for GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis) and the return of bowel function after surgery.

concepts.name: General Anesthesia
concepts.shortExplanation: A medically induced, reversible state of unconsciousness with loss of sensation and reflexes so surgery can be performed. The airway is usually controlled with an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway.

sections.targetConcern: Allows major or painful surgery by producing unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, and muscle relaxation while the anesthesia team supports breathing and hemodynamics.
sections.whatToMonitor: Airway patency and ventilation, oxygen saturation and end-tidal CO2, blood pressure and heart rate, temperature, and level of consciousness on emergence. Watch for airway obstruction, laryngospasm, hypotension, hypothermia, and postoperative nausea after extubation.

concepts.name: Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure
concepts.shortExplanation: A generalized seizure with a tonic (stiffening) phase followed by a clonic (rhythmic jerking) phase and loss of consciousness - the classic 'grand mal' seizure. Distinguished by the whole-body convulsion, possible tongue biting and incontinence, and a postictal period of confusion.

sections.presentation: Sudden loss of consciousness, generalized body stiffening (tonic phase), then rhythmic jerking of all extremities (clonic phase); possible cyanosis, tongue biting, and urinary or fecal incontinence, followed by a postictal period of confusion, drowsiness, and headache.
sections.typicalTreatments: During the event, protect the airway and prevent injury - turn the patient to their side, lower to the floor and pad the area, do NOT restrain or put anything in the mouth, and time the seizure. Give a benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam, or midazolam) if prolonged; escalate to the status epilepticus protocol if it lasts longer than 5 minutes. Maintenance antiseizure medications include valproate, levetiracetam, phenytoin, or carbamazepine.
sections.riskFactors: Known epilepsy, missed antiseizure medication doses, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbances, head trauma, stroke, and sleep deprivation.

concepts.name: Gestational Diabetes
concepts.shortExplanation: Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy, typically screened at 24 to 28 weeks. Unlike pre-existing diabetes, it usually resolves after delivery but raises the mother's future risk of type 2 diabetes and threatens the fetus with macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia.

sections.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and detected by screening (a 50 g glucose challenge followed by a 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test, or a one-step 75 g OGTT) at 24 to 28 weeks.
sections.typicalTreatments: Start with medical nutrition therapy, exercise, and glucose self-monitoring; if targets are not met, insulin is the first-line pharmacologic agent in pregnancy (metformin or glyburide are alternatives). Postpartum glucose screening at 4 to 12 weeks is recommended.
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, older maternal age, prior gestational diabetes or macrosomic infant, family history of diabetes, and polycystic ovary syndrome.

concepts.name: Glasgow Coma Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized scale for grading level of consciousness by testing eye, verbal, and motor responses, used most often after head injury or with any acute change in mental status.

sections.purpose: Quantifies level of consciousness and tracks neurologic status over time, especially in traumatic brain injury, stroke, and other acute neurologic changes.
sections.steps: Three components: Eye opening (1-4), Verbal response (1-5), and Motor response (1-6); summed for a total of 3-15. Record the best response in each category, and note if a component is untestable (e.g. intubated).
sections.abnormalMeaning: 13-15 = mild, 9-12 = moderate, 3-8 = severe injury. A total of 8 or less indicates coma - consider airway protection and urgent intervention. A drop of 2 or more points signals deterioration.

concepts.name: Glipizide
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral sulfonylurea that lowers blood glucose in type 2 diabetes by stimulating insulin release.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates pancreatic beta cells to secrete more insulin by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels; requires functioning beta cells to work.
sections.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, and dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: Prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in older adults, with skipped meals, or in renal impairment; rare allergic skin reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Give about 30 minutes before a meal and ensure the patient eats. Monitor blood glucose and teach hypoglycemia recognition and treatment. Use cautiously in the elderly and in kidney or liver disease.

concepts.name: Glucagon
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone that raises blood sugar, used as rescue treatment for severe hypoglycemia when a person cannot safely swallow.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose, raising blood sugar; also relaxes GI smooth muscle.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Ineffective when liver glycogen is depleted (starvation, alcohol use disorder, adrenal insufficiency); rare hypersensitivity. Can cause rebound low sugar, so oral carbohydrate is needed once the patient can eat.
sections.nursingImplications: Give by IM, subcutaneous, IV, or intranasal route for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose is unavailable. Position the patient on their side because of vomiting risk. Recheck blood glucose and give oral carbohydrate once alert; teach families how to administer the kit.

concepts.name: Glucose
concepts.shortExplanation: Blood sugar level — closely monitored in patients with diabetes, on insulin therapy, or during critical illness.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 70–100 mg/dL fasting; targets differ for hospitalized/critically ill patients and vary by institution protocol.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low (hypoglycemia): shakiness, confusion, risk of loss of consciousness if severe. High (hyperglycemia): can indicate poor diabetes control or acute illness stress response; markedly elevated with ketosis suggests DKA.

concepts.name: Guaifenesin
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral expectorant that thins and loosens airway mucus to make coughs more productive.

sections.mechanism: Increases the water content and reduces the viscosity of respiratory secretions, helping clear mucus from the airways.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and headache; generally well tolerated.
sections.adverseEffects: Uncommon; excessive doses may cause GI upset. Kidney-stone risk with very high chronic doses is rare.
sections.nursingImplications: Encourage increased fluid intake to help thin secretions. It loosens mucus but does not suppress cough; often combined with other cold medicines, so check for duplicate ingredients.

concepts.name: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: An autoimmune disorder in which the body attacks peripheral nerves, causing rapidly progressive, usually ascending muscle weakness. It often follows a recent infection.

sections.presentation: Symmetric ascending weakness starting in the legs, diminished or absent reflexes, paresthesias, and possible progression to respiratory muscle and cranial nerve involvement. Autonomic instability (blood pressure and heart rate swings) can occur.
sections.typicalTreatments: IVIG or plasmapheresis; close monitoring of respiratory function with serial vital capacity and negative inspiratory force; intubation and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure develops; DVT prophylaxis and supportive care; rehabilitation during recovery.
sections.riskFactors: Recent respiratory or GI infection (notably Campylobacter jejuni), recent viral illness, occasionally recent surgery or vaccination.

concepts.name: Haloperidol
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-generation (typical) antipsychotic used for psychosis and severe agitation.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, reducing psychotic symptoms and agitation.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, restlessness (akathisia), and dry mouth.
sections.adverseEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms including acute dystonia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia; QT prolongation; and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but life-threatening reaction.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor for muscle stiffness, abnormal movements, and restlessness, and for signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as high fever and rigidity. Obtain an ECG when high doses or IV use raise QT concerns. Anticholinergic medications can treat acute dystonic reactions.

concepts.name: Heart Chambers
concepts.shortExplanation: The heart's four rooms — two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it — working as a right and left pump in series.

sections.purpose: Move blood through the body. The right atrium and ventricle receive deoxygenated blood and pump it to the lungs; the left atrium and ventricle receive oxygenated blood and pump it to the body — the left ventricle does the hardest work.
sections.careConsiderations: Right-sided failure shows as systemic congestion (JVD, peripheral edema); left-sided failure shows as pulmonary congestion (crackles, dyspnea); the left ventricle's function is summarized by the ejection fraction.

concepts.name: Heart Failure
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump or fill well enough to meet the body's needs, leading to fluid congestion and reduced perfusion. It is classified by ejection fraction (HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF) and by which side of the heart is affected.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and fluid retention (weight gain, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, crackles). Symptoms are graded by NYHA functional class. An acute worsening of these symptoms is called decompensated heart failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Chronic guideline-directed medical therapy tailored to ejection fraction. For reduced EF (HFrEF), the four pillars are an ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Diuretics manage congestion. Daily weights, sodium and fluid restriction, and monitoring of potassium and renal function are core nursing measures. Device therapy (ICD/CRT) in selected patients.
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease and prior MI, hypertension, valvular disease, diabetes, obesity, cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and excess alcohol.

concepts.name: Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFmrEF)
concepts.shortExplanation: An intermediate category of heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 41-49%. Patients often trend toward improvement or decline over time, so ejection fraction should be rechecked and many benefit from HFrEF-style therapy.

sections.presentation: Typical heart failure symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, congestion) with an ejection fraction between 41% and 49% plus evidence of increased filling pressures (elevated natriuretic peptides). Because this range is dynamic, the ejection fraction may move up into the preserved range or down into the reduced range on follow-up imaging.
sections.typicalTreatments: SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended; diuretics for congestion. ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta blockers, and MRAs carry weaker (2b) recommendations and are reasonable, particularly if the ejection fraction is at the lower end. Repeat echocardiography to reclassify over time; treat comorbidities and ischemia aggressively.
sections.riskFactors: Prior heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that has partly recovered, coronary disease, hypertension, and the same shared cardiovascular risk factors as other heart failure types.

concepts.name: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)
concepts.shortExplanation: Diastolic heart failure in which the left ventricle is stiff and fills poorly despite a normal ejection fraction of 50% or greater. Unlike HFrEF, there are fewer mortality-reducing drugs, so treatment focuses on congestion, comorbidities, and SGLT2 inhibitors.

sections.presentation: Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and congestion (edema, crackles, elevated JVP) with a preserved ejection fraction (50% or higher) on echo and evidence of elevated filling pressures (elevated natriuretic peptides, diastolic dysfunction). Often seen in older women with hypertension, obesity, and atrial fibrillation.
sections.typicalTreatments: SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended to reduce hospitalizations; diuretics manage volume overload. Aggressively control the drivers: blood pressure, atrial fibrillation rate/rhythm, obesity, and ischemia. MRAs and ARNI have weaker (adjunctive) recommendations. Rate control matters because a stiff ventricle depends on adequate diastolic filling time. Avoid overdiuresis, which can drop preload and output.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension (especially with left ventricular hypertrophy), older age, female sex, obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease.

concepts.name: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
concepts.shortExplanation: Systolic heart failure in which the left ventricle is weak and cannot contract forcefully, defined by a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less. It is the form with the strongest evidence-based drug therapy (the four pillars of GDMT).

sections.presentation: Signs of low output and congestion: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema, and elevated jugular venous pressure. Echocardiogram shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 40% or less; BNP/NT-proBNP is elevated.
sections.typicalTreatments: Four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy: an ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB, an evidence-based beta blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone), and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Loop diuretics for volume overload. ICD/CRT for eligible patients. Monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function while up-titrating.
sections.riskFactors: Ischemic heart disease and prior MI, longstanding hypertension, dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, and toxins such as alcohol or chemotherapy (e.g., anthracyclines).

concepts.name: HEART Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A chest-pain risk score used in the emergency department to estimate the short-term risk of a major cardiac event.

sections.purpose: Risk-stratifies patients with undifferentiated chest pain in the ED to estimate the short-term risk of major adverse cardiac events and guide disposition. Not for confirmed STEMI or clearly noncardiac pain.
sections.steps: Five components - History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin - each scored 0, 1, or 2; total 0-10.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 0-3 is low risk (often suitable for early discharge with follow-up), 4-6 moderate risk (typically admit/observe), and 7-10 high risk (early aggressive workup). A low score does not fully exclude ACS; use with serial troponins and clinical judgment.

aliases.text: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin

concepts.name: Heart Valves
concepts.shortExplanation: The four one-way valves that keep blood moving in the right direction through the heart — the mitral, tricuspid, aortic, and pulmonic valves.

sections.purpose: Prevent backflow as the heart pumps. The tricuspid and mitral (AV) valves sit between atria and ventricles; the pulmonic and aortic (semilunar) valves guard the outflow to the lungs and body.
sections.careConsiderations: Valves can narrow (stenosis) or leak (regurgitation), each producing a characteristic murmur; severe disease is treated with repair or replacement (surgical or transcatheter, e.g. TAVR); prosthetic valves often require anticoagulation and raise endocarditis risk.

concepts.name: HELLP Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A severe variant of preeclampsia defined by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets that can rapidly threaten the mother's life.

sections.presentation: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, malaise, and headache, often with hypertension. Labs show breakdown of red cells, elevated liver enzymes, and a falling platelet count.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, blood pressure control, correction of coagulation problems, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and prompt delivery.
sections.riskFactors: Preeclampsia, prior HELLP, and multiparity; it can occur even when blood pressure elevation is only mild.

concepts.name: Hemodialysis
concepts.shortExplanation: Filters waste, excess fluid, and electrolytes from the blood using an external machine — used when the kidneys can no longer do this on their own.

sections.targetConcern: Acute kidney injury or end-stage renal disease with dangerous fluid overload, electrolyte imbalance, or uremia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure during treatment (intradialytic hypotension is common), fluid removal amount versus goal, vascular access site (fistula/graft/catheter) patency and infection signs, post-dialysis electrolytes.

concepts.name: Hemoglobin A1c
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that reflects average glucose control over the past two to three months, used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.

sections.normalRange: Below 5.7% is normal, 5.7-6.4% indicates prediabetes, and 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher values reflect poorer average glucose control. A common target for many adults with diabetes is under about 7%, individualized to the patient.

concepts.name: Hemoptysis
concepts.shortExplanation: Coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum from the lower respiratory tract; massive hemoptysis is a life-threatening airway emergency.

sections.presentation: Blood-tinged or frankly bloody sputum, often frothy and bright red. Massive hemoptysis presents with large-volume bleeding, respiratory distress, and risk of asphyxiation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway, position bleeding side down, provide oxygen, and correct coagulopathy. Bronchoscopy, CT angiography, and bronchial artery embolization localize and control bleeding; treat the underlying cause.
sections.riskFactors: Bronchitis, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis and other infections, lung cancer, pulmonary embolism, anticoagulation, and vasculitis.

concepts.name: Hemorrhagic Stroke
concepts.shortExplanation: Bleeding into or around the brain from a ruptured vessel, causing sudden neurologic deficits and dangerous pressure on brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden severe headache (often described as the worst ever), vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, focal weakness or speech changes, seizures, and signs of rising intracranial pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent CT to confirm and locate bleeding, tight blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation, and management of intracranial pressure (hyperosmolar therapy, head-of-bed elevation). Neurosurgical intervention for select cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, anticoagulant use, aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation, older age, and heavy alcohol use.

concepts.name: Heparin
concepts.shortExplanation: An anticoagulant that prevents blood clots from forming or growing larger — used for DVT/PE treatment and prevention.

sections.mechanism: Potentiates antithrombin III, inactivating thrombin and factor Xa. IV (unfractionated) requires continuous infusion with frequent aPTT monitoring; subcutaneous dosing used for prophylaxis.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, bleeding, injection site irritation (subQ).
sections.adverseEffects: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — a serious immune reaction; major bleeding, especially with supratherapeutic aPTT.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor aPTT (IV) or anti-Xa levels, platelet counts (watch for HIT), signs of bleeding. Have protamine sulfate available as reversal agent.

concepts.name: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
concepts.shortExplanation: An immune reaction to heparin (type II HIT) in which antibodies to the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets, causing a paradoxical drop in platelets WITH a high clotting risk. Distinguished by a greater than 50% platelet fall 5-10 days after heparin, and by treatment with a non-heparin anticoagulant - platelet transfusions are avoided.

sections.presentation: A platelet count fall of more than 50% (or a new thrombosis) typically 5-10 days after starting heparin - sooner with recent prior exposure. New venous or arterial clots (DVT, PE, limb ischemia) and skin necrosis at injection sites can occur. The 4Ts score estimates pretest probability; confirm with an anti-PF4 antibody assay and serotonin release assay.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop ALL heparin immediately (including flushes and low-molecular-weight heparin) - but understand this alone is not enough. Start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban (a direct thrombin inhibitor; monitor aPTT) or fondaparinux, later transitioning to a DOAC or warfarin once platelets recover. Avoid platelet transfusions (they may worsen thrombosis), and do not start warfarin until platelets have recovered.
sections.riskFactors: Unfractionated heparin exposure (higher risk than LMWH), longer duration of heparin therapy, surgical or postoperative patients, and prior heparin exposure.

concepts.name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
concepts.shortExplanation: Brain dysfunction from a failing liver's inability to clear toxins such as ammonia. Causes confusion ranging from subtle to coma.

sections.presentation: Confusion, personality changes, sleep reversal, and slurred speech progressing to lethargy and coma. Asterixis (a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands) is characteristic. Often elevated blood ammonia, though levels correlate poorly with severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lactulose to trap and eliminate ammonia through the stool (titrated to 2-3 soft stools daily), rifaximin to reduce ammonia-producing gut bacteria, and identifying precipitants (GI bleeding, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbances, dehydration). Protect the airway if obtunded.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis or acute liver failure, GI bleeding, infection, constipation, dehydration, and sedating medications.

concepts.name: High-Flow Nasal Cannula
concepts.shortExplanation: A system delivering heated, humidified oxygen at high flow rates through wide nasal prongs, providing precise FiO2 and some positive airway pressure.

sections.purpose: Delivers up to 60 L/min of warmed, humidified gas with an adjustable FiO2 up to 100 percent, generating a small amount of PEEP and washing out CO2. Used for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure as an alternative to noninvasive ventilation.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure the water chamber and heated circuit are working so gas is well humidified. Monitor SpO2, work of breathing, and respiratory rate closely; escalate to noninvasive ventilation or intubation if the patient tires. Keep prongs correctly sized and check nares for pressure injury.

concepts.name: HIV / AIDS
concepts.shortExplanation: Human immunodeficiency virus infection progressively weakens the immune system by attacking CD4 T-cells; advanced infection is called AIDS. Treatment allows many to live long, healthy lives.

sections.presentation: Acute infection may cause a flu-like or mononucleosis-like illness. Without treatment, progressive immune decline leads to opportunistic infections and cancers (AIDS-defining illnesses) as the CD4 count falls. Many are asymptomatic for years.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) to suppress the virus and preserve immune function; prophylaxis against opportunistic infections at low CD4 counts; treat coinfections; standard precautions; pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis for prevention. Monitor viral load and CD4 count.
sections.riskFactors: Unprotected sex, sharing injection equipment, exposure to infected blood or body fluids, perinatal transmission, and other sexually transmitted infections.

concepts.name: Home Oxygen Therapy
concepts.shortExplanation: Supplemental oxygen delivered in the home for patients with chronic low blood oxygen, such as those with advanced COPD or heart failure. It is usually supplied by a concentrator or portable tanks.

sections.purpose: Maintains adequate blood oxygen levels to reduce breathlessness, support organ function, and improve activity tolerance and survival in patients with chronic hypoxemia.
sections.careConsiderations: Deliver oxygen at the prescribed flow through nasal cannula or mask; do not change the rate without an order, since some patients rely on a lower drive to breathe. Teach fire safety strictly (no smoking, flames, or heat sources near oxygen, since it strongly supports combustion), secure tubing to prevent falls, provide skin and nasal care to prevent breakdown, humidify at higher flows, and have a backup plan and supplier contact for equipment or power failure.

concepts.name: Hospice Care
concepts.shortExplanation: A model of care focused on comfort and quality of life for people near the end of life who are no longer seeking curative treatment. An interdisciplinary team supports the patient and family, often at home.

sections.triggerCriteria: Generally for patients with a terminal illness and a life expectancy of about six months or less if the disease follows its usual course, who choose comfort-focused care over curative treatment. Eligibility is periodically recertified.
sections.steps: An interdisciplinary team (nurse, physician, aide, social worker, chaplain, and volunteers) manages symptoms such as pain, dyspnea, nausea, and agitation, and supports psychosocial and spiritual needs. Care emphasizes comfort measures, advance care planning, medication and equipment for the home, caregiver teaching and respite, and bereavement support for the family after death.

concepts.name: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)
concepts.shortExplanation: Pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after admission in a non-intubated patient. Unlike community-acquired pneumonia, it requires broad empiric coverage for multidrug-resistant organisms including Pseudomonas and (in at-risk patients) MRSA.

sections.presentation: New or worsening infiltrate on imaging plus clinical signs of infection - fever, leukocytosis, purulent secretions, increased oxygen requirement, or hypotension - beginning at least 48 hours into the hospital stay. Higher likelihood of resistant gram-negative and staphylococcal pathogens than community-acquired pneumonia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Empiric therapy must cover Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas/gram-negatives - e.g., an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam. Add MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) when the patient has resistance risk factors (recent IV antibiotics, high-MRSA unit) or high mortality risk, and add a second antipseudomonal agent for high-risk patients (avoid aminoglycoside monotherapy). Obtain respiratory cultures to de-escalate around 48 hours; typical duration is 7 days.
sections.riskFactors: Hospitalization 48 hours or more, recent IV antibiotics within 90 days, reduced level of consciousness or aspiration, immunosuppression, and prolonged/severe illness.

concepts.name: Hydralazine
concepts.shortExplanation: A direct arterial vasodilator used for hypertension and, combined with a nitrate, for heart failure; an IV form treats hypertensive emergencies.

sections.mechanism: Directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, reducing systemic vascular resistance and afterload.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, flushing, palpitations, reflex tachycardia, and fluid retention.
sections.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia (often paired with a beta-blocker), orthostatic hypotension, and a lupus-like syndrome with long-term high doses.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate closely, especially with IV dosing in hypertensive crisis. Used with isosorbide dinitrate for heart failure in certain patients. Report joint pain, rash, or fever (drug-induced lupus).

concepts.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
concepts.shortExplanation: A thiazide diuretic used as first-line therapy for hypertension and for mild edema.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing sodium and water excretion and lowering blood pressure.
sections.sideEffects: Increased urination, dizziness, and photosensitivity.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia (can trigger gout), hyperglycemia, and dehydration/orthostatic hypotension.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor electrolytes (especially potassium and sodium), blood pressure, and glucose. Give in the morning to avoid nocturia. Encourage potassium-rich foods and sun protection; watch for signs of dehydration.

concepts.name: Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen
concepts.shortExplanation: A combination oral opioid pain reliever pairing hydrocodone with acetaminophen, used for moderate to moderately severe pain.

sections.mechanism: Hydrocodone is an opioid agonist that binds central mu-opioid receptors to reduce pain perception; acetaminophen adds non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, lightheadedness, and euphoria.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, sedation, and dependence with opioid overuse; hepatotoxicity from the acetaminophen component if the daily acetaminophen limit is exceeded.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess pain, respiratory rate, and sedation before and after dosing. Count total daily acetaminophen from all sources to stay under the maximum. Screen bowel function and start a stool softener. Have naloxone available and teach non-opioid measures.

concepts.name: Hydrocortisone
concepts.shortExplanation: A corticosteroid identical to the body's cortisol, used for adrenal insufficiency, shock, inflammation, and stress-dose steroid coverage.

sections.mechanism: A glucocorticoid (with some mineralocorticoid activity) that suppresses inflammation and the immune response and supports vascular tone and glucose metabolism.
sections.sideEffects: Increased appetite, fluid retention, mood changes, insomnia, and elevated blood glucose.
sections.adverseEffects: With prolonged use: hyperglycemia, infection risk, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, GI ulcers, and impaired wound healing. Abrupt withdrawal after chronic use can precipitate adrenal crisis.
sections.nursingImplications: In adrenal (Addisonian) crisis, give IV promptly with fluids. For stress dosing, higher doses cover physiologic stress such as surgery or infection. Monitor blood glucose, blood pressure, electrolytes, and signs of infection; do not stop chronic therapy abruptly.

concepts.name: Hydromorphone
concepts.shortExplanation: A potent opioid for severe pain; because it is stronger than morphine by weight, small dosing errors can cause serious harm.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors; more potent than morphine on a milligram basis.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence.
sections.nursingImplications: A high-alert medication: verify the dose carefully and do not confuse with morphine. Monitor respiratory rate and sedation closely; keep naloxone available; start a bowel regimen.

concepts.name: Hypercalcemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A higher-than-normal blood calcium level that slows nerve and muscle activity. Most often caused by overactive parathyroid glands or cancer.

sections.presentation: Often summarized as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric moans': kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, and confusion or depression. Also increased thirst and urination, muscle weakness, and a shortened QT interval. Severe cases cause lethargy and coma.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV isotonic fluids to restore volume and promote calcium excretion, and bisphosphonates or calcitonin to lower calcium, especially in malignancy. Treat the underlying cause; avoid thiazide diuretics. Monitor cardiac rhythm, fluid status, and calcium trend.
sections.riskFactors: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, prolonged immobilization, excessive vitamin D or calcium intake, and certain medications (thiazides, lithium).

concepts.name: Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure (Type 2)
concepts.shortExplanation: Respiratory failure that is primarily a ventilation problem - the patient cannot clear CO2 (PaCO2 over 45 mmHg with pH under 7.35). Management focuses on assisting ventilation, and oxygen must be given cautiously to avoid worsening CO2 retention.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, drowsiness or confusion (CO2 narcosis), headache, and asterixis. ABG shows elevated PaCO2 with acidosis (pH under 7.35) in acute failure; chronic compensation shows a raised bicarbonate with near-normal pH. Caused by alveolar hypoventilation - COPD exacerbations, neuromuscular disease, chest-wall disorders, and CNS/opioid depression.
sections.typicalTreatments: Support ventilation: BiPAP (noninvasive ventilation) is first-line for acute hypercapnic failure such as a COPD exacerbation and reduces intubation and mortality; escalate to intubation if it fails. Use CONTROLLED oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia and CO2 narcosis. Treat the cause (bronchodilators and steroids for COPD, naloxone for opioid overdose). Reassess ABG within a few hours of starting NIV.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, obesity-hypoventilation and obstructive sleep apnea, neuromuscular disease (e.g., myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre), chest-wall deformity, and sedative or opioid use.

concepts.name: Hyperkalemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A high blood potassium level that can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes and is common in kidney failure.

sections.presentation: Often no symptoms; may cause muscle weakness. Cardiac effects include peaked T waves, a widening QRS, and risk of fatal arrhythmias.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV calcium to stabilize the heart; insulin with glucose and inhaled albuterol to shift potassium into cells; and removal of potassium with diuretics, binders (SPS or patiromer), or dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Kidney disease, potassium-sparing drugs and ACE inhibitors, tissue breakdown, acidosis, and large blood transfusions.

concepts.name: Hyperlipidemia
concepts.shortExplanation: Elevated blood cholesterol and/or triglycerides that promote atherosclerosis, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

sections.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and detected on a lipid panel. Severe cases may show xanthomas, xanthelasma, or corneal arcus; very high triglycerides can trigger pancreatitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Diet (reduce saturated fat), exercise, weight loss, and smoking cessation, plus statins (atorvastatin) as first-line drug therapy; ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, or fibrates when needed. Monitor lipid panel and liver enzymes.
sections.riskFactors: Diet high in saturated/trans fats, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and genetics (familial hypercholesterolemia).

concepts.name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
concepts.shortExplanation: A life-threatening complication of type 2 diabetes with extremely high blood sugar and severe dehydration, but little or no ketoacidosis.

sections.presentation: Very high blood glucose (often above 600 mg/dL), profound dehydration, increased thirst and urination, and altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma. High serum osmolality. Unlike DKA, minimal ketones and little or no acidosis. Often develops over days.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the priority, then insulin infusion to lower glucose gradually, and careful correction of electrolytes (especially potassium). Identify and treat the precipitant (often infection). Monitor glucose, electrolytes, and neurologic status closely.
sections.riskFactors: Type 2 diabetes (often previously undiagnosed), older age, infection or acute illness, poor access to fluids, and missed medications.

concepts.name: Hypertensive Crisis
concepts.shortExplanation: Severely elevated blood pressure. When it starts damaging organs (brain, heart, kidneys) it's an emergency needing carefully controlled lowering.

sections.presentation: Very high BP (often >180/120); emergency if with target-organ signs: headache, vision changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or neuro deficits.
sections.typicalTreatments: Hypertensive emergency: IV agents (e.g. nicardipine, labetalol) with gradual, controlled BP reduction to avoid hypoperfusion; hypertensive urgency: oral agents and close follow-up.
sections.riskFactors: Poorly controlled or untreated hypertension, medication non-adherence, kidney disease, stimulant use.

concepts.name: Hypertensive Emergency
concepts.shortExplanation: Severely elevated blood pressure (usually above 180/120 mmHg) WITH acute target-organ damage such as stroke, MI, pulmonary edema, acute kidney injury, or aortic dissection. It requires immediate IV therapy in a monitored/ICU setting with a controlled, gradual reduction.

sections.presentation: Very high blood pressure plus evidence of acute end-organ injury: neurologic changes (encephalopathy, stroke), chest pain (ACS, aortic dissection), acute pulmonary edema, acute kidney injury, retinal hemorrhages/papilledema, or eclampsia in pregnancy. It is the acute organ damage, not the specific number, that defines an emergency.
sections.typicalTreatments: Admit to ICU/monitored setting for titratable IV antihypertensives (e.g., nicardipine, labetalol, nitroglycerin, or clevidipine) with an arterial line for continuous monitoring. Lower blood pressure in a controlled, gradual way - generally by no more than about 25% in the first hour - to avoid organ hypoperfusion; the target and agent depend on the specific end-organ syndrome (e.g., aortic dissection and acute stroke have distinct goals).
sections.riskFactors: Longstanding or poorly controlled hypertension, medication nonadherence, cocaine or other sympathomimetic use, renal disease, and pregnancy (preeclampsia/eclampsia).

concepts.name: Hypertensive Urgency
concepts.shortExplanation: Severely elevated blood pressure (typically above 180/120 mmHg) WITHOUT acute target-organ damage. Because there is no active organ injury, it is lowered gradually with oral medication over hours to days, not with rapid IV therapy.

sections.presentation: Markedly elevated blood pressure (often systolic over 180 or diastolic over 120 mmHg) with no signs of acute end-organ damage. Patients may be asymptomatic or have mild headache or anxiety, but there is no acute neurologic deficit, chest pain, pulmonary edema, or acute kidney injury. Chronic changes (e.g., stable CKD, LVH) may be present.
sections.typicalTreatments: Gradual blood pressure reduction over 24-48 hours using or restarting oral agents (e.g., resuming home medications, adding an oral agent), with outpatient follow-up. Avoid rapid lowering, which can cause hypoperfusion. Reassess for adherence, pain, or anxiety as reversible contributors. Rest and repeat measurement, since readings often fall without aggressive treatment. IV drugs are NOT indicated - the key distinction from hypertensive emergency.
sections.riskFactors: Poorly controlled or untreated essential hypertension, medication nonadherence, high-sodium diet, and stimulant or NSAID use.

concepts.name: Hyperthyroidism
concepts.shortExplanation: An overactive thyroid producing too much thyroid hormone, speeding up metabolism. Graves disease is the most common cause.

sections.presentation: Weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, and frequent stools. Graves disease can cause a goiter and bulging eyes (exophthalmos). Labs show a low TSH with elevated thyroid hormones.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antithyroid medications (methimazole, or propylthiouracil in specific situations), beta-blockers to control symptoms such as tachycardia and tremor, radioactive iodine ablation, or thyroidectomy. Monitor heart rate and rhythm.
sections.riskFactors: Graves disease (autoimmune), toxic nodular goiter, thyroiditis, excess iodine, and female sex.

concepts.name: Hypertonic Saline
concepts.shortExplanation: Concentrated salt solution (such as 3%) given IV to reduce brain swelling and treat dangerously low sodium.

sections.mechanism: Raises blood osmolality and sodium, drawing water out of swollen brain tissue to lower intracranial pressure; also corrects symptomatic hyponatremia.
sections.sideEffects: Thirst, elevated sodium, and fluid overload.
sections.adverseEffects: Overly rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination; fluid overload and pulmonary edema; phlebitis or tissue injury with peripheral extravasation of higher concentrations.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor serum sodium frequently and correct at a controlled rate to avoid overcorrection. Higher concentrations are usually given through a central line. Watch neuro status, volume status, and the IV site closely.

concepts.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
concepts.shortExplanation: A usually genetic disease in which the heart muscle (especially the septum) becomes abnormally thick, which can obstruct outflow and stiffen the ventricle. It is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, and exertional syncope; some patients are asymptomatic until sudden cardiac arrest. A harsh systolic murmur that increases with maneuvers reducing preload (standing, Valsalva) suggests outflow obstruction. Echo shows asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved or high ejection fraction.
sections.typicalTreatments: Beta blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem/verapamil) to improve filling and reduce obstruction; a myosin inhibitor (mavacamten) in select obstructive cases; septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for refractory obstruction. AVOID preload/afterload reducers such as nitrates, aggressive diuretics, and vasodilators, which can worsen obstruction. Activity restriction and ICD for high sudden-death risk; family screening.
sections.riskFactors: Family history/autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutations; it is the primary consideration in a young athlete with syncope or a family history of sudden cardiac death.

concepts.name: Hypocalcemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A lower-than-normal blood calcium level that increases nerve and muscle excitability, causing cramps, tingling, and, when severe, tetany or seizures.

sections.presentation: Numbness and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, muscle cramps, and hyperactive reflexes. Classic signs are Chvostek sign (facial twitch when tapping the cheek) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff). Severe cases cause tetany, laryngospasm, prolonged QT interval, and seizures.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral or IV calcium replacement depending on severity and symptoms; IV calcium (such as calcium gluconate) for severe or symptomatic cases. Replace vitamin D and correct low magnesium, which can cause refractory hypocalcemia. Use continuous cardiac monitoring during IV calcium.
sections.riskFactors: Hypoparathyroidism (including after thyroid or parathyroid surgery), vitamin D deficiency, low magnesium, kidney disease, and pancreatitis.

concepts.name: Hypoglycemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A low blood glucose level that can quickly cause confusion and, if untreated, loss of consciousness or seizures.

sections.presentation: Shakiness, sweating, palpitations, and hunger, progressing to confusion and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness or seizures. It is typically defined as glucose below about 70 mg/dL.
sections.typicalTreatments: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate (juice or glucose tablets) if the patient is awake and able to swallow; use IV dextrose or IM glucagon if they cannot. Recheck glucose and re-treat as needed (the rule of 15).
sections.riskFactors: Insulin or sulfonylureas, missed meals, kidney disease, alcohol, and tighter glucose targets.

concepts.name: Hypomagnesemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A lower-than-normal blood magnesium level that increases neuromuscular and cardiac excitability. Frequently occurs alongside low potassium and low calcium.

sections.presentation: Muscle cramps, twitching, tremor, weakness, and hyperactive reflexes; severe cases cause seizures and dangerous heart arrhythmias (including torsades de pointes) and a prolonged QT interval. Often accompanies and worsens hypokalemia and hypocalcemia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium replacement, oral for mild deficiency and IV magnesium sulfate for severe or symptomatic cases. Because low magnesium makes potassium and calcium hard to correct, replace magnesium to fix those as well. Use cardiac monitoring with IV replacement and monitor reflexes.
sections.riskFactors: Alcohol use disorder, poor intake or malnutrition, GI losses (diarrhea, malabsorption), diuretics and proton pump inhibitors, and refeeding syndrome.

concepts.name: Hyponatremia
concepts.shortExplanation: A low blood sodium level, the most common electrolyte disorder, which in severe cases causes brain swelling.

sections.presentation: Headache, nausea, confusion, and lethargy; severe or rapid drops can cause seizures and cerebral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Depends on the cause and fluid status - fluid restriction, treating the underlying cause, or careful hypertonic saline for severe symptoms. Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
sections.riskFactors: SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretics, excess water intake, and older age.

concepts.name: Hypothyroidism
concepts.shortExplanation: An underactive thyroid that produces too little thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism. Most often caused by autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.

sections.presentation: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, depression, and slowed thinking. Labs show a high TSH with a low free T4 in primary disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifelong thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, titrated by monitoring TSH. Take on an empty stomach and separate from interfering foods and medications. Symptoms improve gradually over weeks.
sections.riskFactors: Autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, prior thyroid surgery or radioiodine, certain medications (amiodarone, lithium), iodine deficiency, and female sex.

concepts.name: Hypovolemic Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: Shock caused by a large loss of blood or fluid, so there is not enough volume to perfuse the organs.

sections.presentation: Fast, weak pulse, low blood pressure, cool and clammy skin, rapid breathing, thirst, low urine output, and confusion. With hemorrhage there may be obvious or hidden bleeding.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the source of loss (control bleeding), rapid IV fluid or blood product resuscitation, and treat the underlying cause. Massive transfusion protocol for severe hemorrhage. Vasopressors are a temporizing measure, not a substitute for volume.
sections.riskFactors: Trauma, gastrointestinal or surgical bleeding, ruptured aneurysm, severe vomiting or diarrhea, burns, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

concepts.name: Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure (Type 1)
concepts.shortExplanation: Respiratory failure that is primarily an oxygenation problem - low arterial oxygen (PaO2 under 60 mmHg) with a normal or low CO2. Management centers on delivering more oxygen, distinguishing it from the ventilation-focused hypercapnic (Type 2) form.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, restlessness, and cyanosis with low SpO2. ABG shows PaO2 below 60 mmHg with a normal or reduced PaCO2. Driven by V/Q mismatch or shunt from conditions like pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, and ARDS. When already on oxygen, use the PaO2/FiO2 ratio to gauge severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Escalating oxygen to target SpO2 roughly 94-98%: nasal cannula, then high-flow nasal cannula, then CPAP (first-line for cardiogenic pulmonary edema). Treat the underlying cause. Intubation and mechanical ventilation, often with PEEP to recruit alveoli, when oxygenation cannot be maintained noninvasively.
sections.riskFactors: Pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema/heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and aspiration.

concepts.name: Ibuprofen
concepts.shortExplanation: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used for pain, inflammation, and fever.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits COX enzymes, lowering prostaglandins to reduce pain, inflammation, and fever.
sections.sideEffects: Stomach upset, dyspepsia, heartburn.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding and ulcers, kidney injury (especially with dehydration or existing kidney disease), fluid retention and raised blood pressure, and increased cardiovascular risk.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food. Use cautiously or avoid in kidney disease, heart failure, GI bleed risk, and older adults. Monitor renal function and watch for signs of GI bleeding.

concepts.name: ICD Placement
concepts.shortExplanation: Implantation of a device that continuously watches the heart rhythm and delivers a shock automatically if a life-threatening arrhythmia occurs.

sections.targetConcern: High risk of sudden cardiac death — e.g. survived cardiac arrest, reduced ejection fraction, or dangerous ventricular arrhythmias.
sections.whatToMonitor: Implant pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, device function and any delivered shocks, signs of lead dislodgement.

concepts.name: Implanted Port
concepts.shortExplanation: A small device placed under the skin, usually on the chest, connected to a catheter in a large central vein. It gives durable access for chemotherapy, blood draws, and infusions, and is accessed with a special non-coring needle.

sections.purpose: Provides reliable, long-term central venous access for repeated chemotherapy, infusions, transfusions, and blood sampling, sparing peripheral veins and reducing the risk of vesicant extravasation when used correctly.
sections.careConsiderations: Access with a non-coring (Huber) needle using sterile technique, confirm blood return before infusing, and flush per protocol (often with saline and sometimes heparin) to keep it patent. Monitor for infection at the site or bloodstream, occlusion, catheter migration, and (rarely) the needle dislodging from the port during infusion of a vesicant. Teach the patient the signs of infection and how the port is used.

concepts.name: Incentive Spirometer
concepts.shortExplanation: A handheld breathing device that encourages slow, deep breaths to keep the lungs expanded after surgery or during immobility.

sections.purpose: Promotes deep breathing to prevent atelectasis (collapsed air sacs) and reduce the risk of pneumonia after surgery or with limited mobility.
sections.careConsiderations: Teach the patient to inhale slowly and deeply, hold a few seconds, and aim for a target volume, roughly 10 times per hour while awake. Provide it after pain is controlled and have the patient splint incisions with a pillow when coughing.

concepts.name: Increased Intracranial Pressure
concepts.shortExplanation: Dangerously high pressure inside the skull that reduces blood flow to the brain and can cause brain tissue to shift or herniate.

sections.presentation: Headache, vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, and pupil changes. Late signs include the Cushing triad (rising blood pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing) and posturing, which signal impending herniation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Elevate the head of the bed and keep the neck midline, ensure oxygenation and normal carbon dioxide, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), sedation and analgesia, and CSF drainage via an external ventricular drain. Neurosurgery for select causes.
sections.riskFactors: Traumatic brain injury, hemorrhagic stroke, large ischemic stroke, brain tumor, hydrocephalus, and CNS infection.

concepts.name: Indwelling Urinary Catheter (Device)
concepts.shortExplanation: A Foley catheter that stays in the bladder with a small inflated balloon to drain urine continuously.

sections.purpose: Continuously drains the bladder for urinary retention, close monitoring of output in critical illness, perioperative needs, or comfort in select situations. A balloon holds it in place and urine collects in a drainage bag.
sections.careConsiderations: Because it is the leading cause of hospital urinary infections (CAUTI), keep it only as long as truly needed and remove it early. Maintain a closed system, keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor, secure the tubing to prevent traction, and perform routine perineal care. Assess for output, obstruction, and signs of infection.

concepts.name: Infective Endocarditis
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection of the heart's inner lining or valves, usually bacterial — dangerous because clumps of infection can break off and travel through the body.

sections.presentation: Fever, new or changed heart murmur, fatigue; classic embolic/immune signs (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages), positive blood cultures, vegetations on echo.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged IV antibiotics guided by cultures, blood cultures before antibiotics, surgery for valve destruction or persistent infection, monitor for embolic complications.
sections.riskFactors: Prosthetic heart valve, IV drug use, structural heart disease, indwelling lines, prior endocarditis.

concepts.name: Influenza
concepts.shortExplanation: A contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It can cause mild to severe disease and dangerous complications, especially in high-risk groups.

sections.presentation: Abrupt fever, chills, myalgias, headache, fatigue, dry cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Complications include pneumonia (viral or secondary bacterial), worsening of chronic conditions, and respiratory failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care and antipyretics; antiviral medications (such as oseltamivir) are most effective when started early, especially for high-risk or hospitalized patients; droplet precautions; annual vaccination for prevention.
sections.riskFactors: Age extremes, pregnancy, chronic lung, heart, kidney, or metabolic disease, immunocompromise, obesity, and residence in long-term care.

concepts.name: INR
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized measure of how long blood takes to clot — used to monitor and dose warfarin therapy.

sections.normalRange: About 0.8–1.1 without anticoagulation; therapeutic range on warfarin is usually 2.0–3.0 depending on indication.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Too low: inadequate anticoagulation, clot risk. Too high: bleeding risk — may require holding warfarin or reversal with vitamin K.

concepts.name: Insulin
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping cells absorb sugar from the blood — used to manage diabetes and to treat diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

sections.mechanism: Rapid-acting forms (e.g. lispro) peak quickly and are short-lived; long-acting forms (e.g. glargine) give steady basal coverage. IV regular insulin is used in DKA for rapid, titratable effect.
sections.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, injection site reactions, weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypoglycemia (confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness); hypokalemia with IV insulin therapy (drives potassium intracellularly).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood glucose closely, especially with IV infusions; monitor potassium during DKA treatment; know the onset/peak/duration of the specific formulation in use.

concepts.name: Insulin Aspart
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid-acting insulin analog used for mealtime (bolus) coverage and in insulin pumps. Its very fast onset means it is given right at the meal and must be held if the patient is not eating, unlike basal insulins.

sections.mechanism: Rapid-acting human insulin analog. Onset is about 10 to 15 minutes, peak 1 to 3 hours, and duration 3 to 5 hours - closely matching the post-meal glucose rise.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia, which can occur early after the dose; hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Give within about 15 minutes before (or just after) the start of a meal; confirm the meal tray is present and the patient will eat before dosing. It is a clear solution and is commonly used in insulin pumps. Watch for early postprandial hypoglycemia.

concepts.name: Insulin Degludec
concepts.shortExplanation: An ultra-long-acting basal insulin analog with a flat, peakless effect lasting beyond 42 hours. Its very long duration allows flexible once-daily timing but also means residual insulin action persists for days after the last dose.

sections.mechanism: Ultra-long-acting analog that forms soluble multi-hexamer depots in subcutaneous tissue, releasing monomers slowly for a flat, stable effect. Onset is about 1 hour, essentially peakless, with duration beyond 42 hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia (lower nocturnal risk than NPH) and hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously once daily; timing is flexible day to day because of the ultra-long duration. Do NOT mix or give IV. Remember residual action can last up to about 42 hours - keep this in mind when a patient is made NPO for surgery or is switched to a different basal insulin.

concepts.name: Insulin Detemir
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting basal insulin analog that binds albumin to prolong its action. Compared with glargine it has a somewhat shorter and less flat profile, so it is often dosed twice daily, especially in type 1 diabetes.

sections.mechanism: Long-acting insulin analog acylated with a fatty-acid chain that binds albumin, slowing absorption and distribution. Onset is about 1 to 2 hours with a relatively flat, prolonged effect lasting up to about 24 hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain (typically less than NPH).
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia (less nocturnal hypoglycemia than NPH) and hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously once or twice daily at consistent times; it is a clear solution but must NOT be mixed with other insulins. Provides background coverage only - the patient still needs mealtime insulin. Do not give IV.

concepts.name: Insulin Glargine
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting basal insulin that provides steady background glucose control over roughly 24 hours.

sections.mechanism: A recombinant long-acting insulin analog that precipitates after subcutaneous injection and is released slowly, giving a relatively peakless, prolonged glucose-lowering effect.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions, weight gain, and lipohypertrophy with repeated use of the same site.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia and, less commonly, hypokalemia; hypoglycemia risk rises when meals are missed or with other glucose-lowering drugs.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously once daily at the same time and rotate sites. Do not mix in a syringe with other insulins and do not give IV. It provides basal coverage, so it is not for correcting acute high glucose. Monitor blood glucose and teach hypoglycemia recognition.

concepts.name: Insulin Lispro
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid-acting insulin analog given at mealtimes to control the rise in blood glucose after eating.

sections.mechanism: A rapid-acting insulin analog with quick onset and short duration that promotes cellular glucose uptake, covering the glucose load of a meal.
