sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions, weight gain, and lipohypertrophy.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia, which can occur quickly because of the rapid onset, and hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously within about 15 minutes before or just after eating, and ensure food is available. Used for mealtime and correction dosing and in insulin pumps. Monitor blood glucose and act promptly on hypoglycemia. Confirm dose and product carefully given look-alike names.

concepts.name: Intermediate-Acting Insulin (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: NPH insulin - the cloudy, protamine-based class that gives basal-type coverage but with a distinct peak. That peak is what separates it from the peakless long-acting analogs and drives its hypoglycemia timing.

sections.mechanism: Insulin bound to protamine to slow absorption. Onset is about 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, and duration 12 to 18 hours; usually dosed twice daily.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia during the pronounced peak, including nocturnal hypoglycemia with evening dosing; hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Gently roll to resuspend the cloudy suspension before dosing; never give IV. May be mixed with regular insulin (clear before cloudy). Anticipate hypoglycemia around the peak and ensure meals align with dosing.

concepts.name: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump
concepts.shortExplanation: A balloon in the aorta that inflates and deflates with the heartbeat to boost coronary blood flow and ease the heart's workload — used in severe heart failure or cardiogenic shock.

sections.purpose: Provide temporary mechanical circulatory support — inflating in diastole to improve coronary perfusion and deflating in systole to reduce afterload, increasing cardiac output.
sections.careConsiderations: Verify timing to the cardiac cycle (inflation on the dicrotic notch), keep the affected leg straight and monitor distal pulses/perfusion, watch the insertion site for bleeding, monitor platelets and for limb/renal ischemia, and never let the balloon sit idle (clot risk).

concepts.name: Intrinsic (Intrarenal) AKI
concepts.shortExplanation: Acute kidney injury from direct damage to the kidney tissue itself, most often acute tubular necrosis. Unlike prerenal AKI, the damaged tubules can no longer conserve sodium, so FENa is high and the injury does not simply reverse with fluids.

sections.presentation: Rising creatinine with a BUN:creatinine ratio under 20:1, FENa over 2%, urine sodium over 20 mEq/L, and muddy brown granular casts in acute tubular necrosis. May follow prolonged ischemia or a nephrotoxic exposure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Remove the offending cause (nephrotoxins, contrast), maintain euvolemia and renal perfusion, manage electrolytes and acidosis, and provide supportive care while the tubules recover. Dialysis if refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, or volume overload develops.
sections.riskFactors: Ischemia (prolonged prerenal states, sepsis, hypotension), nephrotoxins (vancomycin, aminoglycosides, contrast), rhabdomyolysis, and glomerular or interstitial disease.

concepts.name: Ionized Calcium
concepts.shortExplanation: The free, biologically active fraction of blood calcium; a more accurate measure in critically ill patients than total calcium.

sections.normalRange: About 4.5-5.6 mg/dL (roughly 1.1-1.3 mmol/L).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Not affected by albumin, so it is preferred when albumin is abnormal or during massive transfusion (citrate binds calcium). Low ionized calcium causes tetany, tingling, and QT prolongation; high levels cause lethargy and arrhythmias. Often trended during CRRT and large transfusions.

concepts.name: Ipratropium
concepts.shortExplanation: A short-acting inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator used for COPD and, combined with albuterol, for acute bronchospasm.

sections.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airways, reducing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, cough, throat irritation, and a bitter taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Paradoxical bronchospasm, worsening narrow-angle glaucoma if sprayed in the eyes, and urinary retention. Use caution in glaucoma and prostatic hypertrophy.
sections.nursingImplications: Often given nebulized with albuterol (as DuoNeb). It is a maintenance/adjunct bronchodilator, not a fast rescue like albuterol. Have patient rinse mouth and avoid eye contact with the mist.

concepts.name: Iron Studies
concepts.shortExplanation: A panel (serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, and ferritin) used to classify anemia by iron status.

sections.normalRange: Serum iron about 60-170 mcg/dL; TIBC about 240-450 mcg/dL; transferrin saturation about 20-50%.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Iron deficiency shows low iron, low saturation, and high TIBC with low ferritin. Anemia of chronic disease shows low iron with low or normal TIBC and normal/high ferritin. High iron with high saturation suggests iron overload (hemochromatosis).

concepts.name: Iron-Deficiency Anemia
concepts.shortExplanation: Anemia from inadequate iron for hemoglobin production, the most common anemia worldwide. Its signature lab pattern - low ferritin with a high TIBC - distinguishes it from anemia of chronic disease.

sections.presentation: Fatigue and pallor with a microcytic, hypochromic smear (though early disease may be normocytic). Distinctive findings include koilonychia (spoon nails), atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, and pica/pagophagia (craving ice).
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral iron (take with vitamin C to boost absorption; expect GI upset and dark stools) or IV iron when oral is not tolerated or absorbed. Always investigate the cause, especially GI blood loss in adults.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic blood loss (menstrual or GI), poor dietary intake, malabsorption (celiac disease, gastric surgery), and pregnancy.

concepts.name: Isolation Precautions
concepts.shortExplanation: A tiered set of infection-control practices used to prevent the spread of infectious agents in healthcare, built on standard precautions plus transmission-based precautions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Standard precautions apply to all patients at all times. Transmission-based precautions are added when a patient is known or suspected to be infected or colonized with an organism spread by contact, droplet, or airborne routes (for example MRSA or C. difficile for contact, influenza for droplet, and tuberculosis, measles, or varicella for airborne).
sections.steps: Standard precautions: hand hygiene, gloves and other PPE based on anticipated exposure, safe injection practices, and respiratory hygiene. Contact: gown and gloves; dedicated or disinfected equipment; note that C. difficile and other spores require soap-and-water handwashing. Droplet: surgical mask within about 6 feet and a private room when possible. Airborne: an N95 or higher respirator and a negative-pressure (airborne infection isolation) room with the door closed. Educate patients and visitors, and don and doff PPE correctly to avoid self-contamination.

concepts.name: Isosorbide (Mononitrate / Dinitrate)
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral long-acting nitrate used to prevent angina and, combined with hydralazine, to treat heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Converted to nitric oxide, which relaxes vascular smooth muscle and dilates veins (and arteries), reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, flushing, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Significant hypotension, especially with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil), which is contraindicated. Continuous use causes nitrate tolerance.
sections.nursingImplications: Provide a daily nitrate-free interval (often overnight) to prevent tolerance. Monitor blood pressure and counsel about headache and rising slowly. This is for prevention, not acute chest pain (use sublingual nitroglycerin for that).

concepts.name: IV Infusion Pump
concepts.shortExplanation: An electronic pump that delivers IV fluids and medications at a precise, programmed rate.

sections.purpose: Delivers a controlled volume of fluid or medication over time, allowing accurate titration of drips such as vasopressors, heparin, and insulin. Smart pumps include drug libraries with dose limits ('guardrails') to catch programming errors.
sections.careConsiderations: Verify the drug, concentration, rate, and channel against the order at the pump. Watch for occlusion, air-in-line, and infiltration alarms and troubleshoot promptly. Trace each line from bag to patient before changing settings, and label lines to avoid mix-ups with multiple infusions.

concepts.name: Kawasaki Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: An acute inflammation of blood vessels in young children that, if untreated, can damage the coronary arteries of the heart.

sections.presentation: Fever lasting five or more days plus features such as bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge, cracked red lips and strawberry tongue, rash, swelling and redness of the hands and feet with later peeling, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Children are typically very irritable.
sections.typicalTreatments: Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and aspirin to reduce inflammation and lower the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Echocardiography is used to monitor the coronary arteries. Prompt treatment within the first days of illness improves outcomes.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 5 years, male sex, and Asian ancestry, though it occurs in all populations.

concepts.name: Ketamine
concepts.shortExplanation: A dissociative anesthetic used for sedation, induction during intubation, procedural sedation, and analgesia, notable for preserving airway reflexes and blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Blocks NMDA receptors to produce a dissociative, trance-like state with analgesia and amnesia. Stimulates the sympathetic system, which tends to support blood pressure and heart rate.
sections.sideEffects: Increased blood pressure and heart rate, increased secretions, nystagmus, and emergence reactions (vivid dreams, hallucinations) on waking.
sections.adverseEffects: Emergence delirium, laryngospasm (especially with copious secretions), and hypertension/tachycardia that may be undesirable in some patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Useful for induction in hypotensive or bronchospastic patients because it supports hemodynamics and bronchodilates. Provide a calm, low-stimulation recovery to limit emergence reactions. Monitor airway, secretions, and blood pressure.

concepts.name: Ketorolac
concepts.shortExplanation: A potent injectable and oral NSAID used short term for moderate to severe acute pain.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis to relieve pain and inflammation without opioid effects.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, dyspepsia, drowsiness, and injection-site pain.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding and ulceration, acute kidney injury, bleeding from platelet inhibition, and fluid retention; risk rises with duration, so combined use is limited to about 5 days.
sections.nursingImplications: Limit to short-term use and avoid in renal impairment, active bleeding, or peptic ulcer disease. Assess renal function and bleeding risk and give with food if oral. Useful as an opioid-sparing analgesic; monitor urine output.

concepts.name: Lactate
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood marker that rises when tissues aren't getting enough oxygen — trended to gauge severity and response to treatment in sepsis and shock.

sections.normalRange: Typically <2 mmol/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated lactate suggests tissue hypoperfusion; a downward trend with treatment suggests improving perfusion, while a persistently high or rising lactate is a poor prognostic sign.

concepts.name: Lactulose
concepts.shortExplanation: A non-absorbable sugar used to treat constipation and, importantly, hepatic encephalopathy by lowering blood ammonia.

sections.mechanism: Fermented by colonic bacteria into acids that acidify the gut, converting ammonia into ammonium that is trapped and excreted; its osmotic effect draws water into the bowel to produce stools.
sections.sideEffects: Bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramping, and a sweet taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Diarrhea with excessive dosing can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalances (hypernatremia, hypokalemia).
sections.nursingImplications: For encephalopathy, titrate to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day and monitor mental status and ammonia trend. Can be given orally, by NG tube, or as a retention enema. Monitor fluids and electrolytes.

concepts.name: Lacunar Stroke
concepts.shortExplanation: A small ischemic stroke deep in the brain from occlusion of a small penetrating artery, strongly linked to chronic hypertension and diabetes. Distinguished by classic lacunar syndromes (e.g., pure motor or pure sensory deficits) and small deep infarcts on imaging without cortical signs.

sections.presentation: A small, deep infarct producing a classic lacunar syndrome - pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory stroke, sensorimotor stroke, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome - typically without cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect, or visual field loss. Symptoms may be subtle.
sections.typicalTreatments: Acute ischemic stroke care as eligible. Secondary prevention focuses on aggressive risk-factor control - blood pressure management, antiplatelet therapy, a statin, glycemic control, and smoking cessation.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic hypertension (the primary driver, via small-vessel hyaline arteriolosclerosis), diabetes mellitus, smoking, older age, and hyperlipidemia.

concepts.name: Left-Sided Heart Failure
concepts.shortExplanation: Heart failure in which the left ventricle fails, causing blood to back up into the lungs. The hallmark is pulmonary congestion - dyspnea, orthopnea, and crackles - and it is the most common cause of right-sided failure.

sections.presentation: Pulmonary congestion dominates: dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bibasilar crackles, cough (sometimes pink frothy sputum in acute pulmonary edema), fatigue, and hypoxia. Distinguish from right-sided failure, which causes systemic (peripheral) congestion rather than pulmonary congestion.
sections.typicalTreatments: Loop diuretics for pulmonary congestion, guideline-directed therapy based on ejection fraction, and oxygen or noninvasive ventilation for acute pulmonary edema. Vasodilators (nitroglycerin) reduce preload/afterload in acute presentations. Daily weights, strict intake/output, sodium and fluid restriction, and monitoring of respiratory status and oxygenation.
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease and prior MI, hypertension, aortic and mitral valve disease, and cardiomyopathy.

concepts.name: Levetiracetam
concepts.shortExplanation: A widely used antiseizure medication for many seizure types, valued for few drug interactions and no required blood level monitoring.

sections.mechanism: Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release and reducing abnormal neuronal firing.
sections.sideEffects: Somnolence, dizziness, headache, weakness, and coordination problems.
sections.adverseEffects: Behavioral and mood changes including irritability, agitation, depression, and rarely suicidal ideation; serious hypersensitivity reactions are rare.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor mood and behavior changes and report them. Available oral and IV; do not stop abruptly to avoid precipitating seizures. Adjust dose in renal impairment. Available IV for status epilepticus.

concepts.name: Levodopa-Carbidopa
concepts.shortExplanation: The mainstay medication for Parkinson disease, replacing the brain's missing dopamine to improve movement. Carbidopa boosts its effect and reduces side effects.

sections.mechanism: Levodopa is a dopamine precursor that crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine; carbidopa blocks peripheral conversion so more levodopa reaches the brain and reduces nausea.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, and involuntary movements (dyskinesias); dark-colored urine or sweat.
sections.adverseEffects: Motor fluctuations and 'wearing off,' hallucinations and confusion, impulse-control problems, and sudden sleep onset; abrupt withdrawal can cause a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.
sections.nursingImplications: Give doses on time to avoid 'off' periods; high-protein meals can reduce absorption. Monitor for orthostatic hypotension and dyskinesias; do not stop abruptly. Effects may take time to optimize.

concepts.name: Levofloxacin
concepts.shortExplanation: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for respiratory and urinary infections when broad coverage is needed.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA enzymes (gyrase/topoisomerase) needed for DNA replication.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: Boxed warnings for tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects; also QT prolongation, blood glucose swings, and C. difficile.
sections.nursingImplications: Separate dosing from antacids, iron, and calcium, which impair absorption. Monitor glucose in patients with diabetes and watch for new tendon or joint pain and confusion.

concepts.name: Levothyroxine
concepts.shortExplanation: A synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) used to replace missing hormone in hypothyroidism. One of the most commonly prescribed medications.

sections.mechanism: A synthetic form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine (T4) that is converted to active T3 in the body, restoring normal metabolic function.
sections.sideEffects: When properly dosed, few. Signs of over-replacement mimic hyperthyroidism: palpitations, tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance, and insomnia.
sections.adverseEffects: Excess dosing can cause arrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation) and, long term, bone loss. Angina can worsen; start low in older adults and those with heart disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Take on an empty stomach, typically 30-60 minutes before breakfast, with water and consistently. Separate from calcium, iron, antacids, and certain other drugs and foods that reduce absorption. Do not switch brands without rechecking TSH; monitor TSH to guide dosing.

concepts.name: Lipid Panel
concepts.shortExplanation: A cholesterol blood test used to estimate cardiovascular risk and guide statin therapy — LDL is the main treatment target.

sections.normalRange: LDL is risk-dependent (often a goal <100 mg/dL, or <70 for high-risk patients); HDL >40–50 mg/dL; triglycerides <150 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High LDL and triglycerides with low HDL raise atherosclerotic risk; used to start or intensify statin therapy after events like ACS.

concepts.name: Lisinopril
concepts.shortExplanation: Relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and take pressure off the heart.

sections.mechanism: ACE inhibitor — blocks conversion of angiotensin I to II.
sections.sideEffects: Dry cough, dizziness, elevated potassium.
sections.adverseEffects: Angioedema (rare but serious), hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury in volume-depleted patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure and potassium; watch for signs of angioedema.

concepts.name: Lithium
concepts.shortExplanation: A mood stabilizer used to treat and prevent episodes of mania in bipolar disorder.

sections.mechanism: Its exact action is not fully understood, but it modulates neurotransmission and intracellular signaling to stabilize mood.
sections.sideEffects: Fine hand tremor, increased thirst and urination, weight gain, nausea, and mild cognitive dulling.
sections.adverseEffects: A narrow therapeutic window means toxicity can occur with small increases in level: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, ataxia, slurred speech, seizures, and coma. Long-term use can cause hypothyroidism and kidney impairment, and it is teratogenic.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor lithium levels along with kidney and thyroid function. Maintain steady salt and fluid intake, since dehydration, low sodium, and certain drugs (NSAIDs, some diuretics, ACE inhibitors) raise levels. Teach patients to recognize early signs of toxicity.

concepts.name: Lithium Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that measures the concentration of lithium to keep it in the effective range and avoid toxicity.

sections.normalRange: Maintenance therapeutic range is generally about 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, drawn as a trough roughly 12 hours after the last dose. Levels above about 1.5 mEq/L are considered toxic.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low levels may mean the dose is inadequate or doses were missed. High levels signal toxicity, with rising severity from tremor and GI upset to confusion, ataxia, seizures, and coma. Dehydration, low sodium, kidney impairment, and drugs such as NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, and ACE inhibitors can raise the level.

concepts.name: Liver Function Tests (AST/ALT/Bilirubin)
concepts.shortExplanation: A group of blood tests that assess liver injury and function, including the enzymes AST and ALT and the pigment bilirubin.

sections.normalRange: Approximate adult ranges (assay-dependent): AST about 10-40 U/L, ALT about 7-56 U/L, and total bilirubin about 0.1-1.2 mg/dL. Albumin and INR reflect the liver's synthetic function.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated AST and ALT indicate liver cell injury (hepatitis, toxins, ischemia); very high levels suggest acute injury. Elevated bilirubin causes jaundice and reflects impaired processing or excretion, bile duct obstruction, or hemolysis. A rising INR and falling albumin indicate impaired liver synthetic function seen in advanced disease.

concepts.name: Long-Acting Insulin (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: The basal analogs (glargine, detemir, degludec) that provide steady background insulin with little or no peak. Their flat profile and long duration distinguish them from NPH and mean they are never mixed and cannot substitute for mealtime insulin.

sections.mechanism: Insulin analogs engineered for slow, prolonged absorption to mimic basal secretion. Effect is relatively flat (peakless) lasting about 24 hours or more (degludec beyond 42 hours), giving a lower and less peaked hypoglycemia profile than NPH.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia (less nocturnal hypoglycemia than NPH) and hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously at consistent times, usually once daily; these are clear solutions but must NOT be mixed with other insulins or given IV. They cover background needs only, so patients still require mealtime insulin. Do not omit basal insulin in type 1 patients even when NPO.

concepts.name: Loop Diuretics (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: The drug class furosemide belongs to — more potent than thiazide diuretics.

sections.mechanism: Act on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle rather than the distal tubule, producing a stronger diuretic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Electrolyte depletion (potassium, magnesium, sodium), dehydration.
sections.adverseEffects: Ototoxicity with rapid IV administration, especially at high doses.

concepts.name: Loperamide
concepts.shortExplanation: An over-the-counter antidiarrheal that slows gut motility to reduce the frequency of loose stools.

sections.mechanism: Acts on opioid receptors in the intestinal wall to slow peristalsis and increase transit time, allowing more water reabsorption; it does not cross into the brain at normal doses.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, abdominal cramping, dizziness, and dry mouth.
sections.adverseEffects: At high (misused) doses it can cause serious cardiac arrhythmias and QT prolongation. It can worsen infectious or inflammatory diarrhea and precipitate toxic megacolon.
sections.nursingImplications: Avoid in bloody diarrhea, high fever, or suspected C. difficile or other invasive infection. Teach patients not to exceed the labeled dose and to seek care if diarrhea persists beyond about 48 hours or worsens.

concepts.name: Loratadine
concepts.shortExplanation: A once-daily second-generation antihistamine for allergic rhinitis and hives that causes little drowsiness.

sections.mechanism: Selectively blocks peripheral histamine H1 receptors with minimal central penetration, relieving allergy symptoms without much sedation.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, dry mouth, and mild drowsiness in some people.
sections.adverseEffects: Generally well tolerated; far fewer anticholinergic and sedative effects than first-generation antihistamines.
sections.nursingImplications: Give once daily and note it can be taken during the day because it is non-sedating for most patients. Teach that it controls symptoms rather than curing allergies. Preferred over diphenhydramine in older adults.

concepts.name: Lorazepam
concepts.shortExplanation: A benzodiazepine used for anxiety, agitation, seizures, and alcohol withdrawal.

sections.mechanism: Enhances the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, producing calming, sedative, and anticonvulsant effects.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, and confusion.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, especially when combined with opioids or alcohol, and physical dependence with tolerance and withdrawal after prolonged use. Paradoxical agitation can occur.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor level of consciousness and respiratory status, particularly with IV use or opioid co-administration. Use fall precautions. Flumazenil can reverse benzodiazepines but is used cautiously because it may precipitate seizures. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.

concepts.name: Losartan
concepts.shortExplanation: An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used for hypertension, heart failure, and kidney protection in diabetes.

sections.mechanism: Blocks angiotensin II receptors, causing vasodilation and reduced aldosterone, which lowers blood pressure and reduces cardiac/renal strain.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, fatigue, and orthostatic hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury (especially with renal artery stenosis or NSAIDs), and angioedema (less common than with ACE inhibitors). Contraindicated in pregnancy.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function. Often used when ACE inhibitors cause cough. Counsel about orthostatic hypotension and avoiding potassium supplements/salt substitutes unless directed.

concepts.name: Lower GI Bleed
concepts.shortExplanation: Bleeding originating below the ligament of Treitz (small bowel, colon, rectum, or anus), classically presenting as hematochezia (bright red or maroon blood per rectum). Distinguished from an upper GI bleed, which more often causes melena and hematemesis and is worked up with upper endoscopy.

sections.presentation: Hematochezia (bright red or maroon blood per rectum), sometimes with clots; usually painless (diverticular disease, angiodysplasia) but may include cramping. Melena is less common than in upper GI bleeds. Signs of hypovolemia (tachycardia, hypotension) appear if bleeding is brisk. A normal or low BUN-to-creatinine ratio helps distinguish it from an upper GI bleed.
sections.typicalTreatments: Assess and resuscitate - two large-bore IVs, fluids, type and crossmatch, transfuse as needed, and correct any coagulopathy. Localize and treat the source with colonoscopy (which may allow endoscopic hemostasis), CT angiography, or a tagged RBC scan. Angiographic embolization or surgery is used for uncontrolled bleeding.
sections.riskFactors: Diverticulosis (the most common cause), angiodysplasia, colorectal cancer or polyps, hemorrhoids, ischemic or inflammatory colitis, anticoagulant, antiplatelet, or NSAID use, and older age.

concepts.name: Lumbar Puncture
concepts.shortExplanation: Needle sampling of cerebrospinal fluid from the lower spine — used to diagnose conditions like meningitis or to relieve elevated pressure around the brain.

sections.targetConcern: Suspected CNS infection (e.g. meningitis) or need to measure/relieve elevated intracranial pressure.
sections.whatToMonitor: Post-procedure headache (positional, from CSF leak), neuro checks, insertion site for bleeding or CSF leakage.

concepts.name: Magnesium
concepts.shortExplanation: An electrolyte essential for stable heart rhythm and muscle function — low levels raise the risk of dangerous arrhythmias.

sections.normalRange: About 1.7–2.2 mg/dL (varies by lab).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low (hypomagnesemia): increases arrhythmia risk (including torsades de pointes) and worsens hypokalemia and digoxin toxicity. High (hypermagnesemia): can cause weakness, hypotension, and bradycardia.

concepts.name: Magnesium Sulfate
concepts.shortExplanation: An electrolyte given IV to prevent seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia, and used in obstetrics for fetal neuroprotection and short-term slowing of preterm labor.

sections.mechanism: Central nervous system depressant and smooth-muscle relaxant that raises the seizure threshold and reduces vascular and uterine tone.
sections.sideEffects: Flushing, warmth, nausea, drowsiness, blurred vision.
sections.adverseEffects: Magnesium toxicity progresses from loss of deep tendon reflexes to respiratory depression, hypotension, and cardiac arrest as levels rise.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, level of consciousness, and urine output during infusion, since magnesium is renally cleared. Loss of reflexes is an early warning of toxicity. Keep calcium gluconate available as the antidote.

concepts.name: Malignant Hyperthermia
concepts.shortExplanation: A rare, inherited, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. It is an anesthesia emergency treated with dantrolene.

sections.presentation: Early signs are an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, and masseter or generalized muscle rigidity. Later signs include a rapidly rising temperature, mixed acidosis, hyperkalemia, dark cola-colored urine from rhabdomyolysis, and unstable vital signs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the triggering agent and call for the MH cart, give IV dantrolene, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, and start active cooling. Treat hyperkalemia and acidosis, support urine output, and monitor for recurrence in the ICU.
sections.riskFactors: Inherited RYR1 or related gene mutation (autosomal dominant), personal or family history of an MH event or of certain muscle disorders, and exposure to volatile anesthetics (such as sevoflurane) or succinylcholine.

concepts.name: Mannitol
concepts.shortExplanation: An osmotic diuretic given IV to reduce elevated intracranial pressure and brain swelling by pulling fluid out of tissue and increasing urine output.

sections.mechanism: An osmotically active sugar that raises blood osmolality, drawing water out of brain tissue and into the bloodstream, then is excreted by the kidneys, producing diuresis.
sections.sideEffects: Large urine output, thirst, and electrolyte shifts.
sections.adverseEffects: Dehydration and hypotension from brisk diuresis, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury; rebound rise in intracranial pressure is possible.
sections.nursingImplications: Administer through an in-line filter because it can crystallize. Monitor serum osmolality (and the osmolar gap), electrolytes, kidney function, and strict intake and output. Watch neuro status and hold or reassess if the patient becomes hypotensive or oliguric.

concepts.name: Mechanical Ventilator
concepts.shortExplanation: A machine that delivers breaths through a breathing tube to support or fully take over a patient's breathing when they cannot breathe adequately on their own.

sections.purpose: Support or replace spontaneous breathing by delivering controlled oxygen and pressure, ensuring adequate oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal in respiratory failure, during sedation and paralysis, or after major surgery.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm tube placement and secure it, monitor settings (mode, tidal volume, rate, FiO2, PEEP) and alarms, and respond promptly to high-pressure or low-pressure alarms. Provide oral care and elevate the head of the bed to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia, manage sedation to a goal, and assess readiness for weaning with spontaneous breathing trials.

concepts.name: Meninges
concepts.shortExplanation: The three protective membranes (dura, arachnoid, and pia mater) that surround the brain and spinal cord.

sections.purpose: Protect and support the brain and spinal cord and contain the cerebrospinal fluid that cushions them. The layers, from outer to inner, are the dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater.
sections.careConsiderations: The meninges are clinically central to lumbar puncture (the needle passes into the subarachnoid space to sample CSF) and to bleeds named by layer (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid). Infection of the meninges is meningitis - watch for fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.

concepts.name: Metformin
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes that lowers blood glucose and does not by itself cause hypoglycemia.

sections.mechanism: Reduces glucose production by the liver and improves the body's sensitivity to insulin.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset, diarrhea, metallic taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare lactic acidosis, especially with kidney impairment, low oxygen states, or after iodinated contrast; vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.
sections.nursingImplications: Often held around iodinated contrast and in acute kidney injury. Assess kidney function and take with food to reduce GI effects.

concepts.name: Methimazole
concepts.shortExplanation: An antithyroid medication that reduces thyroid hormone production. First-line drug therapy for hyperthyroidism and Graves disease.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking synthesis of thyroid hormones.
sections.sideEffects: Rash, itching, joint pain, nausea, and altered taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Agranulocytosis (a dangerous drop in white cells) and hepatotoxicity are the most serious; also rare vasculitis. Associated with birth defects in the first trimester, so propylthiouracil is generally preferred in early pregnancy.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach patients to report fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers promptly (possible agranulocytosis) and signs of liver injury. Monitor CBC and liver tests and thyroid function. Effects on hormone levels take several weeks.

concepts.name: Methylergonovine
concepts.shortExplanation: An ergot medication used after delivery to firm up the uterus and control postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony.

sections.mechanism: Directly stimulates sustained uterine smooth-muscle contraction, clamping down on bleeding vessels at the placental site.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, cramping, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Causes vasoconstriction and can trigger severe hypertension; it is contraindicated in preeclampsia and pre-existing hypertension. Rapid IV administration risks dangerous blood pressure spikes and is avoided.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given intramuscularly for postpartum bleeding. Check blood pressure before and after administration and hold the dose if the patient is hypertensive. Assess uterine tone and lochia for response.

concepts.name: Methylprednisolone
concepts.shortExplanation: A corticosteroid given orally or IV to reduce inflammation in conditions such as asthma or COPD flares, severe allergic reactions, and autoimmune disease.

sections.mechanism: A synthetic glucocorticoid that suppresses inflammation and immune activity by altering gene expression and reducing inflammatory mediators.
sections.sideEffects: Increased appetite, insomnia, mood changes, fluid retention, and elevated blood glucose.
sections.adverseEffects: Hyperglycemia, infection risk, GI bleeding, hypertension, and, with prolonged use, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, and Cushingoid changes; abrupt withdrawal after longer courses can cause adrenal crisis.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood glucose, blood pressure, and signs of infection. Give oral doses with food. Do not stop prolonged therapy abruptly; taper. The IV form (Solu-Medrol) and oral taper pack (Medrol Dosepak) are common; teach not to skip doses.

concepts.name: Metoclopramide
concepts.shortExplanation: A prokinetic and antiemetic that speeds stomach emptying and reduces nausea. Used for gastroparesis, GERD, and nausea/vomiting.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine receptors (antiemetic effect) and enhances the response to acetylcholine in the upper GI tract, increasing gastric motility and emptying.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, restlessness, fatigue, and diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms and acute dystonic reactions, and tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use (carries a boxed warning). Also neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Use limited to short courses.
sections.nursingImplications: Limit therapy duration (generally up to 12 weeks) to reduce tardive dyskinesia risk. Watch for involuntary movements. Use cautiously in Parkinson disease and bowel obstruction; can be given before meals and at bedtime.

concepts.name: Metoprolol
concepts.shortExplanation: Slows and steadies the heartbeat so the heart doesn't have to work as hard.

sections.mechanism: Beta-1 selective blocker — reduces heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand.
sections.sideEffects: Fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, slowed heart rate.
sections.adverseEffects: Symptomatic bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm in susceptible patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Check apical pulse and blood pressure before administration.

concepts.name: Metronidazole
concepts.shortExplanation: An antibiotic that covers anaerobic bacteria and some protozoa, used for abdominal, pelvic, and certain intestinal infections.

sections.mechanism: Enters microbes and damages their DNA, killing anaerobic bacteria and protozoa.
sections.sideEffects: Metallic taste, nausea, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, vomiting) with alcohol.
sections.nursingImplications: Advise avoiding alcohol during treatment and for a few days after. Used for intra-abdominal, anaerobic, and some C. difficile infections.

concepts.name: Midazolam
concepts.shortExplanation: A short-acting IV benzodiazepine used for sedation, anxiety and agitation, seizures, and as part of intubation.

sections.mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation, anxiolysis, amnesia, and anticonvulsant effects.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, and anterograde amnesia.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and apnea, especially when combined with opioids. Prolonged infusions accumulate and can delay awakening; abrupt withdrawal after long use can cause agitation and seizures.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor airway, respiratory rate, and oxygenation. Have flumazenil available as the reversal agent, though it is used cautiously. Combine cautiously with opioids because of additive respiratory depression.

concepts.name: Misoprostol
concepts.shortExplanation: A prostaglandin used in obstetrics to ripen the cervix and induce labor, and to contract the uterus in postpartum hemorrhage.

sections.mechanism: A prostaglandin E1 analog that softens and dilates the cervix and stimulates uterine contractions.
sections.sideEffects: Fever, chills, shivering, nausea, and diarrhea are common.
sections.adverseEffects: Uterine tachysystole with fetal heart rate changes and, rarely, uterine rupture, especially with a prior uterine scar.
sections.nursingImplications: Route and use depend on indication (cervical ripening versus postpartum bleeding). When used for induction, monitor contraction pattern and fetal heart rate closely. Fever and shaking after a postpartum dose are expected side effects rather than infection.

concepts.name: Moderate Sedation
concepts.shortExplanation: Drug-induced depression of consciousness in which the patient responds purposefully to voice or light touch and keeps their own airway and breathing. It is used for procedures such as endoscopy, cardioversion, and line placement.

sections.targetConcern: Provides comfort, anxiolysis, and analgesia for shorter procedures without the airway support and full unconsciousness of general anesthesia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Level of responsiveness, respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation, capnography where available, and blood pressure and heart rate. Watch for oversedation and airway obstruction; have oxygen, suction, and reversal agents (naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines) immediately available.

concepts.name: Montelukast
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral leukotriene receptor antagonist used for maintenance control of asthma and allergic rhinitis, and to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm.

sections.mechanism: Blocks leukotriene receptors, reducing airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and mucus.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, abdominal pain, and upper respiratory symptoms.
sections.adverseEffects: Neuropsychiatric effects, including mood changes, agitation, depression, and suicidal thoughts, which prompted an FDA boxed warning. Report new behavioral or mood changes.
sections.nursingImplications: Taken once daily, usually in the evening; it is a controller, not a rescue drug. Counsel patients and families to watch for and report mood or behavior changes.

concepts.name: Morphine
concepts.shortExplanation: A strong opioid used for moderate to severe pain and, at times, for the breathlessness of heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors that reduces pain perception; also dilates veins.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching, urinary retention.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence; risk rises when combined with other CNS depressants.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor respiratory rate, sedation level, and pain; hold and reassess if oversedated. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity. Start a bowel regimen. Use caution in kidney impairment, where active metabolites accumulate.

concepts.name: Morse Fall Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A quick nursing tool that scores a patient's risk of falling to guide fall-prevention measures.

sections.purpose: Estimates a hospitalized patient's risk of falling so appropriate fall-prevention interventions can be put in place.
sections.steps: Six items - history of falling, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, IV/heparin lock, gait, and mental status - each with set point values; total 0-125.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Commonly cited thresholds: 0-24 low, 25-44 moderate, and 45 or higher high risk. Higher scores trigger more aggressive fall precautions, though many facilities use their own cutoffs.

concepts.name: MRSA Infection
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium resistant to many common antibiotics. It ranges from skin infections to life-threatening bloodstream or lung infections.

sections.presentation: Skin and soft-tissue infections (red, swollen, painful areas, abscesses, or 'spider bite'-like lesions) are common; invasive disease can cause bacteremia, pneumonia, endocarditis, bone infection, and sepsis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Drainage of abscesses; antibiotics active against MRSA such as vancomycin or others based on culture and sensitivity; source control; contact precautions to limit spread. De-escalate therapy per culture results.
sections.riskFactors: Recent hospitalization or surgery, indwelling devices and catheters, hemodialysis, crowded settings, injection drug use, prior antibiotic exposure, and skin breakdown.

concepts.name: Mucositis
concepts.shortExplanation: Painful inflammation and ulceration of the mucous membranes lining the mouth and GI tract, caused by chemotherapy or radiation. Oral mucositis can make eating, drinking, and swallowing very difficult.

sections.presentation: Redness, soreness, swelling, and ulcers of the mouth and throat, pain with eating or swallowing, and sometimes bleeding. It can extend along the GI tract, causing diarrhea, and open sores create a route for infection.
sections.typicalTreatments: Frequent gentle oral care with a soft brush and bland rinses, topical and systemic analgesia (including opioids for severe pain), treating superimposed infections such as candidiasis, and supporting nutrition and hydration. Cryotherapy (ice chips) during certain infusions can help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Chemotherapy (especially agents like fluorouracil and methotrexate), head and neck radiation, high-dose therapy and transplant conditioning, neutropenia, and poor baseline oral hygiene.

concepts.name: Multiple Sclerosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic autoimmune disease that damages the myelin covering nerves in the brain and spinal cord, disrupting nerve signaling. It commonly follows a relapsing-remitting course.

sections.presentation: Variable and often relapsing: vision changes (optic neuritis), numbness or tingling, weakness, spasticity, fatigue, gait and balance problems, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive changes. Symptoms may worsen with heat.
sections.typicalTreatments: Disease-modifying therapies to reduce relapses; corticosteroids for acute relapses; symptom management for spasticity, fatigue, pain, and bladder issues; physical and occupational rehabilitation.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex, ages roughly 20 to 40 at onset, higher latitudes, low vitamin D, family history, smoking, certain viral exposures.

concepts.name: Myasthenia Gravis
concepts.shortExplanation: An autoimmune disease where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity.

sections.presentation: Fatigable weakness worsening through the day and with use: ptosis, diplopia, difficulty chewing or swallowing, slurred speech, and proximal limb weakness. Severe cases threaten respiratory muscles.
sections.typicalTreatments: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine); immunosuppression (corticosteroids, other agents); thymectomy in selected patients; IVIG or plasmapheresis for crisis. Avoid medications that worsen weakness.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex in younger adults, male sex in older adults, thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, other autoimmune diseases.

concepts.name: Myasthenic Crisis
concepts.shortExplanation: A life-threatening worsening of myasthenia gravis in which respiratory muscle weakness leads to respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support.

sections.presentation: Rapidly worsening generalized and respiratory weakness, dyspnea, weak cough, difficulty clearing secretions, dysphagia, and declining vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, progressing to respiratory failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Airway protection and mechanical ventilation as needed; IVIG or plasmapheresis; identify and treat triggers (infection, certain medications, surgery, tapering of immunotherapy); ICU monitoring of respiratory parameters. Distinguish from cholinergic crisis.
sections.riskFactors: Infection, aspiration, surgery, pregnancy, physiologic stress, undertreatment or abrupt medication changes, drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission.

concepts.name: Myoclonic Seizure
concepts.shortExplanation: A generalized seizure causing brief, sudden, shock-like muscle jerks, usually without loss of consciousness. Distinguished from tonic-clonic seizures by the very brief, lightning-quick jerks and preserved awareness, and it is a hallmark of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

sections.presentation: Sudden, brief, shock-like jerks of a muscle or muscle group (often the arms and shoulders), usually bilateral and typically without loss of consciousness. Jerks commonly occur on awakening and may cause the patient to drop objects.
sections.typicalTreatments: Valproate is commonly used; levetiracetam, clonazepam, and topiramate are alternatives. Avoid agents that can worsen myoclonus, such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, and gabapentin. Provide safety counseling given the clustering of jerks on awakening.
sections.riskFactors: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, other genetic generalized epilepsies, sleep deprivation, alcohol, and photic stimulation; also seen in metabolic and anoxic states.

concepts.name: Myxedema Coma
concepts.shortExplanation: A rare, life-threatening extreme of severe hypothyroidism, marked by altered mental status, hypothermia, and slowed body functions. A medical emergency.

sections.presentation: Decreased mental status or coma, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, and hyponatremia and hypoglycemia. Often precipitated by infection, cold exposure, surgery, or sedating drugs in a person with underlying hypothyroidism.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU care with IV thyroid hormone replacement, IV corticosteroids (given until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), gentle rewarming, ventilatory and hemodynamic support, and treating the trigger. Correct hyponatremia and hypoglycemia carefully.
sections.riskFactors: Undertreated hypothyroidism plus a precipitant such as infection, cold, surgery, or sedatives; more common in older women in winter.

concepts.name: Naloxone
concepts.shortExplanation: The reversal drug for opioid overdose that rapidly restores breathing by displacing opioids from their receptors.

sections.mechanism: Competitive opioid receptor antagonist that quickly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation.
sections.sideEffects: Acute opioid withdrawal in dependent patients: agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension.
sections.adverseEffects: Precipitated withdrawal, rare pulmonary edema, and re-narcotization when the opioid outlasts naloxone, causing sedation and apnea to return.
sections.nursingImplications: Support airway and breathing first. Titrate to restore adequate respirations rather than full arousal to limit withdrawal. Because many opioids last longer than naloxone, keep monitoring and be ready to redose; repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

concepts.name: Naproxen
concepts.shortExplanation: A long-acting NSAID for pain, inflammation, and fever, available over the counter and by prescription.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes to reduce prostaglandin production, relieving pain, inflammation, and fever.
sections.sideEffects: Stomach upset, heartburn, nausea, and dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding and ulceration, kidney injury, fluid retention with worsening hypertension or heart failure, and increased cardiovascular risk; can raise bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food or milk. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and avoid in renal impairment, active GI bleeding, or heart failure. Monitor blood pressure and renal function on chronic use and review anticoagulant interactions.

concepts.name: Nasal Cannula
concepts.shortExplanation: A lightweight two-pronged tube that delivers low-flow supplemental oxygen through the nostrils; the most common oxygen device.

sections.purpose: Delivers low-flow oxygen, typically 1-6 L/min, providing roughly 24-44 percent FiO2. Comfortable and allows eating and talking, making it ideal for stable patients needing modest oxygen.
sections.careConsiderations: Delivered FiO2 varies with the patient's breathing pattern. Check ears, cheeks, and nostrils for skin breakdown and pad tubing as needed. Humidify flows above about 4 L/min to reduce nasal drying. Ensure prongs curve downward into the nares.

concepts.name: Nasogastric Tube Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of a tube through the nose into the stomach for gastric decompression, medication delivery, or short-term enteral feeding.

sections.targetConcern: Bowel obstruction requiring decompression, inability to take oral intake, or need for short-term enteral nutrition/medication access.
sections.whatToMonitor: Placement confirmation (x-ray and/or aspirate pH), drainage amount/color, nasal and throat skin integrity, aspiration risk during feeds.

concepts.name: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
concepts.shortExplanation: A serious intestinal disease of mostly premature infants in which the bowel becomes inflamed and can die, sometimes leading to perforation.

sections.presentation: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and tenderness, bloody stools, bilious gastric residuals, and systemic signs such as lethargy, apnea, and temperature instability. Abdominal x-ray may show gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis).
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop feeds and rest the gut (NPO), decompress the stomach with a tube, give IV fluids, nutrition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor closely. Surgery is needed if the bowel perforates or the infant deteriorates.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, formula feeding, rapid advancement of feeds, and conditions reducing intestinal blood flow.

concepts.name: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy
concepts.shortExplanation: A wound vacuum system that applies gentle suction through a sealed dressing to speed healing of complex wounds.

sections.purpose: A sealed foam or gauze dressing connected to suction removes wound fluid, reduces swelling, and stimulates granulation tissue, helping deep or chronic wounds heal.
sections.careConsiderations: Maintain an airtight seal and the prescribed suction level; monitor canister output and change the dressing per protocol. Watch for bleeding (it should not be placed over exposed vessels or organs) and protect the skin around the seal.

concepts.name: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
concepts.shortExplanation: A high level of bilirubin in a newborn that causes jaundice, and if severe and untreated can injure the brain.

sections.presentation: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes, typically starting on the face and progressing downward, along with sleepiness or poor feeding when severe. Bilirubin levels are trended against age in hours.
sections.typicalTreatments: Phototherapy to break down bilirubin, ensuring adequate feeding and hydration to promote excretion, and exchange transfusion for dangerously high levels. Very high untreated bilirubin can cause kernicterus, a permanent brain injury.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity, blood type incompatibility between mother and baby, bruising or cephalohematoma, poor feeding, and a sibling who required phototherapy.

concepts.name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A breathing disorder of premature newborns caused by a lack of surfactant, which keeps the tiny air sacs in the lungs from staying open.

sections.presentation: Within hours of birth a preterm infant develops tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions, and cyanosis, with worsening oxygenation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Exogenous surfactant given through the breathing tube, respiratory support with CPAP or mechanical ventilation, and supplemental oxygen. Antenatal corticosteroids given to the mother before preterm birth help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (the more premature, the higher the risk), maternal diabetes, cesarean delivery without labor, and lack of antenatal steroids.

concepts.name: Neonatal Sepsis
concepts.shortExplanation: A bloodstream infection in a newborn that can progress rapidly and requires prompt recognition and antibiotics.

sections.presentation: Often subtle and nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or low temperature), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, apnea, respiratory distress, and poor perfusion. Early-onset appears within the first days of life and late-onset after.
sections.typicalTreatments: Obtain blood cultures and other cultures, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (commonly ampicillin plus gentamicin) without delay, and provide supportive care for breathing and circulation. Narrow therapy once culture results return.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal group B strep colonization, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, prematurity, and invasive lines or devices.

concepts.name: Neostigmine
concepts.shortExplanation: A cholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse non-depolarizing muscle relaxants at the end of surgery. It is given with an anticholinergic to blunt its slowing effect on the heart.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction so it can outcompete residual non-depolarizing blocker and restore muscle strength.
sections.sideEffects: Bradycardia, increased salivation and secretions, nausea, and abdominal cramping.
sections.adverseEffects: Profound bradycardia, bronchospasm, and recurarization (residual weakness) if reversal is incomplete.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given with glycopyrrolate or atropine to prevent bradycardia. Monitor heart rate, respiratory effort, and evidence of adequate reversal such as sustained head lift and strong grip before extubation.

concepts.name: Nephron
concepts.shortExplanation: The microscopic filtering unit of the kidney; each kidney has about a million of them.

sections.purpose: Filters blood and forms urine. The glomerulus filters plasma, and the tubules reabsorb water, electrolytes, and nutrients while secreting wastes, regulating fluid balance, blood pressure, acid-base status, and electrolytes.
sections.careConsiderations: Nephron injury underlies acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. Because nephrons are damaged by low perfusion, nephrotoxic drugs, and obstruction, nurses monitor urine output, creatinine, and BUN and use caution with contrast and nephrotoxins.

concepts.name: Neurogenic Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: A form of distributive shock after acute spinal cord injury (usually at or above T6) in which loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation. Its distinguishing feature is hypotension WITH bradycardia (not the tachycardia seen in other shock).

sections.presentation: The classic triad is hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, dry, pink skin below the level of injury (loss of sympathetic vasoconstriction and sweating). Hypothermia can occur from impaired thermoregulation. The bradycardia is the key discriminator from hypovolemic shock (which causes tachycardia) - and coexisting hemorrhage must be ruled out first, since a trauma patient can have both.
sections.typicalTreatments: Spinal immobilization and airway protection first. Give judicious IV isotonic fluids for the relative hypovolemia, avoiding overload. Add vasopressors when fluids are inadequate - norepinephrine is preferred because it provides both vasoconstriction and heart-rate support; phenylephrine (pure alpha) can worsen the reflex bradycardia. Treat symptomatic bradycardia with atropine, and use pacing for refractory cases. Maintain MAP around 85-90 mmHg for the first 5-7 days to protect spinal cord perfusion.
sections.riskFactors: Acute traumatic spinal cord injury, especially cervical or high-thoracic (at or above T6) levels.

concepts.name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) medications marked by high fever and severe muscle rigidity.

sections.presentation: High fever, generalized lead-pipe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability (fluctuating blood pressure, tachycardia, sweating). Laboratory tests often show a markedly elevated creatine kinase. It usually develops over days.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, and use medications such as dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases. Monitor for complications like kidney injury from muscle breakdown.
sections.riskFactors: Starting or increasing antipsychotics, high-potency agents, rapid dose escalation, dehydration, and abruptly stopping dopaminergic medications.

concepts.name: Neutropenia
concepts.shortExplanation: An abnormally low number of neutrophils, the white blood cells that fight bacterial infection. It is a common effect of chemotherapy and greatly raises infection risk.

sections.presentation: Often asymptomatic until infection develops. Because there are few neutrophils, the usual signs of infection may be blunted, so fever may be the only clue. Severity is graded by the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), with an ANC below 500 considered severe.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat and prevent infection with meticulous hand hygiene and neutropenic precautions, prompt evaluation of any fever, growth factor support such as filgrastim when indicated, and delaying or dose-reducing chemotherapy when counts are too low.
sections.riskFactors: Cytotoxic chemotherapy (the most common cause), radiation, bone marrow cancers and transplant, certain drugs, and severe infection. Risk of serious infection rises as the count falls and the neutropenic period lengthens.

concepts.name: Neutropenic Precautions
concepts.shortExplanation: Protective measures used to reduce infection exposure in patients with very low neutrophil counts. The goal is to shield an immunocompromised patient from avoidable germs.

sections.triggerCriteria: Initiated for patients with significant neutropenia (for example an ANC below 500, or a falling count expected to reach that range), most often during chemotherapy or after transplant.
sections.steps: Strict hand hygiene by everyone entering the room, a private room, and screening out visitors and staff who are ill. Avoid fresh flowers and standing water, follow food-safety practices, provide meticulous skin, oral, and perineal care, and minimize invasive procedures. Monitor temperature closely and report any fever immediately, since fever may be the only sign of a life-threatening infection.

concepts.name: NEWS2
concepts.shortExplanation: An aggregate early-warning score from routine vital signs that flags deteriorating adult patients for a timely response.

sections.purpose: Detects clinical deterioration in adult inpatients by combining routine physiologic measurements into a single score that drives an escalation response.
sections.steps: Points (0-3 each) are assigned for respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, systolic blood pressure, pulse, level of consciousness/new confusion, and temperature, plus 2 points for supplemental oxygen; aggregate 0-20.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher scores mean greater risk: roughly 1-4 low, 5-6 medium, and 7 or more high risk. A score of 5 or more (or a 3 in any single parameter) is a key threshold prompting urgent clinical review.

concepts.name: NIH Stroke Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A structured neurologic exam that quantifies stroke severity, used to guide treatment decisions and track a stroke patient's course.

sections.purpose: Measures the severity of neurologic deficit in acute ischemic stroke and helps guide decisions about thrombolysis and thrombectomy while tracking improvement or decline.
sections.steps: 11 items scored and summed for a total of 0-42: level of consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, motor arm and leg, limb ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, and extinction/inattention. Higher scores mean greater deficit.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 0 = no stroke symptoms; roughly 1-4 = minor, 5-15 = moderate, 16-20 = moderate to severe, 21-42 = severe. Higher scores predict worse outcomes; any acute rise signals worsening and prompts urgent reassessment.

concepts.name: Nimodipine
concepts.shortExplanation: A calcium channel blocker given after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage to reduce brain damage from vasospasm. It is one of the few drugs shown to improve outcomes in SAH.

sections.mechanism: A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with preferential effects on cerebral vessels; improves neurologic outcomes after subarachnoid hemorrhage, thought to relate to reducing ischemic injury from vasospasm.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, headache, flushing, and nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Significant hypotension; giving the contents intravenously has caused death and severe cardiovascular events, so it must never be given IV.
sections.nursingImplications: Give orally or by feeding tube only, never IV (boxed warning). Monitor blood pressure closely and hold or adjust for hypotension. Administer on an empty stomach and on schedule, typically for 21 days after SAH.

concepts.name: Nitrofurantoin
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral antibiotic used specifically for uncomplicated urinary tract infections and UTI prophylaxis.

sections.mechanism: Concentrated in the urine, it is reduced by bacterial enzymes to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA, ribosomes, and other components; it is effective in the bladder but not for kidney or systemic infection.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, and harmless brown discoloration of the urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Acute and chronic pulmonary reactions (cough, dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis with long-term use), hepatotoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy; less effective and higher-risk in significant renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food to improve absorption and reduce GI upset. Avoid in poor kidney function. Teach patients that urine may turn brown and to report new cough, shortness of breath, or numbness and tingling. Not used for pyelonephritis.

concepts.name: Nitroglycerin
concepts.shortExplanation: A vasodilator that relieves chest pain (angina) by widening blood vessels and reducing the heart's workload.

sections.mechanism: Releases nitric oxide, relaxing vascular smooth muscle — venodilation lowers preload (the main effect) with some coronary vasodilation. Available sublingual, IV, and topical.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypotension, especially with volume depletion, right-ventricular/inferior MI, or recent PDE-5 inhibitor (e.g. sildenafil) use — a dangerous interaction.
sections.nursingImplications: Check blood pressure before and after each dose; sublingual angina dosing is one tab every 5 minutes up to 3 doses — call for help if pain persists; titrate IV to pain and BP.
sections.commonBrandName: Nitrostat, Nitro-Dur. Often called NTG or "nitro."

concepts.name: Non-Rebreather Mask
concepts.shortExplanation: A high-concentration oxygen mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves used for critically ill or severely hypoxemic patients.

sections.purpose: Delivers the highest oxygen concentration of the standard masks (up to about 90-95 percent FiO2) at 10-15 L/min, used for acute hypoxemia, trauma, and pre-oxygenation.
sections.careConsiderations: Set flow high enough to keep the reservoir bag inflated (never let it fully collapse on inspiration). One-way valves prevent rebreathing of exhaled air. Reassess frequently; a patient still hypoxemic on a non-rebreather may need noninvasive ventilation or intubation.

concepts.name: Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)
concepts.shortExplanation: A heart attack with elevated troponin but no ST-segment elevation on ECG, usually from partial coronary occlusion. Unlike STEMI, management centers on medical stabilization and risk-stratified (often next-day) catheterization rather than immediate reperfusion.

sections.presentation: Chest pain or pressure similar to STEMI, sometimes at rest, with dyspnea and diaphoresis. ECG may show ST depression, T-wave inversion, or be nonspecific, but there is NO ST elevation. Cardiac troponin is elevated, confirming myocardial injury and distinguishing NSTEMI from unstable angina.
sections.typicalTreatments: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor), anticoagulation (heparin or enoxaparin), beta blocker, nitroglycerin for pain, and high-intensity statin. Risk stratification (e.g., HEART or TIMI score) guides timing of invasive coronary angiography, typically within 24-72 hours rather than emergently; unstable patients go sooner. Serial troponins and continuous telemetry.
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, chronic kidney disease, and older age.

concepts.name: Norepinephrine
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication that raises blood pressure by tightening blood vessels — used when fluids alone aren't maintaining adequate blood pressure, especially in septic shock.

sections.mechanism: Potent alpha-1 agonist (with some beta-1 activity) causing vasoconstriction and increased cardiac contractility. First-line vasopressor in septic shock.
sections.sideEffects: Reflex bradycardia, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Peripheral/digital ischemia with prolonged or high-dose use, especially with extravasation — should be given via central line when possible; arrhythmia.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous BP monitoring, ideally via arterial line; assess extremities/IV site for signs of extravasation; titrate to MAP goal per orders.

concepts.name: NPH Insulin
concepts.shortExplanation: Intermediate-acting insulin that provides basal-type coverage, usually dosed twice daily. Unlike the peakless long-acting analogs, NPH has a pronounced peak that drives predictable hypoglycemia risk, notably overnight with evening doses.

sections.mechanism: Human insulin complexed with protamine to slow absorption, giving a cloudy suspension. Onset is about 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, and duration 12 to 18 hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia, especially during its 4-12 hour peak; an evening dose raises nocturnal hypoglycemia risk. Hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Gently roll the vial or pen to resuspend the cloudy insulin before drawing up; never give NPH IV. It may be mixed with regular insulin in one syringe - draw clear before cloudy. Teach patients to eat on schedule and watch for hypoglycemia around the peak.

concepts.name: Numeric Pain Rating Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A simple self-report scale where the patient rates pain from 0 to 10, used for any patient who can communicate their pain.

sections.purpose: Lets a patient self-report current pain intensity so it can be tracked and treatment response measured.
sections.steps: Patient chooses a whole number from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable). Reassess after interventions to gauge effect.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Commonly grouped as 1-3 mild, 4-6 moderate, and 7-10 severe pain. Higher scores and inadequate relief after treatment prompt escalation, but the goal is a functional level meaningful to the patient.

concepts.name: Obstructive Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: Shock from a mechanical block to blood flow into or out of the heart, even though the heart muscle itself is normal. The classic reversible causes are tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, and massive pulmonary embolism.

sections.presentation: Hypotension and tachycardia with signs of impaired venous return: distended (engorged) neck veins, respiratory distress, and chest pain. Cause-specific clues - absent or decreased breath sounds with tracheal deviation (tension pneumothorax), muffled heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus (cardiac tamponade), or sudden dyspnea and hypoxia with signs of right-heart strain (massive PE). Bedside ultrasound (RUSH exam) and echocardiography help localize the obstruction.
sections.typicalTreatments: The obstruction itself must be relieved - vasopressors and fluids alone will not fix it. Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube. Cardiac tamponade: emergent pericardiocentesis. Massive PE: thrombolytics or embolectomy. Provide oxygen and cautious fluids as a temporizing measure while arranging the definitive intervention.
sections.riskFactors: Chest trauma, mechanical ventilation with high PEEP, pericardial effusion (malignancy, uremia, infection), venous thromboembolism, and severe pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
concepts.shortExplanation: Repeated collapse of the upper airway during sleep causing pauses in breathing, oxygen desaturation, and fragmented sleep.

sections.presentation: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping/choking at night, daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and difficulty concentrating. Often accompanied by hypertension and obesity.
sections.typicalTreatments: CPAP is first-line; weight loss, positional therapy, oral appliances, and avoiding alcohol/sedatives at night. Diagnosis confirmed by polysomnography (sleep study).
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, older age, enlarged tonsils, and alcohol or sedative use.

concepts.name: Octreotide
concepts.shortExplanation: A synthetic hormone (somatostatin analog) used to reduce bleeding from esophageal varices and to control secretory diarrhea and certain hormone-secreting tumors.

sections.mechanism: Mimics somatostatin, causing splanchnic vasoconstriction that lowers portal blood flow and pressure, and suppressing secretion of several GI hormones.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, abdominal cramping, and injection-site reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Bradycardia and other arrhythmias, hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, and gallstones with long-term use.
sections.nursingImplications: In acute variceal bleeding it is typically given as an IV bolus followed by a continuous infusion. Monitor blood glucose, heart rate and rhythm, and signs of ongoing bleeding.

concepts.name: Olanzapine
concepts.shortExplanation: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and acute agitation.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors, improving psychotic and mood symptoms.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain, increased appetite, and dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: Metabolic effects including significant weight gain, high blood sugar, and abnormal lipids; neuroleptic malignant syndrome; and lower risk of movement disorders than typical antipsychotics. Combining intramuscular olanzapine with benzodiazepines has been linked to excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor weight, blood glucose, and lipids over time. Watch for oversedation, and use caution about pairing the IM form closely with parenteral benzodiazepines. Assess for movement disorders and signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

concepts.name: Omeprazole
concepts.shortExplanation: A proton pump inhibitor taken by mouth for heartburn, GERD, and peptic ulcer disease.

sections.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) of parietal cells, markedly reducing stomach acid production.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, and flatulence.
sections.adverseEffects: With long-term use: low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, increased fracture risk, C. difficile infection, and reduced effect of clopidogrel through CYP2C19 inhibition.
sections.nursingImplications: Give before the first meal of the day, and instruct patients to swallow delayed-release capsules whole. Reassess the need for long-term therapy. Monitor magnesium on prolonged use and review interactions such as with clopidogrel.

concepts.name: Ondansetron
concepts.shortExplanation: A widely used anti-nausea medication that prevents and treats nausea and vomiting.

sections.mechanism: Blocks 5-HT3 serotonin receptors in the gut and brainstem that trigger nausea and vomiting.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, constipation, fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: QT prolongation, which can lead to arrhythmias, particularly with other QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte abnormalities.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess for nausea and response. Use caution with other QT-prolonging medications and check potassium/magnesium. Not effective for motion sickness.

concepts.name: Opioid Withdrawal
concepts.shortExplanation: The uncomfortable but usually not life-threatening symptoms that occur when someone dependent on opioids stops or cuts back.

sections.presentation: Anxiety and drug craving, muscle aches, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, runny nose and tearing, yawning, sweating, dilated pupils, goosebumps, and restlessness. Symptoms are very distressing but rarely dangerous in otherwise healthy adults.
sections.typicalTreatments: Medications such as buprenorphine or methadone ease withdrawal and support recovery, and clonidine helps with autonomic symptoms. Symptomatic care addresses nausea, diarrhea, and muscle aches. Severity is often tracked with the COWS scale.
sections.riskFactors: Physical dependence from chronic opioid use, abrupt cessation, and administration of an opioid antagonist such as naloxone or naltrexone.

concepts.name: Oropharyngeal Airway (OPA)
concepts.shortExplanation: A rigid curved device inserted into the mouth to hold the tongue away from the back of the throat and keep the airway open in an unconscious patient.

sections.purpose: Prevents the tongue from obstructing the airway in an unresponsive patient without a gag reflex, aiding bag-mask ventilation. A nasopharyngeal airway is the alternative used when a gag reflex is present.
sections.careConsiderations: Use only in patients without a gag reflex; it can trigger gagging, vomiting, and aspiration or laryngospasm in responsive patients. Size by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe/angle of the jaw. Reassess airway patency and remove if the patient regains a gag reflex.

concepts.name: Oropharyngeal and Nasotracheal Suctioning
concepts.shortExplanation: Using a suction catheter to clear secretions from the mouth, throat, or airway in patients who cannot clear them on their own.

sections.targetConcern: Removes secretions to maintain a patent airway, improve oxygenation, and reduce aspiration and infection risk in patients with a weak cough or excessive secretions.
sections.whatToMonitor: Pre-oxygenate and limit each pass to about 10-15 seconds; apply suction only while withdrawing. Watch oxygen saturation, heart rate, and rhythm - suctioning can cause hypoxia, vagal-mediated bradycardia, and mucosal trauma. Stop and reoxygenate for desaturation or arrhythmia, and note secretion color and amount.

concepts.name: Osteomyelitis
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection of bone, usually bacterial, that can arise from the bloodstream, adjacent tissue infection, or a wound. It often requires prolonged antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

sections.presentation: Localized bone pain, warmth, swelling, and tenderness; fever and malaise; a draining sinus tract or non-healing wound in chronic cases (common in diabetic foot ulcers). Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) support the diagnosis; imaging and bone culture confirm it.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged, often IV, antibiotics guided by culture and sensitivity (frequently weeks); surgical debridement or removal of infected or dead bone and hardware when needed; source control and glucose optimization in diabetics.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes and peripheral vascular disease, open fractures or orthopedic hardware, pressure injuries, IV drug use, recent surgery, and immunocompromise.

concepts.name: Ostomy Care
