concepts.shortExplanation: The care of a surgical stoma that diverts stool or urine into an external pouch, including skin protection and output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Manages a colostomy, ileostomy, or urostomy - a surgically created opening (stoma) that routes waste into an external appliance.
sections.whatToMonitor: A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist; report a dusky, pale, or black stoma immediately. Protect the surrounding (peristomal) skin, ensure a good pouch seal, and monitor output, since high-volume ileostomy output can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

concepts.name: Otitis Media
concepts.shortExplanation: A middle ear infection that is one of the most common illnesses of early childhood, causing ear pain and fever.

sections.presentation: Ear pain, tugging at the ear in nonverbal children, fever, irritability, trouble sleeping, and sometimes drainage if the eardrum ruptures. The eardrum appears red, bulging, and poorly mobile on exam.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pain and fever control with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin when treatment is indicated. Some cases are observed without antibiotics. Recurrent infections may lead to ear tube placement.
sections.riskFactors: Young age, daycare attendance, bottle feeding while lying down, pacifier use, secondhand smoke, and recent upper respiratory infection.

concepts.name: Oxycodone
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral opioid for moderate to severe pain, often given as a combination product with acetaminophen.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors that reduces pain perception.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence, especially with other CNS depressants.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor sedation and respiratory rate; start a bowel regimen; naloxone reverses toxicity. Combination products (such as Percocet) contain acetaminophen, so track total daily acetaminophen. Extended-release forms are not to be crushed.

concepts.name: Oxycodone-Acetaminophen
concepts.shortExplanation: A combination oral opioid analgesic pairing oxycodone with acetaminophen, commonly prescribed for moderate to severe pain including after surgery.

sections.mechanism: Oxycodone is a mu-opioid receptor agonist that blunts pain perception; acetaminophen provides additional non-opioid analgesia and fever reduction.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, pruritus, and lightheadedness.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, oversedation, hypotension, and physical dependence; acetaminophen-related hepatotoxicity if the daily limit is exceeded.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor pain, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and sedation level. Track total daily acetaminophen across all products. Anticipate constipation and start bowel management. Keep naloxone accessible and educate on safe storage and dependence risk.

concepts.name: Oxygen (Supplemental Oxygen Therapy)
concepts.shortExplanation: A prescribed therapy that delivers a higher concentration of oxygen than room air to treat or prevent hypoxemia.

sections.mechanism: Increases the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2), raising alveolar and arterial oxygen and improving tissue oxygen delivery.
sections.sideEffects: Nasal dryness, mucosal irritation, and skin breakdown at contact points from the device.
sections.adverseEffects: High concentrations over time can cause oxygen toxicity and absorption atelectasis. In some COPD patients, uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can blunt respiratory drive and worsen CO2 retention.
sections.nursingImplications: Treat oxygen as a drug: titrate to the ordered SpO2 target (often 92-96 percent, or 88-92 percent in chronic CO2 retainers). Humidify higher flows, ensure no smoking/open flame near oxygen, and choose the delivery device to match the needed FiO2.

concepts.name: Oxytocin
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone given IV to start or strengthen labor contractions and, after delivery, to contract the uterus and control bleeding.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates uterine smooth muscle to contract by increasing intracellular calcium; also promotes milk letdown.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, and with strong contractions, maternal discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Uterine tachysystole (too-frequent contractions) causing fetal heart rate decelerations and distress; uterine rupture; and, at high sustained doses, water intoxication/hyponatremia from its antidiuretic effect. Rapid IV bolus can cause hypotension.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by controlled infusion pump and titrated to contraction pattern. Continuously monitor contraction frequency and fetal heart rate; stop the infusion and reposition/give oxygen if tachysystole or a nonreassuring tracing develops. Track intake/output and watch for signs of fluid overload during prolonged infusions.

concepts.name: Pacemaker Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Implantation of a small device under the skin with leads into the heart that deliver electrical impulses to keep the heart beating at an adequate rate.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade heart block, or another conduction problem where the heart's own rate is too slow to meet the body's needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, heart rate and rhythm to confirm capture, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, signs of lead dislodgement (hiccups, failure to pace).

concepts.name: Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion
concepts.shortExplanation: Infusion of donor red blood cells to treat significant blood loss or anemia that's causing symptoms or instability.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic anemia or acute blood loss where the patient's own red cell count is too low to meet oxygen delivery needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs closely (especially the first 15 minutes), signs of transfusion reaction (fever, chills, rash, back pain, dyspnea) — stop the transfusion immediately and notify the provider if suspected.

concepts.name: PAINAD
concepts.shortExplanation: A short observational pain scale for people with advanced dementia or others who cannot describe their pain.

sections.purpose: Estimates pain in patients with advanced dementia or other noncommunicative older adults by observing behavior over a brief period.
sections.steps: Five items - breathing, negative vocalization, facial expression, body language, and consolability - each scored 0-2, for a total of 0-10.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher totals suggest more pain; some sources group 1-3 as mild, 4-6 moderate, and 7-10 severe, though these cutoffs are not firmly validated. Rising scores prompt comfort measures and analgesia with reassessment.

concepts.name: Palliative Care
concepts.shortExplanation: Specialized care focused on relieving the symptoms and stress of a serious illness and improving quality of life. Unlike hospice, it can be given at any stage of illness and alongside curative or life-prolonging treatment.

sections.triggerCriteria: Appropriate for any patient with a serious illness (such as cancer, heart failure, COPD, or advanced kidney disease), at any stage and any age, regardless of whether they are also pursuing curative treatment.
sections.steps: An interdisciplinary team assesses and manages distressing symptoms (pain, dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, anxiety), clarifies goals of care and prognosis, supports complex decision-making and advance care planning, and coordinates care across settings. Nurses reassess symptoms frequently, support the patient and family emotionally, and help transition to hospice when appropriate.

concepts.name: Pantoprazole
concepts.shortExplanation: A proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that reduces stomach acid, used for reflux, ulcers, and GI bleeding.

sections.mechanism: Blocks the stomach's acid (proton) pump, markedly reducing gastric acid production.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Long-term use is associated with low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, C. difficile infection, and bone fractures.
sections.nursingImplications: Give oral doses before meals. IV infusions are used in acute GI bleeding. Reassess ongoing need to avoid unnecessary long-term use.

concepts.name: Paracentesis
concepts.shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the abdominal cavity — relieves pressure from ascites and can help identify its cause.

sections.targetConcern: Large-volume ascites causing abdominal distension, discomfort, or respiratory compromise; or ascites of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs for hypotension from fluid shifts (especially with large-volume taps), insertion site for leakage, need for albumin replacement after large-volume removal.

concepts.name: Parkinson Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder from loss of dopamine-producing neurons, causing tremor, stiffness, and slowed movement.

sections.presentation: Resting tremor (often 'pill-rolling'), bradykinesia, rigidity (cogwheeling), postural instability, shuffling festinating gait, masked facial expression, soft speech, micrographia, and later cognitive and autonomic changes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Dopaminergic therapy, especially levodopa-carbidopa; dopamine agonists and other adjuncts; deep brain stimulation for select advanced cases; physical, occupational, and speech therapy; fall prevention and careful timing of medication doses.
sections.riskFactors: Advancing age, male sex, family history, certain pesticide or toxin exposures.

concepts.name: Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: Atrial fibrillation that comes and goes, converting back to normal sinus rhythm on its own (or with treatment) within 7 days, usually within 48 hours. Because episodes are intermittent, it is easy to miss and still carries stroke risk.

sections.presentation: Self-terminating episodes of irregularly irregular rhythm, often felt as sudden palpitations, fluttering, breathlessness, or lightheadedness that resolve spontaneously. Patients may be in normal sinus rhythm between episodes, so it can be missed without prolonged or ambulatory monitoring.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate or rhythm control during episodes; antiarrhythmics (e.g., flecainide, amiodarone) or a 'pill-in-the-pocket' strategy in selected patients; catheter ablation for recurrent symptomatic cases. Anticoagulation decisions are based on CHA2DS2-VASc score, not on how brief the episodes are, since stroke risk persists. Identify and treat triggers (alcohol, caffeine, stress, sleep apnea).
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, excess alcohol, hyperthyroidism, older age, and structural heart disease. May progress over time to persistent atrial fibrillation.

concepts.name: Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) Pump
concepts.shortExplanation: An infusion pump that lets a patient self-administer preset doses of IV pain medication by pressing a button.

sections.purpose: Gives the patient control over analgesia (commonly morphine, hydromorphone, or fentanyl) with programmed dose, lockout interval, and hourly limits, improving pain control while limiting overdose.
sections.careConsiderations: Only the patient should press the button - warn family against 'PCA by proxy.' Monitor sedation level, respiratory rate, and pulse oximetry (and capnography per policy) because oversedation is the main danger. Verify pump settings with a second nurse, and keep naloxone available.

concepts.name: Peak Flow Meter
concepts.shortExplanation: A handheld device that measures peak expiratory flow rate to monitor asthma control and detect worsening airway obstruction.

sections.purpose: Measures how fast a patient can forcefully exhale (peak expiratory flow), reflecting airway narrowing. Used at home to track asthma control and guide an asthma action plan (green/yellow/red zones based on personal best).
sections.careConsiderations: Teach a full deep breath and a fast, hard blow while standing, taking the best of three attempts. Establish the patient's personal best when well. A falling peak flow can warn of an exacerbation before symptoms worsen, prompting action-plan steps.

concepts.name: Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation
concepts.shortExplanation: An acute flare of asthma in a child, with narrowing of the airways causing wheezing, cough, and increased work of breathing.

sections.presentation: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness, prolonged expiration, retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles. Severe attacks may show a silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, and falling oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Inhaled short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol), often with ipratropium in the acute setting, systemic corticosteroids, and supplemental oxygen. Severe cases may need continuous nebulization or magnesium. Reassess respiratory effort and oxygenation frequently.
sections.riskFactors: Known asthma, viral respiratory infections, allergen or smoke exposure, exercise, cold air, and poor adherence to controller medications.

concepts.name: Pediatric Dehydration
concepts.shortExplanation: A loss of body fluids in children, often from vomiting and diarrhea, that can progress quickly and become dangerous in infants.

sections.presentation: Dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output and fewer wet diapers, absent tears, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, and lethargy. In infants a sunken fontanelle is a sign, and severe cases show tachycardia and low blood pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral rehydration therapy is preferred for mild to moderate dehydration, given in small frequent amounts. IV fluids are used for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, or shock. Treat the underlying cause and monitor weight, urine output, and electrolytes.
sections.riskFactors: Gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea, young age, fever, poor oral intake, and limited access to fluids.

concepts.name: PEG Tube Placement
concepts.shortExplanation: Endoscopic placement of a feeding tube directly through the abdominal wall into the stomach — used when a patient needs long-term enteral nutrition.

sections.targetConcern: Inability to safely swallow or take adequate oral nutrition long-term (e.g. after stroke, in progressive neurologic disease).
sections.whatToMonitor: Stoma site for infection/leakage, tube placement before each feed, feeding tolerance (nausea, distension), skin integrity around the site.

concepts.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: Open sores in the lining of the stomach or first part of the small intestine, most often from H. pylori infection or NSAID use. Can bleed or perforate.

sections.presentation: Burning or gnawing upper abdominal pain, often related to meals (gastric ulcers worse with food, duodenal ulcers relieved by food and worse at night). Bloating, nausea. Bleeding presents as melena, hematemesis, or coffee-ground emesis; perforation causes sudden severe pain and a rigid abdomen.
sections.typicalTreatments: Proton pump inhibitors to suppress acid and promote healing, H. pylori eradication with combination antibiotics plus a PPI, and stopping NSAIDs. Endoscopy to diagnose and treat bleeding; surgery for perforation.
sections.riskFactors: H. pylori infection, chronic NSAID or aspirin use, smoking, alcohol, and physiologic stress (critical illness).

concepts.name: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
concepts.shortExplanation: Threading a catheter through an artery to open a blocked coronary vessel — a balloon widens the narrowing and a stent is usually left behind to hold it open, restoring blood flow to the heart.

sections.targetConcern: A blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery, most urgently in an acute heart attack (STEMI) where fast reperfusion limits heart muscle damage.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site (radial/femoral) for bleeding or hematoma, distal pulses of the cannulated limb, chest pain and ECG changes (possible re-occlusion or stent thrombosis), renal function after contrast dye.

concepts.name: Pericardiocentesis
concepts.shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the sac around the heart — relieves pressure that keeps the heart from filling and pumping, most urgently in cardiac tamponade.

sections.targetConcern: Pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), or an effusion of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure and heart rate for rapid improvement or re-accumulation, ECG changes, insertion site for bleeding, signs of recurring tamponade.

concepts.name: Pericarditis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing sharp chest pain that often eases when sitting forward. Usually treatable, but can lead to fluid buildup.

sections.presentation: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.
sections.typicalTreatments: NSAIDs and colchicine, treat the underlying cause, monitor for progression to a pericardial effusion or tamponade.
sections.riskFactors: Recent viral infection, recent MI (Dressler syndrome), cardiac surgery, autoimmune disease, uremia.

concepts.name: Perioperative Hypothermia
concepts.shortExplanation: An unintended drop in core body temperature below about 36 degrees Celsius around the time of surgery. Anesthesia impairs the body's ability to hold heat in a cold operating room.

sections.presentation: Low core temperature, shivering on emergence, cold extremities, and patient-reported chilling. It contributes to discomfort and delayed recovery.
sections.typicalTreatments: Active warming with forced-air warming blankets, warmed IV fluids and irrigation, raising the ambient temperature, and covering exposed skin. Prewarming before induction helps prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: General or neuraxial anesthesia, cold operating rooms, long procedures, large exposed surgical fields, extremes of age, low body weight, and infusion of cool fluids. Consequences include increased surgical site infection, coagulopathy and bleeding, cardiac events, and prolonged drug effects.

concepts.name: Perioperative VTE Prophylaxis
concepts.shortExplanation: Measures used around surgery to prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, since surgery and immobility raise clotting risk. It combines mechanical and, when appropriate, pharmacologic methods.

sections.triggerCriteria: Assess every surgical patient for clot risk (for example with a Caprini score) and balance it against bleeding risk. Higher risk comes with major or orthopedic surgery, cancer, prolonged immobility, prior VTE, obesity, and advanced age.
sections.steps: Mechanical prophylaxis such as sequential compression devices and early ambulation for most patients, with pharmacologic prophylaxis (low-dose heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) added when bleeding risk allows. Ensure compression devices are worn and functioning, encourage early mobilization, monitor for signs of DVT (unilateral leg swelling and pain) and PE (sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia), and reassess as bleeding risk changes.

concepts.name: Peripheral Arterial Disease
concepts.shortExplanation: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries to the limbs (usually legs) that reduces blood flow, causing pain with walking and, if severe, tissue loss.

sections.presentation: Intermittent claudication (calf pain with walking relieved by rest), cool pale extremities, diminished or absent distal pulses, hair loss, shiny skin, and slow-healing wounds. Critical limb ischemia causes rest pain and ulcers/gangrene.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, supervised exercise, statins, antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), and BP/diabetes control. Revascularization (angioplasty, stenting, or bypass) for severe disease. Meticulous foot care.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, older age, and known coronary or cerebrovascular disease.

concepts.name: Peripheral IV Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Placing a short catheter into a peripheral vein, usually in the arm or hand, for fluids and medications.

sections.targetConcern: Establishes venous access to give IV fluids, medications, contrast, and blood products, and to draw blood at insertion.
sections.whatToMonitor: After insertion, check the site regularly for infiltration (swelling, coolness), extravasation of vesicants, phlebitis (redness, pain, a cordlike vein), and signs of infection. Ensure a brisk flush and blood return, secure the catheter and date the dressing, and rotate sites per policy.

concepts.name: Peritoneal Dialysis
concepts.shortExplanation: A home-capable form of dialysis that uses the lining of the abdomen (peritoneum) as a natural filter to remove wastes and fluid.

sections.targetConcern: Removes waste products and excess fluid in kidney failure by instilling dialysate into the abdomen, letting it dwell, and draining it.
sections.whatToMonitor: Cloudy drained fluid (effluent), which signals peritonitis; catheter exit-site infection; fluid balance and daily weights; dwell and drain volumes; and blood glucose, since the dialysate contains dextrose.

concepts.name: Permanent Atrial Fibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: Longstanding atrial fibrillation in which the patient and clinician have jointly accepted the rhythm and no longer attempt to restore sinus rhythm. Care shifts entirely to rate control and stroke prevention.

sections.presentation: Continuous atrial fibrillation, often with a controlled or minimally symptomatic ventricular rate on medication. Many patients are asymptomatic at rest but note fatigue or breathlessness with exertion. The rhythm is chronic and accepted rather than actively converted.
sections.typicalTreatments: The goal is a controlled ventricular rate with beta blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, or digoxin, plus long-term anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC such as apixaban/rivaroxaban) guided by CHA2DS2-VASc. Rhythm control and cardioversion are no longer pursued by definition. AV node ablation with pacemaker placement is an option when rate control fails.
sections.riskFactors: Advanced or longstanding AFib, older age, significant structural heart disease, heart failure, and prior failed rhythm-control attempts.

concepts.name: Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: Atrial fibrillation that lasts longer than 7 days and does not stop on its own, requiring medication or cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm. It reflects more established atrial remodeling than the paroxysmal form.

sections.presentation: Sustained irregularly irregular rhythm lasting more than 7 days. Symptoms range from palpitations, fatigue, and exertional breathlessness to few or no symptoms. Does not self-terminate; conversion requires pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control (beta blocker, diltiazem) plus a rhythm-control decision: antiarrhythmic drugs, elective synchronized cardioversion (with adequate anticoagulation or a TEE to exclude atrial thrombus beforehand), or ablation. Anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc. 'Longstanding persistent' AFib refers to continuous AFib for more than 12 months when a rhythm-control strategy is still being pursued.
sections.riskFactors: Longer duration of AFib, hypertension, heart failure, valvular disease, obesity, sleep apnea, and atrial enlargement. Tends to evolve from paroxysmal AFib and can progress to permanent AFib.

concepts.name: Phenylephrine
concepts.shortExplanation: A vasopressor that raises blood pressure by tightening blood vessels, commonly used for hypotension in the PACU and OR and for anesthesia-related low blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that constricts blood vessels to raise systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. A reflex slowing of the heart rate can occur.
sections.sideEffects: Reflex bradycardia, hypertension, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypertension, reflex bradycardia, and reduced organ perfusion or extravasation tissue injury if it leaks from the IV site.
sections.nursingImplications: Preferred when hypotension is paired with tachycardia because it does not increase heart rate. Monitor blood pressure and heart rate continuously, ideally with an arterial line for infusions, and give through a secure, well-monitored IV or central line per policy.

concepts.name: Phenytoin
concepts.shortExplanation: An antiseizure medication used for focal and tonic-clonic seizures and status epilepticus. It requires blood level monitoring because of a narrow therapeutic range.

sections.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, stabilizing neuronal membranes and limiting the spread of seizure activity.
sections.sideEffects: Gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia), hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, nystagmus, ataxia, and drowsiness.
sections.adverseEffects: Signs of toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion) at high levels; serious skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome; IV administration too fast can cause hypotension and arrhythmias; purple glove syndrome with IV extravasation.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor serum levels (typical therapeutic total level about 10 to 20 mcg/mL); many drug interactions. Give IV slowly with cardiac monitoring; use only compatible IV fluids (normal saline) to avoid precipitation. Emphasize meticulous oral hygiene and adherence.

concepts.name: Phosphate
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood mineral that becomes elevated in kidney failure and contributes to bone and mineral disease.

sections.normalRange: About 2.5-4.5 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High phosphate is common in kidney failure and contributes to bone and mineral disease and itching; low phosphate can occur with refeeding, malnutrition, or during treatment of DKA.

concepts.name: Phototherapy
concepts.shortExplanation: Treatment that uses special blue light to lower a newborn's bilirubin level and clear jaundice.

sections.targetConcern: Reduces elevated bilirubin by converting it into water-soluble forms the baby can excrete, preventing progression to brain injury.
sections.whatToMonitor: Protect the infant's eyes with shielding and expose as much skin as possible for maximum light exposure. Monitor temperature (both overheating and cooling can occur), hydration and urine output, feeding, and skin integrity. Track bilirubin levels to gauge response, and watch for loose stools and rash as expected effects.

concepts.name: PICC Line Insertion
concepts.shortExplanation: Placement of a long catheter through an arm vein that terminates near the heart — used for extended IV access without repeated peripheral sticks.

sections.targetConcern: Need for extended IV access, e.g. multi-week antibiotic courses or medications that irritate peripheral veins.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion site for infection/phlebitis, arm swelling or pain (possible thrombosis), catheter tip position confirmed by x-ray.

concepts.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
concepts.shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic combination used empirically for serious infections and sepsis, covering many gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria.

sections.mechanism: Piperacillin is a penicillin that disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis; tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects piperacillin from bacterial enzymes, broadening coverage.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic and anaphylactic reactions (penicillin class), Clostridioides difficile colitis, and a risk of acute kidney injury when combined with vancomycin.
sections.nursingImplications: Screen for penicillin allergy. Often given as an extended infusion for better effect. Draw cultures before the first dose when possible and give antibiotics promptly in sepsis. Monitor renal function, especially when co-administered with vancomycin.

concepts.name: Placental Abruption
concepts.shortExplanation: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before delivery, which can cut off the baby's oxygen supply and cause dangerous maternal bleeding.

sections.presentation: Sudden painful vaginal bleeding, a firm, tender, or rigid uterus, frequent contractions, and often a nonreassuring or absent fetal heart rate. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so blood loss can be underestimated.
sections.typicalTreatments: Continuous fetal and maternal monitoring, IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often cesarean) when the mother or fetus is unstable. Watch for disseminated intravascular coagulation.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal hypertension or preeclampsia, abdominal trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, advanced maternal age, and multiple gestation.

concepts.name: Platelet Count
concepts.shortExplanation: The number of platelets in the blood; platelets form the first plug that stops bleeding.

sections.normalRange: 150,000-400,000 per microliter.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low platelets (thrombocytopenia) raise bleeding risk and can result from sepsis, DIC, chemotherapy, heparin (HIT), or liver disease; bleeding risk climbs sharply at very low counts. High platelets (thrombocytosis) may be reactive to inflammation or a bone-marrow disorder. Check for petechiae, bruising, and bleeding.

concepts.name: Pleural Effusion
concepts.shortExplanation: An abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space that compresses the lung and causes dyspnea; classified as transudative or exudative by cause.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the fluid, decreased tactile fremitus, and sometimes pleuritic chest pain or cough.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause; thoracentesis for diagnosis and symptom relief; chest tube for large or infected (empyema) effusions; diuresis for heart-failure-related transudates.
sections.riskFactors: Heart failure, pneumonia, malignancy, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and recent cardiothoracic surgery.

concepts.name: Pneumonia
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection of the lung tissue that fills air sacs with fluid or pus, causing cough, fever, and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Cough (often productive), fever, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, crackles on auscultation, and low oxygen saturation. Older adults may present with new confusion or falls rather than classic symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by whether it is community- or hospital-acquired, supplemental oxygen, fluids, antipyretics, and pulmonary hygiene such as incentive spirometry and early mobility.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, smoking, COPD, immobility, aspiration risk, recent hospitalization, and immunosuppression.

concepts.name: Pneumothorax
concepts.shortExplanation: Air trapped in the pleural space that collapses part of the lung, causing sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

sections.presentation: Sudden, sharp, one-sided pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, decreased or absent breath sounds and hyperresonance over the affected side, and tachypnea.
sections.typicalTreatments: Small stable pneumothoraces may be observed with oxygen; larger or symptomatic ones need needle aspiration or chest tube drainage. Supplemental oxygen speeds reabsorption of pleural air.
sections.riskFactors: Tall thin young males (primary spontaneous), COPD or other lung disease (secondary), chest trauma, and invasive procedures such as central line placement or thoracentesis.

concepts.name: Polyethylene Glycol 3350
concepts.shortExplanation: An osmotic laxative that draws water into the stool to relieve constipation. High-volume PEG solutions are also used to cleanse the bowel before colonoscopy.

sections.mechanism: An osmotic agent that holds water in the intestine, softening stool and increasing bowel movement frequency.
sections.sideEffects: Bloating, cramping, nausea, and loose stools.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive use or large bowel-prep volumes can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances, especially in older adults or those with kidney or heart disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Mix the powder in water or another beverage. For colonoscopy prep, encourage completing the full volume and maintaining hydration; monitor electrolytes in at-risk patients.

concepts.name: Post-Acute Care Levels
concepts.shortExplanation: The different settings a patient may go to after a hospital stay, ranging from home with services to specialized facilities. Choosing the right level matches the patient's care needs with the appropriate intensity of services.

sections.triggerCriteria: Considered during discharge planning when a patient cannot safely go straight home or needs ongoing skilled care, rehabilitation, or supervision.
sections.steps: Common options, from lower to higher intensity, include home with home health services (intermittent skilled nursing and therapy), skilled nursing facility (SNF) for short-term rehab and skilled care, inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) for intensive daily therapy in patients who can tolerate it, and long-term acute care hospital (LTACH) for medically complex patients needing extended hospital-level care. Match the setting to the patient's medical and functional needs and therapy tolerance, verify insurance coverage and qualifying criteria, and coordinate the transfer and records.

concepts.name: Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
concepts.shortExplanation: Nausea and vomiting occurring in the first day or so after anesthesia and surgery. It is one of the most common and distressing complications for surgical patients.

sections.presentation: Nausea, retching, and vomiting in the recovery unit or on the ward after surgery, which can delay discharge and, rarely, cause aspiration or wound strain.
sections.typicalTreatments: Multimodal prophylaxis and treatment with antiemetics from different classes (for example a serotonin antagonist plus dexamethasone), reducing opioids with multimodal analgesia, adequate hydration, and using regional or total IV anesthesia in high-risk patients.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex, nonsmoking status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioid use are the main risk factors (Apfel score); volatile anesthetics, nitrous oxide, and certain surgery types also increase risk.

concepts.name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
concepts.shortExplanation: Excessive bleeding after childbirth, a leading cause of maternal death that requires rapid recognition and treatment.

sections.presentation: Heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery, a soft (boggy) or poorly contracted uterus, passage of large clots, and signs of blood loss such as tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: The cause is often summarized as the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony, the most common), Trauma (lacerations), Tissue (retained placenta), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management includes firm fundal massage, uterotonic medications (oxytocin, methylergonovine, misoprostol, carboprost), IV fluids and blood products, and procedures such as uterine tamponade or surgery if bleeding continues.
sections.riskFactors: Uterine atony, prolonged or induced labor, overdistended uterus (large baby, twins, polyhydramnios), retained placenta, operative delivery, and clotting disorders.

concepts.name: Postrenal AKI
concepts.shortExplanation: Acute kidney injury from obstruction of urine outflow anywhere from the tubules to the urethra. The distinguishing feature is that relieving the obstruction can rapidly restore function, so it must not be missed.

sections.presentation: Rising creatinine with decreased or fluctuating urine output; a distended bladder or high post-void residual on bladder scan points to lower-tract obstruction. Common causes include BPH, stones, tumors, and clots.
sections.typicalTreatments: Relieve the obstruction: bladder catheterization for outlet obstruction, or ureteral stent/nephrostomy for upper-tract blockage. Watch for post-obstructive diuresis afterward, with large urine output and electrolyte shifts requiring replacement.
sections.riskFactors: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, nephrolithiasis, pelvic or GU malignancy, neurogenic bladder, and blocked or clamped urinary catheters.

concepts.name: Potassium
concepts.shortExplanation: An electrolyte critical for heart and muscle function — closely monitored in patients on diuretics.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low: muscle weakness, arrhythmia risk — common with loop diuretics. High: cardiac arrhythmia risk.

concepts.name: Potassium Chloride
concepts.shortExplanation: Furosemide causes the body to lose potassium along with fluid, so this tops it back up to a safe level.

sections.mechanism: Electrolyte replacement. IV formulations must always be diluted and infused at a controlled rate.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset (oral form), infusion site discomfort (IV form).
sections.adverseEffects: Cardiac arrhythmia if infused too quickly or given undiluted IV.
sections.nursingImplications: Verify potassium level and renal function before administering.

concepts.name: Prednisone
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation and calm the immune system in many conditions, including COPD and asthma flares.

sections.mechanism: A glucocorticoid that broadly suppresses inflammation and immune activity.
sections.sideEffects: Increased appetite, insomnia, mood changes, fluid retention, elevated blood glucose.
sections.adverseEffects: With prolonged use: high blood sugar, infection risk, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, GI ulcers, and muscle wasting.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food. Do not stop abruptly after prolonged use; taper as ordered. Monitor blood glucose and for signs of infection.

concepts.name: Preeclampsia
concepts.shortExplanation: A pregnancy complication of new high blood pressure with signs of organ stress (such as protein in the urine) after 20 weeks of gestation.

sections.presentation: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or other end-organ signs. Warning features include severe headache, visual changes (blurring, flashing lights), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, rapid swelling, and shortness of breath.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease, antihypertensives such as labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine for dangerous blood pressures, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm, and ultimately delivery, which is the definitive treatment.
sections.riskFactors: First pregnancy, prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, obesity, multiple gestation, and extremes of maternal age.

concepts.name: Pregabalin
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral medication for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and as an add-on for seizures.

sections.mechanism: Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing release of excitatory neurotransmitters and dampening abnormal nerve signaling.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, drowsiness, peripheral edema, weight gain, and blurred vision.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants, mood changes, and dependence with withdrawal on abrupt discontinuation; it is a controlled substance.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess pain and sedation and fall risk. Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid withdrawal. Use cautiously with opioids and adjust dose in renal impairment. Teach caution with driving.

concepts.name: Preoperative Fasting (NPO)
concepts.shortExplanation: Withholding food and drink for a set time before anesthesia to reduce the risk of stomach contents being aspirated into the lungs. It is often shortened to NPO, meaning nothing by mouth.

sections.triggerCriteria: Applies to patients scheduled for anesthesia or sedation. Standard minimum fasting times for healthy patients are about 2 hours for clear liquids, 6 hours for a light meal or non-human milk, and 8 hours or more for fried or fatty foods and full meals.
sections.steps: Confirm and document the last oral intake, clarify NPO status with the anesthesia team, and hold or clarify oral medications per orders (many are taken with a sip of water). Encourage clear fluids up to the allowed window to avoid unnecessary dehydration, verify NPO before transport, and reassess if surgery is delayed. Watch for aspiration risk in emergencies, pregnancy, obesity, diabetes with gastroparesis, and bowel obstruction.

concepts.name: Prerenal AKI
concepts.shortExplanation: Acute kidney injury from reduced blood flow to otherwise healthy kidneys - the most common and most reversible type. Distinguished from intrinsic AKI by intact tubular function that avidly conserves sodium and water.

sections.presentation: Rising BUN and creatinine, often oliguria, in the setting of hypovolemia, low cardiac output, or hypotension. Labs classically show BUN:creatinine ratio over 20:1, FENa under 1%, and urine sodium under 20 mEq/L, reflecting preserved tubular reabsorption.
sections.typicalTreatments: Restore perfusion: volume repletion for hypovolemia, hemodynamic support for low output, and stop nephrotoxins including NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs. Prompt correction usually reverses it before it progresses to acute tubular necrosis.
sections.riskFactors: Dehydration, hemorrhage, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis, and drugs that impair renal autoregulation (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics).

concepts.name: Pressure Injury
concepts.shortExplanation: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue from sustained pressure over a bony prominence, staged by depth.

sections.presentation: Staged as: Stage 1 (intact skin with non-blanchable redness), Stage 2 (partial-thickness loss or blister), Stage 3 (full-thickness loss into fat), and Stage 4 (exposed muscle, tendon, or bone). Unstageable wounds are covered by slough or eschar; deep tissue injury shows persistent maroon or purple discoloration.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pressure redistribution with repositioning and support surfaces, offloading, moisture and nutrition management, stage-appropriate dressings, and debridement of nonviable tissue.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, poor nutrition, moisture and incontinence, friction and shear, reduced sensation, and poor perfusion; risk is screened with tools such as the Braden scale.

concepts.name: Prior Authorization
concepts.shortExplanation: A requirement by an insurer to approve a medication, test, procedure, or level of care before it will be covered. Delays in authorization can hold up treatment and discharge.

sections.triggerCriteria: Required by many insurance plans for certain high-cost drugs, imaging, procedures, durable medical equipment, and post-acute placements before the service is delivered or covered.
sections.steps: Identify services that need authorization early, submit the clinical documentation supporting medical necessity, and track the request to approval or denial. If denied, pursue peer-to-peer review or appeal, or arrange a covered alternative. Case managers coordinate with providers, pharmacy, and the payer, communicate expected timelines, and work to prevent authorization delays from postponing care or discharge.

concepts.name: Procalcitonin
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood marker that tends to rise with serious bacterial infection, sometimes used to support decisions about starting or stopping antibiotics.

sections.normalRange: Typically low (often under about 0.1 ng/mL) in healthy people; interpretation depends on the clinical context and the lab's reference thresholds.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher levels are associated with bacterial infection and sepsis, and a falling trend can support de-escalating or stopping antibiotics. It is less elevated in most viral infections. It is an adjunct only and should never replace clinical judgment or cultures; it can rise in non-infectious conditions such as major trauma or surgery.

concepts.name: Promethazine
concepts.shortExplanation: A first-generation antihistamine used for nausea and vomiting, motion sickness, allergies, and sedation.

sections.mechanism: Blocks histamine H1 receptors and central dopamine receptors, giving antihistamine, antiemetic, and sedative effects.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and blurred vision.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe tissue injury and gangrene if extravasated or given intra-arterially, so IV use is high-risk; respiratory depression in young children (contraindicated under age 2), extrapyramidal symptoms, and anticholinergic effects.
sections.nursingImplications: For IV use, dilute well, give slowly through a running line, and monitor the site closely for burning or pain, stopping immediately if it occurs. Assess sedation and fall risk. Avoid in very young children.

concepts.name: Propofol
concepts.shortExplanation: A fast-acting IV sedative-hypnotic used for procedural sedation, induction of anesthesia, and continuous sedation of intubated patients.

sections.mechanism: Enhances inhibitory GABA-A receptor activity in the brain, producing rapid sedation and hypnosis. Very short-acting, so sedation deepens or lightens quickly when the infusion rate changes.
sections.sideEffects: Dose-dependent hypotension, respiratory depression, apnea, pain at the injection site, and green-tinged urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Propofol infusion syndrome (rare but often fatal) with prolonged high-dose use: metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and cardiac failure. Formulated in a lipid emulsion, so it adds calories and can raise triglycerides.
sections.nursingImplications: Requires continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway support. Titrate to a sedation goal (RASS). Change the bottle and tubing per protocol (usually every 12 hours) because the lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth. Monitor triglycerides on prolonged infusions.

concepts.name: Prothrombin Time (PT)
concepts.shortExplanation: A clotting test that measures the extrinsic and common pathways; standardized as the INR to monitor warfarin.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 11-13.5 seconds (lab dependent); reported with the INR.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A prolonged PT suggests warfarin effect, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, or clotting-factor deficiency. It reflects factors I, II, V, VII, and X. Paired with aPTT, it helps localize a bleeding or clotting abnormality.

concepts.name: Pulmonary Embolism
concepts.shortExplanation: A blockage in a lung artery, usually caused by a blood clot that traveled from the legs (DVT) — a potentially life-threatening emergency.

sections.presentation: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain (often pleuritic), tachycardia, low oxygen saturation, sometimes hemoptysis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin, then often transitioned to an oral anticoagulant), thrombolytics in severe/massive PE, supportive oxygen therapy.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, DVT history, cancer, pregnancy, clotting disorders.

concepts.name: Pulmonary Function Test (PFT)
concepts.shortExplanation: A set of breathing tests, usually spirometry, that measure lung volumes and airflow to diagnose and classify lung disease.

sections.targetConcern: Diagnoses and monitors obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) versus restrictive disease by measuring values such as FEV1, FVC, and the FEV1/FVC ratio; often repeated after a bronchodilator to assess reversibility.
sections.whatToMonitor: During testing watch for dizziness, lightheadedness, or bronchospasm from repeated forced breathing. Hold short-acting bronchodilators before the test if reversibility is being assessed and per protocol. Ensure the patient is rested afterward and reassess respiratory status.

concepts.name: Pulmonary Hypertension
concepts.shortExplanation: Elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries that strains the right heart and can progress to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

sections.presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope, a loud pulmonic heart sound, and signs of right heart failure such as jugular venous distension, ascites, and peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause (left heart disease, lung disease, chronic PE); pulmonary vasodilators for select types; diuretics for volume overload; and long-term oxygen for hypoxemia.
sections.riskFactors: Left heart failure, COPD and chronic lung disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, obstructive sleep apnea, connective tissue disease, and certain congenital heart defects.

concepts.name: Pulse Oximeter
concepts.shortExplanation: A noninvasive sensor, usually clipped to a finger, that estimates blood oxygen saturation and heart rate.

sections.purpose: Continuously or intermittently measures oxygen saturation (SpO2) to detect hypoxemia and guide oxygen therapy. It is a core vital sign on nearly every unit.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure a good waveform or signal; poor perfusion, motion, cold digits, and nail polish cause false readings. It cannot detect carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal) and may read less accurately at low saturations and on darker skin tones. Correlate a surprising value with the patient's clinical picture before acting.

concepts.name: Pulse Oximetry
concepts.shortExplanation: A noninvasive sensor that estimates blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate by shining light through a fingertip, toe, or earlobe.

sections.purpose: Provides continuous or spot-check measurement of oxygen saturation, allowing rapid detection of hypoxemia and titration of oxygen therapy. Normal SpO2 is generally 95-100 percent (often 88-92 percent target in chronic CO2 retainers).
sections.careConsiderations: Accuracy is reduced by poor perfusion, motion, nail polish, cold extremities, and severe anemia. It cannot detect carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal) and does not measure ventilation/CO2. Rotate probe sites to prevent skin/pressure injury and correlate readings with the patient's clinical picture and, when needed, an ABG.

concepts.name: qSOFA
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid three-point bedside screen that flags patients with suspected infection who are at higher risk of poor outcomes.

sections.purpose: Quickly identifies patients with suspected infection who are at higher risk of sepsis-related deterioration and death, without needing lab tests.
sections.steps: Three criteria, each worth 1 point: respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mental status (GCS under 15), and systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less; total 0-3.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A score of 2 or more identifies patients at greater risk of poor outcomes and should prompt closer assessment and consideration of sepsis. It is a screen, not a diagnosis.

concepts.name: Quetiapine
concepts.shortExplanation: An atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and as add-on for depression, often sedating at low doses.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, and its antihistamine activity contributes to sedation.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Metabolic effects (weight gain, high glucose and lipids), QT prolongation, extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia (less than older agents), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor for orthostatic hypotension and fall risk, especially early. Track weight, glucose, and lipids on ongoing therapy. Watch for extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid abrupt discontinuation.

concepts.name: Racemic Epinephrine
concepts.shortExplanation: A nebulized form of epinephrine used to quickly shrink swollen upper airway tissues in children with croup or stridor.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors to constrict blood vessels in the airway mucosa, reducing swelling and easing airflow.
sections.sideEffects: Transient tachycardia, tremor, pallor, and jitteriness.
sections.adverseEffects: Rebound airway swelling can occur as the drug wears off, so children need observation after treatment before discharge.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by nebulizer for moderate to severe stridor. Monitor heart rate, respiratory effort, and oxygen saturation, and observe the child for a period after administration to watch for return of stridor.

concepts.name: Radiation Therapy
concepts.shortExplanation: The use of high-energy radiation to destroy or shrink cancer cells in a targeted area of the body. It can be curative, given with chemotherapy, or used to relieve symptoms such as pain.

sections.targetConcern: Damages the DNA of cancer cells in the treated field so they cannot grow and divide, while sparing surrounding tissue as much as possible; it is often given as a series of daily treatments.
sections.whatToMonitor: Site-specific effects depending on the area treated, such as skin redness and breakdown in the field, fatigue, mucositis and difficulty swallowing with head, neck, or chest treatment, diarrhea with abdominal or pelvic treatment, and low blood counts. Provide gentle skin care in the treated area, protect it from sun and irritation, and manage fatigue and local symptoms.

concepts.name: Rapid Response Team
concepts.shortExplanation: A dedicated team called to the bedside when a patient shows early signs of deterioration, aiming to intervene before a full cardiac or respiratory arrest.

sections.triggerCriteria: Acute changes in vital signs or condition, such as a marked rise or fall in heart rate, respiratory rate, or blood pressure, falling oxygen saturation, new altered mental status, decreased urine output, or simply staff or family concern that the patient is deteriorating.
sections.steps: Any staff member activates the team. The responders (often ICU nurse, respiratory therapist, and provider) rapidly assess airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status, begin interventions such as oxygen, fluids, or medications, order labs and imaging, and decide on escalation - including transfer to a higher level of care - while communicating with the primary team.

concepts.name: Rapid Sequence Intubation
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid method to secure the airway by giving a sedative and a paralytic almost simultaneously, then placing a breathing tube, used in emergencies to reduce the risk of aspiration.

sections.targetConcern: Quickly and safely securing a definitive airway in patients who need intubation but are at risk of vomiting and aspiration, such as those with full stomachs, trauma, or respiratory failure.
sections.whatToMonitor: Continuous pulse oximetry and waveform capnography to confirm tube placement, heart rate and blood pressure, and end-tidal CO2. After placement, confirm tube position, secure the tube, monitor ventilation and sedation, and obtain a chest X-ray to verify depth.

concepts.name: Rapid-Acting Insulin (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: The mealtime bolus insulins (lispro, aspart, glulisine) with the fastest onset and shortest duration. Their defining nursing rule: give with the meal and hold if the patient is not eating.

sections.mechanism: Insulin analogs modified to absorb quickly for prandial coverage. Onset is roughly 15 minutes, peak about 1 hour, and duration 3 to 5 hours - the quickest and shortest of all insulins.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia, particularly early after the dose if the meal is delayed or missed; hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Dose right before eating and confirm the patient will eat. These are the analogs used in insulin pumps and correction (sliding-scale) dosing. Clear solutions; do not confuse with basal insulins.

concepts.name: RASS Sedation Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A 10-point scale for rating a patient's level of agitation or sedation, used to titrate sedatives in ventilated and critically ill patients.

sections.purpose: Standardizes assessment of agitation and depth of sedation so sedatives can be titrated to a target, most often in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
sections.steps: A single score from +4 (combative) through 0 (alert and calm) down to -5 (unarousable). Positive scores describe agitation; negative scores describe increasing sedation based on response to voice then physical stimulation.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Positive scores indicate agitation needing attention; -1 to -3 is light to moderate sedation; -4 to -5 is deep sedation or unarousable. A common goal is a light target (around 0 to -2) unless deeper sedation is clinically required.

concepts.name: Readmission Risk Reduction
concepts.shortExplanation: Efforts to identify patients likely to return to the hospital soon after discharge and to prevent it. Reducing avoidable readmissions improves outcomes and lowers costs.

sections.triggerCriteria: Screen patients for readmission risk during the admission. Higher-risk features include multiple chronic conditions, prior recent admissions, polypharmacy, older age, mental health or substance use issues, limited health literacy or social support, and unstable housing or finances.
sections.steps: Target high-risk patients with enhanced interventions: careful medication reconciliation, clear teach-back education on the condition and warning signs, timely follow-up appointments, follow-up phone calls after discharge, connection to home health or community resources, and attention to social barriers such as transportation and medication cost. Ensure a warm handoff to outpatient and post-acute providers so nothing falls through the cracks.

concepts.name: Regular Insulin
concepts.shortExplanation: Short-acting human insulin and the only insulin that can be given IV, making it the workhorse for DKA drips and hyperkalemia. Its slower onset and longer tail than rapid-acting analogs mean it is dosed about 30 minutes before meals.

sections.mechanism: Human insulin that lowers glucose by driving cellular uptake, promoting glycogen synthesis, and suppressing hepatic glucose production. Given subcutaneously, onset is about 30 minutes, peak 2 to 3 hours, and duration 5 to 8 hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia (risk greatest around the 2-3 hour peak) and hypokalemia, since insulin drives potassium into cells.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously 30 minutes before meals; it is a clear solution. Only regular insulin may be given IV (DKA, hyperkalemia) - monitor glucose and potassium closely on a drip. When mixing with NPH, draw up the clear regular insulin first, then the cloudy NPH.

concepts.name: Respiratory Acidosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A drop in blood pH from inadequate ventilation causing CO2 retention (hypercapnia); the lungs fail to blow off enough carbon dioxide.

sections.presentation: Low pH with high PaCO2 on ABG. Signs include headache, drowsiness, confusion, flushed skin, and (in acute cases) somnolence progressing to CO2 narcosis. Chronic cases show renal compensation with elevated bicarbonate.
sections.typicalTreatments: Improve ventilation: bronchodilators, reversal of sedation/opioids (naloxone), noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP), or intubation. Treat the underlying cause of hypoventilation.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, respiratory depression from opioids or sedatives, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall disorders, and airway obstruction.

concepts.name: Respiratory Alkalosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A rise in blood pH from excessive ventilation that blows off too much CO2 (hypocapnia), often from hyperventilation.

sections.presentation: High pH with low PaCO2 on ABG. Signs include lightheadedness, perioral and fingertip numbness/tingling, carpopedal spasm, and anxiety. Often triggered by rapid breathing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause of hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, hypoxemia, sepsis, PE). Reassurance and coached slow breathing help anxiety-driven cases; correct hypoxemia if present.
sections.riskFactors: Anxiety/panic, pain, fever, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, high altitude, pregnancy, and salicylate toxicity.

concepts.name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
concepts.shortExplanation: Abnormal growth of blood vessels in the eyes of premature infants that, if severe, can lead to retinal detachment and blindness.

sections.presentation: There are no outward symptoms; the condition is found on screening dilated eye exams performed on at-risk preterm infants. Disease is graded by stage and location within the retina.
sections.typicalTreatments: Many mild cases resolve on their own with monitoring. Advanced disease is treated with laser therapy or anti-VEGF injections to prevent retinal detachment. Careful oxygen management helps reduce the risk.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, prolonged or high supplemental oxygen exposure, and unstable oxygen saturations.

concepts.name: Rho(D) Immune Globulin
concepts.shortExplanation: An injection given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent their immune system from making antibodies against an Rh-positive baby's blood, which protects future pregnancies.

sections.mechanism: Provides passive anti-D antibodies that bind and clear any Rh-positive fetal red cells before the mother's immune system is sensitized to them.
sections.sideEffects: Soreness at the injection site, low-grade fever.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic/hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon.
sections.nursingImplications: Typically given intramuscularly around 28 weeks and again within 72 hours after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive, and after events like miscarriage, amniocentesis, or trauma. Verify maternal Rh-negative status and antibody screen before giving. It prevents sensitization but does not treat existing antibodies.

concepts.name: Rifaximin
concepts.shortExplanation: A poorly absorbed antibiotic that acts in the gut. Used to reduce recurrence of hepatic encephalopathy and to treat travelers' diarrhea and IBS with diarrhea.

sections.mechanism: A non-systemic antibiotic that stays largely within the gut, reducing ammonia-producing bacteria in the colon.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, bloating, dizziness, and peripheral edema; generally well tolerated because little is absorbed.
sections.adverseEffects: Rarely C. difficile infection; hypersensitivity reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Used with lactulose to lower the risk of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy. Can be taken with or without food. Monitor mental status.

concepts.name: Right-Sided Heart Failure
concepts.shortExplanation: Heart failure in which the right ventricle fails, causing blood to back up into the body. The hallmark is systemic congestion - peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and hepatic congestion - most often triggered by left-sided failure or lung disease (cor pulmonale).

sections.presentation: Systemic venous congestion: dependent peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly and right-upper-quadrant fullness, ascites, weight gain, and nausea/anorexia from gut congestion. Lungs are typically clear unless left-sided failure coexists.
sections.typicalTreatments: Diuretics to relieve systemic congestion, treatment of the underlying cause (left-sided heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, COPD, or acute PE), and optimization of volume status. Daily weights, intake/output, abdominal girth for ascites, and edema monitoring. When caused by chronic lung disease it is termed cor pulmonale; managing hypoxia and the lung disease is central.
sections.riskFactors: Left-sided heart failure (the most common cause), pulmonary hypertension, chronic lung disease (COPD), pulmonary embolism, and right ventricular infarction.

concepts.name: Risperidone
concepts.shortExplanation: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and irritability associated with autism.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors to reduce psychotic and mood symptoms.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain, dizziness, and increased prolactin, which can cause breast changes or menstrual irregularities.
sections.adverseEffects: Higher rates of extrapyramidal symptoms and prolactin elevation than some other atypicals, metabolic changes, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor for movement disorders, orthostatic hypotension, weight, glucose, and lipids, and ask about prolactin-related symptoms. A long-acting injectable form exists for adherence. Assess for signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

concepts.name: Rivaroxaban
concepts.shortExplanation: A direct oral anticoagulant (factor Xa inhibitor) used to prevent stroke in atrial fibrillation and to treat and prevent venous thromboembolism.

sections.mechanism: Directly inhibits factor Xa in the clotting cascade, reducing thrombin generation and clot formation without requiring routine coagulation monitoring.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding, and nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding, including gastrointestinal and intracranial hemorrhage; increased clotting risk if stopped abruptly, and higher spinal hematoma risk with neuraxial procedures.
sections.nursingImplications: Give treatment doses with food for absorption. Monitor for bleeding and do not stop abruptly without provider guidance. Andexanet alfa is a reversal agent for life-threatening bleeding. Assess renal function and review interacting drugs.

concepts.name: Rocuronium
concepts.shortExplanation: A non-depolarizing paralytic that relaxes skeletal muscle to enable intubation and mechanical ventilation. It does not provide any sedation or pain relief.

sections.mechanism: Competitively blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, preventing muscle contraction. Rapid onset makes it a common choice for rapid sequence intubation.
sections.sideEffects: Prolonged paralysis if metabolism is impaired; injection-site discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Complete inability to breathe or move while the drug is active - the patient must be ventilated. Awareness with paralysis if sedation and analgesia are inadequate; rare anaphylaxis.
sections.nursingImplications: Never give without adequate sedation and analgesia - the patient can be fully aware but unable to move. Ensure the airway is secured and ventilation is controlled. Sugammadex reverses rocuronium; monitor recovery with a train-of-four nerve stimulator.

concepts.name: Scopolamine
concepts.shortExplanation: An anticholinergic drug used to dry up excess secretions and to prevent nausea and motion sickness. In hospice it is often used to reduce noisy respiratory secretions (the death rattle) near the end of life.

sections.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing secretions from salivary and respiratory glands and dampening the nausea and vomiting pathways.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, drowsiness, urinary retention, and constipation.
sections.adverseEffects: Confusion, delirium, and agitation (especially in older adults), tachycardia, and worsening of narrow-angle glaucoma.
sections.nursingImplications: Available as a transdermal patch and other forms. For end-of-life secretions, combine with repositioning and reassure the family that the sound is usually not distressing to the patient. Monitor for anticholinergic effects such as confusion and urinary retention, and keep the patch away from the eyes (wash hands after handling).

concepts.name: Second-Degree AV Block
concepts.shortExplanation: Intermittent failure of AV conduction so some P waves do not reach the ventricles; includes Mobitz I (Wenckebach) and the more dangerous Mobitz II.

sections.presentation: Mobitz I shows progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped and is often benign. Mobitz II shows dropped beats without PR prolongation and can progress abruptly to complete block; may cause fatigue, dizziness, or syncope.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mobitz I usually needs only monitoring and medication review. Mobitz II often requires a permanent pacemaker; use atropine cautiously and transcutaneous pacing for symptomatic bradycardia while awaiting a pacemaker.
sections.riskFactors: Myocardial ischemia/infarction (especially inferior for Mobitz I, anterior for Mobitz II), AV-nodal blocking drugs, increased vagal tone, and conduction system disease.

concepts.name: Semaglutide
concepts.shortExplanation: A GLP-1 receptor agonist used for type 2 diabetes and, at higher doses, for weight management, given by weekly injection or daily tablet.

sections.mechanism: Mimics the incretin hormone GLP-1: stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and increases satiety.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and decreased appetite, usually greatest when the dose is increased.
sections.adverseEffects: Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, and a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents; low hypoglycemia risk alone but higher when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
sections.nursingImplications: Inject subcutaneously once weekly (or give the oral form on an empty stomach with a sip of water). Titrate slowly to limit GI effects. Teach patients to report severe abdominal pain. Hold per protocol before procedures because delayed gastric emptying raises aspiration risk.

concepts.name: Senna
concepts.shortExplanation: A stimulant laxative used for constipation, including opioid-induced constipation.

sections.mechanism: A plant-derived stimulant laxative whose active compounds irritate the intestinal lining to increase peristalsis and fluid secretion into the bowel.
sections.sideEffects: Abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and harmless brown discoloration of the urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Fluid and electrolyte loss with overuse, and dependence on the laxative with chronic use.
sections.nursingImplications: Often paired with a stool softener for opioid-induced constipation. Give at bedtime because effect typically occurs in 6 to 12 hours. Encourage fluids and monitor for cramping and diarrhea.

concepts.name: Sepsis
concepts.shortExplanation: A life-threatening response to infection that can lead to organ dysfunction and shock if not treated quickly.

sections.presentation: Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension in severe cases (septic shock).
sections.typicalTreatments: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if hypotension persists, source control of the underlying infection.
sections.riskFactors: Immunosuppression, indwelling catheters/lines, recent surgery, advanced age, chronic illness.

concepts.name: Sepsis Bundle
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized set of time-sensitive actions performed when sepsis is suspected, designed to improve survival by acting quickly.

sections.triggerCriteria: Suspected infection plus signs of organ dysfunction or meeting systemic inflammatory criteria, per unit/hospital sepsis screening tool.
sections.steps: Draw blood cultures before antibiotics, measure lactate, start broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, begin IV fluid resuscitation, reassess and add vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluids.

concepts.name: Septic Shock
concepts.shortExplanation: The most severe form of sepsis, where infection causes dangerously low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion that persist despite fluids and require vasopressors.

sections.presentation: Signs of infection plus persistent low blood pressure needing vasopressors to maintain perfusion, an elevated lactate, fever or low temperature, fast heart rate, altered mental status, mottled skin, and low urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Early broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures, IV fluid resuscitation, and vasopressors (norepinephrine first) to maintain a mean arterial pressure goal; source control; and serial lactate measurement following the sepsis bundle.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, immunosuppression, chronic illness, recent surgery or invasive devices, and untreated or severe infection.

concepts.name: Sequential Compression Device (SCD)
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflatable leg sleeves that squeeze the calves in a cycle to promote venous return and prevent blood clots.

sections.purpose: Provides mechanical prophylaxis against deep vein thrombosis in immobile or postoperative patients by mimicking the calf muscle pump and reducing venous stasis. Used alone when anticoagulation is contraindicated, or with it for higher-risk patients.
sections.careConsiderations: Apply correctly sized sleeves and keep them on except during ambulation, hygiene, and skin checks. Assess skin and neurovascular status, and do not apply over an existing DVT or ischemic limb. Reinforce that they only work when actually worn and connected.

concepts.name: Serotonin Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A potentially life-threatening reaction from too much serotonin activity, usually from combining serotonergic medications.

sections.presentation: A triad of mental status changes (agitation, confusion), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, high blood pressure, sweating, dilated pupils), and neuromuscular abnormalities (tremor, hyperreflexia, and clonus that is often more pronounced in the legs). Onset is usually rapid, within hours of a change in serotonergic drugs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop all serotonergic agents, provide supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, control agitation and muscle rigidity with benzodiazepines, and use cyproheptadine as a serotonin blocker in more severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, certain opioids like tramadol, triptans, linezolid), overdose, or adding a new serotonergic agent.

concepts.name: Sertraline
concepts.shortExplanation: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used to treat depression and various anxiety disorders.

sections.mechanism: Blocks reuptake of serotonin in the brain, increasing its availability to improve mood and anxiety over time.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, insomnia or drowsiness, and sexual dysfunction; gastrointestinal effects often ease after the first weeks.
sections.adverseEffects: Serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, increased bleeding risk, hyponatremia, and a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children, adolescents, and young adults early in treatment.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach that full benefit takes several weeks, so adherence matters. Monitor mood and for emerging suicidal thoughts, especially early on. Do not stop abruptly to avoid discontinuation symptoms, and review other medications for serotonergic interactions.

concepts.name: Serum Amylase
concepts.shortExplanation: An enzyme from the pancreas and salivary glands that rises in pancreatitis; less specific than lipase.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 30-110 U/L (assay dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated amylase supports acute pancreatitis but can also rise with salivary gland disease, bowel obstruction, and kidney impairment. Because lipase is more specific, amylase is now often used as a supporting rather than primary test.

concepts.name: Serum Bicarbonate (CO2)
concepts.shortExplanation: The bicarbonate (often reported as CO2) on a metabolic panel reflects the body's acid-base buffer status.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis (as in DKA, sepsis, renal failure, or diarrhea) or respiratory compensation for alkalosis. High bicarbonate suggests metabolic alkalosis (as with vomiting or diuretics) or compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis such as COPD.

concepts.name: Serum Calcium (Total)
concepts.shortExplanation: Total blood calcium supports bones, nerves, muscle contraction, and clotting; results should be interpreted with the albumin level.

sections.normalRange: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (varies slightly by lab).
sections.abnormalMeaning: High calcium (hypercalcemia) is often from hyperparathyroidism or malignancy and causes fatigue, constipation, confusion, and kidney stones. Low calcium (hypocalcemia) can follow kidney disease, low vitamin D, or thyroid surgery and causes numbness, tingling, and muscle spasms. Low albumin lowers total calcium without lowering the active (ionized) fraction.

concepts.name: Serum Chloride
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood electrolyte that moves with sodium and helps maintain acid-base and fluid balance.

sections.abnormalMeaning: High chloride (hyperchloremia) is often seen with dehydration, large-volume normal saline infusion, and metabolic acidosis. Low chloride (hypochloremia) can occur with vomiting, gastric suction, and some diuretics. It is usually interpreted alongside sodium, bicarbonate, and the anion gap.

concepts.name: Serum Lipase
concepts.shortExplanation: A pancreatic enzyme that is the preferred blood test for diagnosing acute pancreatitis.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0-160 U/L (assay dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A lipase three or more times the upper limit of normal strongly supports acute pancreatitis. Lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase. The degree of elevation does not predict severity of the pancreatitis.

concepts.name: Serum Sodium
concepts.shortExplanation: The main electrolyte in the blood outside cells; it tracks the body's water and salt balance.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low (hyponatremia) often reflects fluid overload, SIADH, diuretics, or heart/liver/kidney disease and can cause confusion or seizures. High (hypernatremia) usually reflects water loss or dehydration and causes thirst, lethargy, and irritability. Sodium should be corrected slowly to avoid brain injury.

concepts.name: Sevelamer
concepts.shortExplanation: A phosphate binder taken with meals to lower high phosphate levels in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients.

sections.mechanism: A non-calcium binder that traps dietary phosphate in the gut so it passes in the stool rather than being absorbed.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, bloating, constipation or diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: GI intolerance; rare bowel obstruction with prior GI motility problems.
sections.nursingImplications: Must be taken with meals to work. Separate from certain other oral medications. Monitor phosphate and calcium levels.

concepts.name: Sevoflurane
concepts.shortExplanation: An inhaled volatile anesthetic used to induce and maintain general anesthesia. It is well tolerated for mask induction, especially in children.

sections.mechanism: A halogenated volatile agent that enhances inhibitory neurotransmission (largely GABA-A) in the central nervous system to produce unconsciousness and amnesia; dose is titrated by inhaled concentration.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, respiratory depression, and postoperative nausea and vomiting; emergence agitation, particularly in children.
sections.adverseEffects: A known trigger of malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients; dose-dependent cardiorespiratory depression.
