sections.nursingImplications: Delivered by the anesthesia team through an anesthesia machine and scavenging system. Monitor airway, ventilation, blood pressure, and temperature, and watch for signs of malignant hyperthermia such as rising end-tidal CO2 and rigidity.

concepts.name: Short-Acting Insulin (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: Regular human insulin - the class given about 30 minutes before meals and the only insulin that can be given IV. Its slower onset and longer tail set it apart from the rapid-acting analogs.

sections.mechanism: Unmodified human insulin for prandial coverage. Given subcutaneously, onset is about 30 minutes, peak 2 to 3 hours, and duration 5 to 8 hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reactions and weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypoglycemia around the 2-3 hour peak; hypokalemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Administer 30 minutes before meals. This is the class used IV for DKA drips and hyperkalemia - monitor glucose and potassium. Clear solution; may be mixed with NPH (clear before cloudy).

concepts.name: Simethicone
concepts.shortExplanation: An over-the-counter anti-gas agent that relieves bloating and pressure from excess gastrointestinal gas.

sections.mechanism: An antifoaming agent that lowers the surface tension of gas bubbles so they coalesce and are more easily passed; it is not absorbed systemically.
sections.sideEffects: Generally none; occasional mild loose stools.
sections.adverseEffects: Essentially none because it is not absorbed; it does not prevent gas formation, only helps eliminate trapped gas.
sections.nursingImplications: Give after meals and at bedtime as needed. Chewable tablets should be chewed thoroughly. Often used for postoperative or functional bloating; set expectations that it relieves symptoms rather than treating an underlying cause.

concepts.name: Simple Face Mask
concepts.shortExplanation: A soft mask covering the nose and mouth that delivers moderate-concentration oxygen at medium flow rates.

sections.purpose: Delivers roughly 40-60 percent FiO2 at flows of about 5-10 L/min for patients needing more oxygen than a nasal cannula provides.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep flow at least 5-6 L/min to flush exhaled CO2 from the mask and prevent rebreathing. Watch for skin breakdown at the ears, nose bridge, and cheeks. The mask must be removed for eating and drinking, so plan care around it.

concepts.name: Sliding-Scale Insulin
concepts.shortExplanation: An ordered plan in which the dose of rapid- or short-acting insulin increases as the measured blood glucose rises.

sections.triggerCriteria: Scheduled blood glucose checks (commonly before meals and at bedtime) that map to a prescribed insulin dose, with larger doses at higher glucose values.
sections.steps: Check glucose at the ordered times, give the corresponding insulin dose per the order, treat and recheck for hypoglycemia if low, and document. It is usually paired with scheduled basal insulin; reactive sliding scale alone is discouraged for ongoing diabetes control.

concepts.name: Small Bowel Obstruction
concepts.shortExplanation: A blockage of the small intestine that stops the normal passage of contents, causing pain, vomiting, and distension.

sections.presentation: Crampy abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or gas; bowel sounds may be high-pitched then absent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest (nothing by mouth), a nasogastric tube for decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction. Surgery is needed for strangulation or if it does not resolve.
sections.riskFactors: Prior abdominal surgery (adhesions), hernias, tumors, and Crohn disease.

concepts.name: Social Determinants of Health
concepts.shortExplanation: The non-medical conditions in which people live and work that strongly influence their health, such as housing, food, income, and access to care. Addressing them is central to case management and reducing readmissions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Screen all patients, and especially those with frequent admissions, poor disease control, or complex social situations, for unmet social needs that could undermine their care plan.
sections.steps: Key domains include economic stability, housing and neighborhood safety, food security, education and health literacy, transportation, and access to health care and social support. Use a screening tool to identify needs, then connect patients to resources such as financial assistance, medication and food programs, transportation, home services, and community organizations. Tailor discharge plans to real-world barriers and document and communicate needs so the care team can follow up.

concepts.name: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
concepts.shortExplanation: A resin given by mouth or rectally that removes potassium through the stool to treat high potassium.

sections.mechanism: A cation-exchange resin that binds potassium in the gut in exchange for sodium, which is then eliminated in the stool.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, nausea, anorexia.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare intestinal necrosis, particularly after surgery or with bowel disease; adds a sodium load.
sections.nursingImplications: Works slowly and is not for emergency lowering of potassium. Assess bowel function and ensure the patient can have a bowel movement. Monitor potassium and sodium. Newer binders such as patiromer are also used.

concepts.name: Spinal Anesthesia
concepts.shortExplanation: A single injection of local anesthetic into the cerebrospinal fluid of the lower back that numbs the lower body for surgery. It is common for cesarean sections, and lower-abdominal, pelvic, and lower-extremity procedures.

sections.targetConcern: Provides dense sensory and motor block below the injection level so surgery can be done without general anesthesia, letting the patient stay awake or lightly sedated.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure closely (sympathetic blockade causes hypotension and bradycardia), block level, respiratory effort if the block rises too high, urinary retention, and return of motor/sensory function. Watch for post-dural-puncture headache in the days afterward.

concepts.name: Spinal Cord Injury
concepts.shortExplanation: Damage to the spinal cord that causes loss of motor, sensory, or autonomic function below the level of injury. It may be complete or incomplete.

sections.presentation: Weakness or paralysis and sensory loss below the injury level, loss of bowel and bladder control, and possible respiratory compromise with high cervical injuries. Neurogenic shock (hypotension with bradycardia) may occur acutely; later, autonomic dysreflexia can cause dangerous blood pressure spikes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Spinal immobilization and airway protection; maintain perfusion and oxygenation to limit secondary injury; surgical decompression and stabilization as indicated; prevent complications (pressure injury, DVT, respiratory issues); intensive rehabilitation. For autonomic dysreflexia, sit the patient up and remove the trigger (often bladder distension) urgently.
sections.riskFactors: Motor vehicle crashes, falls (especially in older adults), sports injuries, violence, osteoporosis, and conditions narrowing the spinal canal.

concepts.name: Spironolactone
concepts.shortExplanation: A potassium-sparing diuretic and aldosterone antagonist used for heart failure, resistant hypertension, and edema from cirrhosis.

sections.mechanism: Blocks aldosterone receptors in the distal nephron, promoting sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium; also reduces cardiac remodeling in heart failure.
sections.sideEffects: Hyperkalemia, dizziness, GI upset, and gynecomastia or breast tenderness.
sections.adverseEffects: Dangerous hyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs, or renal impairment; can also cause hyponatremia and metabolic acidosis.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor potassium and renal function closely. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes. Counsel that it is a mild diuretic added for its aldosterone-blocking benefit in heart failure.

concepts.name: Spontaneous Breathing Trial
concepts.shortExplanation: A test of whether a ventilated patient can breathe on their own with minimal support, used to decide readiness for removing the breathing tube.

sections.triggerCriteria: Considered when the reason for intubation is improving, oxygenation is adequate on low support, the patient is hemodynamically stable with minimal or no vasopressors, is able to initiate breaths, and often after a sedation pause (spontaneous awakening trial).
sections.steps: Reduce ventilator support to a minimal level (such as low pressure support or a T-piece) and observe the patient breathing on their own for roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours. Watch respiratory rate, tidal volume, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, and work of breathing or distress. If the patient tolerates it, proceed toward extubation; if they fail, resume full support and reassess the causes.

concepts.name: Sputum Culture
concepts.shortExplanation: A laboratory test that grows and identifies bacteria or other organisms in respiratory secretions to guide antibiotic therapy for lung infections.

sections.normalRange: Normal respiratory flora with no pathogenic organisms and few epithelial cells (a good deep-cough specimen has many neutrophils and few squamous cells). Final culture results typically take 24-72 hours.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Growth of a pathogen (for example Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas, or Staphylococcus aureus) indicates a respiratory infection such as pneumonia; sensitivities guide targeted antibiotics. A specimen with mostly squamous epithelial cells is likely saliva and should be recollected.

concepts.name: ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
concepts.shortExplanation: The most time-critical form of heart attack, caused by complete occlusion of a coronary artery and marked by ST-segment elevation on ECG. It requires emergent reperfusion, with a door-to-balloon goal of 90 minutes for primary PCI.

sections.presentation: Sudden, severe crushing chest pain or pressure, often radiating to the arm, jaw, or back, with diaphoresis, nausea, and dyspnea. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in contiguous leads (or a new left bundle branch block), and troponin rises. Women, older adults, and diabetics may have atypical or 'silent' presentations.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate cath lab activation for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI); fibrinolytics if timely PCI is unavailable. Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor such as ticagrelor or clopidogrel), anticoagulation (heparin), and anti-ischemic measures (nitroglycerin, beta blocker when appropriate). High-intensity statin. Continuous telemetry for lethal arrhythmias; oxygen only if hypoxic.
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, obesity, family history, and older age.

concepts.name: Stable Angina
concepts.shortExplanation: Predictable chest pain brought on by exertion or stress and relieved within minutes by rest or nitroglycerin, caused by fixed coronary narrowing. It is a chronic condition, not an acute coronary syndrome, and troponin stays normal.

sections.presentation: Substernal chest pressure or tightness triggered by a reproducible amount of exertion or emotional stress, lasting a few minutes and relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin. The pattern is stable and predictable over time. ECG and troponin are typically normal at rest.
sections.typicalTreatments: Chronic management: sublingual nitroglycerin for acute episodes; beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and long-acting nitrates for prevention; aspirin and high-intensity statin for secondary prevention. Aggressive risk-factor modification (blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, smoking cessation). Stress testing and, if indicated, coronary angiography with revascularization. Teach patients that a change to rest pain or worsening pattern signals unstable angina and warrants emergency care.
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, and family history.

concepts.name: Status Asthmaticus
concepts.shortExplanation: A severe asthma exacerbation that does not respond to initial bronchodilators and corticosteroids and threatens respiratory failure. It differs from a routine asthma attack by requiring escalated therapy and close monitoring for intubation.

sections.presentation: Severe, persistent dyspnea and wheezing that continue despite repeated albuterol; accessory-muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences, and low peak flow (often under 40% predicted). Ominous signs of impending respiratory failure: a 'silent chest' (no air movement), rising or normalizing PaCO2 with fatigue, drowsiness, and falling oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Continuous or frequent nebulized short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol) plus ipratropium, early systemic corticosteroids, and controlled oxygen to keep SpO2 above 90%. For refractory cases add IV magnesium sulfate, which can rapidly reverse bronchospasm and help avert intubation. Escalate to noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP) in selected patients or to intubation and mechanical ventilation for progressive failure; ventilate carefully given high air-trapping and pneumothorax risk. Avoid sedatives outside of intubation.
sections.riskFactors: Poorly controlled or undertreated asthma, prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, frequent rescue-inhaler use, and recent respiratory infection or allergen/irritant exposure.

concepts.name: Status Epilepticus
concepts.shortExplanation: A seizure that lasts too long or repeated seizures without full recovery in between - a neurologic emergency that needs immediate treatment.

sections.presentation: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without returning to baseline. Nonconvulsive status may show only altered consciousness and requires EEG to detect.
sections.typicalTreatments: Airway and oxygen support, benzodiazepines as first-line, followed by an antiseizure medication (such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate). Refractory cases may need continuous infusions and intubation. Check and treat glucose and other reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Known epilepsy with missed medication, acute brain injury or stroke, infection, metabolic disturbances, alcohol or drug withdrawal, and low glucose.

concepts.name: STEMI Protocol
concepts.shortExplanation: A time-critical pathway to reopen a blocked coronary artery fast in a full-thickness heart attack — "time is muscle."

sections.triggerCriteria: ST-elevation on a 12-lead ECG with ischemic symptoms — activates the cath lab immediately.
sections.steps: Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, activate the cath lab, give aspirin and a second antiplatelet plus anticoagulation, manage pain/ischemia, and get the patient to PCI with a door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes (fibrinolytics if timely PCI isn't available).

concepts.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
concepts.shortExplanation: Bleeding into the space between the brain and its surrounding membranes, most often from a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. It is a neurologic emergency.

sections.presentation: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache often described as the worst of life, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea and vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, seizures, focal deficits. Diagnosed by CT and, if needed, lumbar puncture showing blood or xanthochromia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Secure the aneurysm by surgical clipping or endovascular coiling; nimodipine to reduce vasospasm-related deficits; blood pressure control before securing; monitor for rebleeding, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia. Frequent neuro checks in ICU.
sections.riskFactors: Cerebral aneurysm, hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol use, family history, polycystic kidney disease, arteriovenous malformation.

concepts.name: Subdural Hematoma
concepts.shortExplanation: A collection of blood between the dura and the brain surface, usually from torn bridging veins after head trauma. It can develop acutely or slowly over weeks.

sections.presentation: Headache, confusion, drowsiness, focal weakness, unequal pupils, and declining level of consciousness. Chronic subdurals in older or anticoagulated patients may cause gradual cognitive decline or gait changes; acute subdurals present rapidly after trauma.
sections.typicalTreatments: Surgical evacuation (burr holes or craniotomy) for large or symptomatic bleeds; small ones may be observed with serial imaging; reverse anticoagulation; control intracranial pressure and prevent secondary injury.
sections.riskFactors: Head trauma, falls, older age with brain atrophy, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, alcohol misuse, coagulopathy.

concepts.name: Succinylcholine
concepts.shortExplanation: A very fast, short-acting depolarizing paralytic used to relax muscles for intubation. It provides no sedation or analgesia.

sections.mechanism: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that continuously stimulates then desensitizes the acetylcholine receptor, causing brief muscle fasciculations followed by paralysis. Very rapid onset and offset.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle fasciculations, post-procedure muscle aches, and a small transient rise in potassium.
sections.adverseEffects: Dangerous hyperkalemia in at-risk patients (burns, crush injury, prolonged immobility, certain neuromuscular disease), malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients, and bradycardia.
sections.nursingImplications: Confirm no contraindications for hyperkalemia risk before use. Ensure sedation is given because it provides none. Have emergency airway equipment ready; know malignant hyperthermia protocol and dantrolene location.

concepts.name: Sucralfate
concepts.shortExplanation: A mucosal protectant that forms a barrier over ulcers, shielding them from acid so they can heal. Used for ulcers and mucosal injury.

sections.mechanism: In the acidic stomach it forms a sticky paste that adheres to ulcer sites, creating a protective barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation is most common; also dry mouth and nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Can bind other medications and reduce their absorption; risk of bezoar formation, especially in critically ill patients. Aluminum accumulation in renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Give on an empty stomach, typically before meals and at bedtime. Separate from other oral medications and from antacids by about 2 hours to avoid interfering with absorption. Requires an acidic environment to work.

concepts.name: Sugammadex
concepts.shortExplanation: A reversal agent that rapidly ends paralysis from rocuronium or vecuronium, commonly used at the end of anesthesia to restore breathing and muscle strength.

sections.mechanism: Encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium molecules and removes them from the neuromuscular junction, quickly reversing paralysis.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, hypotension, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Anaphylaxis and hypersensitivity, bradycardia (sometimes severe), and reduced effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives for a period after the dose.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor recovery of muscle strength with a train-of-four nerve stimulator and watch for return of adequate breathing. Watch for bradycardia and allergic reactions. Counsel patients on hormonal contraceptives about temporarily reduced efficacy.

concepts.name: Suicidal Ideation and Safety Precautions
concepts.shortExplanation: The nursing approach to assessing and protecting a patient who is having thoughts of suicide.

sections.triggerCriteria: A patient expresses thoughts of death or suicide, has a plan or intent, has a history of attempts, or screens positive on a suicide risk screening tool. Sudden calm after distress can also be a warning sign.
sections.steps: Ask directly and nonjudgmentally about thoughts, plan, intent, and access to means. Place the patient on the appropriate level of observation (up to one-to-one continuous observation) and remove dangerous items from the environment. Maintain a safe, searched room, document risk assessment and interventions, communicate risk at handoff, and involve the mental health team. Provide a supportive, nonjudgmental presence and reassess risk regularly.

concepts.name: Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim
concepts.shortExplanation: A combination oral or IV antibiotic used for urinary tract infections, certain skin infections including MRSA, and Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis.

sections.mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim block sequential steps in bacterial folic acid synthesis, together impairing DNA production and giving a synergistic bactericidal effect.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, rash, photosensitivity, and loss of appetite.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), hyperkalemia, elevated creatinine, hematologic suppression, and increased warfarin effect. Sulfa allergy is a contraindication.
sections.nursingImplications: Ask about sulfa allergy before giving. Encourage generous fluid intake and sun protection. Monitor potassium, renal function, and CBC on prolonged therapy, and INR in patients on warfarin. Teach patients to report rash promptly.

concepts.name: Surfactant (Exogenous)
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication instilled into a premature baby's lungs to replace the natural substance that keeps the air sacs from collapsing.

sections.mechanism: Lowers surface tension inside the alveoli so they stay open at the end of each breath, improving oxygenation and lung compliance.
sections.sideEffects: Transient drop in oxygen saturation, heart rate changes, or reflux of the dose during administration.
sections.adverseEffects: Airway obstruction from the instilled dose, and rarely pulmonary hemorrhage.
sections.nursingImplications: Delivered through the endotracheal tube. Monitor oxygen saturation and heart rate closely during administration and be prepared for transient desaturation. Lung compliance can improve quickly, so ventilator settings and oxygen often need prompt adjustment to avoid overinflation.

concepts.name: Surgical Safety Checklist
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized team checklist used before, during, and after an operation to prevent avoidable harm such as wrong-site surgery. The surgical time-out is its central pause.

sections.triggerCriteria: Performed for every operative procedure, at three points: sign-in before anesthesia induction, time-out before skin incision, and sign-out before the patient leaves the room.
sections.steps: Sign-in: confirm patient identity, procedure, site marking, consent, allergies, and airway/aspiration risk. Time-out: the whole team pauses to confirm correct patient, procedure, and site, review anticipated critical events, and confirm antibiotic prophylaxis and imaging. Sign-out: confirm the procedure performed, correct instrument, sponge, and needle counts, specimen labeling, and equipment issues, and review recovery concerns.

concepts.name: Surgical Site Infection
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection at or near a surgical incision occurring after an operation. It is a common and largely preventable surgical complication.

sections.presentation: Redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, and purulent drainage at the incision, sometimes with wound dehiscence and fever. It may be superficial or extend to deep tissue or the organ space.
sections.typicalTreatments: Wound cultures, opening and draining the wound when needed, dressing changes, and antibiotics targeted to the organism. Deep or organ-space infections may need return to the operating room.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes and hyperglycemia, obesity, smoking, prolonged or contaminated surgery, immunosuppression, and lapses in prevention such as mistimed prophylactic antibiotics, hypothermia, or shaving (rather than clipping) the surgical site.

concepts.name: Symptomatic Bradycardia
concepts.shortExplanation: A heart rate too slow to meet the body's needs — often from a conduction problem (heart block) — causing dizziness, fatigue, or low blood pressure.

sections.presentation: Heart rate typically <60 with symptoms: lightheadedness, fatigue, syncope, hypotension, chest pain, or shortness of breath. ECG may show sinus bradycardia or AV block.
sections.typicalTreatments: Atropine first-line, transcutaneous pacing if atropine fails, dopamine or epinephrine infusion; permanent pacemaker for persistent high-grade block.
sections.riskFactors: Inferior MI, degenerative conduction disease, medications (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin), hyperkalemia, increased vagal tone.

concepts.name: Synchronized Cardioversion
concepts.shortExplanation: A timed electrical shock delivered to reset an abnormal heart rhythm back to a normal pattern — used when a fast, unstable rhythm needs to be corrected quickly.

sections.targetConcern: Unstable or persistent symptomatic tachyarrhythmia, commonly atrial fibrillation, that hasn't responded to (or can't wait for) medication alone.
sections.whatToMonitor: Rhythm and pulse immediately before/after, sedation level and airway, skin at pad placement sites, blood pressure.

concepts.name: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
concepts.shortExplanation: A condition where the body makes too much antidiuretic hormone, causing water retention and dilutional low sodium (hyponatremia).

sections.presentation: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine and a normal-to-slightly-volume-expanded state (euvolemic). Symptoms depend on how low and how fast sodium falls: nausea, headache, confusion, and, when severe, seizures and coma. Low serum osmolality with inappropriately high urine osmolality.
sections.typicalTreatments: Fluid (water) restriction is the mainstay; treat the underlying cause. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia may need hypertonic (3%) saline. Correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination. Vaptans or salt tablets are used in selected cases.
sections.riskFactors: CNS disorders, lung disease, malignancies (especially small-cell lung cancer), medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, others), and surgery or pain.

concepts.name: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS)
concepts.shortExplanation: A widespread inflammatory state defined by meeting 2 or more of four bedside criteria (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, WBC). Distinguished from sepsis in that SIRS can be triggered by non-infectious causes such as trauma, burns, pancreatitis, or surgery; sepsis is SIRS caused by infection.

sections.presentation: Two or more of the following: temperature above 38 C (100.4 F) or below 36 C (96.8 F); heart rate above 90 beats per minute; respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute (or PaCO2 below 32 mmHg); and WBC above 12,000 or below 4,000 cells/mm3 or more than 10% immature (band) forms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Identify and treat the underlying cause. If infection is suspected, treat as sepsis - obtain cultures and lactate, give early broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids per the sepsis bundle. Provide supportive care with fluids, oxygen, and source control, and reassess frequently for progression to sepsis or organ dysfunction.
sections.riskFactors: Infection, major trauma, burns, major surgery, acute pancreatitis, ischemia, and malignancy.

concepts.name: Targeted Temperature Management
concepts.shortExplanation: Deliberately controlling a patient's body temperature (often after cardiac arrest) to protect the brain and prevent fever.

sections.targetConcern: Reducing brain injury and improving neurologic outcomes in comatose survivors of cardiac arrest by maintaining a controlled target temperature and preventing fever.
sections.whatToMonitor: Core temperature via a reliable probe (bladder, esophageal, or blood), continuous cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, and neuro exam. Watch for shivering, bradycardia, electrolyte shifts (potassium, magnesium), hyperglycemia, and coagulopathy. Rewarm slowly and avoid rebound fever.

concepts.name: TAVR
concepts.shortExplanation: A minimally invasive procedure that replaces a narrowed aortic valve without open-heart surgery.

sections.targetConcern: Severe aortic stenosis in patients who are poor candidates for open surgical valve replacement.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site for bleeding/hematoma, rhythm changes, blood pressure, signs of stroke.

concepts.name: Temazepam
concepts.shortExplanation: An intermediate-acting benzodiazepine used short term for insomnia.

sections.mechanism: Potentiates GABA at the GABA-A receptor to promote sedation and sleep onset and maintenance.
sections.sideEffects: Daytime drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and grogginess on waking.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression with other CNS depressants, complex sleep behaviors, next-day impairment, and dependence with withdrawal on abrupt discontinuation.
sections.nursingImplications: Give at bedtime with enough time for sleep, and ensure a safe environment because of fall and confusion risk, especially in older adults. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives. Recommend short-term use and taper after prolonged use.

concepts.name: Tension Pneumothorax
concepts.shortExplanation: A life-threatening emergency where trapped pleural air progressively builds up, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum to compress the heart and great vessels.

sections.presentation: Severe respiratory distress, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, distended neck veins, hypotension, and tachycardia progressing to cardiac arrest.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate emergency needle decompression (large-bore catheter, typically second intercostal space midclavicular line or fifth intercostal space) followed by chest tube placement. Do not wait for a chest x-ray if unstable.
sections.riskFactors: Chest trauma, positive-pressure mechanical ventilation, CPR, and an untreated simple pneumothorax.

concepts.name: Third-Degree (Complete) AV Block
concepts.shortExplanation: Total failure of AV conduction where the atria and ventricles beat independently; a slow escape rhythm sustains output and often needs a pacemaker.

sections.presentation: ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes marching out independently (AV dissociation) with a slow ventricular escape rate. Symptoms include fatigue, dizziness, syncope, hypotension, and heart failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergency transcutaneous pacing for unstable patients (atropine is usually ineffective), followed by a permanent pacemaker. Hold AV-nodal blocking drugs and treat reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Myocardial infarction, degenerative conduction disease, AV-nodal blocking medications, cardiac surgery, and Lyme carditis.

concepts.name: Thoracentesis
concepts.shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the space around the lung — done to relieve breathing difficulty or to diagnose the cause of a pleural effusion.

sections.targetConcern: Pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise, or an effusion of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Respiratory status during and after the procedure, signs of pneumothorax (sudden dyspnea, decreased breath sounds), insertion site for bleeding.

concepts.name: Thrombocytopenia
concepts.shortExplanation: A low platelet count (typically below 150,000/uL) that increases bleeding risk. An umbrella term with many causes - decreased production, increased destruction or consumption, or splenic sequestration - that guide management.

sections.presentation: Often asymptomatic if mild; petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, mucosal bleeding (gums, nose), and prolonged bleeding. With severe drops there is a risk of spontaneous or internal bleeding. CBC shows a low platelet count.
sections.typicalTreatments: Identify and treat the cause; hold or avoid agents that worsen bleeding. Platelet transfusion is used for severe thrombocytopenia or active bleeding, with important exceptions such as HIT and TTP where platelet transfusion is generally avoided. Institute bleeding precautions.
sections.riskFactors: Sepsis and DIC, chemotherapy and bone marrow suppression, medications (including heparin - see HIT), immune thrombocytopenia, liver disease with splenomegaly, alcohol, viral infections, and massive transfusion.

concepts.name: Thrombotic Ischemic Stroke
concepts.shortExplanation: An ischemic stroke caused by a clot forming directly on an atherosclerotic plaque within a brain-supplying artery. Distinguished by an often gradual or stuttering onset, frequent preceding TIAs, and antiplatelet-based secondary prevention.

sections.presentation: Focal neurologic deficits that may develop gradually or in a stepwise, stuttering fashion, sometimes noticed on awakening. Onset is often preceded by transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), and the patient usually has an atherosclerotic risk profile, frequently involving large vessels (carotid or vertebral arteries).
sections.typicalTreatments: Acute ischemic stroke care - thrombolysis if eligible and thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Secondary prevention centers on antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel), a high-intensity statin, and control of blood pressure and diabetes. Carotid revascularization (endarterectomy or stenting) is considered for significant carotid stenosis.
sections.riskFactors: Atherosclerosis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, older age, and carotid artery stenosis.

concepts.name: Thyroid Storm
concepts.shortExplanation: A rare, life-threatening extreme of hyperthyroidism with high fever and severe cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction. A medical emergency.

sections.presentation: High fever, marked tachycardia and often atrial fibrillation, heart failure, agitation, delirium or coma, and GI symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea). Frequently triggered by infection, surgery, trauma, or stopping antithyroid medication.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU-level care: beta-blockers to control heart rate, antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil or methimazole), iodine given after the antithyroid drug to block hormone release, corticosteroids, aggressive cooling and fluids, and treating the trigger.
sections.riskFactors: Untreated or undertreated hyperthyroidism plus a precipitant such as infection, surgery, trauma, or iodine load.

concepts.name: Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
concepts.shortExplanation: A pituitary hormone that regulates the thyroid; TSH is the primary screening test for thyroid function.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 0.4-4.0 mIU/L (reference ranges vary by lab and pregnancy).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high TSH usually indicates an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), causing fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain. A low TSH usually indicates an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism), causing palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss. Free T4 is often checked alongside to confirm.

concepts.name: Ticagrelor
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral antiplatelet (P2Y12 inhibitor) used with aspirin to prevent clots after acute coronary syndrome and coronary stenting.

sections.mechanism: Reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, inhibiting platelet aggregation.
sections.sideEffects: Dyspnea (often transient), bruising, and minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding and bradyarrhythmias. Effectiveness drops when aspirin doses above 100 mg are used; taken twice daily unlike clopidogrel.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with low-dose aspirin only. Monitor for bleeding and new-onset shortness of breath. Emphasize not stopping early after stent placement due to stent thrombosis risk; hold before surgery as directed.

concepts.name: Tiotropium
concepts.shortExplanation: A once-daily long-acting inhaled anticholinergic (LAMA) used for maintenance control of COPD and, in some formulations, asthma.

sections.mechanism: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist that produces sustained bronchodilation by blocking airway muscarinic receptors.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, constipation, and pharyngitis.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsening narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, and rarely paradoxical bronchospasm.
sections.nursingImplications: Maintenance therapy only, not for acute attacks. Teach correct use of the dry-powder inhaler (do not swallow the capsules) or soft-mist inhaler. Reinforce daily dosing for prevention.

concepts.name: Total Bilirubin
concepts.shortExplanation: A yellow breakdown product of red blood cells cleared by the liver; high levels cause jaundice.

sections.normalRange: Total bilirubin about 0.1-1.2 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated bilirubin causes yellowing of the skin and eyes. A high unconjugated (indirect) fraction suggests red-cell breakdown or Gilbert syndrome; a high conjugated (direct) fraction suggests liver disease or bile-duct obstruction. In newborns, high bilirubin risks brain injury (kernicterus).

concepts.name: Tracheostomy
concepts.shortExplanation: Surgical creation of an airway opening in the neck directly into the trachea — used when a patient needs prolonged mechanical ventilation or has an upper airway obstruction.

sections.targetConcern: Anticipated prolonged mechanical ventilation, or upper airway obstruction that an endotracheal tube can't safely address long-term.
sections.whatToMonitor: Stoma site for bleeding/infection, cuff pressure, secretion volume and suctioning needs, signs of accidental decannulation.

concepts.name: Tramadol
concepts.shortExplanation: A centrally acting oral analgesic for moderate pain that combines weak opioid activity with effects on serotonin and norepinephrine.

sections.mechanism: Binds mu-opioid receptors and inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, modulating pain signaling through both pathways.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, dizziness, constipation, headache, drowsiness, and dry mouth.
sections.adverseEffects: Seizures (especially at higher doses or with lowered seizure threshold), serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, respiratory depression, and dependence.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess pain and sedation and screen for seizure history and serotonergic medications. Watch for agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, or clonus suggesting serotonin syndrome. Avoid abrupt discontinuation. Keep naloxone available, recognizing it only partially reverses tramadol.

concepts.name: Transient Ischemic Attack
concepts.shortExplanation: A brief episode of stroke-like symptoms from temporary loss of blood flow to the brain, resolving without permanent infarction. It is a warning sign of high stroke risk.

sections.presentation: Sudden focal deficits that fully resolve, typically within an hour: unilateral weakness or numbness, facial droop, slurred speech, vision loss, or difficulty speaking. No lasting infarct on imaging.
sections.typicalTreatments: Urgent workup to find the cause (carotid imaging, ECG for atrial fibrillation, labs); antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel) or anticoagulation if cardioembolic; statin, blood pressure and diabetes control; carotid revascularization if indicated.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia, prior TIA or stroke, older age.

concepts.name: Traumatic Brain Injury
concepts.shortExplanation: Brain dysfunction caused by an external force such as a blow or jolt to the head. Severity ranges from mild concussion to life-threatening injury.

sections.presentation: Ranges from brief confusion, headache, and dizziness (mild/concussion) to loss of consciousness, unequal pupils, vomiting, seizures, and coma (severe). Watch for signs of rising intracranial pressure and secondary deterioration. Graded with the Glasgow Coma Scale.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prevent secondary injury by maintaining oxygenation and cerebral perfusion; manage intracranial pressure (head-of-bed elevation, osmotic therapy such as mannitol or hypertonic saline, sedation, and sometimes surgery); frequent neuro assessments; seizure prophylaxis in select cases.
sections.riskFactors: Falls, motor vehicle crashes, assaults, sports and combat injuries, older age, alcohol use, anticoagulation.

concepts.name: Trazodone
concepts.shortExplanation: An antidepressant most often used at low doses off-label as a sleep aid, and at higher doses for depression.

sections.mechanism: Blocks serotonin reuptake and antagonizes certain serotonin and histamine receptors; the sedating antihistamine effect underlies its use for sleep.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, orthostatic hypotension, and blurred vision.
sections.adverseEffects: Priapism (a urologic emergency), serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, QT prolongation, and orthostatic falls.
sections.nursingImplications: Give at bedtime and rise slowly to limit orthostatic hypotension. Institute fall precautions. Teach male patients that a prolonged or painful erection requires emergency care. Watch for serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic agents.

concepts.name: Troponin
concepts.shortExplanation: A protein released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged — the key lab value used to help diagnose a heart attack.

sections.normalRange: Typically <0.04 ng/mL, but the exact cutoff and assay type vary by lab — trended serially rather than interpreted from a single value.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated and rising troponin suggests myocardial injury; the pattern of rise/fall over serial measurements helps distinguish acute injury from other causes of elevation (e.g. renal failure, sepsis).

concepts.name: Tuberculosis
concepts.shortExplanation: A bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that primarily affects the lungs and spreads through the air. It exists as latent (inactive) and active disease.

sections.presentation: Active pulmonary TB: chronic productive cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Latent TB has no symptoms and is not contagious. Diagnosed with skin (TST) or blood (IGRA) tests, chest imaging, and sputum studies.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged multidrug regimens (commonly isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for months, often with directly observed therapy; latent TB is treated to prevent progression; airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room for suspected active pulmonary disease.
sections.riskFactors: Close contact with an active case, HIV or immunocompromise, birth or travel in high-prevalence regions, crowded or congregate living, injection drug use, and diabetes.

concepts.name: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
concepts.shortExplanation: A metabolic emergency in which rapidly dying cancer cells dump their contents into the blood, usually just after starting treatment. The released chemicals can cause dangerous electrolyte swings, kidney failure, and arrhythmias.

sections.presentation: High potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, and low calcium, leading to nausea, weakness, muscle cramps, tetany, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and acute kidney injury with reduced urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV hydration, close monitoring of electrolytes and kidney function, uric-acid-lowering therapy with allopurinol or rasburicase, and treatment of hyperkalemia. Cardiac monitoring and, in severe cases, dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Bulky, rapidly proliferating, treatment-sensitive cancers such as acute leukemias and high-grade lymphomas, high tumor burden, pre-existing kidney impairment, and the initiation of chemotherapy.

concepts.name: Type 1 Diabetes
concepts.shortExplanation: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing an absolute lack of insulin, so the patient depends on insulin for life and is prone to diabetic ketoacidosis. Distinct from type 2, which is driven by insulin resistance.

sections.presentation: Often abrupt onset in children or young adults with polyuria, polydipsia, and unintended weight loss; may first present in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Little to no endogenous insulin.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifelong insulin by basal-bolus (multiple daily injections) or pump; carbohydrate counting. Key nursing point that distinguishes it from type 2: never withhold basal insulin, even when the patient is NPO, because stopping insulin can precipitate DKA.
sections.riskFactors: Genetic predisposition (HLA associations), family history, and coexisting autoimmune disorders. Not caused by lifestyle or obesity.

concepts.name: Type 2 Diabetes
concepts.shortExplanation: Insulin resistance combined with a relative insulin deficiency, usually tied to obesity and metabolic syndrome. Unlike type 1, it often responds to lifestyle and oral agents before insulin is needed, and severe hyperglycemia tends toward HHS rather than DKA.

sections.presentation: Gradual, often asymptomatic onset; found on screening or with polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, or recurrent infections. Frequently accompanied by hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stepwise: lifestyle change, then metformin, then additional agents (GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide, SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin), with insulin added as beta-cell function declines. A1c is trended to guide escalation.
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, physical inactivity, older age, family history, prior gestational diabetes, and certain ethnicities.

concepts.name: Ulcerative Colitis
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colon lining, starting at the rectum. Marked by bloody diarrhea.

sections.presentation: Bloody diarrhea with mucus, urgency and tenesmus, crampy lower abdominal pain, and weight loss. Severe flares cause fever and dehydration. Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication. Inflammation is continuous and limited to the colon and rectum.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aminosalicylates (5-ASA) for maintenance, corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators, and biologics. Colectomy can be curative for refractory disease or complications. Monitor stool frequency, bleeding, and hydration; long-standing disease raises colon cancer risk requiring surveillance.
sections.riskFactors: Family history and age (often diagnosed in young adulthood); risk of colorectal cancer increases with disease duration and extent.

concepts.name: Unstable Angina
concepts.shortExplanation: Cardiac chest pain that is new, worsening (crescendo), or occurs at rest, signaling an unstable coronary plaque. Unlike NSTEMI, troponin is NOT elevated, but it is treated as an acute coronary syndrome because it can progress to infarction.

sections.presentation: Angina that is new-onset, more frequent or severe than the patient's usual pattern, occurs at rest, or is no longer relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. ECG may show transient ST depression or T-wave changes or be normal. By definition, troponin is NOT elevated (no myocardial necrosis), which separates it from NSTEMI.
sections.typicalTreatments: Managed like NSTEMI without evidence of necrosis: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation, nitroglycerin, beta blocker, and statin. Serial troponins and ECGs to detect evolution to NSTEMI. Risk stratification (HEART/TIMI) determines whether and when to pursue coronary angiography. Continuous telemetry and prompt reassessment of any recurrent pain.
sections.riskFactors: Established coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, and prior cardiac events.

concepts.name: Upper Endoscopy (EGD)
concepts.shortExplanation: A procedure using a flexible scope to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. Used to diagnose and treat problems such as ulcers, bleeding, and reflux damage.

sections.targetConcern: Evaluates upper GI symptoms and bleeding, ulcers, varices, strictures, tumors, and reflux injury; allows biopsy, band ligation of varices, cautery of bleeding, and dilation of strictures.
sections.whatToMonitor: After the procedure, monitor level of consciousness and vital signs as sedation wears off, and confirm the gag reflex has returned before giving food or fluids. Watch for signs of perforation or bleeding: severe abdominal or chest pain, fever, difficulty swallowing, hematemesis, or melena.

concepts.name: Upper GI Bleed
concepts.shortExplanation: Bleeding from the upper digestive tract (esophagus, stomach, or duodenum) that can range from minor to life-threatening hemorrhage.

sections.presentation: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools (melena), and with brisk bleeding, red blood per rectum. Large losses cause lightheadedness, fast heart rate, low blood pressure, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: Large-bore IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, proton pump inhibitor therapy, and urgent endoscopy to find and control the source. Octreotide and antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding; transfusion guided by a restrictive strategy for most patients.
sections.riskFactors: Peptic ulcer disease, NSAID or anticoagulant use, H. pylori infection, liver disease with varices, and heavy alcohol use.

concepts.name: Urinalysis
concepts.shortExplanation: A screening test of the urine's chemistry and microscopic contents used to detect infection, kidney disease, and dehydration.

sections.normalRange: Clear, yellow urine; specific gravity about 1.005-1.030; pH about 4.5-8.0; negative for protein, glucose, ketones, blood, nitrites, and leukocyte esterase.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase with white cells suggest a urinary tract infection. Protein suggests kidney disease; glucose and ketones suggest hyperglycemia or DKA; blood may indicate infection, stones, or trauma. A high specific gravity suggests dehydration.

concepts.name: Urinary Tract Infection
concepts.shortExplanation: An infection of the bladder or kidneys; it is a very common reason for admission and can progress to life-threatening urosepsis.

sections.presentation: Burning with urination, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine. Flank pain and fever suggest a kidney infection (pyelonephritis); older adults may show new confusion.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by urine culture, hydration, and removing or changing indwelling catheters when possible.
sections.riskFactors: Female anatomy, indwelling urinary catheters, urinary retention, diabetes, older age, and immobility.

concepts.name: Urine Culture
concepts.shortExplanation: A test that grows and identifies bacteria in the urine to confirm a urinary tract infection and guide antibiotics.

sections.normalRange: No growth or fewer than about 10,000 CFU/mL is generally considered negative.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Growth of a single organism at 100,000 CFU/mL or more usually confirms infection, and sensitivities guide antibiotic choice. Positive cultures without symptoms (asymptomatic bacteriuria) usually are not treated except in pregnancy or before urologic procedures. Proper clean-catch or catheter technique limits contamination.

concepts.name: Valsartan
concepts.shortExplanation: An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) for hypertension and heart failure, also combined with sacubitril for heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Blocks angiotensin II receptors to produce vasodilation and reduced aldosterone, lowering blood pressure and cardiac workload.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, fatigue, and hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia, renal impairment, and angioedema. Contraindicated in pregnancy. Do not combine with an ACE inhibitor.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function. As part of sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto), do not give within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor due to angioedema risk.

concepts.name: Vancomycin
concepts.shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum antibiotic used to treat serious infections, including resistant bacteria — often started empirically while cultures are pending in suspected sepsis.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; effective against many gram-positive organisms including MRSA. Requires trough-level monitoring for dosing and renal function tracking.
sections.sideEffects: Redness/flushing with rapid infusion ("red man syndrome"), phlebitis at the infusion site.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe infusion reactions if given too quickly.
sections.nursingImplications: Infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes, monitor trough levels and renal function, watch for signs of red man syndrome.

concepts.name: Vasopressin
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone given as a fixed-dose infusion to raise blood pressure in shock, usually added to norepinephrine in septic shock.

sections.mechanism: Acts on vascular V1 receptors to constrict blood vessels through a pathway separate from catecholamines, raising blood pressure without directly stimulating the heart.
sections.sideEffects: Pallor, abdominal cramping, and hyponatremia.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive vasoconstriction causing digital, mesenteric, or cardiac ischemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Typically run at a fixed dose (not titrated like other pressors) as an adjunct to norepinephrine. Monitor blood pressure, urine output, and perfusion to the fingers, toes, and gut. Give through a central line when possible.

concepts.name: Venipuncture (Blood Draw)
concepts.shortExplanation: Puncturing a vein with a needle to collect blood samples for laboratory testing.

sections.targetConcern: Obtains venous blood for diagnostic testing. Correct technique and tube handling protect the accuracy of results.
sections.whatToMonitor: Draw tubes in the correct order and fill to volume; mix additive tubes gently to avoid clots or hemolysis. Avoid drawing above an IV or from the arm with a fistula or on the mastectomy side. After removal, hold pressure and check for hematoma; watch for lightheadedness or fainting in anxious patients. Label tubes at the bedside.

concepts.name: Venous Stasis Ulcer
concepts.shortExplanation: A chronic lower-leg wound caused by poor vein circulation, and the most common type of leg ulcer.

sections.presentation: Shallow, irregular wounds around the ankle or inner lower leg, with surrounding brown-stained (hemosiderin) and swollen skin; usually mild pain but moderate to heavy drainage.
sections.typicalTreatments: Compression therapy is the cornerstone once adequate arterial flow is confirmed, along with leg elevation, moist wound dressings, and skin care.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic venous insufficiency, prior DVT, obesity, prolonged standing, and older age.

concepts.name: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)
concepts.shortExplanation: Pneumonia arising more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation. Distinguished by its strong link to the breathing tube, its high rate of resistant organisms, and a bundle of nursing measures aimed at prevention.

sections.presentation: New infiltrate plus new fever, leukocytosis, purulent tracheal secretions, worsening oxygenation or rising ventilator requirements developing after 48 hours of mechanical ventilation. Obtain lower respiratory (endotracheal aspirate) cultures before starting or changing antibiotics.
sections.typicalTreatments: Empiric regimen covering S. aureus and Pseudomonas/gram-negatives (antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam), adding vancomycin or linezolid for MRSA and dual antipseudomonal coverage in high-risk patients; de-escalate by culture at ~48 hours, treat ~7 days. Prevention is central: the VAP bundle - elevate head of bed 30-45 degrees, daily sedation interruption and readiness-to-extubate assessment, oral care with chlorhexidine, and DVT/stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
sections.riskFactors: Prolonged mechanical ventilation, reintubation, supine positioning, heavy sedation, aspiration, and prior antibiotic exposure.

concepts.name: Ventricular Fibrillation
concepts.shortExplanation: The ventricles quiver chaotically instead of pumping, so there's no effective heartbeat — a form of cardiac arrest that requires immediate CPR and defibrillation.

sections.presentation: Sudden loss of pulse and consciousness; ECG shows disorganized, irregular waveforms with no identifiable QRS complexes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR and defibrillation (a shockable rhythm), epinephrine and amiodarone per ACLS, and treatment of reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Acute MI/ischemia, cardiomyopathy, severe electrolyte imbalance, prolonged QT, prior cardiac arrest.

concepts.name: Ventricular Tachycardia
concepts.shortExplanation: A fast rhythm arising from the ventricles — it can be stable, or become pulseless and life-threatening. Treatment depends on whether the patient has a pulse and is stable.

sections.presentation: Palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness; may deteriorate to loss of pulse. ECG shows a wide-complex, regular, fast rhythm.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pulseless VT: CPR and defibrillation per ACLS. Unstable with a pulse: synchronized cardioversion. Stable: antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone.
sections.riskFactors: Prior MI/scar, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte abnormalities, prolonged QT, structural heart disease.

concepts.name: Venturi Mask
concepts.shortExplanation: A high-flow oxygen mask with color-coded adapters that delivers a precise, fixed oxygen concentration regardless of the patient's breathing.

sections.purpose: Delivers an exact FiO2 (commonly 24-50 percent) using interchangeable color-coded valves. Preferred when precise, controlled oxygen is needed, such as in COPD patients at risk of CO2 retention.
sections.careConsiderations: Match the correct adapter and flow rate to the ordered FiO2 (each color specifies a flow). Keep the air-entrainment ports unobstructed. Remove for meals and monitor SpO2 and, in CO2 retainers, watch for rising drowsiness or CO2 retention.

concepts.name: Vinca Alkaloids (class)
concepts.shortExplanation: A class of plant-derived chemotherapy drugs, including vincristine and vinblastine, used for leukemias, lymphomas, and other cancers. Peripheral neuropathy is their signature side effect.

sections.mechanism: Bind tubulin and block microtubule assembly, arresting the mitotic spindle so dividing cells cannot complete cell division.
sections.sideEffects: Peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, weakness), constipation and ileus, and hair loss; vinblastine causes more myelosuppression than vincristine.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe or disabling neuropathy, and vesicant tissue injury on extravasation. These drugs are fatal if given intrathecally and must only be given intravenously.
sections.nursingImplications: Give IV only, never into the spinal fluid, and verify labeling carefully. Assess for neuropathy and bowel function, encourage a bowel regimen to prevent constipation, and monitor the IV site for extravasation.

concepts.name: Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Inflammation of the meninges caused by a virus, most often an enterovirus; the most common and usually self-limiting form of meningitis. Distinguished from bacterial meningitis by clearer CSF with lymphocytic predominance, normal glucose, and mainly supportive treatment.

sections.presentation: Headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, malaise, and nausea - typically less severe and less rapidly progressive than bacterial meningitis. CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and normal to mildly elevated protein, with a negative Gram stain and culture.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mainly supportive - fluids, analgesics and antipyretics, and rest. Empiric antibiotics (and acyclovir if HSV is suspected) are often started until bacterial meningitis is ruled out; acyclovir is used for herpes-related cases. The illness is usually self-limited with a good prognosis.
sections.riskFactors: Enteroviral exposure (the most common cause, peaking in summer and fall), young age, immunocompromise, and HSV, HIV, mumps, or arbovirus infection.

concepts.name: Viral Hepatitis
concepts.shortExplanation: Liver inflammation caused by hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, E). A and E spread through contaminated food/water; B, C, and D spread through blood and body fluids.

sections.presentation: Fatigue, nausea, poor appetite, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Elevated liver enzymes. Hepatitis A and E are usually acute and self-limited; B and C can become chronic and lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care for acute infection. Chronic hepatitis B and C are treated with antiviral medications; hepatitis C is often curable with direct-acting antivirals. Vaccination prevents hepatitis A and B. Use standard precautions and avoid hepatotoxins such as alcohol.
sections.riskFactors: Injection drug use, unprotected sex, needlestick exposure, contaminated food or water (A and E), and perinatal transmission (B).

concepts.name: Warfarin
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral anticoagulant used for long-term prevention of blood clots, commonly in atrial fibrillation or after a DVT/PE.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Requires regular INR monitoring due to a narrow therapeutic window and many drug/food interactions.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding (GI, intracranial) especially if INR is supratherapeutic; skin necrosis (rare, early therapy).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor INR regularly, educate on consistent vitamin K intake, watch for interacting medications.

concepts.name: WBC Differential
concepts.shortExplanation: A breakdown of the white blood cell types that helps identify infection, inflammation, and immune problems.

sections.normalRange: Approximate percentages of total WBCs: neutrophils 40-60%, lymphocytes 20-40%, monocytes 2-8%, eosinophils 1-4%, basophils 0.5-1%.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High neutrophils suggest bacterial infection or stress; a 'left shift' (more immature bands) signals active infection. High lymphocytes often accompany viral illness. High eosinophils suggest allergy or parasites. A low absolute neutrophil count (neutropenia) means high infection risk. The absolute neutrophil count guides neutropenic precautions.

concepts.name: Wells Criteria
concepts.shortExplanation: A clinical scoring rule that estimates the pretest probability of a blood clot (DVT or PE) to guide testing.

sections.purpose: Estimates the pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism so clinicians can decide whether to use D-dimer testing or proceed to imaging. Separate versions exist for DVT and PE.
sections.steps: Points are assigned for clinical features (e.g. active cancer, immobilization/recent surgery, prior VTE, leg swelling and tenderness for DVT; tachycardia, hemoptysis, clinical signs of DVT for PE), with one DVT item subtracting points if an alternative diagnosis is as likely.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Scores stratify patients into low, moderate, and high probability (or unlikely vs likely in the two-tier model). Lower probability with a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer can rule out clot; higher probability warrants imaging (ultrasound for DVT, CT angiography for PE).

concepts.name: Wong-Baker FACES Pain Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A pain scale using a row of faces from smiling to crying, useful for children and others who struggle with number-based rating.

sections.purpose: Provides a self-report pain measure for children (generally 3 and older) and others who find numbers difficult, by having them pick the face that matches their pain.
sections.steps: Six faces ranging from a smiling face to a crying face, mapped to scores of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. The patient selects the face; the corresponding number is recorded.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Interpreted like the 0-10 scale: higher scores mean more pain (roughly mild, moderate, severe as the number rises), guiding treatment and reassessment.

concepts.name: Wound Culture Collection
concepts.shortExplanation: Sampling a wound to identify infecting organisms and guide antibiotic therapy.

sections.targetConcern: Identifies the organisms causing a wound infection and their antibiotic sensitivities in cellulitis, surgical-site infection, or a non-healing ulcer.
sections.whatToMonitor: Cleanse the wound with saline first so you sample infected tissue, not surface colonizers; the Levine technique (rotating a swab over viable tissue) is preferred, and deep tissue or aspirate is best. Note wound appearance, drainage, and odor. Collect before starting antibiotics when feasible, and follow up on culture results and healing.

concepts.name: Wound Debridement
concepts.shortExplanation: The removal of dead, damaged, or infected tissue from a wound to promote healing.

sections.targetConcern: Removes nonviable tissue (slough and eschar) and debris that block healing and harbor infection, converting a chronic wound toward a healing state.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assess for bleeding and pain during and after the procedure, signs of infection, and the appearance of healthy granulation tissue. Methods include sharp/surgical, enzymatic, autolytic (moist dressings), and mechanical debridement.

concepts.name: Zolpidem
concepts.shortExplanation: A non-benzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic (a Z-drug) used short term for insomnia.

sections.mechanism: Selectively binds the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor to promote sleep with relatively less muscle-relaxant and anticonvulsant effect.
sections.sideEffects: Daytime drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and a metallic taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-walking, driving, or eating with no memory of the event; next-morning impairment and falls, especially in older adults.
sections.nursingImplications: Give immediately before bed with at least 7 to 8 hours available for sleep, and only when the patient will stay in bed. Institute fall precautions. Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants. Teach to stop and report any complex sleep behaviors.

concepts.name: Dopamine
concepts.shortExplanation: A titrated IV drip that supports blood pressure and heart function, with effects that change depending on the dose.

sections.mechanism: Dose-dependent adrenergic agonist - lower rates favor beta-1 effects (increased contractility and heart rate) and higher rates add alpha-1 vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure.
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, palpitations, headache, nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, increased myocardial oxygen demand and ischemia, and tissue necrosis with extravasation - give through a central line when possible.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring (ideally arterial line), titrate to hemodynamic goals, assess the IV site for extravasation, and never stop abruptly.

concepts.name: Milrinone
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV medication that strengthens the heart's pumping while relaxing blood vessels, used in severe heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor "inodilator" - increases contractility and causes vasodilation, improving cardiac output and lowering filling pressures.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, headache, palpitations.
sections.adverseEffects: Ventricular arrhythmias and significant hypotension; accumulates in renal impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring, titrate carefully as hypotension is common, and monitor renal function; often used in acute decompensated heart failure and after cardiac surgery.

concepts.name: Labetalol
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV/oral blood-pressure medication that blocks both alpha and beta receptors, favored in hypertensive emergencies and pregnancy.

sections.mechanism: Combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta-blocker - lowers blood pressure by reducing vascular resistance and heart rate without reflex tachycardia.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, fatigue, scalp tingling, orthostatic hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm, and hypotension; avoid in decompensated heart failure and severe asthma.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate closely with IV use, keep the patient supine during IV administration, and lower pressure gradually to avoid hypoperfusion; a first-line agent in stroke and pregnancy-related hypertension.

concepts.name: Nicardipine
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV calcium channel blocker drip that smoothly lowers blood pressure, used in hypertensive emergencies and neuro patients.

sections.mechanism: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker - relaxes arterial smooth muscle to reduce vascular resistance and blood pressure, easily titratable as an infusion.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, flushing, reflex tachycardia, peripheral edema.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypotension and reflex tachycardia if titrated too quickly.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous blood pressure monitoring (often arterial line), titrate to a target range to avoid abrupt drops, and monitor the IV site; commonly used for controlled BP reduction in stroke and aortic dissection.

concepts.name: Sodium Nitroprusside
concepts.shortExplanation: A fast, powerful IV vasodilator drip used for severe high blood pressure, with a risk of cyanide buildup.

sections.mechanism: Releases nitric oxide, dilating both arteries and veins to rapidly reduce blood pressure and cardiac workload.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, headache, nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Profound hypotension and, with prolonged or high-dose use or renal impairment, cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity (altered mental status, metabolic acidosis).
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring, titrate carefully, protect the solution from light, use the shortest effective duration, and watch for signs of cyanide toxicity.

concepts.name: Esmolol
concepts.shortExplanation: A very short-acting IV beta-blocker used to quickly slow the heart in fast rhythms or aortic emergencies.

sections.mechanism: Ultra-short-acting cardioselective beta-1 blocker - lowers heart rate and blood pressure with an effect that wears off within minutes of stopping.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: Symptomatic bradycardia, heart block, hypotension, and bronchospasm in susceptible patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring, useful when a quickly reversible beta-blockade is desired (e.g., SVT, aortic dissection, perioperative tachycardia); titrate to heart rate/BP goals.

concepts.name: Lidocaine
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication that numbs tissue as a local anesthetic and, given IV, can treat certain dangerous heart rhythms.

sections.mechanism: Class Ib antiarrhythmic and local anesthetic - blocks sodium channels, stabilizing cardiac cells (for ventricular arrhythmias) and blocking nerve conduction (for local anesthesia).
sections.sideEffects: Local: numbness/tingling. Systemic: dizziness, drowsiness, perioral numbness.
sections.adverseEffects: CNS toxicity (confusion, seizures) and cardiac depression with high systemic levels; watch total dose for local anesthesia.
sections.nursingImplications: For IV antiarrhythmic use, continuous ECG monitoring and watch for neuro signs of toxicity; for local use, aspirate before injecting and track cumulative dose.

concepts.name: Sodium Bicarbonate
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV base used to correct severe acid buildup in the blood and to treat certain overdoses and high potassium.

sections.mechanism: Buffers acid by raising blood pH; in sodium-channel-blocker/TCA overdose it narrows a widened QRS, and it can temporarily shift potassium into cells.
sections.sideEffects: Fluid/sodium load, metabolic alkalosis if over-corrected.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and fluid overload; extravasation can injure tissue.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor arterial blood gases and electrolytes, use for documented severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, or specific toxicities, and do not mix with calcium in the same line (precipitation).

concepts.name: Digoxin Immune Fab
concepts.shortExplanation: The antidote for life-threatening digoxin poisoning.

sections.mechanism: Antibody fragments that bind digoxin and remove it from its site of action, reversing toxicity.
sections.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated; rarely allergic reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsening heart failure or rapid ventricular response as digoxin effect is removed, and hypokalemia (potassium shifts back into cells).
sections.nursingImplications: Give for life-threatening digoxin toxicity (dangerous arrhythmias, severe hyperkalemia from acute overdose); monitor rhythm, potassium, and for return of the underlying condition digoxin was treating.

concepts.name: Dextrose 50% (D50)
concepts.shortExplanation: A concentrated sugar solution pushed into a vein to rapidly treat dangerously low blood sugar.

sections.mechanism: Provides an immediate source of glucose to raise blood sugar.
sections.sideEffects: Local vein irritation, transient hyperglycemia.
sections.adverseEffects: Tissue necrosis with extravasation (it is very concentrated), rebound hypoglycemia, and hyperglycemia; give thiamine first in suspected alcohol use to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.
sections.nursingImplications: Confirm hypoglycemia, give through a secure IV (ideally larger vein), recheck glucose after administration, and feed the patient when able; use glucagon if no IV access.

concepts.name: Cefepime
concepts.shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic (4th-generation cephalosporin) used for serious hospital infections, including those with Pseudomonas.

sections.mechanism: Fourth-generation cephalosporin - inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis with broad gram-negative (including Pseudomonas) and gram-positive coverage.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, rash, injection-site reaction.
sections.adverseEffects: Neurotoxicity (confusion, myoclonus, seizures) especially with renal impairment or high doses, C. difficile infection, and allergic reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Adjust dose for renal function, monitor for neuro changes in at-risk patients, assess for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy, and watch for diarrhea suggesting C. difficile.

concepts.name: Meropenem
concepts.shortExplanation: A very broad-spectrum IV antibiotic (carbapenem) reserved for serious or resistant infections.

sections.mechanism: Carbapenem - inhibits cell-wall synthesis with very broad coverage including many resistant (ESBL) gram-negative organisms and anaerobes.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, headache, injection-site reaction.
sections.adverseEffects: Seizures (lower risk than older carbapenems), C. difficile infection, and allergic reactions; some cross-reactivity in severe penicillin allergy.
sections.nursingImplications: Adjust for renal function, reserve for serious/resistant infections per stewardship, monitor for diarrhea and neuro effects, and note it lowers valproate levels if co-administered.

concepts.name: Gentamicin / Tobramycin
concepts.shortExplanation: Aminoglycoside antibiotics used against serious gram-negative infections, requiring blood-level monitoring to protect the kidneys and hearing.

sections.mechanism: Aminoglycosides - bind the bacterial 30S ribosome to block protein synthesis, with potent gram-negative activity often used for synergy.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reaction; effects are mostly dose/level related.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity (usually reversible) and ototoxicity (can be permanent - hearing loss, vertigo); neuromuscular blockade at high doses.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor peak and trough levels, renal function, and for hearing/balance changes; ensure adequate hydration and coordinate accurate draw timing around doses.
sections.commonBrandName: Generic gentamicin; tobramycin (Tobrex ophthalmic; inhaled for cystic fibrosis).

concepts.name: Linezolid
concepts.shortExplanation: An antibiotic (oral or IV) for resistant gram-positive infections like MRSA and VRE.

sections.mechanism: Oxazolidinone - inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; active against MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE).
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Thrombocytopenia and other cytopenias with prolonged use, peripheral/optic neuropathy, and serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic drugs (it has weak MAO-inhibitor activity).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor CBC with longer courses, screen for concurrent serotonergic medications, and watch for serotonin syndrome; excellent oral bioavailability allows IV-to-PO switch.

concepts.name: Daptomycin
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV antibiotic for serious MRSA bloodstream and skin infections.

sections.mechanism: Cyclic lipopeptide - disrupts the bacterial cell membrane; active against MRSA and other resistant gram-positive organisms.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reaction, GI upset, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (monitor CK); eosinophilic pneumonia; it is inactivated by lung surfactant, so it is not used for pneumonia.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor weekly CK and for muscle pain/weakness, hold interacting statins if directed, and do not use for pneumonia; dose by weight and renal function.

concepts.name: Aztreonam
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV antibiotic for gram-negative infections, useful when a patient has a severe penicillin allergy.

sections.mechanism: Monobactam - inhibits cell-wall synthesis with activity limited to aerobic gram-negative bacteria (including Pseudomonas).
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reaction, rash, GI upset.
sections.adverseEffects: Generally low cross-reactivity with penicillins/cephalosporins (except ceftazidime, which shares a side chain), rare hepatic enzyme elevation.
sections.nursingImplications: A useful gram-negative option in serious beta-lactam allergy; still assess allergy history, adjust for renal function, and combine with gram-positive coverage when needed.

concepts.name: Ampicillin-Sulbactam
concepts.shortExplanation: A common IV antibiotic combination that covers a broad range of bacteria, including anaerobes.

sections.mechanism: Ampicillin (a penicillin) plus sulbactam (a beta-lactamase inhibitor) - broadens coverage to many resistant organisms and anaerobes.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, rash, injection-site reaction.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions (including anaphylaxis in penicillin allergy), C. difficile infection.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess for penicillin allergy before giving, adjust for renal function, and monitor for diarrhea; commonly used for aspiration pneumonia, intra-abdominal, and skin/soft-tissue infections.

concepts.name: Micafungin
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV antifungal that is first-line for serious yeast (Candida) infections in the hospital.

sections.mechanism: Echinocandin - inhibits fungal cell-wall synthesis; first-line for invasive candidiasis and candidemia.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, injection-site reaction.
