sections.adverseEffects: Liver enzyme elevation, infusion reactions, and rare hepatotoxicity.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor liver function, infuse over the recommended time to reduce infusion reactions, and note fewer drug interactions and less nephrotoxicity than azoles or amphotericin.

concepts.name: Amphotericin B
concepts.shortExplanation: A powerful IV antifungal for severe systemic fungal infections, known for infusion reactions and kidney effects.

sections.mechanism: Polyene - binds fungal cell-membrane ergosterol to create pores; broad, fungicidal activity for serious systemic mycoses.
sections.sideEffects: Fever, chills, rigors during infusion ("shake and bake"), nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, and infusion reactions; lipid formulations reduce toxicity.
sections.nursingImplications: Pre-medicate per protocol, monitor renal function and electrolytes (replace potassium/magnesium), hydrate to protect the kidneys, and watch closely during infusion; verify the exact formulation and dose.

concepts.name: Oseltamivir
concepts.shortExplanation: An oral antiviral that shortens the flu and can prevent it after exposure, most effective when started early.

sections.mechanism: Neuraminidase inhibitor - blocks release of influenza virus from infected cells, reducing viral spread.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare neuropsychiatric events (confusion, abnormal behavior), and hypersensitivity reactions.
sections.nursingImplications: Start as early as possible (ideally within 48 hours of symptoms), give for treatment or post-exposure prophylaxis in at-risk/hospitalized patients, and take with food to reduce nausea; apply droplet precautions for influenza.

concepts.name: Phytonadione (Vitamin K1)
concepts.shortExplanation: Vitamin K given to reverse the blood-thinning effect of warfarin and treat a high INR.

sections.mechanism: Provides vitamin K needed to make clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, reversing warfarin's effect over hours.
sections.sideEffects: Injection-site reaction; flushing.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare anaphylactoid reactions with IV administration (give slowly, diluted); over-correction can make re-anticoagulation difficult.
sections.nursingImplications: Choose the route by urgency (oral for mild elevation, slow IV for serious bleeding, often with FFP or PCC), monitor INR response, and reassess the need for ongoing anticoagulation.

concepts.name: Protamine Sulfate
concepts.shortExplanation: The antidote that reverses the anticoagulant heparin, used for bleeding or after heart/vascular surgery.

sections.mechanism: A positively charged protein that binds and neutralizes negatively charged heparin, reversing its anticoagulant effect (partial for low-molecular-weight heparin).
sections.sideEffects: Flushing, hypotension with rapid administration.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylaxis (higher risk in patients with fish allergy, prior protamine exposure, or NPH insulin use); too much can itself have an anticoagulant effect.
sections.nursingImplications: Give slowly with continuous monitoring, dose based on the amount and timing of heparin, and recheck coagulation (aPTT); have resuscitation support available.

concepts.name: Idarucizumab
concepts.shortExplanation: A specific antidote that rapidly reverses the blood thinner dabigatran in life-threatening bleeding.

sections.mechanism: A monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity, immediately neutralizing its anticoagulant effect.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, constipation.
sections.adverseEffects: Thrombotic risk returns once anticoagulation is reversed; rare hypersensitivity.
sections.nursingImplications: Give for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding or before emergency surgery in dabigatran-treated patients, monitor for bleeding control and for return of the clotting risk, and reassess anticoagulation needs.

concepts.name: Andexanet Alfa / 4-Factor PCC
concepts.shortExplanation: Agents used to reverse factor Xa-inhibitor blood thinners (like apixaban and rivaroxaban) during major bleeding.

sections.mechanism: Andexanet alfa is a decoy factor Xa that binds and neutralizes Xa-inhibitors; 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) replaces clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X to restore clotting.
sections.sideEffects: Infusion-related reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Thrombotic events (MI, stroke, DVT/PE) as clotting is restored; PCC also carries a thrombotic risk.
sections.nursingImplications: Reserve for life-threatening bleeding on apixaban/rivaroxaban, monitor for bleeding control and thrombosis, and know your institution's preferred agent and dosing; PCC is also used for urgent warfarin reversal.

concepts.name: Argatroban
concepts.shortExplanation: An IV blood thinner used when heparin can't be given, especially in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

sections.mechanism: Direct thrombin inhibitor - blocks thrombin directly, providing anticoagulation without the platelet cross-reactivity of heparin.
sections.sideEffects: Bleeding, hypotension, nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding; it prolongs the INR, which complicates transitioning to warfarin.
sections.nursingImplications: The anticoagulant of choice in HIT, titrated to aPTT; reduce dose in hepatic impairment, monitor for bleeding, and follow the specific protocol when bridging to warfarin.

concepts.name: Prochlorperazine
concepts.shortExplanation: An antinausea medication also used for migraines, from the same family as some antipsychotics.

sections.mechanism: Phenothiazine - blocks dopamine (D2) receptors in the brain's vomiting center to relieve nausea and vomiting.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, orthostatic hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms including acute dystonia and akathisia, QT prolongation, and rarely neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
sections.nursingImplications: Watch for restlessness and dystonic reactions (treatable with diphenhydramine/benztropine), monitor blood pressure, and use cautiously with other QT-prolonging drugs; distinct from promethazine and metoclopramide.

concepts.name: Valproic Acid
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication that controls seizures and stabilizes mood, available in an IV form for status epilepticus.

sections.mechanism: Increases GABA activity and blocks sodium channels; broad-spectrum antiseizure agent also used for bipolar mania and migraine prevention.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, tremor, weight gain, sedation, hair thinning.
sections.adverseEffects: Hepatotoxicity, hyperammonemia (can cause encephalopathy), thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, and teratogenicity (avoid in pregnancy).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor LFTs, ammonia, platelets, and drug levels; assess for confusion (check ammonia), avoid in pregnancy and liver disease, and note carbapenems dramatically lower its level.

concepts.name: Fosphenytoin
concepts.shortExplanation: A form of the seizure drug phenytoin that can be given IV quickly and more safely, used in status epilepticus.

sections.mechanism: A water-soluble prodrug rapidly converted to phenytoin, a sodium-channel blocker that stops seizure activity.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, itching/paresthesias during infusion, nystagmus.
sections.adverseEffects: Hypotension and arrhythmias with rapid infusion (less than phenytoin), and it avoids the severe tissue injury (purple glove syndrome) seen with IV phenytoin extravasation.
sections.nursingImplications: Dosed in "phenytoin equivalents," monitor ECG and blood pressure during infusion, and follow phenytoin levels afterward; a safer IV loading option than phenytoin for status epilepticus.

concepts.name: Dexamethasone
concepts.shortExplanation: A potent, long-acting steroid used for many conditions, from brain swelling and croup to nausea and COVID-19.

sections.mechanism: Long-acting corticosteroid - strongly reduces inflammation and immune activity with minimal mineralocorticoid (salt-retaining) effect.
sections.sideEffects: Hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood changes, increased appetite, fluid effects.
sections.adverseEffects: Hyperglycemia, immunosuppression/infection risk, GI ulceration, adrenal suppression with prolonged use, and psychosis at high doses.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood glucose, do not stop abruptly after prolonged use, watch for infection and GI symptoms, and know its many uses (cerebral edema, croup, chemo-induced nausea, COVID-19, adrenal testing).

concepts.name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
concepts.shortExplanation: A vitamin given to prevent and treat a serious brain condition (Wernicke encephalopathy), especially in alcohol use.

sections.mechanism: An essential vitamin (B1) required for glucose metabolism in the brain; deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy.
sections.sideEffects: Generally very well tolerated.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare hypersensitivity with IV administration.
sections.nursingImplications: Give before or with glucose in at-risk patients (chronic alcohol use, malnutrition) to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy, a core part of alcohol-withdrawal and "banana bag" protocols; watch for confusion, ataxia, and eye-movement changes.

concepts.name: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
concepts.shortExplanation: An antithyroid drug that lowers thyroid hormone, preferred in thyroid storm and early pregnancy.

sections.mechanism: Blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and also reduces conversion of T4 to active T3, making it useful in thyroid storm.
sections.sideEffects: Rash, nausea, joint aches.
sections.adverseEffects: Agranulocytosis (watch for fever/sore throat) and hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole); vasculitis rarely.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach patients to report fever or sore throat immediately (check CBC), monitor LFTs, and note it is preferred over methimazole in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm.

concepts.name: Buprenorphine
concepts.shortExplanation: A medication for opioid use disorder and pain that eases withdrawal and cravings with a lower overdose risk than full opioids.

sections.mechanism: Partial opioid agonist (often combined with naloxone) - activates opioid receptors enough to prevent withdrawal and cravings while having a ceiling effect that limits respiratory depression.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, headache, sweating, nausea.
sections.adverseEffects: Precipitated withdrawal if given too soon after a full opioid, respiratory depression (especially with benzodiazepines/alcohol), and QT effects at high doses.
sections.nursingImplications: Confirm the patient is in early withdrawal (e.g., by COWS) before induction to avoid precipitated withdrawal, give sublingually as directed, and coordinate with addiction-medicine protocols.

concepts.name: Clozapine
concepts.shortExplanation: An antipsychotic for schizophrenia that hasn't responded to other drugs, requiring close blood monitoring.

sections.mechanism: Atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors; uniquely effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reducing suicidality.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, drooling, weight gain, constipation, orthostatic hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Agranulocytosis (mandatory ANC monitoring), myocarditis, seizures, severe constipation/ileus, and metabolic effects.
sections.nursingImplications: Requires enrollment in a monitoring program with regular ANC checks; teach patients to report fever/infection, chest pain, or severe constipation, and monitor metabolic parameters.

concepts.name: Acetaminophen Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that measures acetaminophen (Tylenol) to detect overdose and guide the antidote.

sections.normalRange: Therapeutic levels are roughly 10-20 mcg/mL; in overdose the level is plotted against time since ingestion on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram (a 4-hour level >=150 mcg/mL indicates likely toxicity).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A toxic level (or being above the treatment line on the nomogram) risks acute liver failure and is the trigger for N-acetylcysteine; a single acetaminophen level should be drawn no earlier than 4 hours after ingestion.

concepts.name: Vancomycin Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood level used to keep the antibiotic vancomycin effective while avoiding kidney damage.

sections.normalRange: Traditional trough goals are about 10-20 mcg/mL depending on the infection; many centers now dose to an AUC/MIC target. The trough is drawn just before the next scheduled dose.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Levels too low risk treatment failure; levels too high increase the risk of nephrotoxicity (and possibly ototoxicity). Timing the draw correctly (right before the dose) is essential for accurate dosing.

concepts.name: Blood Alcohol Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test measuring the amount of alcohol (ethanol) in the blood.

sections.normalRange: Normally none (0 mg/dL). The legal driving limit is commonly 80 mg/dL (0.08%); values are reported in mg/dL or as a percentage.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher levels correlate with intoxication severity; very high levels risk respiratory depression. A rising or high level in an intoxicated patient, or a surprisingly low one in a chronic drinker with symptoms, helps anticipate withdrawal timing and evaluate altered mental status.

concepts.name: Salicylate Level
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that measures aspirin (salicylate) to diagnose overdose.

sections.normalRange: Therapeutic anti-inflammatory levels are roughly 10-30 mg/dL; toxicity generally begins above about 40-50 mg/dL and levels are trended because absorption can be prolonged.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels cause the classic mixed picture of respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis, tinnitus, tachypnea, and altered mental status; rising levels may require alkalinization or dialysis.

concepts.name: Serum & Urine Osmolality
concepts.shortExplanation: Tests that measure how concentrated the blood and urine are, used to work up sodium and water problems.

sections.normalRange: Serum osmolality is about 275-295 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality varies widely (roughly 50-1200 mOsm/kg) with hydration.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Comparing serum and urine osmolality distinguishes causes of hyponatremia (e.g., SIADH shows inappropriately concentrated urine) and dehydration. A gap between measured and calculated serum osmolality (osmolar gap) suggests a toxic alcohol ingestion.

concepts.name: Estimated GFR (eGFR)
concepts.shortExplanation: A calculated number that estimates how well the kidneys are filtering, used to stage kidney disease and dose medications.

sections.normalRange: About 90 mL/min/1.73m2 or higher with no other signs of kidney damage; it is estimated from creatinine, age, and sex.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Declining eGFR stages chronic kidney disease (e.g., <60 for 3 months) and signals acute kidney injury when it falls quickly. It guides renal dosing of drugs and decisions about contrast and nephrotoxins.

concepts.name: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
concepts.shortExplanation: An enzyme found in most tissues that rises in the blood when cells are damaged.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 140-280 U/L, varying by lab and method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A nonspecific marker of tissue damage or cell turnover; elevations occur with hemolysis, tumor lysis, tissue infarction, and some cancers. It is interpreted alongside the clinical picture and other labs rather than alone.

concepts.name: Uric Acid
concepts.shortExplanation: A waste product measured in the blood; high levels can cause gout and signal rapid cell breakdown.

sections.normalRange: About 3.5-7.2 mg/dL, slightly higher in men than women.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels can trigger gout flares and kidney stones, and rise sharply in tumor lysis syndrome during cancer treatment. Low levels are usually not clinically significant.

concepts.name: Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa)
concepts.shortExplanation: A calculation using blood and urine sodium and creatinine to find the cause of acute kidney injury.

sections.normalRange: Interpreted rather than "normal/abnormal": FeNa is calculated from paired serum and urine sodium and creatinine, ideally before diuretics are given.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A FeNa below 1% suggests prerenal AKI (the kidneys are avidly holding sodium due to poor perfusion), while above 2% suggests intrinsic (tubular) injury. Diuretics invalidate FeNa, so a urine urea fraction may be used instead.

concepts.name: Microalbumin (Albumin-Creatinine Ratio)
concepts.shortExplanation: A urine test that detects small amounts of protein, the earliest sign of kidney damage from diabetes or high blood pressure.

sections.normalRange: A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio under 30 mg/g is normal.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 30-300 mg/g indicates moderately increased albuminuria (early kidney damage) and above 300 mg/g is severely increased; persistent elevation guides blood-pressure and kidney-protective treatment in diabetes and hypertension.

concepts.name: Prealbumin
concepts.shortExplanation: A protein that reflects recent nutritional status, used to monitor at-risk and tube-fed patients.

sections.normalRange: About 15-36 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Because it has a short half-life (~2 days), a low or falling prealbumin can reflect recent poor nutrition; however, it also drops with inflammation, so it is interpreted alongside CRP and the clinical picture rather than as a pure nutrition marker.

concepts.name: Reticulocyte Count
concepts.shortExplanation: A measure of young red blood cells that shows whether the bone marrow is responding to anemia.

sections.normalRange: About 0.5-2.5% of red cells (reported as a percentage or absolute count).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high count means the marrow is appropriately making new red cells (blood loss or hemolysis), while a low count with anemia means the marrow is under-producing (iron/B12 deficiency, marrow suppression, kidney disease).

concepts.name: Peripheral Blood Smear
concepts.shortExplanation: A microscope look at a drop of blood to examine the size, shape, and appearance of blood cells.

sections.normalRange: Reported descriptively rather than as a number; normal shows uniform red cells, normal white cells, and adequate platelets.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Morphology flags specific problems - schistocytes (fragmented cells) in TTP/DIC/HELLP, blasts in leukemia, sickle cells, spherocytes, and toxic granulation in infection - directing further workup.

concepts.name: Haptoglobin
concepts.shortExplanation: A protein that binds free hemoglobin; a low level points to red blood cells being destroyed.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 30-200 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low haptoglobin supports intravascular hemolysis (it gets used up binding hemoglobin released from broken red cells) - seen in hemolytic transfusion reactions, TTP, and HELLP - and is interpreted with LDH, bilirubin, and the reticulocyte count.

concepts.name: G6PD
concepts.shortExplanation: A test for an enzyme that, when deficient, makes red blood cells break down after certain drugs, foods, or infections.

sections.normalRange: Reported as normal enzyme activity; deficiency is an inherited (X-linked) low level.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Deficiency predisposes to hemolysis when exposed to oxidant stress (certain antibiotics/antimalarials, fava beans, infection). Knowing status before oxidant drugs helps prevent a hemolytic episode.

concepts.name: Blood Type & Crossmatch
concepts.shortExplanation: Tests that determine a patient's blood group and confirm donor blood is compatible before a transfusion.

sections.normalRange: Reports the ABO group and Rh(D) status plus an antibody screen; the crossmatch confirms compatibility with specific donor units.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive antibody screen means the patient has antibodies that can react with donor cells, requiring specially matched units and more time. Nurses verify the type and crossmatch and perform the two-person identity check before hanging blood.

concepts.name: Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs)
concepts.shortExplanation: A test that detects antibodies stuck to red blood cells, used to investigate hemolysis.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive direct Coombs indicates antibody-coated red cells, seen in hemolytic transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and hemolytic disease of the newborn; it helps confirm an immune cause of hemolysis.

concepts.name: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
concepts.shortExplanation: A hormone that controls blood calcium; its level helps explain calcium problems and bone disease in kidney patients.

sections.normalRange: About 15-65 pg/mL, interpreted together with the calcium level.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High PTH with high calcium suggests hyperparathyroidism; high PTH with low calcium suggests a compensatory response (as in vitamin D deficiency or CKD mineral-bone disease); low PTH with low calcium suggests hypoparathyroidism (e.g., after thyroid surgery).

concepts.name: Vitamin B12 & Folate
concepts.shortExplanation: Blood tests for two vitamins whose deficiency causes a specific type of anemia and, for B12, nerve problems.

sections.normalRange: B12 is roughly 200-900 pg/mL and folate about >4 ng/mL, varying by lab.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low B12 or folate causes macrocytic (large-cell) anemia; low B12 also causes neuropathy and cognitive changes and must be corrected before or with folate. These are part of the workup of an elevated MCV or unexplained neuro symptoms.

concepts.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
concepts.shortExplanation: The blood test that measures vitamin D status, important for bone health and calcium balance.

sections.normalRange: Sufficiency is commonly defined as 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 30 ng/mL or higher; 20-30 is often called insufficient and below 20 deficient.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Deficiency contributes to low calcium, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and bone disease, and is common in chronic kidney disease and limited sun exposure; it guides supplementation.

concepts.name: Thyroid Antibodies
concepts.shortExplanation: Blood tests that identify an autoimmune cause of an underactive or overactive thyroid.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative or low; includes thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO) and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated TPO antibodies support Hashimoto thyroiditis (a common cause of hypothyroidism), while elevated TSI supports Graves disease (hyperthyroidism). They confirm an autoimmune cause when thyroid function is abnormal.

concepts.name: Beta-hCG (Quantitative)
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test measuring the pregnancy hormone, used to confirm and monitor pregnancy and detect complications.

sections.normalRange: Very low or undetectable when not pregnant; in early pregnancy the level roughly doubles every ~48 hours.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive result confirms pregnancy (a key safety check before imaging with radiation or certain medications); levels that rise abnormally slowly or plateau can suggest ectopic or nonviable pregnancy, and very high levels can occur with molar pregnancy.

concepts.name: C. difficile Testing
concepts.shortExplanation: A stool test to diagnose Clostridioides difficile, a common cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative; testing is done only on unformed (diarrheal) stool from symptomatic patients.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive result (toxin or PCR for the toxin gene) indicates C. difficile infection and triggers contact precautions and treatment; testing formed stool or after treatment can give misleading positives, so it is used judiciously.

concepts.name: Respiratory Pathogen Panel
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid test (often a nasal swab) that identifies common respiratory viruses like flu, COVID-19, and RSV at once.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative for pathogens; a multiplex PCR panel detects several respiratory viruses and some bacteria from one specimen.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive result identifies the organism, guiding isolation precautions, antiviral treatment (e.g., oseltamivir for influenza), and cohorting decisions; results are interpreted with symptoms and exposure history.

concepts.name: HIV Screening
concepts.shortExplanation: A blood test that screens for HIV infection, used for diagnosis and after possible exposures.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative; the 4th-generation antigen/antibody test detects both the p24 antigen and antibodies.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A reactive screen must be confirmed with follow-up testing before a diagnosis is made; early detection allows treatment and, after occupational exposures, guides post-exposure prophylaxis decisions.

concepts.name: Hepatitis Panel
concepts.shortExplanation: Blood tests that screen for hepatitis A, B, and C infection.

sections.normalRange: Normally negative/non-reactive; the panel checks antigens and antibodies for hepatitis A, B, and C to identify current or past infection and immunity.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Positive markers distinguish acute vs chronic vs resolved infection or vaccine immunity (e.g., hepatitis B surface antigen indicates active infection). Used before certain procedures/treatments and in the workup of abnormal liver tests.

concepts.name: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Analysis
concepts.shortExplanation: Testing of the fluid around the brain and spinal cord, obtained by lumbar puncture, to diagnose infections and other neurologic conditions.

sections.normalRange: Normal CSF is clear with low white cells, normal protein (~15-45 mg/dL), glucose about two-thirds of blood glucose, and no organisms; opening pressure is roughly 10-20 cm H2O.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Patterns point to the cause: high neutrophils with low glucose suggest bacterial meningitis; lymphocytes with normal glucose suggest viral meningitis; blood in all tubes suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage. Nurses position for the LP and monitor for post-procedure headache.

concepts.name: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) / BLS
concepts.shortExplanation: Chest compressions and rescue breaths that keep blood and oxygen moving to vital organs during cardiac arrest.

sections.targetConcern: Cardiac arrest - a pulseless, unresponsive patient who is not breathing normally.
sections.whatToMonitor: Compression quality (rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4 inches, full recoil, minimal interruptions), rhythm at each pulse check for a shockable rhythm, return of spontaneous circulation, and end-tidal CO2 as a marker of effective compressions.

concepts.name: Transcutaneous Pacing
concepts.shortExplanation: A noninvasive way to speed up a dangerously slow heart by delivering electrical impulses through pads on the chest.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade heart block that hasn't responded to atropine and is causing hypotension or poor perfusion.
sections.whatToMonitor: Electrical capture (a pacer spike followed by a wide QRS) AND mechanical capture (a matching pulse and improved blood pressure), skin under the pads, and the patient's pain/sedation - pacing is uncomfortable.

concepts.name: Platelet Transfusion
concepts.shortExplanation: Infusion of donor platelets to prevent or treat bleeding when a patient's platelet count is very low or platelets don't work.

sections.targetConcern: Thrombocytopenia with bleeding or a very low count (transfusion thresholds vary, e.g., prophylaxis often around 10,000, higher before procedures), or platelet dysfunction.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs and for transfusion reactions (fever, chills, rash, respiratory distress) especially early, the post-transfusion platelet count for expected rise, and fluid status; ABO-preferred but compatibility rules differ from red cells.

concepts.name: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) Transfusion
concepts.shortExplanation: Infusion of the liquid part of donor blood, which contains clotting factors, to treat bleeding from coagulopathy.

sections.targetConcern: Active bleeding or a planned procedure in a patient with multiple clotting-factor deficiencies (e.g., liver disease, warfarin reversal with active bleeding, massive transfusion, DIC).
sections.whatToMonitor: Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) response, vital signs and for reactions including TACO (volume overload) and TRALI (acute lung injury), and fluid status; FFP must be ABO-compatible and thawed before use.

concepts.name: Cryoprecipitate Transfusion
concepts.shortExplanation: Infusion of a concentrated blood product rich in fibrinogen and clotting factors, used mainly for low fibrinogen in severe bleeding.

sections.targetConcern: Low fibrinogen with bleeding - as in DIC, massive hemorrhage, or obstetric bleeding - or specific factor deficiencies.
sections.whatToMonitor: Fibrinogen level response, vital signs and for transfusion reactions, and ongoing bleeding; like other products it requires the two-person verification check before administration.

concepts.name: Physical Restraint Application
concepts.shortExplanation: The temporary, last-resort use of devices to restrict a patient's movement to protect them or others from harm.

sections.targetConcern: Imminent risk of harm to self or others (or to essential medical devices) when less-restrictive measures have failed - never for staff convenience or punishment.
sections.whatToMonitor: Circulation, skin, and range of motion of restrained limbs at frequent intervals, hydration/toileting/nutrition needs, the least-restrictive effective option, and required provider orders, re-evaluation, and documentation per regulation.

concepts.name: PPE Donning and Doffing
concepts.shortExplanation: The correct order for putting on and safely taking off protective gear to avoid spreading or catching infections.

sections.targetConcern: Preventing transmission of infectious organisms to and from healthcare workers when caring for patients on isolation precautions.
sections.whatToMonitor: Correct sequence and technique - don gown, mask/respirator, goggles, then gloves; doff the most contaminated items first (gloves, then gown) and perform hand hygiene between steps and at the end to avoid self-contamination.

concepts.name: Pressure Injury Prevention / Repositioning
concepts.shortExplanation: Regular turning, offloading, and skin care to keep immobile patients from developing pressure injuries.

sections.targetConcern: Patients at risk for pressure injury from immobility, poor perfusion, moisture, or malnutrition (e.g., a high Braden score risk).
sections.whatToMonitor: Skin over bony prominences at each turn, adherence to the turning schedule (commonly every ~2 hours), heel offloading, moisture and continence care, nutrition, and support-surface use.

concepts.name: Tracheostomy Care & Suctioning
concepts.shortExplanation: Ongoing cleaning of a tracheostomy site and clearing of secretions to keep the airway open and prevent infection.

sections.targetConcern: Maintaining a patent, clean tracheostomy in a patient with a long-term airway - distinct from creating the tracheostomy.
sections.whatToMonitor: Oxygen saturation before/during/after suctioning, secretion amount and character, stoma site for bleeding/infection, cuff pressure, and signs of accidental decannulation; keep a spare tube and obturator at the bedside.

concepts.name: Prone Positioning
concepts.shortExplanation: Turning a patient face-down to improve oxygenation in severe lung failure.

sections.targetConcern: Moderate-to-severe ARDS with refractory hypoxemia, where prone positioning improves oxygen exchange and survival (PROSEVA evidence).
sections.whatToMonitor: Oxygenation and ventilator pressures, security of the endotracheal tube and all lines during the coordinated turn, pressure points and the face/eyes for skin injury, and hemodynamic tolerance; a trained team is needed to turn safely.

concepts.name: Wound Dressing Change
concepts.shortExplanation: Removing an old dressing, cleaning a wound, and applying a new dressing using clean or sterile technique.

sections.targetConcern: Promoting healing and preventing infection in surgical, pressure, or chronic wounds by maintaining an appropriate wound environment.
sections.whatToMonitor: Wound appearance, size, drainage, and odor, signs of infection, periwound skin, and the patient's pain (pre-medicate as needed); use correct technique and the ordered dressing type.

concepts.name: Wound Irrigation
concepts.shortExplanation: Flushing a wound with fluid to remove debris and bacteria and support healing.

sections.targetConcern: Cleansing contaminated, chronic, or draining wounds to reduce infection risk and prepare the wound bed.
sections.whatToMonitor: Adequate but not excessive irrigation pressure, complete removal of debris, wound-bed appearance, patient comfort, and protection of surrounding skin; use the ordered solution and technique.

concepts.name: Incision & Drainage (Abscess)
concepts.shortExplanation: Cutting open and draining a pocket of pus to treat an abscess.

sections.targetConcern: A fluctuant skin or soft-tissue abscess that needs drainage for source control (antibiotics alone often aren't enough).
sections.whatToMonitor: Bleeding and drainage after the procedure, packing if placed, signs of spreading infection or systemic illness, and pain; provide wound-care and follow-up teaching.

concepts.name: Laceration Repair / Suturing
concepts.shortExplanation: Closing a cut with sutures, staples, or skin adhesive to stop bleeding and help it heal.

sections.targetConcern: A laceration that needs closure for hemostasis, function, and a good cosmetic result, after the wound is cleaned and assessed.
sections.whatToMonitor: Wound hemostasis and approximation, neurovascular and tendon function distal to the wound, signs of infection, and tetanus status; provide wound-care and suture/staple-removal timing teaching.

concepts.name: Splint Application / Immobilization
concepts.shortExplanation: Applying a rigid support to immobilize an injured bone or joint and reduce pain.

sections.targetConcern: Fractures, sprains, or soft-tissue injuries that need immobilization for pain control and to prevent further injury before or instead of casting.
sections.whatToMonitor: Neurovascular status (pulses, color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation, movement) before and after application, for compartment syndrome (severe pain, especially with passive stretch), and skin/pressure under the splint.

concepts.name: Arthrocentesis
concepts.shortExplanation: Using a needle to withdraw fluid from a joint to diagnose or relieve a joint problem.

sections.targetConcern: Evaluating a swollen joint - most urgently to rule out septic arthritis - or relieving a painful effusion; synovial fluid is sent for cell count, crystals, Gram stain, and culture.
sections.whatToMonitor: The joint for bleeding, infection, and swelling after the tap, pain, and the synovial fluid results; maintain sterile technique to avoid introducing infection.

concepts.name: External Ventricular Drain (Ventriculostomy)
concepts.shortExplanation: A catheter placed into the brain's fluid spaces to drain cerebrospinal fluid and measure intracranial pressure.

sections.targetConcern: Elevated intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus (e.g., after hemorrhage or traumatic brain injury) needing CSF drainage and pressure monitoring.
sections.whatToMonitor: ICP and CSF drainage amount/color/clarity, the transducer/drain leveled to the reference point (often the tragus/foramen of Monro), clamping during position changes per order, and the insertion site for infection or leakage.

concepts.name: Intracranial Pressure (ICP) Monitoring
concepts.shortExplanation: Continuous measurement of the pressure inside the skull to guide treatment of brain injury.

sections.targetConcern: Patients at risk of raised intracranial pressure (severe traumatic brain injury, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus) where trends guide therapy and preserve brain perfusion.
sections.whatToMonitor: ICP and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP), waveform quality, response to interventions (head of bed, sedation, osmotherapy), and signs of herniation such as pupil changes and Cushing triad.

concepts.name: Vaginal Delivery
concepts.shortExplanation: The birth of a baby through the birth canal, supported and monitored by the nursing team.

sections.targetConcern: Progression of labor to birth in a mother and fetus without indications for cesarean delivery.
sections.whatToMonitor: Fetal heart rate pattern and contractions, cervical progress and maternal vital signs, and after birth, uterine tone and bleeding (for postpartum hemorrhage), perineal integrity, and newborn transition/Apgar.

concepts.name: Cesarean Delivery
concepts.shortExplanation: Surgical birth of a baby through incisions in the abdomen and uterus.

sections.targetConcern: Situations where vaginal birth is unsafe or not progressing - e.g., nonreassuring fetal status, malposition, failure to progress, placenta previa, or maternal indications.
sections.whatToMonitor: Perioperative maternal vital signs, uterine tone and incisional/vaginal bleeding, anesthesia effects, fluid status and urine output, VTE prophylaxis, pain control, and newborn transition.

concepts.name: Amniocentesis
concepts.shortExplanation: Withdrawing a small sample of amniotic fluid with a needle to test the fetus during pregnancy.

sections.targetConcern: Prenatal testing for genetic conditions or fetal lung maturity, usually in the second trimester or later, done under ultrasound guidance.
sections.whatToMonitor: Fetal heart rate before and after, the needle site for bleeding or fluid leakage, uterine cramping or contractions, and signs of infection; Rh-negative mothers may need Rho(D) immune globulin.

concepts.name: FAST Exam
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid bedside ultrasound in trauma that looks for internal bleeding around the organs and heart.

sections.targetConcern: Rapidly detecting free fluid (usually blood) in the abdomen, pelvis, or around the heart in an unstable trauma patient to guide emergent decisions.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hemodynamic status during and after the scan, the exam findings (positive views suggest internal bleeding), and the need for rapid escalation to CT or the operating room; the nurse assists and continues resuscitation.

concepts.name: Pulmonary Artery (Swan-Ganz) Catheterization
concepts.shortExplanation: Threading a special catheter through the heart into the pulmonary artery to measure pressures and cardiac output.

sections.targetConcern: Advanced hemodynamic assessment in undifferentiated or severe shock, heart failure, or pulmonary hypertension when other data are insufficient.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion for arrhythmias during passage, the waveform to confirm position and avoid persistent wedging, the balloon deflated except for brief readings, and the site for bleeding/infection; interpret pressures and cardiac output with the team.

concepts.name: Arterial Pressure Monitoring
concepts.shortExplanation: Setting up and maintaining an arterial line so blood pressure can be read continuously and accurately.

sections.targetConcern: Critically ill patients needing beat-to-beat blood pressure (e.g., titrating vasopressors) or frequent arterial blood gases.
sections.whatToMonitor: A leveled and zeroed transducer at the phlebostatic axis, a good (non-damped, non-whipping) waveform, distal limb perfusion, and the site and connections for bleeding; troubleshoot damping and re-zero as needed.

concepts.name: Pulmonary Artery Catheter
concepts.shortExplanation: A long, multi-channel catheter floated through the heart into the pulmonary artery to measure pressures and cardiac output in the sickest patients.

sections.purpose: Provides advanced hemodynamic data - right atrial and pulmonary artery pressures, a wedge pressure that estimates left-heart filling, and cardiac output - to guide management of shock, heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension.
sections.careConsiderations: Monitor the waveform for the correct position and for spontaneous "wedging," keep the balloon deflated except during brief wedge readings, watch for arrhythmias and pulmonary artery rupture, and maintain a leveled, zeroed transducer and sterile line care.

concepts.name: ECMO Circuit
concepts.shortExplanation: A machine that pumps a patient's blood through an artificial lung outside the body to add oxygen and remove carbon dioxide when the heart or lungs are failing.

sections.purpose: Provides temporary extracorporeal life support - VV-ECMO supports failing lungs and VA-ECMO supports both heart and lungs - buying time for recovery or bridging to further therapy.
sections.careConsiderations: Continuously monitor the circuit (flows, pressures, oxygenator, for clots or air), cannula sites for bleeding and position, and anticoagulation labs; watch for hemolysis and limb ischemia and know the emergency response to circuit failure or cannula dislodgement.

concepts.name: Ventricular Assist Device
concepts.shortExplanation: An implanted mechanical pump that helps a weak heart push blood to the body, used in advanced heart failure.

sections.purpose: Most often a left ventricular assist device (LVAD), it takes over pumping for a failing ventricle as a bridge to transplant or as long-term (destination) therapy.
sections.careConsiderations: Many patients have a continuous-flow pump and no palpable pulse, so use a Doppler MAP; protect and monitor the driveline exit site for infection, respond to controller alarms, and know that CPR chest compressions may be contraindicated per protocol - follow the VAD team.

concepts.name: Percutaneous VAD (Impella)
concepts.shortExplanation: A small catheter-based pump placed across the aortic valve to temporarily boost the heart's output in cardiogenic shock or high-risk procedures.

sections.purpose: A temporary axial-flow pump that pulls blood from the left ventricle and ejects it into the aorta, unloading the heart and supporting circulation during cardiogenic shock or high-risk PCI.
sections.careConsiderations: Monitor the console for correct catheter position and "suction" alarms, watch for hemolysis (check plasma-free hemoglobin), keep the affected leg straight and check distal perfusion, and manage anticoagulation and the purge solution per protocol.

concepts.name: Arterial Line & Pressure Transducer
concepts.shortExplanation: A catheter in an artery connected to a transducer that shows continuous, beat-to-beat blood pressure and allows frequent blood draws.

sections.purpose: Delivers real-time arterial blood pressure and easy access for arterial blood gases, used when precise, continuous pressure monitoring is needed (e.g., titrating vasopressors).
sections.careConsiderations: Keep the transducer leveled at the phlebostatic axis and zeroed, verify a good waveform, and check distal perfusion of the cannulated limb. A disconnection can cause rapid blood loss, so keep connections tight and alarms on.

concepts.name: Bag-Valve-Mask
concepts.shortExplanation: A handheld device with a mask and squeeze bag used to deliver rescue breaths to someone who isn't breathing adequately.

sections.purpose: Provides manual positive-pressure ventilation and high-concentration oxygen during respiratory or cardiac arrest and before or between intubation attempts.
sections.careConsiderations: Achieve a tight mask seal (E-C technique, ideally two rescuers), squeeze smoothly to make the chest rise, avoid over-ventilating (rate and volume), attach oxygen and a reservoir, and coordinate with compressions during CPR.

concepts.name: Nasopharyngeal Airway
concepts.shortExplanation: A soft tube passed through the nose to keep the upper airway open, tolerated even by patients who still have a gag reflex.

sections.purpose: Bypasses soft-tissue obstruction at the back of the throat to maintain an open airway, useful in semiconscious patients or when an oral airway can't be used (e.g., clenched jaw).
sections.careConsiderations: Size by measuring nare to earlobe, lubricate and insert along the floor of the nostril, and avoid in suspected basilar skull fracture. Watch for nasal bleeding and ensure it doesn't dislodge.

concepts.name: Laryngeal Mask Airway
concepts.shortExplanation: A tube with an inflatable cuff that sits over the voice box to keep the airway open without passing a tube through the vocal cords.

sections.purpose: A supraglottic airway used for planned anesthesia and as a rescue airway when bag-mask ventilation fails and intubation is difficult or delayed.
sections.careConsiderations: Insert to seat over the laryngeal opening and inflate the cuff, confirm ventilation and capnography, and remember it does not fully protect against aspiration. Have suction and intubation backup ready.

concepts.name: Nebulizer
concepts.shortExplanation: A device that turns liquid medication into a fine mist the patient breathes in, commonly used for asthma and COPD.

sections.purpose: Delivers aerosolized medications - most often bronchodilators like albuterol/ipratropium - directly to the airways over several minutes of tidal breathing.
sections.careConsiderations: Assemble with the correct medication and oxygen/air flow, have the patient sit upright and breathe slowly, and reassess respiratory status, heart rate, and lung sounds before and after. Watch for tachycardia and tremor from bronchodilators.

concepts.name: Yankauer Suction Catheter
concepts.shortExplanation: A rigid, angled plastic tip used to suction secretions, blood, or vomit from the mouth to protect the airway.

sections.purpose: Clears the oral cavity of thick secretions, blood, or emesis to keep the airway open and prevent aspiration.
sections.careConsiderations: Suction the mouth (not deep in the throat, to avoid gagging/vomiting), apply suction only while withdrawing, keep it within reach at aspiration-risk and post-op bedsides, and monitor oxygen saturation during suctioning.

concepts.name: Forced-Air Warming Device
concepts.shortExplanation: A blanket connected to a warm-air blower used to prevent or treat low body temperature, especially around surgery.

sections.purpose: Actively warms patients by circulating heated air through a disposable blanket, preventing and treating perioperative hypothermia and its complications.
sections.careConsiderations: Use only the matched blanket with the hose attached (never "free-hose" warming, which can burn skin), monitor temperature to a normothermia goal, and protect skin and surgical sites. Avoid over-warming.

concepts.name: Rigid Cervical Collar
concepts.shortExplanation: A stiff neck brace applied to limit movement of the cervical spine when a neck injury is suspected.

sections.purpose: Restricts cervical spine motion to protect against worsening a possible spinal injury during assessment, transport, and imaging.
sections.careConsiderations: Size and apply correctly (a poor fit is ineffective), keep the head and neck aligned, log-roll for repositioning, and inspect skin under the collar for pressure injury during prolonged use. Remove only when the spine is cleared per protocol.

concepts.name: Traction Splint
concepts.shortExplanation: A device that applies steady pull to a fractured thigh bone to reduce pain, bleeding, and further injury.

sections.purpose: Applies longitudinal traction to realign and stabilize a mid-shaft femur fracture, reducing pain, muscle spasm, and blood loss before definitive care.
sections.careConsiderations: Perform neurovascular checks before and after application, do not use with certain injuries (e.g., pelvic fracture, or lower-leg/ankle injury on the same limb per protocol), and monitor distal pulses, sensation, and skin under straps.

concepts.name: Lungs & Pleura
concepts.shortExplanation: The paired organs of gas exchange and the thin double membrane that surrounds them and lets them slide against the chest wall.

sections.purpose: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two; each is wrapped by a visceral pleura, with a parietal pleura lining the chest wall and a thin fluid film between them that reduces friction during breathing.
sections.careConsiderations: Lobar anatomy grounds breath-sound assessment and interpreting infiltrates. Air in the pleural space causes pneumothorax and fluid causes effusion - both can compress the lung and are drained with a chest tube or thoracentesis.

concepts.name: Tracheobronchial Tree
concepts.shortExplanation: The branching airway from the windpipe down through the bronchi and bronchioles that carries air into the lungs.

sections.purpose: The trachea splits at the carina into right and left main bronchi (the right is more vertical, so aspirated material and a too-deep ETT tend to go right), branching into progressively smaller bronchi and bronchioles that end at the alveoli.
sections.careConsiderations: This anatomy underlies endotracheal tube placement, suctioning depth, and why aspiration and mucus plugging favor the right lung. Bronchospasm narrows these airways in asthma and COPD.

concepts.name: Diaphragm
concepts.shortExplanation: The dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs that is the main driver of breathing.

sections.purpose: Innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), it contracts and flattens to pull air into the lungs on inhalation and relaxes on exhalation; it also separates the chest from the abdomen.
sections.careConsiderations: High cervical spinal cord injury (above C3-C5) can paralyze the diaphragm and require ventilation. Watch for paradoxical or labored breathing, hiccups from diaphragmatic irritation, and splinting after abdominal or thoracic surgery.

concepts.name: Aorta & Great Vessels
concepts.shortExplanation: The body's largest artery and the major vessels leaving the heart that carry blood to the whole body.

sections.purpose: The aorta rises from the left ventricle (ascending aorta), curves at the arch giving off vessels to the head and arms, then descends through the chest and abdomen; its wall has three layers (intima, media, adventitia).
sections.careConsiderations: A tear between wall layers causes aortic dissection (tearing chest/back pain, unequal pulses/BP) and a weakened bulge is an aneurysm - both are emergencies. This anatomy also underlies central line tip position and blood pressure differences between limbs.

concepts.name: Pericardium
concepts.shortExplanation: The tough, double-layered sac that surrounds the heart and holds a small amount of lubricating fluid.

sections.purpose: An outer fibrous layer and inner serous layer enclose roughly 15-50 mL of fluid that lets the heart move without friction and anchors it in the chest.
sections.careConsiderations: Inflammation causes pericarditis (sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward); rapid fluid buildup causes a pericardial effusion that can progress to tamponade, where the heart cannot fill - watch for hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins.

concepts.name: Kidneys
concepts.shortExplanation: The paired, bean-shaped organs behind the abdomen that filter blood, make urine, and balance fluids and electrolytes.

sections.purpose: Each kidney has an outer cortex and inner medulla organized into pyramids that drain urine into calyces and the renal pelvis; they filter blood through about a million nephrons, regulating fluid, electrolytes, acid-base status, and blood pressure, and produce erythropoietin.
sections.careConsiderations: Because they sit retroperitoneally and depend on perfusion, they are injured by low blood flow, nephrotoxins, and obstruction. Nurses track urine output, creatinine, BUN, and eGFR and use caution with contrast and nephrotoxic drugs.

concepts.name: Ureters
concepts.shortExplanation: The two muscular tubes that carry urine from the kidneys down to the bladder.

sections.purpose: Each ureter propels urine by peristalsis from the renal pelvis to the bladder; it is narrowest where it passes through the bladder wall, a common site for kidney stones to lodge.
sections.careConsiderations: Obstruction (usually a stone) causes severe flank pain radiating to the groin (renal colic), nausea, and hematuria, and can back up urine into the kidney (hydronephrosis). Relevant to stone passage, stents, and urologic surgery.

concepts.name: Urinary Bladder
concepts.shortExplanation: The muscular, balloon-like organ that stores urine until it is voided.

sections.purpose: The detrusor muscle stretches to hold roughly 400-600 mL and contracts to empty; the trigone is a smooth triangle between the ureter openings and the urethral outlet, and internal/external sphincters control continence.
sections.careConsiderations: Retention causes distension and discomfort and is assessed with a bladder scanner and relieved by catheterization. This anatomy underlies Foley insertion, post-void residuals, and catheter-associated UTI prevention.

concepts.name: Liver
concepts.shortExplanation: The large organ in the right upper abdomen that processes nutrients, filters toxins, makes clotting proteins and bile, and metabolizes drugs.

sections.purpose: It receives a dual blood supply (portal vein plus hepatic artery), is organized into lobules with a central vein and peripheral portal triads, and handles metabolism, detoxification, protein/albumin and clotting-factor synthesis, and bile production.
sections.careConsiderations: Failure causes jaundice, coagulopathy, low albumin, and rising ammonia with confusion (hepatic encephalopathy); portal hypertension causes ascites and varices. Impaired metabolism means many drugs need dose adjustment.

concepts.name: Pancreas
concepts.shortExplanation: The gland behind the stomach that makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.

sections.purpose: Its exocrine tissue secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum, while endocrine islets of Langerhans release insulin (lowers glucose) and glucagon (raises glucose) to regulate blood sugar.
sections.careConsiderations: Inflammation (pancreatitis) causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated lipase; islet failure causes diabetes. Relevant to glucose management, enzyme labs, and NPO status in acute pancreatitis.

concepts.name: Gallbladder & Biliary Tree
concepts.shortExplanation: The small sac under the liver that stores bile, and the ducts that carry bile into the intestine.

sections.purpose: The gallbladder concentrates and stores bile made by the liver and releases it via the cystic duct into the common bile duct to help digest fats after meals.
sections.careConsiderations: Gallstones can block the ducts, causing cholecystitis (RUQ pain, fever) or obstructive jaundice; blockage near the pancreas can trigger pancreatitis. Relevant to cholecystectomy care and NPO/pain management.

concepts.name: Stomach
concepts.shortExplanation: The muscular pouch that holds swallowed food and begins digestion with acid and enzymes.

sections.purpose: Divided into the cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus, it secretes acid and pepsin to break down food and churns it before releasing it through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum.
sections.careConsiderations: Anatomy underlies NG tube placement and decompression, acid-related disease (GERD, peptic ulcers), and upper GI bleeding. Watch for aspiration risk and confirm tube position before feeds.

concepts.name: Brainstem
concepts.shortExplanation: The lower part of the brain (midbrain, pons, medulla) that controls breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, and consciousness.

sections.purpose: It relays signals between the brain and body, houses cranial nerve nuclei, and contains centers that drive automatic vital functions and arousal.
sections.careConsiderations: Brainstem compromise from herniation, stroke, or mass causes changes in breathing pattern, pupils, and consciousness and defines brain death. Watch for Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) signaling rising intracranial pressure.

concepts.name: Cerebellum
concepts.shortExplanation: The structure at the back of the brain that coordinates movement, balance, and posture.

sections.purpose: It fine-tunes voluntary movement, gait, and eye movements and maintains balance and coordination, without initiating movement itself.
sections.careConsiderations: Damage (stroke, tumor, alcohol effects) causes ataxia, unsteady gait, and coordination problems that raise fall risk. Posterior fossa swelling can compress the brainstem - watch for headache, vomiting, and declining consciousness.

concepts.name: Spinal Cord
concepts.shortExplanation: The bundle of nerves running through the spine that carries signals between the brain and the body.

sections.purpose: About 31 spinal segments with paired nerve roots relay motor commands down and sensory information up; it usually ends near L1-L2, below which the nerve roots form the cauda equina.
sections.careConsiderations: Injury causes motor/sensory loss below the level and, if high, breathing and blood-pressure instability (neurogenic shock). Anatomy underlies dermatome assessment, spinal precautions, and why lumbar puncture is done below L2.

concepts.name: Cranial Nerves
concepts.shortExplanation: The 12 pairs of nerves emerging from the brain that control the senses, face, and many head and neck functions.

sections.purpose: Numbered I-XII, they handle smell, vision, eye movement and pupils, facial sensation and movement, hearing and balance, taste, swallowing, and shoulder/tongue movement.
sections.careConsiderations: They are the backbone of the neuro exam - pupillary response (CN III), facial droop (CN VII), gag/swallow (CN IX, X), and eye movements localize stroke, raised ICP, and brainstem injury and flag aspiration risk.

concepts.name: Vertebral Column / Spine
concepts.shortExplanation: The stack of bones (vertebrae) that supports the body and protects the spinal cord.

sections.purpose: Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal vertebrae, separated by discs, protect the spinal cord and define the spinal levels used to describe injuries and procedures.
sections.careConsiderations: Suspected spinal injury requires motion restriction (collar, log-rolling) until cleared. The vertebral levels guide lumbar puncture, epidural placement, and localizing cord compression.

concepts.name: Thyroid & Parathyroid Glands
concepts.shortExplanation: The butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that sets metabolism, plus the four tiny glands behind it that control calcium.

sections.purpose: The thyroid makes T3/T4 hormones that regulate metabolic rate, while the parathyroid glands secrete PTH to raise blood calcium; both sit in the anterior neck near the trachea.
sections.careConsiderations: Overactivity causes hyperthyroidism/thyroid storm and underactivity causes hypothyroidism/myxedema. After thyroid surgery, watch for hypocalcemia (from parathyroid injury) - numbness, tingling, and positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs - and airway swelling.

concepts.name: Adrenal Glands
concepts.shortExplanation: The small glands on top of each kidney that make stress and blood-pressure hormones.

sections.purpose: The cortex produces cortisol (stress response), aldosterone (sodium/potassium and blood pressure), and androgens; the medulla releases the catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine.
sections.careConsiderations: Insufficient cortisol causes adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia) requiring stress-dose steroids; excess causes Cushing syndrome. Do not stop long-term steroids abruptly.

concepts.name: Pituitary Gland
concepts.shortExplanation: The pea-sized "master gland" at the base of the brain that directs the body's other hormone glands.

sections.purpose: The anterior lobe releases hormones controlling the thyroid, adrenals, growth, and reproduction; the posterior lobe stores and releases ADH (water balance) and oxytocin.
sections.careConsiderations: Too little ADH causes diabetes insipidus (large dilute urine, high sodium) and too much causes SIADH (retained water, low sodium). Relevant after pituitary surgery, head injury, and in hormone-axis workups.

concepts.name: Skin Layers
concepts.shortExplanation: The three layers of the skin - epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis - that form the body's protective barrier.

sections.purpose: The outer epidermis is the waterproof barrier, the dermis holds blood vessels, nerves, and collagen, and the deeper hypodermis (subcutaneous fat) cushions and insulates; together they protect against infection and regulate temperature and fluid.
sections.careConsiderations: Depth of injury defines pressure injury staging and burn depth. Nurses assess skin integrity, offload pressure points, and protect against breakdown, moisture, and shear.

concepts.name: Spleen
concepts.shortExplanation: The organ in the left upper abdomen that filters blood and supports the immune system.

sections.purpose: The largest lymphatic organ, it filters and recycles old red blood cells, stores platelets, and mounts immune responses against blood-borne organisms.
sections.careConsiderations: It is vulnerable to rupture in blunt trauma (left-upper-quadrant/shoulder pain, hypotension). People without a spleen (asplenia) are at risk for overwhelming infection and need vaccinations and prompt treatment of fevers.

concepts.name: Bone Marrow & Hematopoiesis
concepts.shortExplanation: The spongy tissue inside bones that manufactures red cells, white cells, and platelets.

sections.purpose: Hematopoietic stem cells in the marrow (hematopoiesis) continuously produce red blood cells (oxygen carrying), white blood cells (immunity), and platelets (clotting).
sections.careConsiderations: Marrow suppression from chemotherapy, radiation, or disease causes anemia, neutropenia (infection risk), and thrombocytopenia (bleeding risk). Nurses monitor the CBC, use neutropenic precautions, and prep for marrow biopsy.

concepts.name: SOFA Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A score that grades how badly six organ systems are failing, used to define sepsis and gauge how sick a critically ill patient is.

sections.purpose: Quantifies organ dysfunction in critically ill patients and, with the Sepsis-3 definition, identifies sepsis as a suspected infection plus an acute rise in SOFA; it also tracks trajectory and predicts mortality.
sections.steps: Scores 0-4 in each of six systems - respiration (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP/vasopressors), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine/urine output) - summed for a total.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher totals mean more organ failure and worse prognosis; an acute increase of 2 or more points with suspected infection meets the sepsis definition. Rising scores signal deterioration.

concepts.name: CURB-65
concepts.shortExplanation: A quick pneumonia severity score that helps decide whether a patient can go home or needs the hospital or ICU.

sections.purpose: Risk-stratifies community-acquired pneumonia to guide the site of care (outpatient vs ward vs ICU).
sections.steps: One point each for Confusion, Urea (BUN >19 mg/dL), Respiratory rate >=30, Blood pressure (SBP <90 or DBP <=60), and Age >=65.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 0-1 is low risk (often outpatient), 2 suggests admission, and 3-5 indicates severe pneumonia warranting consideration of ICU care.

concepts.name: Pediatric Early Warning Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A bedside score for hospitalized children that flags early signs of deterioration so the team can act before a child crashes.

sections.purpose: The pediatric counterpart to adult early-warning scores, it detects clinical deterioration in admitted children and triggers escalation or rapid response.
sections.steps: Assigns points for behavior/neuro status, cardiovascular signs (color, heart rate, capillary refill), and respiratory signs (rate, effort, oxygen/nebulizer use), summed to a total.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rising total or any high single-parameter score prompts increased monitoring and provider or rapid-response escalation per local thresholds.

concepts.name: Confusion Assessment Method
concepts.shortExplanation: The most widely used bedside tool for detecting delirium on general wards.

sections.purpose: Screens for delirium in non-ICU patients so it can be recognized and its cause treated, distinct from the ICU-specific CAM-ICU.
sections.steps: Delirium is present when there is (1) acute onset with fluctuating course AND (2) inattention, plus EITHER (3) disorganized thinking OR (4) an altered level of consciousness.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive CAM indicates delirium - prompt a workup for reversible causes (infection, drugs, metabolic, hypoxia), safety measures, and reorientation.

concepts.name: 4AT
concepts.shortExplanation: A rapid, roughly two-minute screen for delirium and cognitive impairment that needs no special training.

sections.purpose: Provides a fast bedside delirium screen usable by any clinician, useful at admission and with any acute mental-status change.
sections.steps: Four items: Alertness, AMT4 (age, date of birth, place, current year), Attention (months of the year backward), and Acute change or fluctuating course.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A total of 4 or more suggests possible delirium (with or without cognitive impairment); 1-3 suggests cognitive impairment; 0 makes delirium unlikely. A positive screen prompts a delirium workup.

concepts.name: Aldrete Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A recovery-room score that judges when a patient is safe to leave the PACU after anesthesia.

sections.purpose: Assesses readiness for discharge from post-anesthesia recovery by measuring return of physiologic function.
sections.steps: Scores 0-2 in each of five areas - Activity (movement), Respiration, Circulation (blood pressure), Consciousness, and Oxygen saturation - for a total of 0-10.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A score of 9-10 generally indicates readiness for discharge from the PACU; lower scores require continued recovery and monitoring.

concepts.name: PHQ-9
concepts.shortExplanation: A nine-question self-report screen that identifies depression and grades its severity.

sections.purpose: Screens for depression and measures symptom severity over the prior two weeks, widely used in primary care and med-surg settings.
sections.steps: Nine items scored 0-3 ("not at all" to "nearly every day") for a total of 0-27; item 9 specifically asks about thoughts of self-harm.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Scores of 5, 10, 15, and 20 mark mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression. Any positive response on item 9 requires immediate suicide-risk assessment.

concepts.name: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A standardized set of questions used to screen for suicide risk at admission or triage.

sections.purpose: Assesses the presence and severity of suicidal ideation and behavior to identify patients who need safety precautions and further evaluation.
sections.steps: A stepped series of yes/no questions about the wish to die, active ideation, methods, intent, plan, and any past suicidal behavior; positive answers guide deeper questions.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Endorsing active ideation with method, intent, or plan - or recent behavior - indicates elevated risk and triggers safety measures (1:1 observation, environment safety, provider/behavioral-health referral).

concepts.name: AUDIT-C
concepts.shortExplanation: A three-question screen for risky alcohol use that helps flag patients who may develop withdrawal.

sections.purpose: Quickly identifies hazardous drinking or alcohol use disorder, helping anticipate withdrawal risk during admission (pairs with the CIWA-Ar for active withdrawal).
sections.steps: Three questions on frequency of drinking, typical number of drinks, and frequency of heavy (6+ drink) episodes, each scored 0-4 for a total of 0-12.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A score of 4 or more in men or 3 or more in women suggests risky use; higher scores mean higher risk and prompt withdrawal monitoring and counseling.

concepts.name: TIMI Risk Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A score that estimates short-term risk of bad outcomes in patients with unstable angina or an NSTEMI.

sections.purpose: Risk-stratifies non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes to guide how aggressively and quickly to treat (complements the HEART Score used in the ED).
sections.steps: One point each for 7 factors: age >=65, >=3 coronary risk factors, known coronary stenosis >=50%, aspirin use in the last 7 days, >=2 anginal episodes in 24 hours, ST deviation, and elevated cardiac markers.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher scores predict greater 14-day risk of death, MI, or urgent revascularization; higher scores favor an early invasive strategy.

concepts.name: Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score
concepts.shortExplanation: A score for upper GI bleeding that identifies low-risk patients who may safely avoid urgent intervention or admission.

sections.purpose: Predicts the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopy, surgery) in upper GI bleeding, using only clinical and lab data available at presentation.
sections.steps: Uses BUN, hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse, and features such as melena, syncope, liver disease, and heart failure, summed to a total.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A score of 0 (or very low) identifies patients at low risk who may be managed as outpatients; higher scores predict a greater need for transfusion and urgent endoscopy.

concepts.name: Modified Rankin Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A simple 0-6 scale that grades overall disability, used most often to describe recovery after a stroke.

sections.purpose: Measures global functional disability and dependence, serving as the standard outcome measure after stroke and other neurologic events.
sections.steps: A single grade from 0 (no symptoms) through 5 (severe disability, bedridden) to 6 (death), based on independence in usual activities.
sections.abnormalMeaning: 0-2 generally indicates functional independence; 3-5 indicates increasing disability and care needs. Used to track recovery and guide rehab and discharge planning.

concepts.name: Katz Index of ADLs
concepts.shortExplanation: A checklist of basic self-care abilities used to gauge how independent a patient is, especially older adults.

sections.purpose: Measures functional independence in activities of daily living to guide care needs, rehab, and discharge planning.
sections.steps: Rates independence (yes/no) in six activities: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, and feeding.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A higher number of independent activities (up to 6) indicates greater independence; lower scores indicate dependence and a need for assistance or a higher level of care.

concepts.name: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
concepts.shortExplanation: A ten-item questionnaire that screens new mothers for postpartum depression.

sections.purpose: Screens for depression during pregnancy and the postpartum period so at-risk mothers can be referred for support and treatment.
sections.steps: Ten self-report items scored 0-3 about mood over the past 7 days (total 0-30); item 10 asks about self-harm thoughts.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A score of 13 or higher suggests likely depression and warrants further evaluation; any positive answer on the self-harm item requires immediate assessment.

concepts.name: New Ballard Score
concepts.shortExplanation: An exam that estimates a newborn's gestational age from physical and neuromuscular signs of maturity.

sections.purpose: Estimates gestational age after birth, useful when dating is uncertain and for anticipating prematurity-related risks.
sections.steps: Scores six neuromuscular signs (posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear) and six physical signs (skin, lanugo, plantar surface, breast, eye/ear, genitalia); the summed score maps to a gestational age.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Lower maturity scores indicate a more premature infant at higher risk for respiratory distress, temperature instability, and feeding difficulty; the estimate guides NICU care.

concepts.name: Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring System
concepts.shortExplanation: A scoring tool that grades how severely a newborn is withdrawing from opioids to guide treatment.

sections.purpose: Measures the severity of neonatal abstinence syndrome in infants exposed to opioids in utero, guiding supportive care and pharmacologic treatment.
sections.steps: Scores a set of signs across CNS (high-pitched cry, tremors, poor sleep), GI (poor feeding, vomiting, loose stools), and autonomic/respiratory (sweating, fever, tachypnea) domains at intervals.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Rising or persistently high scores (commonly 8 or more on serial assessments) indicate more severe withdrawal and prompt escalation of soothing measures and medication such as morphine.
